cases.title: M/s Rukmani Ferro Pvt. Ltd. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.disposition: Writ petition disposed of without interference. The challenge to the provisional assessment notice dated 22 September 2009 under Section 126(2) of the Electricity Act, 2003 was held premature; the petitioner was given liberty to file a detailed objection within fifteen days, which the competent authority must decide by a reasoned order dealing with each objection (including the objection to the competence to issue the notice) after fixing a date of hearing, no opinion being expressed on the merits. The apprehension of coercive action was held misconceived as only a provisional assessment had been made.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. v. Appellate Authority for Industrial & Financial Reconstruction & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.disposition: Writ petition dismissed as devoid of merit. The Corporation, having been heard during and consented to the BIFR-sanctioned rehabilitation scheme (Clause 8(iii)) directing waiver of demand charges, was bound by it and by the BIFR/AAIFR orders; its statutory obligation under the Electricity Act, 2003 to recover tariff did not entitle it to resile. The writ was also barred for not availing the statutory appeal to the AAIFR under Section 25 SICA and for inordinate delay of four to five years.

cases.title: Rajee Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.disposition: Writ petition allowed. The recovery proceedings initiated against petitioner no. 1 in 2010 for electricity dues relating to a 1997 disconnection were held barred by the two-year limitation in Clause 6.15(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 — the Corporation having failed to establish that the dues were continuously shown as recoverable — and were quashed. The petitioners' arguments that liability stood shifted to the auction-purchaser under a sale-deed, and that the Director could not be proceeded against, were rejected but did not affect the result. No order as to costs.

cases.title: Vijay Krishna Agrawal & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.disposition: Writ petition pending; not finally decided. By interim order dated 20 July 2010 the Division Bench directed restoration of the consumer's electricity connection subject to the consumer depositing, within a week, the amount assessed by the order dated 19 May 2010 limited to one year preceding the inspection dated 24 February 2010, with liberty to pay regular bills as raised. The challenge to the assessment — that under Annexure 6.3 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 the assessment period is capped at 365 days, and that the order violated natural justice — remains to be decided. After the deaths of both original petitioners their heirs were substituted (delay condoned, 2023); relief clauses 1(a) and 1(b) were not pressed on 18 March 2026, and the matter was last listed for 2 April 2026.

ARREARS::transferee-liability.code: Electricity Act / Supply Codes (general principle; cf. Clause 4.3(g)&(h))
ARREARS::transferee-liability.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Arrears are not a charge; transferee liable only where statutory rules/terms so provide
cases.holding: (i) Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge over the property, so in general law a transferee cannot be made liable for the previous owner/occupier's dues. (ii) But where statutory rules, or statutory terms and conditions of supply, authorise the supplier to demand the previous owner's arrears from a purchaser seeking re-/fresh connection, the supplier may recover them. Here the Board pleaded no such enabling provision (introduced in Haryana only in 2001), so the demand against the auction-purchaser failed.
cases.flag: Multi-state (Haryana) and general-law principle; the doctrinal foundation of the arrears/transferee cluster (cf. SCJ-005 K.C. Ninan, SCJ-012). The Court expressly notes that provisions like Clause 4.3(g) & (h) of an Electricity Supply Code are necessary to enable such recovery.

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Supply Code can create a statutory charge for a previous owner's arrears recoverable from a new owner (apex authority)
cases.holding: Yes. A condition of supply requiring the new owner to clear the previous owner's arrears has a statutory character (s.49, 1948 Act); the State Commission's regulatory power under s.50, and the rule-making power under s.181 read with s.50, are wide enough to stipulate recovery of a previous owner's arrears from a new/subsequent owner and to create a statutory charge on the premises even where the plenary statute does not provide for one. Such Supply Code recoupment has a reasonable nexus with the objects of the 2003 Act. The power to recover by suit is independent of the disconnection power under s.56; and 'as is where is' puts an auction-purchaser on notice of electricity dues. Outstanding interest from the date of the supply application was waived under Article 142.
cases.flag: Apex authority confirming the arrears/transferee line (cf. SCJ-031 Haryana SEB; applied in SCJ-005 Amir Ahmad). Substantially qualifies Isha Marbles (1995).

cases.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: IBC Section 238 overrides the Electricity Act/Supply Code first-charge and arrears-recovery provisions where the premises were acquired via IBC liquidation and the licensee has submitted its claim to the Liquidator
cases.holding: No. Section 238 of the IBC — a subsequent, non-obstante special enactment — overrides Sections 173-174 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and Clause 4.3(f)(iv) of the Supply Code (first charge on assets), following Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat (P) Ltd. and Southern Power Distribution Co. of Telangana v. Gopal Agarwal. Once the licensee has participated in the liquidation and lodged its claim, it cannot also insist on payment of the arrears as a precondition for a fresh connection to the auction-purchaser; its dues are recoverable only through the IBC Section 53 waterfall mechanism via the Liquidator, not by withholding supply. K.C. Ninan's holding that a Supply Code condition can make arrears run with the premises is confined to its own facts (no IBC liquidation in issue) and does not apply once the IBC framework and the licensee's own participation in it are engaged. The impugned demand/refusal order was set aside and the licensee directed to install the connection, retaining liberty to recover its dues only from the Liquidator.

cases.title: Palika Towns LLP v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Survey and application, by analogy, of the electricity-dues transferee-liability doctrine (dues do not constitute a charge absent specific stipulation) to hold an IBC-auction purchaser of an industrial leasehold liable for the corporate debtor's pre-existing lease-rent arrears, given an express 'first charge' clause in the lease deed and the purchaser's acceptance of the Transfer Memorandum/Sale Certificate
cases.holding: Yes. Surveying the electricity-dues transferee-liability line (Haryana SEB v. Hanuman Rice Mills; Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam v. DVS Steels & Alloys; Telangana State Southern Power Distribution Co.), the Court summarized the settled position: such dues do not themselves constitute a charge over the property, so a transferee is not automatically liable absent a specific statutory/regulatory stipulation authorising recovery from a purchaser, or an auction notice expressly flagging the dues as the purchaser's liability. Applying this by analogy, the Court found the lease deed here contained an express first-charge clause (Clause 3(b), Chapter IV) covering unpaid lease rent/interest/other dues, which displaced the general Transfer of Property Act s.55(1)(g) rule (applicable only 'in absence of a contract to the contrary'); the purchaser had also signed the Transfer Memorandum and accepted the Sale Certificate incorporating the lease covenants, and could not now approbate and reprobate by accepting the beneficial parts of those instruments while disclaiming the burden. GNIDA's failure to register its claim in the IBC liquidation proceedings did not extinguish its right to demand the arrears as a condition of transfer/recognition of the purchaser as lessee. Refund of the amount paid under protest was accordingly refused.

cases.title: Rajee Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Consumer cannot shift its own dues to an auction-purchaser via a sale deed it is not party to
cases.holding: No. The petitioners and the supplier were not parties or signatories to the bilateral sale deed between PICUP and respondent no. 7, and its terms do not bind them; the petitioners cannot take advantage of it to contend that their liability stands shifted to the vendee. The demand for electricity is enforced under the supply contract between the supplier and the consumer, and (applying DVS Steels) a transferee cannot be foisted with a predecessor's dues absent a contract to the contrary. This determination did not affect the result, which turned on limitation.

cases.title: Special Officer, Commerce, North Eastern Electricity Company of Orissa (NESCO) & Anr. v. M/s Raghunath Paper Mills Private Limited & Anr.
cases.topic: An arrears-clearance precondition applicable to transfer of an existing service connection does not extend to a fresh-connection application by a purchaser (e.g., an auction-purchaser of liquidated assets) who has no privity of contract with the licensee and did not seek transfer of the erstwhile consumer's connection
cases.holding: No. Sub-clause 10(b) of Regulation 13 governs transfer of an existing service connection from one consumer's name to another's, not an application for a fresh connection. The auction-purchaser here applied for a fresh connection to its own unit after purchasing the premises from the Official Liquidator, and did not seek transfer of the erstwhile company's connection; the arrears were levied against the erstwhile company, not as a charge on the premises. Synthesising Isha Marbles v. Bihar SEB (1995) 2 SCC 648 (electricity dues create no charge on the property and a third-party purchaser lacking privity cannot be compelled to clear them), Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. (2009) 1 SCC 210 (para 10: a distributor may nonetheless lawfully stipulate, as a condition of a fresh connection, that arrears be cleared, if its statutory rules/regulations or terms of supply so permit), Ahmedabad Electricity Co. Ltd. v. Gujarat Inns Pvt. Ltd. (2004) 3 SCC 587 (auction-purchasers not liable for previous owners' arrears on a fresh connection absent a specific statutory provision), and Haryana State Electricity Board v. Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri (2010) 9 SCC 145 (summarising the position: no charge on property in general law, but the supplier may recover arrears from a purchaser seeking reconnection/fresh connection where statutory rules or supply terms expressly authorise it) — the Court held that, since no such specific authorising provision applied here (Sub-clause 10(b) being confined to transfers), the demand of Rs. 79,02,262 in arrears as a precondition to the fresh connection was unsustainable, affirming the High Court's quashing of the demand order.

BIHAR-2007::4.1.topic: Arrears of an associate/relative: third proviso to Clause 4.1 inapplicable to an unconnected successor

cases.title: Vijay Lakshmi v. Bihar State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.topic: Arrears of an associate/relative: third proviso to Clause 4.1 inapplicable to an unconnected successor
cases.holding: No. The third proviso to Clause 4.1 applies only where the applicant is an associate or relative of the defaulting consumer; the petitioner, being neither an associate nor a relative of the erstwhile tenant, does not fall within it, and it furnishes no ground to deny her a connection.

BIHAR-2007::4.15.topic: Owner's liability for a tenant's arrears arises only where the connection was given with the owner's consent; no retrospective application

cases.title: Vijay Lakshmi v. Bihar State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.topic: Owner's liability for a tenant's arrears arises only where the connection was given with the owner's consent; no retrospective application
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.15(vi) applies only where the electricity connection to the premises was given with the consent of the house-owner; that precondition must be satisfied before the owner can be made liable for the tenant's arrears. There being nothing on record to show the tenant's connection was given with the consent of the petitioner's father, and the Code of 2007 not being in force on the date of disconnection (so the clause cannot operate retrospectively), the Board could not insist on payment of the tenant's arrears and was directed to grant a new connection within one month.

cases.title: Ujala Kumar @ Ujala Singh v. State of Bihar & Ors.
cases.topic: Owner's consent as precondition to liability for a lease-holder's arrears; mere signature on the application is not consent
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.15(vi) makes a person liable for a lease-holder's arrears only where the connection was given with the consent of the house-owner. A mere presence of the owner's signature on the lease-holder's application cannot signify consent unless it is expressed in such terms. There being nothing on record to show the connection was given with the owner's consent, the denial of a fresh connection to the applicant was unjustified, and the authority was directed to provide the connection within four weeks.

CA1956::457.topic: Court-ordered post-winding-up electricity supply as a liquidation expense

cases.title: U.P. State Cement Corporation Ltd. (In Liquidation), In re
cases.topic: Court-ordered post-winding-up electricity supply as a liquidation expense
cases.holding: Electricity supplied to the workmen's residential colonies after the winding-up order, under the Court's directions to prevent hardship and to preserve the assets for a smooth sale, was 'absolutely essential for effective liquidation' and is a liquidation expense to be borne by the Official Liquidator, along with security, valuation and claims-committee costs. It is not a secured debt ranking pari passu with workmen and secured creditors, and the proviso to Section 529(2) is not attracted (the supplier is not a secured creditor realising its own security).
cases.flag: The judgment is primarily a Companies Act winding-up distribution order among workmen, secured creditors, Government, EPF and unsecured creditors; only the U.P. Power Corporation electricity-dues question (paras 111-127) is digested for the supply-code corpus.

CA1956::529A.topic: Priority ceiling on an electricity supplier's dues in liquidation

cases.title: U.P. State Cement Corporation Ltd. (In Liquidation), In re
cases.topic: Priority ceiling on an electricity supplier's dues in liquidation
cases.holding: Section 529-A makes workmen's dues and secured creditors' debts rank pari passu and overrides preferential claims under Section 530 and all other claims; a writ of mandamus or an Article 142 direction to continue supply cannot override these substantive statutory provisions. An electricity supplier therefore obtains no preference over workmen and secured creditors except to the extent its post-winding-up, court-ordered dues qualify as liquidation expenses.
cases.flag: Textile Labour Association distinguished on facts (gas supply ordered before winding up; ONGC an unsecured creditor) but its Section 529-A ratio applied to cap the U.P. Power Corporation's claim.

CA1956::617.topic: DVVNL is a 'Government company' (subsidiary of UPPCL)

cases.title: Ashok Kumar & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: DVVNL is a 'Government company' (subsidiary of UPPCL)
cases.holding: Reading s.4(1) with s.617 of the Companies Act, 1956, DVVNL is a subsidiary of UPPCL (admittedly a Government company) and is therefore itself a 'Government company' under s.617; this bears on its status as a deemed licensee and instrumentality.
cases.flag: Companies-Act/status node; recorded compactly for the ledger.

CGRF-2007::6.10.topic: alternative remedy before CGRF after Clause 6.5 decision

cases.title: Raja Ram Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: alternative remedy before CGRF after Clause 6.5 decision
cases.holding: A further writ challenging the Executive Engineer's decision on a Clause 6.5 billing representation is not entertained where the consumer has an undisputed statutory remedy before the Consumer Grievances Redressal Forum under Clause 6.10; if the consumer approaches the Forum, it is to consider and decide the grievance expeditiously, preferably within three months, by a speaking order in accordance with law.
cases.flag: Court cited Clause 6.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not the CGRF Regulations, 2007.

cases.title: S.N. Singh v. State of U.P. — recovery of disputed energy dues kept in abeyance pending CGRF stay application
cases.topic: interim-stay-of-recovery-pending-forum-complaint
cases.holding: Where a billing complaint against outstanding electricity charges is already pending before the Consumer Grievances Redressal Forum, the High Court will not decide the dues or quash the recovery citation on writ. Regulation 6.10 of the 2007 Forum Regulations empowers the Forum to pass such interim orders as it considers necessary pending final disposal. The consumer may apply to the Forum for stay of recovery; the Forum shall decide that application in accordance with law by a reasoned speaking order after hearing all concerned. Recovery of the disputed amount may be kept in abeyance for a limited period to enable that application, and the protection stands vacated if the stay application is not filed in time.

cases.title: M/S Chandpur Enterprises Ltd. v. Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF stay application — deposit and non-mandatory timeline
cases.holding: A writ directing the CGRF to consider a stay application within a few days under para 6.10 of the UPERC (CGRF & Electricity Ombudsman) Regulations, 2007 is misconceived. The Forum may grant interim orders on regular billing and method of billing. The time in the third proviso to para 6.10(1) is not mandatory and starts running on deposit under the second proviso of the amount calculated as provided or 50% of the impugned demand; the second proviso bars interim relief unless that amount is deposited. Absent inordinate delay, the High Court will not direct the Forum to decide the stay hurriedly. Writ dismissed.

CONTEMPT::special-appeal-maintainability.code: Contempt of Courts Act / High Court Rules
CONTEMPT::special-appeal-maintainability.clause: s.19 CoC Act; Ch. VIII Rule 5 HC Rules
CONTEMPT::special-appeal-maintainability.topic: Special appeal lies where a contempt court exercises writ-court powers beyond the writ order

cases.title: Daya Nand Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Special appeal lies where a contempt court exercises writ-court powers beyond the writ order
cases.holding: A special appeal is maintainable, notwithstanding that no punishment order was passed, where the contempt court issues a direction in the nature of the exercise of writ-court powers, even beyond the scope of the order passed by the writ court.
cases.flag: Procedural node recorded for the ledger; the electricity-law substance is the Rule 3(b) / owner-objection point above.

CPC::47.code: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (applied by analogy to recovery of electricity dues)
CPC::47.topic: Executing authority cannot vary the underlying demand; objection must go to the assessing authority

cases.title: Heera Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Executing authority cannot vary the underlying demand; objection must go to the assessing authority
cases.holding: Recovery is akin to execution; the executing authority (Tehsildar) is confined to the execution, discharge or satisfaction of the demand ('decree') and cannot modify, set aside or vary it. An objection that seeks to vary the demand must be taken before the authority that passed it (the electricity authority) or by appeal, not before the executing Tehsildar; variation and execution cannot proceed simultaneously.

CPC::res-judicata.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred

cases.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cases.topic: Second suit on a different subject-matter/relief not barred
cases.holding: The second suit (challenging the 1998 disconnection threat and disconnection for the previous owner's arrears) was not barred by res judicata by the dismissal of the earlier suit (for a permanent injunction against the 1995 demand), the matters directly in issue and the reliefs being different.

EA1999(UP)::10(a).topic: Commission alone determines tariff/power-purchase price, overriding the contract

cases.title: Noida Power Company Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Commission alone determines tariff/power-purchase price, overriding the contract
cases.holding: From the constitution of the Commission on 25.4.1998, only the Regulatory Commission is competent to determine the tariff/power-purchase price under s.10(a), irrespective of Clause 7(a) of the agreement and despite the agreement's protection under s.47 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. If the Commission can fix the rate in the teeth of the agreement once constituted, it equally has jurisdiction to fix it for the initial six months and subsequent periods.

EA1999(UP)::10(q).clause: 10(q) (r/w s.22(2)(n), U.P. Electricity Reforms Act 1998; s.52)
EA1999(UP)::10(q).topic: Commission's jurisdiction to adjudicate licensee-utility disputes

cases.title: Noida Power Company Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Commission's jurisdiction to adjudicate licensee-utility disputes
cases.holding: Section 10(q) must be given its widest meaning: the Commission's functions include adjudicating disputes and differences between licensees and utilities and referring matters to arbitration (mirroring s.22(2)(n) of the 1998 Act), and s.52 gives the Act overriding effect. The reference of the dispute to the Commission was therefore competent.

EA1999(UP)::24.topic: Tariff is fixed by the Commission; a licensee cannot alter it by circular

cases.title: M/s Saini Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation, Lucknow & Ors.
cases.topic: Tariff is fixed by the Commission; a licensee cannot alter it by circular
cases.holding: No. Tariff is determined by the U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission under Section 24; a licensee has no authority to alter it. Any alteration required the procedure in Section 24(5)-(8), which was not followed; the circulars of 8-9-2000 and 15-12-2000 were therefore void ab initio and acquired no significance, and the theory of 'deemed approval' was rejected. The circular of 31-8-2001 withdrawing them was valid.
cases.flag: REVERSED by the Supreme Court in Badri Kedar Paper (P) Ltd. v. U.P. ERC, (2009) 3 SCC 754 — this holding is no longer good law.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Commission-notified tariff (including minimum monthly/fixed charges) binds the licensee; Ombudsman cannot direct contrary to the Act and Code
cases.holding: No. Minimum monthly/fixed charges are announced by the Commission in accordance with Section 24 of the U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999, consistent with the Electricity Act, 2003. A Tariff Order so notified is binding on the licensee. The licensee cannot waive it on a consumer's request, and the consumer's remedy against the Tariff Order is before the appropriate forum. Following Narinder Chand Hem Raj (AIR 1971 SC 2399), no direction can be issued against the provisions of the Act and the Code. The impugned Ombudsman orders contained no consideration of the Tariff Order or of the Act or the Code.

cases.title: Chandra Bhan Singh v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Licensee publishes Commission-determined tariff; it takes effect seven days after newspaper publication
cases.holding: Yes. Section 24 requires the licensee to follow the prescribed procedure in calculating expected revenue and determining tariffs; the Commission considers objections and may require modification. Sub-section (7) requires each supply licensee to publish the tariff in at least two daily newspapers widely circulating in the area of supply; the tariff comes into force after seven days from the last date of such publication. Clause 3.8(a) of the Code incorporates that publication rule to the extent consistent with the 2003 Act. The 22.11.2004 schedule was fixed by the Commission in accordance with Section 24(7) and published; the tariff as so notified is in accordance with the 2003 Act and the Code, 2005.

EA1999(UP)::24-tariff-fact-forum.topic: Whether guaranteed supply was given is a fact for the prescribed authority, not the Commission

cases.title: M/s Saini Alloys Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation, Lucknow & Ors.
cases.topic: Whether guaranteed supply was given is a fact for the prescribed authority, not the Commission
cases.holding: Whether the licensee actually made the guaranteed supply of 500 hours per month is a question of fact to be determined by the prescribed authority competent to hear objections to the bills; it is not for the Commission (whose role is to determine tariff, not adjudicate factual controversies) nor for the Court.
cases.flag: Part of a judgment reversed by the Supreme Court in Badri Kedar Paper (2009) 3 SCC 754.

EA1999(UP)::26.clause: s.26 (Commission's power to enforce licence conditions/tariff compliance) vis-a-vis s.48 (bar of civil suits)
EA1999(UP)::26.topic: An application alleging that a licensee is charging a surcharge inconsistent with an approved tariff order (violating licence terms/tariff compliance) is properly filed under s.26 of the 1999 Act before the Commission, not a barred civil suit

cases.title: Northern Coalfield Ltd. v. Chairman and Managing Director, U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: An application alleging that a licensee is charging a surcharge inconsistent with an approved tariff order (violating licence terms/tariff compliance) is properly filed under s.26 of the 1999 Act before the Commission, not a barred civil suit
cases.holding: Since a civil suit is barred under s.48 of the 1999 Act, and the consumer's grievance was in substance that the licensee was contravening the terms and conditions of its licence/tariff order by levying an unauthorised surcharge, the application was properly maintainable under s.26 (not Regulation 138's 90-day review-application bar, which did not apply).

cases.title: Dara Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: assessment-recovery-writ
cases.holding: A writ challenging recovery under section 3 of the U.P. State Government Electricity Dues Act, 1958, without challenging the assessment order, is not maintainable; the consumer must pursue remedies under the Electricity Act, 2003 and Electricity Supply Code, 2005 as applicable.

cases.title: Sunil Kumar Gupta — pending new-connection application to be decided in law
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: Without entering the merits of a mandamus for a new electric connection, if the consumer's application has reached and is pending before the Executive Engineer, it is to be dealt with and decided in accordance with law within the timeframe provided under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.
cases.flag: Order invokes EA 2003 and Supply Code 2005 timeframes without naming a section or clause.

cases.title: Sri Ram Yadav v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional assessment — consideration of objections
cases.holding: Where notice of provisional assessment is followed by a detailed objection, the assessing authority must consider that objection before finalising the assessment. An order that overlooks the objection and treats only a later, non-detailed letter is unsustainable and will be quashed, with a direction to take a fresh decision in accordance with law after the consumer files any additional documents.
cases.flag: order cites the Electricity Act and U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 generally, without a numbered clause

EA2003:: / UP-2005::.topic: writ challenge to recovery without assessment or bill

cases.title: Vinay Ranjan v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ challenge to recovery without assessment or bill
cases.holding: A recovery certificate for electricity dues cannot be challenged in writ without challenging the assessment order or bill. The petitioner may pursue the remedy against the assessment or bill under the Electricity Act, 2003 / Electricity Supply Code, 2005, as applicable. The writ, pending since May 2013 without interim relief, was dismissed and any interim order discharged.
cases.flag: Order cites the Electricity Act 2003 and Electricity Supply Code 2005 generally, without a numbered section or clause.

cases.title: Ravi Shankar Tiwari v. Executive Engineer, Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ maintainability; private dispute; statutory remedy
cases.holding: Where a consumer’s writ asking the distribution licensee to ensure supply and to punish private persons for alleged theft is, prima facie, a private dispute between the consumer and those private respondents, the High Court will not grant mandamus. The petitioner may pursue the remedies available under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ is dismissed.

cases.title: Veeri Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ withdrawal; departmental remedy
cases.holding: The writ petition is dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to the petitioner to avail any other departmental remedy available under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.
cases.flag: Order styles the statute as 'U.P.Electricity Act, 2003' (Electricity Act, 2003); no section or Supply Code clause is identified.

cases.title: M/s Janki News Print Ltd. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: alternative remedy — appeal
cases.holding: Following dismissal of identical Writ-C No. 67768 of 2009, the writ seeking refund of system loading charges and vires of Supply Code cls. 4.6(h)(i) and 4.21(a) is dismissed on alternative remedy. If the petitioner files an appeal under s.111 EA 2003 before the Appellate Authority within one month, that authority shall decide it on merits without entering into limitation.
cases.flag: ambiguous_clause

EA2003::126.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with the DERC Supply Code Regulations)
EA2003::126.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Legal fiction of 'deemed' consumption under the Supply Code / s.126 must be given full effect
cases.holding: Yes. Where the statute and the DERC Supply Code Regulations create a legal fiction that assessed energy is 'deemed' consumed (e.g. under the LDHF formula), the fiction must be taken to its logical end: the assessed units must be treated as 'sales'. The DERC's method of back-calculating units from the reduced settlement amount is contrary to law; assessed energy is to be considered as supply, with the impact and carrying costs allowed.

cases.title: Islam v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Agricultural ancillary use (kolhu) within sanctioned load is not unauthorised use
cases.holding: No. Ancillary use of a sanctioned agricultural connection for a kolhu/kutti machine to crush one's own produce, within the sanctioned load, is authorised agricultural use (per the licensee's own policy order of 11.11.2005), not unauthorised use — unless the load exceeds the sanctioned load or a second meter is installed. The burden to prove commercial use/theft is on the department; absent any allegation of crushing for others/hire, excess load, or a second meter, the assessment is illegal and quashed.

cases.title: Kapil Gupta v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd. & Anr.
cases.topic: A Section 126 assessment can be made even in a theft case
cases.holding: Section 126 (Chapter XII, investigation/enforcement) empowers a provisional assessment of charges for unauthorised use, while Section 135 (Chapter XIV, offences) makes unauthorised use a criminal offence; the two operate in different chapters, and a person committing theft/unauthorised use still bears the civil liability to pay for the consumption. A provisional assessment can therefore be made in a theft case.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: Sections 126 and 135 are distinct provisions in different fields; s.126 is civil and intention-neutral
cases.holding: No commonality. Sections 126 and 135 operate in different and distinct fields. Section 135 falls within criminal jurisprudence and mens rea is a relevant factor for theft; Section 126 does not speak of any criminal intendment and is primarily a civil remedy, applying even in the absence of intention.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Southern Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. (SOUTHCO) v. Sri Seetaram Rice Mill
cases.topic: 'Unauthorised use' is a wider, purposively-construed expression covering excess load
cases.holding: 'Unauthorised use of electricity' is an expression of wider connotation, to be construed purposively rather than restrictively by the clauses of the Explanation, keeping in mind the object and purpose of the Act. Consumption in excess of the maximum contracted/sanctioned load falls under Explanation (b)(iv) to Section 126 (besides violating the Regulations and the agreement of supply).

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) is a subset of unauthorised use (s.126); a s.126 assessment is available even in theft cases
cases.holding: Yes. All instances of unauthorised use may not amount to theft, but theft under Section 135 falls within the definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity'; use through a tampered meter is therefore unauthorised use assessable under Section 126(6)(b)(iii). The authorities are empowered to make a provisional and final assessment under Section 126(1) even in cases where electricity is unauthorisedly used by way of theft.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Kapoor v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company & Anr.
cases.topic: Law applicable to the deposit condition and assessment rate is the law in force on the date of the FINAL assessment, not the date of provisional assessment or the underlying cause of action
cases.holding: The amended Act governs. A provisional assessment is not a final assessment and carries no independent right of appeal; the cause of action for the statutory appeal arises only from the final assessment. The law prevailing on the date of the final assessment (here, 2011) applies both to the deposit condition for the appeal and to the assessment rate under Section 126(6) (amended to 'twice' the tariff, from 'one-and-half times'), regardless of when the theft/cause of action arose (2004) or the provisional assessment was made.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: CGRF and Ombudsman have no jurisdiction over Section 126 unauthorised-use assessments or Section 127 appellate orders — a parallel forum by subordinate legislation is impermissible
cases.holding: No. The Assessing Officer under Section 126 is a statutory authority and his order is appealable only under Section 127; where the statute itself creates its own adjudicatory and appellate forum, a parallel forum created by subordinate legislation (CGRF/Ombudsman under the 2007 Regulations) is not permissible and has no jurisdiction at all over such assessments. An earlier writ order that had allowed the consumer to approach CGRF, without the jurisdictional point being raised or contested, does not confer jurisdiction — a judgment lays down a ratio decidendi only on an issue raised, argued and decided, and jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or a court's assumption. The entire CGRF and Ombudsman proceedings (including the order refunding Rs. 14.44 lakh with 16% compound interest) were quashed as a nullity, with liberty to the consumer to pursue objections before the Assessing Officer under Section 126 or an appeal under Section 127, condoning any resulting delay if availed within one month.

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Physical/MRI indicators suffice to ground a theft inference; Ashok Kumar's notice requirement satisfied by the checking report's own disclosed facts
cases.holding: No. A naked conductor found at the LT mains bracket, a broken seal, and an MRI report showing an unexplained wide variance in the power-factor ratio and a reversed phase sequence (which cannot occur without manual manipulation) together well-support the Assessing Officer's inference of direct extraction/theft; this is not a case of no evidence. Ashok Kumar requires only that the consumer be informed of the manner in which he is alleged to have committed theft so he can respond — satisfied here since the checking report itself discloses, under 'observations', the facts from which theft is inferred, even though the consumer was not caught red-handed. No error in the actual quantum of assessment was pointed out.

cases.title: M/S Modern Rice Mill v. MVVNL & Anr.
cases.topic: Where the Code's assessment-rate provision conflicts with the statute, the statute prevails
cases.holding: At the relevant date, Section 126(6) fixed the assessment rate at one-and-a-half times the applicable tariff; any discrepancy in the Code (which the assessing/appellate authorities read as permitting a rate of thrice/twice respectively) must yield to the statute, which prevails over the Code in case of conflict. Both the assessing officer's (thrice) and the appellate authority's (twice) orders were accordingly unsustainable on rate alone, independent of the Clause 5.6 defect.

cases.title: Navi Hasan v. U.P. Power Corporation & Another
cases.topic: A pre-printed, non-speaking demand order passed in defiance of prior court directions to confront the consumer with adverse material and pass a reasoned order after hearing violates natural justice and is quashed with costs; an officer's unexplained recall/withdrawal of such an order mid-litigation, without disclosing statutory basis, is prima facie misconduct
cases.holding: No — the impugned order dated 21.3.2022 was found to be a pre-printed order (only name, checking-report number, notice number, and the demanded amount of Rs. 5,19,525/- filled in by hand), issued in conscious disregard of this Court's earlier order dated 22.10.2021 (Writ-C No. 26241 of 2021) requiring disclosure of adverse material, an opportunity for objections, a hearing, and a reasoned order. This violated the audi alteram partem principle and the order was quashed, with a direction to confront the petitioner with adverse material afresh, permit objections, and pass a reasoned assessment order after a hearing, all within a defined timeline. Costs of Rs. 1,00,000/- were imposed on the respondent officer given the deliberate defiance of the court's earlier directions, compounded by an unexplained mid-litigation withdrawal/recall of the impugned order without disclosing the statutory power under the Electricity Act or Supply Code to do so.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Appellate Authority/Addl. Commissioner & Anr. (Sunita Spat Pvt. Ltd.)
cases.topic: Assessment under Section 126 is available for theft; 'unauthorised use of electricity' in Explanation (b) is comprehensive enough to cover theft under Section 135
cases.holding: Section 126 assessment applies to theft. The definition of 'unauthorised use of electricity' in Explanation (b) to Section 126 is wide and comprehensive enough to cover usage by artificial means, by unauthorised means and through a tampered meter, and therefore to cover the theft of electricity more elaborately defined in Section 135; theft is itself an unauthorised use for which assessment under Section 126 is contemplated. Section 135 falls under the 'Offences and Penalties' chapter, which deals with a different subject (prosecution and penalty) from assessment, and the scheme of the 2003 Act does not exclude assessment under Section 126 in theft cases. This is fortified by the third proviso to Section 135(1A), which requires restoration of supply on deposit or payment of the assessed amount - showing that assessment of charges for theft is itself contemplated. The Legislature thus contemplated assessment under Section 126 for all categories of unauthorised use, including theft.
cases.flag: Source judgment is not paragraph-numbered; pins reference the printed page numbers of the reserved judgment (pp.1-10). Sections 126, 127(1) and 135(1)/(1A) are reproduced at pp.4-7.

cases.title: M/s Rukmani Ferro Pvt. Ltd. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Premature writ challenge to a provisional assessment notice; relegation to the statutory objection process
cases.holding: The Court declined to interfere. A provisional assessment notice is not the stage for the writ court to examine the consumer's pleas (including want of jurisdiction and non-compliance with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005). The notice itself afforded an opportunity to reply, and it was open to the consumer to file a detailed objection raising all its pleas, which the authority could modify, confirm or discharge. The petitioner was given liberty to file a detailed objection within fifteen days, and the competent authority was directed to fix a date of hearing and take a final decision by a reasoned order dealing with each objection raised, including the objection regarding competence to issue the notice, the Court expressing no opinion on the merits of any issue.
cases.flag: Source is an order-sheet compilation; the operative order dated 20.7.2011 carries printed page numbers (pp. 1-6) — pins are those printed pages.

cases.title: M/s Rukmani Ferro Pvt. Ltd. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: No coercive action pending final assessment; no interim protection needed
cases.holding: No. Since only a provisional assessment notice had been issued, there was no occasion for any coercive action against the consumer unless and until a final assessment was made; the apprehension of coercive action was therefore misconceived, and the request for interim protection was declined.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Section 126 assessment must be made even in theft (s.135) cases with a pending Special Court trial; the Special Court's civil-liability jurisdiction under s.154(5)/(6) operates alongside, not instead of, the assessing officer's s.126 process — 'unauthorised use of electricity' is the genus of which theft is a dishonest species
cases.holding: (1)-(2) Yes, s.126 assessment must be made even in theft cases pending Special Court trial. 'Unauthorised use of electricity' under Explanation (b) to s.126 is a wide genus comprehensively covering theft under s.135 as a dishonest species of the same conduct; the sixth proviso to s.135(1), which conditions restoration of supply on payment of the 'assessed amount', itself presupposes a s.126 assessment exists to be paid. Clause 8.1 of the Supply Code, 2005 (framed by the Regulatory Commission under s.50) confirms this understanding by prescribing a provisional-assessment-and-hearing procedure specifically for theft cases under s.135. The now-omitted Clause 8.0(6) (allowing interim-payment restoration pending Special Court decision) was merely an option for restoration, not an indication that s.126 assessment is inapplicable to theft. The Special Court's role under s.154(5)/(6) is to finally determine civil liability (which may differ from — and trigger refund/adjustment against — the s.126-assessed amount already deposited), not to displace the assessing officer's s.126 jurisdiction. Following Paliwal Alloys, Radha Krishna Cold Storage, Ashok Kumar, Mohit Paper Mills, and distinguishing the Andhra Pradesh High Court's Tirumala Modern Rice Mill and clarifying that the Supreme Court's Southco v. Seetaram Rice Mill (holding ss.126/135 operate in 'different fields') did not hold that s.126 assessment is barred in theft cases: (i) assessment under s.126 is to be made even where a s.135 offence is pending trial before the Special Court; (ii) the Special Court finally determines civil liability, with s.154(6) governing any refund if that determination is less than the amount already deposited pursuant to s.126 assessment.

cases.title: Mohd. Ramzan @ Rajan Ali v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reconnection and assessment after alleged theft
cases.holding: A grievance seeking decision of an application for reconnection and restoration of supply and for assessment of electricity charges, where theft is alleged and an FIR has been lodged, is to be redressed by the competent authority under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Clause 6.8 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ court will not examine merits and may dispose of the petition by directing that authority to decide the application within a stipulated time.

cases.title: Rijwan Ahmad v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reconnection and assessment after theft FIR
cases.holding: A writ seeking a direction to decide an application for reconnection and restoration of supply (LMV-6 in place of LMV-2) and for assessment of charges, where a theft FIR has been lodged, is to be left to the competent authority under s.126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with cl.6.8 of the Supply Code; the Court will not go into the merits of that claim.

cases.title: Rajesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: reconnection and assessment after theft allegation
cases.holding: Where a consumer facing a theft FIR seeks a writ for decision of his application for reconnection, restoration, load-category change and assessment of charges, the grievance is to be redressed by the competent assessing authority under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Clause 6.8 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ court will not decide those merits and will only direct that authority to dispose of the application.

cases.title: Reconnection after theft allegation remitted to s.126 and clause 6.8
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: forum for reconnection and assessment after theft allegation
cases.holding: A writ seeking decision of an application for reconnection and restoration (LMV-6 in place of LMV-2) and assessment of charges, raised after a theft allegation and FIR, is to be redressed by the competent authority under s.126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with clause 6.8 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The Court did not examine merits and directed respondent no. 2 to decide the application preferably within two months of production of a certified copy.

cases.title: Shiv Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: assessment grievance; appeal under s.127
cases.holding: If the consumer is aggrieved by assessment proceedings, the grievance lies to the Executive Engineer under section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003, and any grievance against the order of assessment is appealable under section 127. The writ was disposed of with liberty to approach the Executive Engineer, Vidyut Vitaran Khand, Siddharth Nagar, for redressal under the applicable provision, to be decided within three months if entertainable.

cases.title: Smt. Vimla Tiwari v. State of U.P. And Others
cases.topic: A s.126 assessment premised on a 'missing meter' checking report that is internally contradictory and effectively fabricated/backdated (as revealed through compelled personal affidavits of the Assessing/Appellate Authorities and field officials) is vitiated by malice in law and must be quashed, given the assessment's overlap with theft (s.135) and its consequent reputational/character stakes requiring rigorous procedural fairness
cases.holding: No. The Court, having directed personal affidavits from the Assessing Authority, the Appellate Authority (the Commissioner) and the Superintending Engineer (technical member), and multiple field officials involved in the checking, found the record riddled with irreconcilable inconsistencies going to the core factual premise (whether and when the meter was actually found missing/tampered), amounting to fabrication or backdating of the checking report. Such action, taken without just cause or on a misrepresented factual foundation, constitutes 'malice in law' regardless of any personal ill-will (extensively discussed via S.R. Venkatraman v. Union of India, Mukesh Kumar Agrawal v. State of U.P., Somesh Tiwari v. Union of India, HMT Ltd. v. Mudappa and the string of authorities at para 42). Because s.126 assessments frequently share their factual predicate with s.135 theft charges and carry comparable reputational/character consequences for the consumer, the same procedural rigour applicable to quasi-criminal proceedings must govern s.126 assessments — a standard flagrantly breached here. The assessment order and the appellate order affirming it are accordingly quashed.
cases.paras: paras throughout; malice-in-law discussion at para 42

cases.title: Abdul Gaffar @ G. Hussian v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Section 126(3) contemplates a Final Order of Assessment after Provisional Assessment; treating the Provisional as Final without a specific order is questionable
cases.holding: Prima facie, no. The respondents admitted that no Final Assessment Order was passed, the Provisional Assessment itself being treated as the Final Assessment without any specific order, because no objections had been received. The Court observed that sub-section (3) of Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 contemplates the passing of a Final Order of Assessment after a Provisional Assessment, found that the matter required consideration, and stayed recovery on a nominal deposit. The point was not finally decided, the petition being later dismissed as infructuous.
cases.flag: Order-sheet: no printed page numbers or numbered paragraphs; pins are order dates. The substantive prima facie observations are in the 26.4.2011 order (Satya Poot Mehrotra and Rajesh Chandra, JJ.); coram/date reflect the 2.2.2017 disposal (Ran Vijai Singh and Vinod Kumar Srivastava-III, JJ.).

cases.title: Rameshwar v. DVVNL & Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: A demand notice recovering under the provisional assessment is illegal where a final assessment order has been passed
cases.holding: Yes. The demand notice dated 7.2.2011 recovered the amount assessed against the petitioner under the provisional assessment order dated 22.5.2010, while the respondents' counter affidavit did not dispute that the final assessment order was passed on 29.6.2010. A demand notice issued on the basis of the provisional assessment notice, and not the final assessment order, is illegal, and was accordingly quashed. The writ petition was allowed to that extent, the petitioner being left at liberty to challenge the final assessment order in appropriate proceedings.
cases.flag: Order-sheet: no printed page numbers or numbered paragraphs; pins are order dates. The interim order is of 18.5.2011 (Satya Poot Mehrotra and Jayashree Tiwari, JJ.); the operative merits disposal is the 16.3.2023 order (Manoj Kumar Gupta and Prashant Kumar, JJ.).

cases.title: Ram Charan v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Failure to object to a provisional assessment order renders the consequent recovery validly initiated
cases.holding: Validly initiated. The Court found on the affidavits that there were arrears of Rs.46,722 as on 20.3.2009 for which the supply was disconnected, that on a checking on 1.10.2009 the petitioner was found unauthorisedly using electricity, that an FIR was lodged, and that a provisional order dated 10.12.2009 was passed calling upon him to pay Rs.75,198. The petitioner did not file any objection to that provisional order and a recovery certificate consequently issued. The Court held that the petitioner should have filed an objection against the provisional assessment order and, since he did not, the recovery proceedings had been rightly initiated; the writ against the citation could not succeed on the merits.
cases.flag: Order-sheet: 12 pages, multiple dated orders from 31.5.2011 to 22.4.2016, no printed page numbers (a single '(2)' marks the second page of the final order); pins are order dates. The operative disposal is the 13.4.2015 order (Tarun Agarwala and Manoj Kumar Gupta, JJ.); the interim stay of recovery is of 31.5.2011 (Satya Poot Mehrotra and Bharati Sapru, JJ.).

cases.title: Beni Madhav v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: consumer-forum-jurisdiction-over-uue-theft
cases.holding: District Consumer Forum has no jurisdiction over a demand for unauthorised use or theft of electrical energy. Such assessment is not a service rendered to the person committing the unauthorised use or theft and is therefore beyond the Consumer Protection Act, 1986. The field is governed by ss. 126 and 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the Electricity Supply Code (earlier, regulations under s. 79 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948).

cases.title: Beni Madhav v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: recovery-citation-consequential-to-assessment
cases.holding: A recovery citation is only a consequential act. Where the main assessment order is neither produced nor challenged, a writ attacking only the citation is ill-drafted and misconceived and is liable to be dismissed.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors. v. Anis Ahmad (with connected appeals)
cases.topic: A complaint against a final s.126 assessment order, or against action/prosecution for theft/interference offences under ss.135-140 of the Electricity Act, 2003, is not maintainable before a Consumer Forum under the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, since neither falls within the CP Act's narrow definition of 'complaint,' and a person availing a commercial electricity connection is not a 'consumer' under the CP Act at all
cases.holding: No. Overruling the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission's majority view, the Supreme Court held that Sections 173-175 of the Electricity Act, 2003 preserve the Consumer Protection Act's general applicability and resolve any 'inconsistency' in the CP Act's favour, but this does not itself confer Consumer Forum jurisdiction over matters that never fall within the CP Act's 'complaint' definition (s.2(1)(c)) in the first place — namely unfair/restrictive trade practice, defective goods, deficiency in service, hazardous goods/services, or overcharging. The quasi-judicial assessment of 'unauthorised use of electricity' under s.126 (assessed by a public-servant assessing officer at twice the applicable tariff, appealable under s.127, with a further 50%-of-assessed-amount deposit precondition) has no relationship to any of these categories, and offences under ss.135-140 (theft, meter-tampering, interference) are triable exclusively by Special Courts constituted under s.153 — the Civil Court's jurisdiction over both is expressly ousted by s.145. The Electricity Supply Code under s.50 governs billing, disconnection, and tampering-prevention measures, not s.126/135-140 assessment or offences. Separately, all the respondent-complainants here held commercial/industrial electricity connections and so were not 'consumers' under s.2(1)(d) CP Act (which excludes persons availing goods/services for commercial purpose), rendering their complaints independently non-maintainable on that ground too. Section 42 of the Electricity Act (Ombudsman/Forum mechanism, on which the National Commission relied) applies only to distribution licensees under Part VI and does not extend Consumer Forum jurisdiction to assessment/theft matters. All the National Commission's orders were accordingly set aside.

cases.title: Mukesh Chand Agarwal v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: restoration of supply after s.126 assessment
cases.holding: Where assessment proceedings under section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 have been undertaken, notice has been sent, and an assessment order is produced, the High Court will not mandamus resumption of supply. The petitioner is left to the remedy available under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2003 (as described by the Court). The writ petition is dismissed.
cases.flag: Court referred to the residual remedy as under the 'U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2003'; the operative U.P. Supply Code is 2005. No clause of that Code was identified.

cases.title: Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Thomas Joseph Alias Thomas M.J. & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.topic: A consumer's overdrawal of electricity in excess of the sanctioned/connected load constitutes 'unauthorised use of electricity' under Explanation (b)(iv) to s.126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and must be assessed at twice the FULL tariff (both fixed and energy charges) under s.126(6), even where the overdrawal occurs in the same premises, for the same purpose, involves no change of tariff category, has already been metered and paid for, and involves no artificial means or tampering — there is no textual or principled basis to carve out an exception limiting such 'mere overdrawal' cases to twice the fixed charges alone
cases.holding: The overdrawal constitutes 'unauthorised use of electricity' in every such case and must be assessed at twice the FULL tariff under s.126(6); the Kerala High Court's para 31(vi) exception is unsustainable and set aside. Following Seetaram Rice Mill's holding that ss.126-127 together form a 'complete code' whose purpose is to restrict unauthorised consumption and that the Explanation's use of the word 'means' (rather than 'means and includes' or 'does not include') signals the legislature's intent NOT to exhaustively limit the provision's scope, the Court held Explanation (b)(iv) squarely covers excess-load consumption irrespective of whether it also changes the tariff category — a contention to the contrary was expressly rejected in Seetaram Rice Mill's own para 72, which this Court quoted and applied. The decisive point overlooked by the Kerala High Court is that overdrawal is 'prejudicial to the public at large' independent of any revenue effect: it threatens to 'throw out of gear the entire supply system, undermining its efficiency, efficacy and even increasing voltage fluctuations' — a systemic infrastructural concern entirely distinct from whether the individual consumer's bill changes. Since s.45(3)(a) defines 'tariff' to include both a fixed charge and the charge for actual electricity supplied, and s.126(6) requires assessment 'at a rate equal to twice the tariff applicable,' this necessarily includes both fixed and energy charges in every case of unauthorised use — there is no room in the statutory text for a category of case where only fixed charges (and not energy charges) are chargeable. The Court noted staggering real-world stakes: unauthorised-use assessments in Kerala totalled nearly Rs. 60 crore over three years (2014-17), underscoring why a judicially-engrafted revenue-neutral exception was inappropriate.

cases.title: Krishna Gopal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional assessment — objections and further forum
cases.holding: Where reconnection is sought in a matter the licensee treats as theft and a provisional assessment has been made, the writ court will not decide reconnection once a copy of that assessment is supplied in court. The consumer may file statutory objections within a short time; the authority must then take a final decision; further remedies lie under the Electricity Act 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code 2005.
cases.flag: No section numbered. Keyed to s.126 from provisional assessment and statutory objections. Residual forum stated only as EA 2003 read with UP Supply Code 2005.

cases.title: Vinod Kumar Awasathi v. U.P.P.C.L.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional theft bill — statutory objection
cases.holding: Where a provisional bill is issued on a checking report finding theft of electricity, objection does not lie in writ. The consumer must file a reply under s.126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and s.8.5 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; a notice already so filed shall be considered by the concerned Executive Engineer, who will then pass an appropriate assessment order.
cases.flag: Court also cites 'Section 8.5' of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; that clause number is not among the catalogued 8.1/8.2 theft-UUE provisions.

cases.title: Shyam Kumar Awasthi v. U.P.P.C.L.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: objection-to-provisional-assessment
cases.holding: A consumer objecting to a provisional bill raised on a checking report of theft must file a reply under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and clause 8.5 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Where that objection has already been served as a notice, the concerned Executive Engineer shall consider it and pass an appropriate assessment order; the writ court will not itself decide the assessment.

cases.title: Mahboob Ahmad v. Electricity Corp. Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: recovery after s.126 assessment
cases.holding: Once dues have been quantified under Section 126 and the consumer has not deposited the assessed amount, recovery under the 1958 Act is not infirm and a writ to quash the recovery notice will not lie. The validity of the assessment may still be questioned before the competent authority under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Shri Krishna Kumar Sharma v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: The power to make a provisional assessment vests in the Executive Engineer; a proposal for the assessed amount issued by the Assistant Engineer (Revenue) on his behalf is only a calculation sheet, not the assessment, so the 'wrong officer' challenge fails
cases.holding: No. Under the provisions of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 there is no doubt that the power to carry out provisional assessment vests in the Executive Engineer concerned. The proposal for the assessed amount issued by the Assistant Engineer, Revenue on behalf of the Executive Engineer is only a calculation sheet, intended to call upon the petitioner to file his response; it is not itself the assessment. The petitioner's contention - that the Assistant Engineer, Revenue could not have issued the notice and that the consequential notice of the Executive Engineer was bad in law, resting on the State Government notification empowering the Executive Engineer - was therefore not accepted.
cases.flag: Order-sheet of 14 pages, dated orders from 12.10.2012 to the operative disposal of 22.10.2018, no printed page numbers; pins are order dates. The provisional/final assessment scheme is reflected in the interim order's 'Provisional Assessment (8.12.2011)' / 'Final Assessment' language; the Court grounded the Executive Engineer's power in the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and the cited State notification.

cases.title: Shri Krishna Kumar Sharma v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: A writ at the calculation-sheet / proposed-assessment stage is not entertained; the consumer is relegated to raise his objection before the Executive Engineer, the calculation sheet being only a call for his response
cases.holding: The writ is not entertained at that stage. Since the calculation sheet is only intended to call upon the petitioner to file his response, the Court was not inclined to entertain the petition on the arguments advanced, and left it open to the petitioner to raise his objection, if any, before the Executive Engineer himself; the petition was consigned to record. The interim order dated 12.10.2012 restraining the Executive Engineer from making a final assessment pursuant to the provisional assessment dated 8.12.2011 thus lapsed with the disposal, the objection stage before the Executive Engineer remaining open to the petitioner.

cases.title: Ashok Kumar & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Two-stage opportunity of hearing; recorded conclusion of unauthorised use as a condition precedent
cases.holding: The condition precedent to the s.126(1) power is that the assessing officer come to and record a conclusion of unauthorised use. Because that finding overlaps with the s.135 offence and stigmatises the consumer, the officer must, before making the provisional assessment, disclose the specific manner of the alleged unauthorised use and give the consumer an opportunity to defend, then record the conclusion (conferring jurisdiction). Opportunity is required at two distinct stages — first, before concluding that unauthorised use occurred (the guilt stage), and second, before final assessment (the quantum stage); only an assessment conducted in this manner is valid.
cases.flag: This two-stage-hearing statement is the ratio later applied in SCJ-154 (Arup Kumar Mitra), which cites this case (as Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P., (2008) 6 ADJ 660).

cases.title: Shiv Shankar v. U.P. Power Corporation
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional assessment before recovery
cases.holding: Where nothing on record shows a provisional assessment under Section 126, a recovery certificate for alleged theft of electricity cannot be sustained. The licensee must prepare a provisional assessment, serve it on the consumer, and make a final assessment only after considering objections, giving reasons that meet those objections, in the light of Ashok Kumar v. State of U.P., 2008 (6) ADJ 660 (DB) paras 56–64 (Supply Code procedure for theft assessment).

cases.title: Jai Laxmi Cement Company Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A provisional assessment relying on a checking report is not a prejudged 'concluded opinion'
cases.holding: No. A bare reading of the provisional assessment notice shows it does not express a concluded opinion or prejudge the issue; it is based on the checking report and the consumer has been given a right to file objections against both the checking report and the notice, to be examined by the authority finalising the assessment. Oryx Fisheries, where the notice said the charge was 'proved beyond doubt', is on different facts and does not apply.

cases.title: Parmarth Steels & Alloys (Pvt.) Ltd. & Anr. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. (Transco) & Others
cases.topic: Assessing officer must consider all objections (check-meter and sub-station readings) via a speaking order
cases.holding: No. Before making a final assessment under s.126 the assessing officer must consider the consumer's detailed objections and pass a speaking order. The outdoor double-pole meter functions as a check meter and was found O.K., and the sub-station meter maintains line-loss readings that tally at both ends; both were relevant to whether theft occurred and had to be given due consideration. The rejection order, which met a key objection only with 'Assessment is as per rules...', did not do so and is set aside; the matter is remitted for a fresh final assessment after due consideration of the objections.
cases.flag: The Court did not decide whether theft in fact occurred (para 31) — the ratio is the duty to consider objections via a speaking order.

cases.title: Kamil v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Recorded conclusion of UUE and a fair hearing are conditions precedent to assessment
cases.holding: The condition precedent to the s.126(1) power is the assessing officer's conclusion that the consumer indulged in unauthorised use; that satisfaction cannot rest on the officer's mere vagaries without a fair opportunity of hearing. Natural justice, not being excluded by the Act, applies to a serious charge of unauthorised use that may also amount to a s.135 offence; s.126(3) itself contemplates a reasonable opportunity of hearing before final assessment.

cases.title: Ajay Prakash Srivastava v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: final assessment as precondition to recovery
cases.holding: Recovery founded on the 29 March 2016 assessment could not proceed because that order did not consider the petitioners' objections dated 24 February 2016 to the provisional assessment, and instead treated a later compounding affidavit as a request. Final assessment must be made under Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The Executive Engineer was directed to consider those objections and pass a fresh final-assessment order within three weeks; recovery remains in abeyance and depends on the outcome of that order.

cases.title: Ajay Prakash Srivastava v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: final assessment; objections; recovery
cases.holding: The 29 March 2016 final assessment did not consider the petitioners' 24 February 2016 objections to the provisional assessment; the department instead proceeded on a theft-compounding affidavit treated as an Aavedan and reduced the demand by applying a multiplier. Recovery of the assessed amount depends on a final assessment made in accordance with the rules, namely section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The Executive Engineer must consider the objections and pass a fresh final assessment; recovery remains in abeyance until then and is dependent on that outcome.

cases.title: Gajendra Singh Yadav v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: assessment and recovery after theft FIR
cases.holding: On a writ challenging recovery for alleged theft of electricity where the consumer contends that no assessment has been passed and the Executive Engineer has called for a report on the consumer's objection, the Executive Engineer is to pass orders of assessment in terms of section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with clause 6.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 if not already passed, duly inform the consumer, and complete that exercise within three weeks of a certified copy; recovery remains subject to that order. If the consumer is satisfied he may deposit the amount found recoverable; if he disputes it, an appeal under section 127 is the remedy. The writ is disposed of on those observations without adjudicating the theft allegation or the quantum.
cases.flag: Court referred to 'Section 126 of the U.P. Electricity Act, 2003'; the provision is section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003.

cases.title: Sanjay Kumar Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: demand notice for alleged unauthorized use
cases.holding: A demand notice alleging unauthorized use of electricity (consumption for construction contrary to the sanctioned connection) is a billing issue arising out of assessment to be adjudicated by the Executive Engineer under s.126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with cl.6.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The High Court will not decide that dispute in writ; the consumer may approach the Executive Engineer, who shall pass an appropriate order within two weeks if a certified copy of the order is filed within a week.

cases.title: Raj Narayan Mishra v. State of U.P. and others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ-relegation-billing-theft-assessment-remedies
cases.holding: A writ petition raising a factual billing and recovery dispute after a theft case and a dishonoured compounding cheque will not be entertained when a variety of remedies remain available: compounding of theft under Section 152; assessment by the Executive Engineer under Section 126 with appeal under Section 127; the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under Clause 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; a final assessment if only a provisional assessment has been made; and a pure billing dispute before the Executive Engineer under Clause 6.5. The consumer may avail any such remedy in accordance with law. If the authority approached passes an order, recovery proceedings shall abide by it.
cases.flag: The Court referred to compounding as under 'Section 152 of the U.P. Electricity Act, 2003'; the provision applied is Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (EA2003::152). It also described the Section 127 appellate authority as a 'higher Forum'.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division v. District Consumer Forum
cases.topic: consumer-forum-jurisdiction
cases.holding: Prima facie, a District Consumer Forum has no jurisdiction to entertain a complaint against assessment or recovery for theft/unauthorised use under section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003, or against offences under sections 135 to 140 (triable only by a Special Court under section 153), and cannot stay such recovery; applying UPPCL v. Anis Ahmad, the High Court stayed the Forum’s orders dated 1 and 4 August 2018.

cases.title: Gauri Prasad v. State of U.P. Thru. Prin. Secy. Deptt. of Energy, Lko. & 4 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Lucknow Bench)
cases.topic: unexplained delay in serving provisional assessment; demand not served in accordance with law
cases.holding: No. The petitioner's case was that proceedings were started without clear notice, that he had not been served with any provisional assessment, and that the final assessment was not made known, so that Sections 126 and 135 and the Supply Code, 2005 had not been followed. The licensee's letter showed a provisional assessment dated 24.02.2023 sent by registered cover dated 08.05.2023. Nothing on record explained why it took three months to send the provisional assessment, let alone the final assessment. Coupled with incomplete instructions and no decision on the consumer's representation, the Court held there had been a breakdown of communication and that the petitioner had not been served with the assessment or demand notice in accordance with law.
cases.flag: The challenged demand is dated 19.08.2022; the licensee's letter dates the provisional assessment 24.02.2023. Recorded as the judgment states it. Petitioner also invoked Section 135 and the Supply Code, 2005 without a numbered clause; the Court cited neither a Code clause nor Section 126 by number in its own reasoning.

cases.title: Saurabh Agarwal v. State of U.P. And 3 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s.126 assessments not quashed; de novo hearing and reasoned order to be treated as the final assessment
cases.holding: The Court did not quash the assessments. It stayed the impugned order and the demand notice for a limited period and directed the petitioner to file a fresh representation, within one week, before the authority who had passed the assessment orders. That authority shall consider the representation, grant a proper opportunity of hearing, and pass a reasoned order, which shall be treated as the final assessment. The petitioner must deposit 25% of the amount mentioned in the demand notice along with the representation, for the matter to be heard de novo. The entire process is to be completed within six weeks. In the meantime, no coercive measure shall be taken. The writ petition is disposed of.
cases.flag: Source PDF also contains listing orders of 8.4.2025 (Siddhartha Varma, J. and Dr. Y.K. Srivastava, J.) and 16.4.2025; the operative disposal is 24.4.2025. Paragraphs of that order are unnumbered; numbering is of its recitals and directions. The prayers invoked Section 126 'read with the Electricity Supply Code' without a numbered clause (6.8 or 8.1); the Court did not cite a Code clause.

cases.title: Satyam Shukla v. State of U.P. and 3 Others
cases.topic: Assessing officer must himself inspect before provisionally assessing
cases.holding: No. Seetaram Rice Mill is binding. Section 126 requires the assessing officer to conduct the inspection of the premises and then provisionally assess the charges. The licensee's contention that inspection is done by the Assistant Engineer and the Executive Engineer then assesses cannot be acted upon. The 27 July 2024 provisional assessment is set aside because it rests on an inspection the assessing officer did not make. The supply company may proceed afresh in accordance with law; the concurring opinion remands to respondent no. 3 to initiate Section 126 assessment proceedings afresh.
cases.flag: Lead opinion paras 2 and 4 refer to inspection by the Assistant Engineer; para 5 and the concurring opinion refer to the Junior Engineer. The impugned order recited Clause 6.8/8.1 of the Supply Code, 2005; the Court did not decide which clause governed.

cases.title: Managing Director, D.V.V. Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others v. Sri Kartar Singh & Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: A CGRF billing-arrears complaint is not a s.126 assessment or s.135–140/150 matter
cases.holding: No. The Court clarified that these proceedings do not arise out of any action under Section 126 relating to assessment, or under Sections 135 to 140 and Section 150; such complaints are not maintainable before Consumer Forums.
cases.flag: Source PDF also contains 09.05.2014 (notice), 20.08.2014 (stay of the CGRF order), and 10.10.2014 (admit; stay continued; petitioners cited Anis Ahmad against a 'District Consumer Forum' proceeding). The 04.11.2025 judgment treats the body as the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, Agra, and decides a billing-arrears dispute, not a s.126/135 complaint.

cases.title: Saroj Agarwal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: statutory appeal against finalized s.126 assessment
