Documents required for filing the appeal are to be furnished by the licensee within one week.

cases.title: M/S Prem Steel (Pvt.) Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: writ relegation to s.127 against final assessment
cases.holding: A writ challenging a final assessment, including alleged non-compliance with clause 6.8 of the Supply Code and want of theft material in the checking report, is to be left to the appellate authority under section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003, which shall examine those issues; the petition may be disposed of by permitting a short time to appeal, directing an expeditious decision, and adjusting amounts already deposited towards the deposit required in the appeal.

cases.title: Unreasoned theft assessment set aside despite s.127 appeal
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ despite s.127 — unreasoned assessment
cases.holding: Although an appeal under section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003 lay against the theft assessment, the Court set aside the 21 October 2011 order because it was not a reasoned order: the assessing officer referred to the petitioner's 10 October 2011 reply but considered none of the grounds. The licensee was given liberty to pass a fresh order after considering the reply within four weeks of production of a certified copy. The petitioner was directed to continue paying regular bills as they fell due.

cases.title: Jaipal Singh v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: objections to provisional assessment and s.127 appeal
cases.holding: A consumer assessed for unauthorised drawing under Annexure 6.3 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 must object to the provisional assessment and, on a final order, appeal under Section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003; the writ court will not decide the recovery on merits. If objections are filed within fifteen days they shall be decided within a month, recovery remaining stayed for two months. A police final report closing the criminal case, without a detailed investigation of who occupied the premises, does not displace that assessment machinery.

cases.title: Writ against post-checking assessment dismissed for s.127 appeal
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ against assessment barred by s.127 appeal
cases.holding: Where an assessment and demand follow a checking that found unauthorised use and an FIR under Section 135, the consumer’s remedy against that assessment and demand is an appeal under Section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003; a writ petition is dismissed on the ground of that alternative remedy.

cases.title: Manoj Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ against assessed dues; statutory appeal and pending Forum
cases.holding: A consumer who bypassed departmental remedies under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and is already before the District Consumer Forum, cannot maintain a writ against recovery of assessed electricity dues; he also has a right of appeal against the assessment under the Electricity Act (cited as Section 27). The Consumer Protection Act does not empower a District Forum to pass an unreasoned interim mandatory injunction to reconnect supply or to summon the Executive Engineer for non-compliance.
cases.flag: Court cited 'Section 27 of the Electricity Act' for appeal against assessment of electricity dues; catalog key is EA2003::127. Theft case recited as 'Section 138-B'.

cases.title: Ram Kumar v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s127-appeal-against-theft-assessment
cases.holding: Against a theft/final assessment, a consumer's representation seeking correction of the electricity bill is not a statutory appeal under Section 127 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The High Court will not mandamus the licensee to correct the bill or decide that representation; the Act and the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 supply the appeal, which the consumer may pursue.

cases.title: Rajveer Bhati v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ-barred-by-s127-appeal-against-s126-final-assessment
cases.holding: After reciting s.126(1)–(3) (provisional assessment, service, objections, and final order after hearing) and s.127(1), and noting that Clause 6.8 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 also provides for appeal against the final order of assessment, the Court held that the petitioner had an alternative remedy of appeal under s.127 read with Clause 6.8 against the final assessment dated 12.10.2012, declined Article 226 interference, and dismissed the writ on that ground.

EA2003::135.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Proof standard: civil for s.126 assessment, beyond reasonable doubt + mens rea for s.135 theft
cases.holding: To prove theft in a criminal proceeding the case must be proved beyond reasonable doubt with mens rea established; such strict proof is not necessary for assessing liability under Section 126(1), which requires only civil proof.

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Mens rea not required for a Section 126 civil assessment
cases.holding: The question of mens rea does not arise for a Section 126 assessment on an allegation of theft, since that assessment does not require criminal intention; mens rea is required only for prosecution under Section 135. (Agreeing with Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. v. PVVNL, distinguishing Ram Chandra Prasad Sharma v. State of Bihar, which concerned criminal prosecution under the 1910 Act.)

cases.title: Mobin Ahamad v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: FIR disclosing a cognizable s.135 offence will not be quashed, but arrest must follow Cr.P.C. s.41(1)(b)/41-A safeguards, and a compoundable offence's remedy lies via the Supply Code/s.152, not quashing
cases.holding: No — the FIR discloses a cognizable offence and will not be quashed merely because the alleged offence attracts less than 7 years' imprisonment or is compoundable. However, since the sentence would not exceed 7 years, any arrest must comply with the safeguards under Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A of the Cr.P.C.; if the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek his remedy under the provisions of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003.

cases.title: Mohamad Aslam v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Companion ruling to SCJ-081 (Mobin Ahamad) — identical holding on a parallel FIR from the same investigation
cases.holding: As in SCJ-081: the FIR discloses a cognizable offence and is not quashed; any arrest must comply with Cr.P.C. s.41(1)(b)/41-A since the offence would not entail more than 7 years' imprisonment; a compoundable offence's remedy lies under the Supply Code, 2005 and s.152 of the Act.
cases.flag: Near-verbatim companion order to SCJ-081; recorded compactly to avoid duplicating the identical reasoning.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Laur v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: A licensee's authorised officer is competent under s.135(2) to lodge an FIR for theft of electricity; the FIR is not quashed absent ex-facie absence of a cognizable offence or proven malafide
cases.holding: Yes, the officer is competent under s.135(2), which empowers an authorised officer of the licensee to enter, inspect, search and seize in relation to unauthorised use of electricity, supporting the officer's authority to also lodge an FIR under s.135(1). No malafide was made out merely from the FIR's timing relative to the related writ petition (which had only resulted in notice being issued, not a stay of recovery); the FIR disclosed a prima facie cognizable offence (theft found on inspection, and substantial dues outstanding), and following the settled Bhajan Lal/Satya Pal/Ajit Singh line, courts do not interfere with investigation or quash an FIR absent ex-facie absence of a cognizable offence or a statutory bar on investigation.

cases.title: Jay Prakash Yadav v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft assessment challenge and compounding
cases.holding: The petitioner having neither contended that the s.135 theft assessment was on the higher side nor challenged it before the Executive Engineer or by appeal, the writ was dismissed. If aggrieved by quantum he may file a representation and thereafter an appeal under the Electricity Act. It remains open to apply for compounding of the theft offence if an FIR has been lodged under s.135.

cases.title: Javed Ali v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: s.135 FIR quash and compounding
cases.holding: Where an FIR under s.135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 prima facie discloses a cognizable offence, the High Court will not quash it in writ jurisdiction. Compounding, if any, is governed by the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and the accused may pursue that statutory remedy.

cases.holding: Where an FIR under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 prima facie discloses a cognizable offence, the High Court will not quash it in writ jurisdiction. Compounding, if sought, is to be pursued under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Ayodhya Prasad Alias Lala Prajapati v. State of U.P. and others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s.135 FIR quash, arrest safeguards, compounding
cases.holding: An FIR under Section 135 of the Electricity Act that discloses a cognizable offence will not be quashed. Arrest had not been made; a mere apprehension of arrest in breach of Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC does not warrant interference, those provisions being expected to be followed, with a complaint to the Magistrate available if they are violated. If arrest is to be made and the offence will not entail a sentence of more than seven years, the police must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC. If the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek the remedy under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Dinesh Kumar Gupta v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: FIR quashing and compounding liberty
cases.holding: An FIR that discloses a cognizable offence under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 will not be quashed. The accused may still invoke whatever compounding or other remedy is available under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: M/S Kamakhya Steels Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: An inspection that rules out direct theft and records only a 'possibility of theft' from CT/PT-chamber seals and mixed-feeder line losses cannot, without reasoned analysis, be converted into a finding of actual theft supporting a Code assessment
cases.holding: No. The checking/summary report itself stated that although no direct theft had been detected in the metering system, certain facts (tampered CT/PT-chamber seals; feeder energy difference of 9.17%–19.75% across three consumers) led only to a 'possibility of theft'. The Court held there was no analysis converting that possibility into a case of clear theft: the main-meter seal was not found broken, nothing incriminating was found in the meter or metering system, and line loss on a mixed feeder was not shown to be solely attributable to the petitioner (no inspection of the other two consumers having been reported). Theft is a question of fact; a mere doubt or apprehension cannot found a proved case of theft so as to hold the consumer liable for unauthorised-use charges. The assessing authority was directed, on remand, to record specific findings as to how and on what basis a case of possibility of theft can be taken as actual theft within Section 135, leading to provisional and final assessment under the Code.

cases.title: Anil Kumar Upadhyay v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: A s.135 FIR / provisional-assessment writ may be disposed of, without quashing, where the consumer has paid the assessment and the licensee will send a compounding report to the police, and the petitioner so prays
cases.holding: The Court disposed of the petition without quashing either the FIR or the provisional assessment. After the licensee recorded that payment had been received under the assessment notice and that a compounding report would be sent to the police station, the petitioner prayed for disposal in view of that affidavit; the department and the State did not object. The Court found no good reason to keep the petition pending. This is not a decision that the FIR was illegal, that compounding has already extinguished the offence, or that the Code procedure was (or was not) followed.
cases.flag: Thin disposal on consent/payment. Prayer (iv) alleged violation of 'mandatory provisions' of the Act and the Supply Code, 2005, and sought disciplinary action; that was not decided. The FIR describes the statute as the 'Indian Electricity Act, 2003' — the 2003 Act, not the 1910 Act; recorded, not merged. Compounding is spoken of in the affidavit, not attributed by the Court to a numbered Code clause; indexed with the s.135/compounding cluster.

cases.title: Satish Kumar Bharti alias Chhotu v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Non-mention of the specific clause of s.135(1) in the FIR, charge-sheet or cognizance order is not fatal where the narration makes the theft clear
cases.holding: No, on these facts. The five clauses of s.135(1) carry the same punishment (up to three years or fine or both) and are the definition of theft of electricity. The FIR's narration — no authorised connection, electricity used by laying a cable illegally, videographed, no document produced — makes the offence under s.135(1) clear (direct/unauthorised connection). Mere mention of 'Section 135' without the sub-clause does not aid the accused. Ashim @ Hassim is distinguished: it concerned the Gangster Act, where the different offences have a different connotation.

cases.title: Shah Faisal v. State of Uttar Pradesh & 4 Others
cases.topic: A 528 BNSS challenge to a s.135 charge-sheet, withdrawn at the hearing, yields only a direction that a promptly filed bail application be decided in light of Satender Kumar Antil
cases.holding: The charge-sheet and sessions case were not quashed. On the applicant not pressing the 528 application, the Court granted two weeks to appear before the trial court and file bail, to be decided expeditiously following Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI. The State's submission that the allegations are disputed questions of fact for trial was not traversed.
cases.flag: Criminal-procedure disposal of a s.135 prosecution; retained as a node in the theft line.

cases.title: M/s Sangam Crusher Works & Another v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A cable lying on the floor, from which theft 'can be done' if artificial means were obtained, does not establish theft or support the s.135(1) proviso presumption
cases.holding: No. Inspections of 28.10.2022 and 08.12.2022 recorded no evidence of abstraction from the energised double-pole line behind the premises (jumper not attached; no 11 kV cable or wire connected). The 17.12.2022 inside inspection found an 11 kV cable on the floor and concluded only that unauthorised consumption was possible with artificial means. Nothing on the record showed any such artificial means in the premises. The proviso to s.135(1) — that existence of artificial means is presumed to be dishonest abstraction until the contrary is proved — is misplaced where those means were not found. A cable lying in a premises cannot indict the occupier on the footing that if he obtained artificial means he could steal. In the absence of a positive act of unauthorised use by artificial means found on the spot, no presumption of theft lies. Allegation of theft/unauthorised use under s.135 is not established. Presence of stone grits after an NGT-directed shutdown and permanent disconnection cannot itself found a presumption that the crusher was being run unauthorisedly.
cases.flag: Companion to SCJ-273 / SCJ-070 (theft-cannot-rest-on-mere-possibility). Internal date: para 3 has PD after the 23.07.2019 visit; para 18 states PD w.e.f. 12.07.2019. Recorded as the judgment states them. The demand was styled as theft (compounding fee; s.135 language) and assessed under s.126; the Court treated the first issue as s.135 theft and the second as s.126 r/w Clause 6.8.

cases.title: M/s K.G.N. Stone Crusher Mill & Another v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A cable lying on the floor, from which theft 'can be done' if artificial means were obtained, does not establish theft or support the s.135(1) proviso presumption
cases.holding: No. Inspections of 29.10.2022 and 08.12.2022 recorded no evidence of abstraction from the energised double-pole line behind the premises (jumper not attached; no 11 kV cable connected at the rear). The 17.12.2022 inside inspection found an 11 kV cable on the floor and concluded only that unauthorised consumption was possible with artificial means. Nothing on the record showed any such artificial means in the premises. The proviso to s.135(1) — that existence of artificial means is presumed to be dishonest abstraction until the contrary is proved — is misplaced where those means were not found. A cable lying in a premises cannot indict the occupier on the footing that if he obtained artificial means he could steal. In the absence of a positive act of unauthorised use by artificial means found on the spot, no presumption of theft lies. Allegation of theft/unauthorised use under s.135 is not established. Presence of stone grits after an NGT-directed shutdown and permanent disconnection w.e.f. 12.10.2019 cannot itself found a presumption that the crusher was being run unauthorisedly.
cases.flag: Twin of SCJ-285 (Sangam Crusher Works, Writ-C 12783/2024), same Bench, same dates, same reasoning. Distinguishing facts: 140 kW (not 90 kW); PD 12.10.2019 (not 23.07.2019); inspections 29.10.2022 (not 28.10.2022); restart order 18.12.2022; 08.12.2022 report noted an 11 kV wire coming from the premises; provisional Rs. 83,40,994 + compounding Rs. 15,00,000; final Rs. 62,34,761 + compounding Rs. 28,00,000; earlier writ 26481/2023. Same s.126/s.135 mix: compounding on a s.126 assessment; Court treated issue (1) as s.135 theft and issue (2) as s.126 r/w Clause 6.8.

cases.title: Mohan Lal v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: Permanent Lok Adalat rejection of a s.135-origin complaint — no interference
cases.holding: There is no illegality in a Permanent Lok Adalat order rejecting a complaint for want of compromise where the dispute arises out of Section 135. Disputed facts of that kind cannot be decided in writ at the first instance.

cases.title: M/s Kamakhya Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Another v. PVVNL & Another
cases.topic: A checking-report 'possibility of theft' plus a check-meter finding that the original meter was slow-running cannot, without a finding of actual theft, support an assessment of additional units as theft
cases.holding: No. The checking report concluded only a 'possibility of theft' although no direct theft had been detected. The Court held that unless a finding of electricity theft was returned — the matter not having been found to be a case of tampering with a broken seal in that sense — mere slow working of a meter with a lesser reading would not amount to theft. Liability for 2,97,779 additional units, hypothetically derived from the difference between the check meter and the original meter, could not rest on that footing. On remand the assessing authority must record how and under what circumstances a case of possibility of theft can be taken as actual theft so as to make the consumer liable for that difference.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite s.135 by number. Companion to SCJ-273 (Writ-C No. 20210 of 2012), same Bench and date, connected; that order remitted for findings of actual theft under s.135. Keyed accordingly. OCR reads 'tempered' for tampered.

cases.title: Anuradha v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s.135 FIR not quashed; arrest only after s.35 BNSS notice and credible material (Arnesh Kumar)
cases.holding: No. The writ is disposed of without quashing the FIR. Taking the offence as punishable with seven years or less, the Court applied Arnesh Kumar and Md. Asfak Alam: the petitioner's liberty is protected if the investigating officer gives notice under Section 35 BNSS; the petitioner must fully cooperate; arrest may be effected only if credible material is brought on record during investigation, after recording reasons, strictly in those guidelines; and the investigation is to be concluded preferably within 60 days with a report under Section 193(3) BNSS.
cases.flag: Template Arnesh Kumar disposal. The Court did not examine the FIR, any checking report, or clause 8.1. Petitioner invoked ss.126/135 and clause 8.1; those points are not decided. Compounding was not mentioned. The source PDF also contains a 23.8.2025 listing order; the operative disposal is 1.9.2025. Same cluster as SCJ-004, SCJ-081, SCJ-180–186.

cases.title: Udit Narayan v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interim stay of s.135 trial and direction to grant connection
cases.holding: Where a prior recovery citation in a s.135 matter had been quashed for ignoring the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and a fresh Code-compliant assessment (over Rs.1 lakh plus compounding fee) had been raised, the applicant was directed to deposit Rs.50,000 toward that assessment within three weeks. On such deposit the s.135 trial would remain stayed till the next date and the department would provide the electricity connection already applied for. The quashing application was not disposed of.

cases.title: M/S Dev Cold Storage Pvt. Ltd. v. Dakshinachal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: appeal against revised assessment
cases.holding: A revised assessment order and bill of September 2007 passed by the Executive Engineer (Distribution) under s.135 are not quashed on merits. The consumer may appeal them within four weeks without pre-deposit, substantial amounts having already been deposited; the appellate authority shall grant a hearing and pass a reasoned order in accordance with law within eight weeks of filing.

cases.title: Sheelu v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: writ against s.135 recovery
cases.holding: Where recovery proceedings have been initiated under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, a writ to quash the recovery certificate cannot be granted if the consumer has not first challenged those proceedings under the Electricity Act and/or the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Petitioner v. State of U.P. And 4 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: consequential recovery of unchallenged s.135 demand
cases.holding: Where a demand notice is raised pursuant to an order under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003, a writ confined to the consequential recovery cannot be entertained unless the primary order creating the demand is also challenged. Article 226 interference was declined. The petitioner was left to the statutory remedy under the Act read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; if availed within three weeks, that remedy is to be decided on merits without prejudice from this order.

cases.title: Avanish Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s135-consequential-demand-notice
cases.holding: Unless the primary order creating a Section 135 demand is challenged, a writ limited to the consequential recovery notice cannot be considered. The consumer has an adequate statutory remedy under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; Article 226 interference is declined, without prejudice if that remedy is availed within three weeks.

cases.title: Anil Suhala v. Purvanchal Vidhut Vitrana Nigam Ltd., Varanasi
cases.topic: no mandamus to restore while s.135 action is taken
cases.holding: Where the consumer was found drawing supply by a separate cable to the main line, bypassing the meter, and action under Section 135 has been taken, no mandamus can issue to restore the connection. The remedy is to challenge those proceedings in the appropriate forum.

cases.title: Sunil Pandey v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: section 135 theft prosecution — 482 quash refused where ingredients prima facie made out
cases.holding: Where a spot inspection found the consumer indulged in electricity theft and the FIR and record disclose the ingredients of section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003, a petition under section 482 Cr.P.C. to quash the FIR, charge-sheet, summoning order and criminal electricity case will not lie. Questions of fact—including the correctness of charging for a whole year though the assessment was for a month, and whether an objection was considered—are for the trial court. Section 482 is not a forum to appreciate evidence or test the reliability of the prosecution version, and the proceedings were not shown to be mala fide.

cases.title: Syed Avesh Ahmad v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.topic: section 135 theft prosecution — 482 quash refused where a prima facie case is made out
cases.holding: No. From the record it could not be said that no offence was made out. All submissions related to disputed questions of fact, which cannot be adjudicated under section 482 Cr.P.C.; at that stage only a prima facie case is to be seen. The application did not fall under the Bhajan Lal guidelines, followed with Neeharika, R.P. Kapur, P.P. Sharma and Zandu Pharmaceutical: only cases in which no prima facie case is made out can be considered under section 482. Whether the alleged offence was committed is for evidence and trial. The application was dismissed.
cases.flag: Source PDF also contains listing/adjournment orders of 31.10.2023 and 30.11.2023; the operative dismissal is 08.02.2024. The applicant invoked non-compliance with the Electricity Supply Code; the Court did not construe any Code clause.

cases.title: Pramod Kumar v. State of U.P. and 3 Others
cases.topic: FIR under s.135 — quashing not decided; petition dismissed for non-prosecution
cases.holding: The writ sought quashing of the FIR in Case Crime No. 4681 of 2022 under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, Police Station Anti Power Theft, Jalaun. The Court did not quash the FIR. After interim directions (an affidavit from the Executive Engineer, a show-cause for costs of Rs. 1 lakh, and a stay of coercive measures), none appeared for the petitioner on the revised call of 16.07.2026. The petition was dismissed for non-prosecution and the interim order, if any, was vacated.
cases.flag: The 16.07.2026 order is unnumbered; treated as a single paragraph. Dismissal for non-prosecution is not a finding that theft was committed.

cases.title: Ramesh Chandra Kasera v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: authorised-officer search and seizure vs Cr.P.C.
cases.holding: Section 135(2)(a) and (b), empowering the licensee's authorised officer to search and seize, is not inconsistent with Cr.P.C. sections 47, 51, 94 and 100. The Electricity Act, 2003 is a special Act that borrows Cr.P.C. procedure for search and seizure; the two are not at cross-purposes. The further plea that section 154(3) summary trial of sections 135–139 (punishable with up to three years) conflicts with Cr.P.C. section 262(2) (summary-trial imprisonment capped at three months) was rejected as lacking judicial understanding.

cases.title: Joginder Singh v. State of U.P. and Others
cases.topic: Summoning under ss.135/138 is not tested by s.39 IEA 1910 or mens rea at the s.204 stage
cases.holding: No. Ram Chandra Prasad Sharma is inapplicable on these facts. The Indian Electricity Act, 1910 has been repealed by Section 185 of the Electricity Act, 2003. Even if the 1910 Act were still in force, at the stage of summoning under Section 204 CrPC intention is not to be looked into; intention is locked in the heart of the accused and is disclosed, if at all, by his actions in the course of trial. Neither Section 39 nor that precedent has any relevance. A Section 204 summoning order need not give detailed reasons; the reasons given were sufficient and the summoning was legal. Issuing a non-bailable warrant at the first instance was not proper; summons should have been issued. The non-bailable-warrant portion is set aside; the revisionist is directed to appear on 3.1.2011 to stand trial, with liberty to the trial court to secure presence if he does not, and to consider bail in accordance with law.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Mohd. Kasim
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s.135 complaint — maintainability; 2003 Act versus 1999 Reforms Act
cases.holding: The High Court declined to interfere with the Sessions Court's closure of a section 135 Electricity Act, 2003 complaint on maintainability. It held that the finding that proceedings under the 2003 Act and the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 could not continue, and that the prosecution should have been launched under the Electricity Reforms Act, 1999 and the Electricity Code, 2002, disclosed no illegality, infirmity or jurisdictional error; the licensee's revision was dismissed as lacking merit.

cases.title: Ashok Garg v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.topic: Section 135 charge-sheet needs no s.141 NI Act-style 'in charge of business' averment; director-vicarious-liability cases distinguished
cases.holding: No. S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals is distinguished: the mandatory s.141 complaint averment has no counterpart in section 135 fastening any such duty on the prosecution in the report. Sunil Bharti Mittal (no vicarious liability unless the statute so provides) and Datar Switchgear (no presumption that a chairman is responsible for all company acts) are distinguished because the petitioner was the director and the owner who absconded at checking and did not inform change of ownership. M.A.A. Annamalai, where the accused had ceased to be a director before the offences and the FIR contained no allegation against him, could not help. Disputed facts of resignation, takeover and presence are not for section 482. There is no material illegality in the summoning order. The petition is dismissed.

cases.title: M/S Radha Krishna v. M.D., D.V.V.N. and Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: pending revision against acquittal means s.135 proceedings have not attained finality
cases.holding: An FIR under section 135 was lodged the same day as the 22 June 2007 raid. The Special Judge later held the theft charge not made out. A criminal revision against that order having been filed and notices issued, the proceedings have not attained finality; that fact is the reason the refund is against security rather than unconditional.

cases.title: Kailash Chandra Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: bail in s.135/138 theft prosecution
cases.holding: The applicant in Case Crime No. 116 of 2009 under sections 135 and 138 of the Electricity Act, 2003 was held entitled to bail, without any opinion on the merits of the alleged meter tampering or of the clause 8.4 contention that no FIR shall be lodged where a consumer voluntarily declares a tampered meter and pays the requisite charges in time.

cases.title: Dinesh Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: payment of dues does not obliterate theft prosecution
cases.holding: Prosecution of a crime is a different matter from payment of electricity dues. Mere payment of dues does not obliterate an offence under s.135 of the Electricity Act, 2003: crime is against society. Compounding can be done only by the department if it so desires; the accused cannot compel compounding. Even payment of the entire dues with electricity charges leaves the accused liable to prosecution under s.135. A judgment in Misc. Petition No. 31705 of 2009 on recovery under Electricity Supply Code, 2005 clause 8.1 has no application in a criminal matter. The 482 application to quash the order dated 30.7.2010 in Special Case No. 514 of 2008 was dismissed as bereft of merit.

cases.title: Sri Mandir v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: s.135 FIR — quash refused; arrest safeguards; compounding
cases.holding: An FIR under Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003 that discloses a cognizable offence is not liable to be quashed in a criminal miscellaneous writ petition. Because the alleged offence cannot attract a sentence of more than seven years, any arrest must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC. If the offence is compoundable, the petitioner may seek compounding under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The writ petition was disposed of; the quash prayer was refused.

cases.title: Prayag Prakash v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: quashing FIR for unauthorised reconnection
cases.holding: An FIR under Section 138(B) of the Electricity Act, 2003 that discloses a cognizable offence is not liable to be quashed. Arrest, if effectuated for an offence not entailing more than seven years' imprisonment, must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC. If the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek compounding under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Chitranjan Sheel v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: FIR under s.138 — quash refused where cognizable offence disclosed
cases.holding: The FIR under Section 138-B of the Indian Electricity Act discloses a cognizable offence, so it cannot be quashed. Arrest not having been made, if arrest is to be effectuated for an offence that will not entail sentence of more than seven years, police must comply with CrPC s.41(1)(b) read with s.41-A; breach may be complained of before the Magistrate. If the offence is compoundable, the petitioner may seek the remedy under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Petition disposed of.
cases.flag: FIR and order cite 'Section 138-B of the Indian Electricity Act'; EA 2003 has s.138, not 138-B.

cases.title: Adeel Husain v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: FIR quash of reconnection/theft charges; compounding under Supply Code
cases.holding: FIRs under ss. 138-B and 135-E of the Electricity Act, 2003 disclose a cognizable offence and will not be quashed. Arrest, if made for an offence not entailing sentence of more than seven years, must comply with s. 41(1)(b) read with s. 41-A CrPC. If the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek compounding under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.
cases.flag: FIR charges styled as ss. 138-B and 135-E of the Electricity Act; not restated as 138(b)/135(1)(e).

cases.title: Niranjan v. State of U.P. — s.138-B electricity FIR not quashed
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ quash of cognizable s.138 FIR; compounding under Supply Code
cases.holding: Where the FIR under Section 138-B of the Indian Electricity Act discloses a cognizable offence, the High Court will not quash it. Arrest, if at all, in an offence that cannot attract a sentence of more than seven years must follow CrPC s. 41(1)(b) read with s. 41-A; if the electricity offence is compoundable, the accused may seek the remedy under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.
cases.flag: FIR cited as 'Section 138-B of the Indian Electricity Act'; not resolved whether that is EA 2003 s.138(1)(b) (unauthorised reconnection) or another clause.

cases.title: Suresh v. State of U.P. and others
cases.topic: fir-quash-cognizable-offence
cases.holding: Where the FIR under Section 138 B of the Indian Electricity Act discloses a cognizable offence, the High Court will not quash it. Arrest, if effectuated and the offence will not entail sentence of more than seven years, must comply with CrPC s.41(1)(b) read with s.41-A; violation may be complained of before the Magistrate. If the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek his remedy under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.
cases.flag: FIR registered as 'Section 138 B of Indian Electricity Act'; counsel argued EA 2003 s.135. Court did not resolve the section or the statute's title.

cases.title: Vikky v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: quashing FIR for interference with meters or works
cases.holding: An FIR registered under Section 138(d) of the Electricity Act, 2003 that discloses a cognizable offence will not be quashed. If arrest is to be effectuated for an offence that will not entail a sentence of more than seven years, the police must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC.

cases.title: Smt. Anita Devi v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: quashing of FIR under s.138
cases.holding: Where an FIR registered under s.138 of the Electricity Act, 2003 discloses a cognizable offence, the High Court will not quash it. If arrest is to be effectuated and the offence will not entail a sentence of more than seven years, the police must proceed in compliance with CrPC s.41(1)(b) read with s.41-A.

cases.title: Maukeen @ Saukeen v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: FIR quashing for interference with meters or unauthorised reconnection
cases.holding: An FIR registered under Section 138-B of the Electricity Act that discloses a cognizable offence will not be quashed. If the alleged offence would not entail a sentence of more than seven years and arrest is to be effectuated, police must comply with Section 41(1)(b) read with Section 41-A CrPC. If the offence is compoundable, the accused may seek compounding under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and Section 152 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
cases.flag: Order and FIR cite 'Section 138-B' of the Electricity Act; EA 2003 s.138 uses clauses (a)–(d) of sub-section (1), not a separate section 138-B.

cases.title: Shailendra Kumar v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: Unauthorised reconnection (s.138) is distinct from a billing/arrears dispute
cases.holding: No. The s.138 offence of unauthorisedly reconnecting the line after disconnection is entirely different from the arrears/billing dispute (governed by Chapter 6 of the Code); the prosecution was for the reconnection, not for non-payment. A prior consumer-forum order on a different bill does not make the criminal proceedings an abuse of process, especially as the revised bill was neither paid nor challenged. At the pre-trial stage under s.482 the Court will not appreciate evidence; a prima facie s.138 case being made out, the proceedings and the non-bailable warrant were not quashed.

EA2003::14-franchisee-agency.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.2(27) 'franchisee'; seventh proviso to s.14; s.128, investigation of licensees) read with the Conditions of Distribution License Regulations, 2004 (Clauses 4, 5.8-5.11, 7)
EA2003::14-franchisee-agency.clause: Seventh proviso to s.14 and s.2(27) — a distribution franchisee is the agent of the distribution licensee, which alone bears regulatory accountability; s.128 investigation confined to the licensee, not the franchisee
EA2003::14-franchisee-agency.topic: A distribution franchisee, being the statutory agent of the distribution licensee under s.2(27)/seventh proviso to s.14, is not directly subject to ERC regulatory oversight; an ERC's Section 128 investigation power can only be exercised against the distribution licensee (on a showing of licence/Act violation), not to review or micromanage a franchisee's performance metrics

cases.title: Torrent Power Limited v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: A distribution franchisee, being the statutory agent of the distribution licensee under s.2(27)/seventh proviso to s.14, is not directly subject to ERC regulatory oversight; an ERC's Section 128 investigation power can only be exercised against the distribution licensee (on a showing of licence/Act violation), not to review or micromanage a franchisee's performance metrics
cases.holding: No, not directly against the franchisee, and not as a bare performance review. The relationship between distribution licensee and franchisee is one of agency (principal-agent), following APTEL's reasoning in City Corporation Ltd. v. MERC: the franchisee is accountable only to the licensee, and the licensee alone is accountable to consumers and the ERC. The Act contains no provision for direct ERC regulatory oversight of a franchisee — Part IV (ss.12-24) regulates only the licensee. An investigation under s.128 requires the ERC's 'satisfaction,' based on concrete grounds, that the licensee has failed to comply with licence conditions or the Act/Regulations; bare, undocumented allegations (as here, where neither the petitioner nor the subsequently-appointed Expert Committee identified any specific tariff-order or licence violation) do not meet this threshold. While cross-subsidisation of a franchisee's below-bulk-supply input rate by other consumers is a legitimate feature of input-based franchisee models in high-loss areas (a low bid input rate reflects anticipated high capital investment, not misrepresentation), the UPERC and APTEL erred in ordering an open-ended performance review of the franchisee's collection efficiency and loss-reduction trends absent any finding of licensee non-compliance; such micromanagement of a franchisee transaction, without a specific Act/licence violation, exceeds the ERC's statutory mandate. The petition under s.128 was accordingly not maintainable, and the impugned orders were set aside.

EA2003::145.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with Supply Code 2005 & CGRF Regulations 2007)
EA2003::145.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)

cases.title: Divisional Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-I v. Raman Singh & Another
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's tort claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: For a consumer's dispute, the Act and the Supply Code are comprehensive and civil-court jurisdiction is barred by Section 145. A non-consumer's claim for tort damages against the licensee is not a Code/CGRF matter; 'supply of power' is a 'public utility service' under Section 22-A of the LSA Act, 1987, so the Permanent Lok Adalat has jurisdiction, and the CGRF/Ombudsman Regulations, 2007 (covering only consumer grievances) do not apply. The compensation award is upheld.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division-II v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Forum: consumer disputes (Code/civil-court bar) vs a non-consumer's electrocution-damages claim (Lok Adalat)
cases.holding: Yes. 'Public utility service' (LSA Act s.22-A) means supply of power to the public and needs no consumer relationship; the Permanent Lok Adalat has adjudicatory power under s.22-C(8) where conciliation fails. A consumer's electricity dispute is cognizable only by the statutory authorities under the Act/Code, civil-court jurisdiction being barred by Section 145; but a non-consumer's tort claim for electrocution is a civil dispute the Lok Adalat may decide, and a weaker-section claimant cannot be relegated to a civil suit.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Distribution Division & Anr. v. Pacific Promoter
cases.topic: Civil court's jurisdiction barred for a s.126 assessment dispute
cases.holding: No. Section 145 expressly bars the civil court's jurisdiction over matters of assessment under ss.126/127; civil liability for unauthorised use is imposed only through a s.126 assessment (appealable under s.127), and s.9 CPC excludes the civil court where jurisdiction is so barred. A suit for a declaration that the checking report and the consequent assessment are illegal/void is barred; the plaint is rejected and the suit dismissed. The plea of lack of jurisdiction can be raised at any stage, even after long pendency.

EA2003::151.topic: Unamended s.151 does not bar FIR or charge-sheet cognizance of a s.135 offence

cases.title: Ashok Garg v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.topic: Unamended s.151 does not bar FIR or charge-sheet cognizance of a s.135 offence
cases.holding: No. Following Vishal Agrawal, section 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies to offences under the Electricity Act; the Act does not prescribe a special exclusive machinery that shuts out Chapter XII. Section 151 enables specified persons to file a complaint on which the court may take cognizance straightway, but that does not exclude an FIR, investigation, or a police report. It is therefore trite that a charge-sheet can be filed for an offence punishable under section 135. The petition on this ground fails.
cases.flag: The Court quotes unamended s.151, Rule 12 of the Electricity Rules, 2005, the 2007 provisos to s.151 (cognizance on a s.173 Cr.P.C. report; Special Court under s.153), and s.151-A. A 14.2.2017 listing note had reserved the transition period after the 15.6.2007 amendment; the reserved judgment does not decide retrospectivity of that amendment, because Vishal Agrawal already holds FIR and charge-sheet competent under the unamended scheme. Rule 12 is quoted but not independently construed.

EA2003::152.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required

cases.title: Abhinav Seva Sansthan Mahavidyalaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of electricity theft — whether a pending prosecution is required
cases.holding: Section 152(2) and (3) operate at different stages: under s.152(2), where no criminal proceeding has yet been instituted, payment of the compounding sum sets the person at liberty and bars institution of proceedings; s.152(3) (acceptance deemed an acquittal) applies only where a prosecution is already pending. Compounding therefore does not require a pending prosecution.
cases.flag: The judgment refers throughout to 'Section 152(2) of the Electricity Supply Code 2005'; Section 152 is in the Electricity Act, 2003. Recorded, not merged.

cases.title: Om Prakash s/o Gauri Shankar v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Compounding of a theft offence under s.152(3) does not exonerate the consumer from separate civil liability for electricity consumption dues; a quantum dispute over such recovery must go to the Supply Code authority, not the writ court
cases.holding: No — the compounding fee is a penalty for the criminal offence of theft and does not exonerate the consumer from the separate civil liability to pay for electricity actually consumed; a recovery notice for such dues is not barred by compounding. Any grievance as to the quantum of such dues must be raised before the authority under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not by way of writ petition.

cases.title: Vijay Bahadur Maurya v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: compounding of s.135 offence

cases.holding: Where recovery of electricity dues rests on an unchallenged checking report of theft, the High Court will not entertain a writ against the recovery notice. If an FIR has been lodged, the consumer's remedy is compounding under s.152 of the Electricity Act, 2003. If the demand is a provisional assessment arising from theft, the consumer must approach the concerned Executive Engineer; the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 supplies the statutory remedy.

cases.title: Faizul Hasan v. State of U.P.
