cases.title: Anil Kumar Upadhyay v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: After payment of the assessment, the licensee may send a compounding report to the police station; the writ court recorded that statement and disposed of the petition without deciding whether compounding was complete
cases.holding: The licensee’s counsel stated that payment had been received from the petitioner in connection with the inspection and the assessment notice, and (on oral instruction) that a report would be sent to the concerned police station for compounding. The Court recorded that statement and disposed of the writ on the petitioner’s prayer. It did not hold that compounding under Section 152 was complete, nor did it stay or quash the criminal case.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite s.152; compounding is the department’s description. Keyed here as the statutory compounding provision the affidavit was invoking.

cases.title: Pramod Kumar v. State of U.P. and 3 Others
cases.topic: Department conceded s.135 FIR is compoundable under s.152 and inclined to withdraw — not given effect
cases.holding: On 21.03.2024 senior counsel for the electricity department fairly conceded that the FIR under Section 135 is compoundable under Section 152 and that the Department was inclined to withdraw it, and sought time to file an affidavit. The Court passed the matter over. No compounding order was recorded and the FIR was not withdrawn on the writ. The petition was later dismissed for non-prosecution.
cases.flag: Paragraph 3 of the 21.03.2024 order. Compounding was conceded, not applied.

EA2003::153.topic: Theft (s.135) is triable by Special Courts; civil liability via s.126 assessment

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Distribution Division & Anr. v. Pacific Promoter
cases.topic: Theft (s.135) is triable by Special Courts; civil liability via s.126 assessment
cases.holding: Theft of electricity under s.135 is a criminal offence triable by Special Courts constituted under s.153, the procedure being in s.154 read with Clauses 8.1-8.5 of the Code; civil liability for unauthorised use is separately imposed through a s.126 assessment (Chapter 6 of the Code). The Act is a complete Code covering both aspects, leaving no room for a civil suit on the assessment.

EA2003::154.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed

cases.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: The Section 126 assessment and the Special Court's Section 154(5) civil-liability determination are not parallel/mutually exclusive — both may proceed
cases.holding: The Section 126(1) assessment power and the power to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) are not parallel to each other; the High Court erred in holding the two proceedings cannot operate parallelly. Where there is no theft (only unauthorised use), the loss is assessed under Section 126(1) alone; where the unauthorised use amounts to theft, a Section 126(1) assessment AND a Section 135 complaint may both proceed, with the Special Court determining civil liability under Section 154(5) and any excess deposit refunded. Merely because the Special Court is empowered to determine civil liability under Section 154(5) does not mean the authorities lack power to make a Section 126 assessment.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Appellate Authority/Addl. Commissioner & Anr. (Sunita Spat Pvt. Ltd.)
cases.topic: Even a 'no theft' finding by the appellate authority is subject to the Special Court's determination of civil liability for theft under Sections 154(5)-(6); the licensee's revenue interest is thereby protected
cases.holding: No. The proceedings arising from the FIR and charge-sheet are subject to the orders of the Special Court constituted under Section 153, whose powers include the determination, under Section 154(5)-(6), of the consumer's civil liability for theft of energy (not less than twice the tariff for the twelve months preceding detection or the exact period of theft, whichever is less, recoverable as a civil-court decree, with refund of any excess deposit with interest); by Section 155 the Special Court has the powers of a court of session. Consequently, even a finding by the appellate authority that it was not a case of theft is always subject to the order of the Special Court, so that any difference of amount can be realised if theft is proved. The licensee's revenue interest is thereby fully protected, and the writ - which sought only to protect that interest - lacks substance and is dismissed.

cases.title: Om Prakash v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.topic: Compounding = deemed acquittal of the offence, but civil liability survives (Special Court)
cases.holding: Depositing the compounding fee means the consumer is deemed acquitted of the theft offence under s.154, but it does not extinguish the civil liability, which is to be determined and adjudicated by the Special Court (constituted under s.153, empowered under s.154 to deal with both criminal and civil liability). The consumer having an adequate alternative remedy, the writ was dismissed in limine.

cases.title: Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.neutral_citation: Criminal Appeal u/s 413 BNSS Defective No. 78 of 2025
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: review of Special Court assessment
cases.holding: If the assessment arrived at by the Special Court under s.154 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is found incorrect, the remedy of review before that Court is to be availed. A licensee's High Court criminal appeal under s.413 BNSS challenging inadequate sentence and fine (pleaded with s.126 and Supply Code 6.8(c)(iii)), where no such review had been filed, was dismissed as withdrawn with liberty to seek that review.

EA2003::161.topic: Compensation for accidents caused by a licensee's negligence

cases.title: Parmeshwar Prasad v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: Compensation for accidents caused by a licensee's negligence
cases.holding: A writ complaining of the absence of any statutory provision for compensation where injury or death is caused by a licensee's negligence is misconceived when it ignores s.161 of the Electricity Act, 2003, which provides the statutory mechanism for inquiry into such accidents. The petition, filed without examining s.161, is dismissed.

cases.title: Jhanni v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: electrical accident inquiry and compensation representation
cases.holding: Without expressing any opinion on merits, a writ seeking compensation for electrocution death is disposed of by directing a fresh representation; the concerned authority shall submit a report as provided under Section 161, together with the representation, to the Executive Engineer, who shall decide the claim by a speaking order after hearing, in accordance with law.
cases.flag: Order cites 'Section 161 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005'; Section 161 is of the Electricity Act, 2003 (notice of accidents and inquiries), not the Supply Code.

cases.title: Ajay Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: electrical-accident-inquiry-compensation
cases.holding: Without expressing opinion on the merits of a compensation claim for deaths alleged to have been caused by electric short-circuit, the Court disposed of the writ by directing the petitioners to make a fresh representation to the Electrical Inspector and the Executive Engineer within ten days. The Electrical Inspector was to submit a report as provided under Section 161 within 15 days; the Executive Engineer was then to consider and decide the representation by a speaking order after hearing, in accordance with law, within 30 days of receiving that report. Delay was not to be a ground for dismissal.
cases.flag: Court cited 'Section 161 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005'; accident-inquiry jurisdiction is Electricity Act 2003 s.161 (Electrical Inspector).

EA2003::173.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.173, 174) vis-a-vis Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (s.238, s.53 waterfall mechanism)
EA2003::173.clause: ss.173/174 (non-obstante overriding clauses) vis-a-vis IBC s.238 (later, overriding non-obstante clause) and s.53 (liquidation waterfall)
EA2003::173.topic: IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act's ss.173/174 recovery mechanism once liquidation has commenced; a distribution licensee cannot independently attach/auction a corporate debtor's property for electricity dues outside the IBC process, and its dues do not automatically rank as 'government dues' merely due to state shareholding, though they may be a 'secured interest' on the facts

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cases.topic: IBC s.238 overrides the Electricity Act's ss.173/174 recovery mechanism once liquidation has commenced; a distribution licensee cannot independently attach/auction a corporate debtor's property for electricity dues outside the IBC process, and its dues do not automatically rank as 'government dues' merely due to state shareholding, though they may be a 'secured interest' on the facts
cases.holding: (a) No — s.238 of the IBC, being the later special enactment expressly covering corporate insolvency/liquidation, overrides ss.173/174 of the Electricity Act, 2003 despite the latter's non-obstante clauses; once liquidation commences, the licensee cannot independently attach or auction the corporate debtor's property outside the IBC's collective process, and the District Collector's attachment/auction notice for electricity dues was accordingly set aside, with the property released to the liquidator per the NCLT/NCLAT's order. (b) No — dues payable to a distribution licensee, even one with government shareholding, do not fall within s.53(1)(f)'s 'government dues' description, since such licensees are distinct juristic entities carrying on a liberalised activity open to private participation, and are not 'the State Government' merely by virtue of shareholding or historical function. (c) Not automatically — but on the facts here, given the supply agreement's clause making outstanding dues 'a charge on the assets of the company' and the concurrent, unchallenged NCLT/NCLAT findings that PVVNL was a secured creditor, PVVNL's claim proceeds within the s.53 waterfall as a secured creditor's claim (not outside/above the IBC process), to be verified and processed by the liquidator within 10 weeks. State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers, which treated a statutory first-charge as automatically conferring secured-creditor priority, was confined to its facts — it neither considered the s.53 waterfall nor arose in a liquidation (as opposed to resolution-plan) context, and cannot be extended to elevate electricity/quasi-government dues above Parliament's deliberately structured priority.

EA2003::174.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with s.50; Supply Code Para 7.10 / 7.7.1-7.7.5)
EA2003::174.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others v. M/s Prakancha Metal Works Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Overriding effect of the Act does not oust Lok Adalat / Consumer Protection remedies for damages
cases.holding: Section 174 gives the Act overriding effect only for matters provided under it; Section 50 does not empower the Supply Code to ascertain damages for a licensee's wrongful acts, and the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (Para 7.10, Clauses 7.7.1-7.7.5) covers only supply-related matters, not tortious damages for illegal disconnection. The Consumer Protection Act, 1986 is preserved (ss.173/174), and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (Lok Adalat) is a special Act for such damages; the Lok Adalat therefore had jurisdiction, to which the petitioners had in any event submitted.

cases.title: M/S Sri Dauji Cold Storage Pvt Ltd And Another v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd And Others
cases.topic: s.174 gives the Act overriding effect; a Code three-times rate cannot exceed s.126(6)
cases.holding: No. The Court adopted Vijay Pal Singh: Section 174 gives the Act overriding effect, and the Code, being subordinate legislation framed under the Act, cannot travel beyond Section 126(6). A three-times Code rate contrary to the then 1.5-times statutory cap cannot be enforced. Licensee's counsel could not dispute those provisions as already considered in Vijay Pal Singh.

cases.title: Raj Kumar v. KESCO and Others
cases.topic: s.174 overriding effect; scheduled 1999 Reforms Act continues only if consistent with the 2003 Act
cases.holding: No. A conjoint reading of Sections 174 and 175 shows the 2003 Act has overriding effect (save Section 173) over anything inconsistent in any other law or instrument, and is additional, not in derogation of other laws. Section 185(3) continues scheduled enactments, including the U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999, only so far as they are not inconsistent with the 2003 Act. Even if the 2002 Code is treated as framed under that Act, the rate for unauthorised consumption from 10.6.2003 is that in Section 126(6) as it then stood.
cases.flag: Catalog has EA2003::174, not 175 or 185; keyed to 174. Petitioner's submission (para 4) styles the parent as 'U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 2004'; the Court applies U.P. Act No. 24 of 1999 as scheduled to s.185(3).

EA2003::176.clause: 176(2)(e) r/w s.67(2) (Works of Licensees Rules, 2006, Rule 3(b) proviso)
EA2003::176.topic: Owner's objection to supply over his premises; DM's permission required — interim

cases.title: Daya Nand Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Owner's objection to supply over his premises; DM's permission required — interim
cases.holding: Prima facie, no. The writ court had directed a connection on an indemnity bond (Clause 4.4) ignoring the landlord's objection, but did not decide the tenant's occupation nor direct supply despite the owner's resistance. Where an owner objects to supply over his premises, the licensee must obtain the DM's/Commissioner's permission under the proviso to Rule 3(b) of the Works of Licensees Rules, 2006 (s.176(2)(e) r/w s.67(2)). The contempt court's direction to install within 72 hours and bar the owner's objection travelled beyond the writ order and was stayed, along with the contempt proceedings.
cases.flag: Interim order (stay) in a special appeal; the occupation dispute and merits are reserved.

EA2003::2(15).code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.2(15), 'consumer'; s.2(20), 'electric line'; s.2(77), 'works') read with s.135
EA2003::2(15).clause: s.2(15) 'consumer' definition — second limb ('premises connected with works for receiving electricity') vis-a-vis owner's liability for theft detected at leased-out premises
EA2003::2(15).topic: An owner of premises where theft of electricity is detected can be held liable for assessment purposes as a 'consumer' under s.2(15), even where he claims the premises was let out, since the premises' 'works' being connected for receiving electricity suffices — lack of mens rea (relevant to criminal liability under s.135) does not exempt the owner from civil assessment liability, particularly where an unsubstantiated leasing claim caused revenue loss

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: An owner of premises where theft of electricity is detected can be held liable for assessment purposes as a 'consumer' under s.2(15), even where he claims the premises was let out, since the premises' 'works' being connected for receiving electricity suffices — lack of mens rea (relevant to criminal liability under s.135) does not exempt the owner from civil assessment liability, particularly where an unsubstantiated leasing claim caused revenue loss
cases.holding: Yes. Section 135's widest-possible scope (using 'whoever', 'person', 'consumer', 'occupant' interchangeably) shows the legislature did not confine its mischief by any hyper-technical plea as to individual status. The s.2(15) 'consumer' definition's second limb covers any person whose premises are for the time being connected with the works (electric line, transformer, apparatus) of a licensee 'for the purpose of receiving electricity', without requiring a contractual/supply relationship — this is broad enough to include an owner. A bare, unsubstantiated claim of having let out the premises (disbelieved by both the Assessing Officer and Appellate Authority, and not substantiated before the High Court either) does not exempt the owner from assessment liability, though it may bear on the separate criminal-law mens rea requirement under s.135. On the facts, the petitioner did not dispute ownership and did not challenge the theft allegation or quantum in his objections — only bare non-occupancy was pleaded and disbelieved.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitaran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Commissioner, Moradabad Region & Anr.
cases.topic: Owner of premises is a 'consumer' liable to theft assessment (reproduced from the 2011 judgment)
cases.holding: Per the earlier final judgment (reproduced): a person whose premises are connected with anything capable of carrying the licensee's electricity is a 'consumer' under s.2(15); the owner of premises where theft is detected can be proceeded against under s.135 for revenue assessment even if the premises were let out, mens rea for the criminal offence being a matter for trial. On these facts the letting-out plea was disbelieved.
cases.flag: Reproduced from the High Court's final judgment dated 18.11.2011; relied on as the settled position, not decided afresh in this interim order.

cases.title: Anil Shastri v. State of U.P. Thru. Principal Secy. Power & Others
cases.topic: Secretary occupying the premises of a society's connection is a consumer liable for the theft assessment
cases.holding: Yes. Section 2(15), followed in the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, defines 'consumer' as any person supplied with electricity for his own use by a licensee, the Government, or any other person engaged in supplying electricity to the public, and includes any person whose premises are for the time being connected for receiving electricity with the works of a licensee. The petitioner, representing the society as Secretary and occupying the premises of the connection from which electricity was drawn, falls within that definition and is liable to pay the amount to the Power Corporation. The writ is dismissed.
cases.flag: Source PDF also contains listing, notice, pass-over and time-grant orders from 6.7.2010 to 22.2.2011; the operative judgment is 4.7.2011 (paras 1-11 of that order). Inspection, provisional assessment and recovery (2002–2004) predate the 2005 Code; the counter affidavit invoked the 2002 Code structural formula; the Court applied s.2(15) as followed in the 2005 Code without discussing retrospectivity. Amounts are as the judgment states them (difference Rs.9,716 in the counter-affidavit recital and Rs.9,738 later; Amin demand Rs.48,780 against recovery certificate Rs.48,760).

EA2003::2(49).topic: A registered society is a person; its Secretary representing it is liable

cases.title: Anil Shastri v. State of U.P. Thru. Principal Secy. Power & Others
cases.topic: A registered society is a person; its Secretary representing it is liable
cases.holding: A registered society is a 'person' within Section 2(49) of the Electricity Act, 2003 — any company or body corporate or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated or not, or artificial juridical person. The petitioner representing the society as Secretary is liable to pay the theft assessment.
cases.flag: The Court first defines 'person' under 'Section 2 (4)' and then holds the society is a person within 'Section 2 (49)'. Section 2(4) of the Electricity Act, 2003 is 'Appropriate Commission'; 'person' is s.2(49). Keyed to the later, correct citation; the s.2(4) recital is a mis-cite, not a holding on the Commission.

EA2003::42.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (with UPERC CGRF & Ombudsman Regulations, 2007)
EA2003::42.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: CGRF/Ombudsman cannot relegate a consumer's dispute to arbitration
cases.holding: No. Under Section 42(5)-(8) and the Regulations, 2007, the ECGRF and Ombudsman are under a statutory duty to decide a consumer's grievance on merits; an arbitration clause in the agreement is at most an additional forum (Section 42(8) — without prejudice to other rights; right of election) and does not oust the statutory forum. The special statute overrides the general Arbitration Act. Regulation 5.1 bars the Forum only from matters under ss.126, 127, 128, 135-139, 143, 152 and 161; other disputes (Reg. 5.2) it must decide. The ECGRF erred in diverting the dispute to arbitration.
cases.flag: Maintainability: a writ by the Executive Engineer alone (an officer, not a juristic person) without the Distribution Licensee (PVVNL) was held not maintainable, but the Court decided on merits anyway (paras 62-63).

cases.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cases.topic: Only a consumer, not the Distribution Licensee, may approach the Electricity Ombudsman; Regulation 8.1(i) is ultra vires to the extent it includes the licensee
cases.holding: No. Section 42(5) constitutes the Forum for redressal of consumer grievances; Section 42(6) gives only a 'consumer' aggrieved by non-redressal the right to represent to the Ombudsman; Section 42(7) requires the Ombudsman to settle 'the grievance of the consumer'. The Act and Rule 7 of the Electricity Rules, 2005 nowhere contemplate a grievance-redressal remedy for the Distribution Licensee. Regulation 8.1(i) of the 2007 Regulations, in extending the Ombudsman remedy to the Distribution Licensee as well, is inconsistent with and therefore ultra vires Section 42(5)-(7) and Section 181(1) (regulations must be consistent with the Act); a statutory right of appeal/representation must be found in the statute itself, not manufactured by subordinate regulation.

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: A licensee has no remedy of representation before the Ombudsman against a CGRF order
cases.holding: The licensee has no remedy to file a representation under Clause 8 of the 2007 Regulations read with Section 42(6) of the Act before the Ombudsman against an order of the CGRF, following Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal, Lucknow (which struck down Clause 8 to that extent).

cases.title: Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission v. Reliance Energy Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Billing must follow actual meter readings; a Regulatory Commission cannot issue a blanket refund direction for supplementary/amended bills without a proper s.128 investigation, and individual consumer billing grievances go through the s.42(5) Forum/s.42(6) Ombudsman, not the Commission directly
cases.holding: (a) No — billing must be on the basis of actual meter reading; the licensee bears responsibility for meter maintenance/replacement, and any additional/amended billing must follow due statutory process, not an unexplained years-later reassessment on a presumed basis. (b) The Commission does have a general power under Section 128(6) to direct licensees to bring billing practices into conformity with the statute, but exercising that power via a blanket direction to refund all amounts collected — without first conducting an investigation and obtaining a report under Section 128(1)/(5) — exceeds its jurisdiction; and in any event the Commission's own adjudicatory function under Section 86(1)(f) is limited to licensee-generator disputes, not individual consumer grievances. The correct route for individual billing grievances is the Section 42(5) Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, with a further remedy before the Section 42(6) Ombudsman. In substitution of the Commission's blanket refund order, the Court directed licensees to publish notice inviting affected consumers to make representations for redress (decided after a hearing), with a further remedy via ss.42(5)/(6) for those still dissatisfied.

cases.title: Amrita Arya v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: No simultaneous pursuit of inconsistent remedies (Forum contest vs mandamus to pay/restore)
cases.holding: No. A consumer who is contesting her liability before the CGRF cannot simultaneously seek a mandamus to pay the recovery and restore supply — the two are inconsistent, and a litigant cannot avail two remedies simultaneously for the same cause. The writ was not entertained; but if the consumer tenders the amount, the Executive Engineer may accept it and pass an appropriate order under the Code.

cases.title: Suresh Chand Bansal v. Electricity Ombudsman & Others
cases.topic: CGRF has no jurisdiction over compensation for property loss from a transmission-line accident; claimant not a 'consumer' qua transmission lines
cases.holding: No. Transmission lines are, by Section 2(72), not an essential part of a licensee's distribution system, so the affected person is not a 'consumer' (Section 2(15)) qua those lines - the presence of a transformer tapped off the line does not alter this. The CGRF's jurisdiction under Section 42 r/w Section 181 and the 2007 Regulation (cl. 2.1(e)/cl. 5) is confined to defects/deficiency in supply, billing and tariff, and does not extend to loss of public property from a transmission-line accident; the Section 161 accident-inquiry mechanism concerns loss to human/animal life, not property. The Ombudsman rightly held the CGRF without jurisdiction and set aside its compensation award.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division IInd v. Electricity Ombudsman, Lucknow & Ors.
cases.topic: Limited scope of judicial interference with an Electricity Ombudsman's award
cases.holding: Only on limited grounds. The Ombudsman (appointed under s.42(6) and the Regulations) resolves grievances by conciliation/mediation or, failing that, by an award that has the flavour of an arbitral award; it is challengeable only on grounds akin to Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 - jurisdictional error, breach of natural justice, violation of an express provision of the Act/Code/Rules/rate schedule, fraud, or conflict with public policy - reiterating Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Vidyut Lokpal. As none of these grounds was made out, the writ was dismissed.

cases.title: Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., Bhikaripur & Anr. v. Vidyut Lokpal (Electricity Ombudsman) & Anr.
cases.neutral_citation: 2008 SCC OnLine All 376 : AIR 2008 All 127 : (2008) 5 All LJ 683
cases.topic: Limited scope of interference with an Electricity Ombudsman's award/settlement
cases.holding: Only on limited grounds. Where the Ombudsman settles the dispute by conciliation/mediation, the proceedings are not challengeable except for want of jurisdiction or fraud; where he makes an award, the scope of interference is confined to grounds akin to Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (incapacity, want of notice, matters beyond or excepted from the reference, subject-matter not arbitrable, or conflict with public policy). The Court drew the analogy from Section 34 as the measure of permissible challenge.

cases.title: Maula Bux v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: After Clause 6.5, the factual bill dispute goes to the CGRF and then the Ombudsman
cases.holding: If the supplier's competent authority fails to rectify the bill or the consumer remains aggrieved, a further statutory complaint lies to the consumer grievance forum and then to the Ombudsman. Those authorities can look into the factual dispute, so the writ court will not short-circuit them.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite section 42. It styled the forum as the 'Electricity District Redressal Grievance Authority'; that is the CGRF under s.42(5), with the Ombudsman under s.42(6).

EA2003::42(5).clause: 42(5) r/w UPERC (CGRF & Electricity Ombudsman) Regulations, 2007, Regs. 2(e), 2(n), 5.2
EA2003::42(5).topic: The Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum has jurisdiction over a consumer's billing / tariff-interpretation grievance; the restrictive 'grievance' definition in Regulation 2(n) does not oust it

cases.title: M/s. Shree Gopala Iron (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: The Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum has jurisdiction over a consumer's billing / tariff-interpretation grievance; the restrictive 'grievance' definition in Regulation 2(n) does not oust it
cases.holding: The Forum has jurisdiction. Although Regulation 2(n) defines 'grievance' restrictively as a failure of the Distribution Licensee to provide the specified or agreed electricity service, 'complaint' in Regulation 2(e) is wide: it covers billing 'a price in excess of the price fixed by the Commission in tariff order or otherwise' and the breach of any obligation under the Act, the Electricity Supply Code or a tariff order; Regulation 5.2 confers jurisdiction over all complaints except those excepted by Regulation 5.1. On a conjoint reading the Forum is entrusted with jurisdiction to settle such disputes effectively and in a legal manner, and the present billing / tariff dispute can very well be gone into by it. The contention that the restrictive 'grievance' definition ousts the Forum was rejected.
cases.flag: Hybrid source: a ~15-page order-sheet of interim / listing orders (17.2.2011 to the reserving order of 26.3.2012) precedes the reserved judgment of 10.4.2012, which carries its own printed page numbers 2-13; pins are those printed page numbers. The Court's reference to 'Clause (iv) of Regulation 2(e)' appears to be a slip for clause (ii) (billing in excess of the tariff price) / clause (v) (breach of obligation), which are the clauses that in terms cover the dispute.

cases.title: M/s. Shree Gopala Iron (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: The alternative remedy before the CGRF is efficacious - no precondition to deposit the whole demand (only 50% for interim relief), no bar of limitation - so the onerous-deposit / limitation exceptions to the alternative-remedy rule do not apply
cases.holding: No. Those principles apply where recourse to the alternative remedy is onerous because it requires deposit of a huge amount, or the demand is barred by limitation. Here there is no precondition to deposit the entire amount before the Forum and the demand is not barred by limitation; indeed a consumer approaching the Forum need deposit no amount towards the disputed bills, and only 50% (or the prescribed slab) where an interim order is sought. The onerous-deposit / limitation exceptions were therefore not attracted, and the petitioners were relegated to the Forum, to approach it within fifteen days, the complaint to be decided expeditiously without any plea of limitation and the interim orders to continue meanwhile.

cases.title: Obedue Rahaman Khan v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF as forum for disputed billing demand
cases.holding: Where a consumer challenges a demand-cum-disconnection notice for assessed-unit arrears and the dispute turns on disputed questions of fact, the High Court will not decide the bill in writ. The statutory forum is the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under the UPERC (CGRF & Electricity Ombudsman) Regulations, 2007, framed under s.181 read with s.42(5)–(8) of the Electricity Act, 2003. The petitioner was given liberty to complain to the Forum within three weeks; the Forum was directed to dispose of the complaint expeditiously, preferably within three months, by a reasoned speaking order after hearing all concerned. Recovery under the impugned notice dated 21/23.02.2017 was to remain in abeyance for three months or until disposal of the complaint, whichever was earlier.

EA2003::42(6).code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.42(5)-(8), Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and Electricity Ombudsman) read with U.P. ERC (Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum & Electricity Ombudsman) Regulations, 2007 (Regulations 8, 10-12, 14)
EA2003::42(6).clause: s.42(6) (Ombudsman as grievance-redressal mechanism) — institutional character: not an Appellate Authority, not a Tribunal
EA2003::42(6).topic: The Electricity Ombudsman under s.42(6) of the Electricity Act, 2003 is neither an Appellate Authority exercising appellate/revisional jurisdiction nor a Tribunal invested with the State's inherent judicial power, but an alternative dispute-resolution/quasi-judicial authority whose awards lack finality (either party may approach any Court or Tribunal of competent jurisdiction), such that Special Appeal against a Single Judge's writ-petition order concerning the Ombudsman's award is not barred by the Rule 5, Chapter VIII exclusion (which applies only to appellate/revisional orders over a tribunal, or Article 226/227 superintendence over a tribunal)

cases.title: U.P. Power Corporation Limited Thru' Executive Engineer v. Electricity Ombudsman & Ors. (M/S Suresh Automobiles)
cases.topic: The Electricity Ombudsman under s.42(6) of the Electricity Act, 2003 is neither an Appellate Authority exercising appellate/revisional jurisdiction nor a Tribunal invested with the State's inherent judicial power, but an alternative dispute-resolution/quasi-judicial authority whose awards lack finality (either party may approach any Court or Tribunal of competent jurisdiction), such that Special Appeal against a Single Judge's writ-petition order concerning the Ombudsman's award is not barred by the Rule 5, Chapter VIII exclusion (which applies only to appellate/revisional orders over a tribunal, or Article 226/227 superintendence over a tribunal)
cases.holding: No, the Special Appeal is maintainable. On the 'Appellate Authority' question: though a party's approach to the Ombudsman under Regulation 8.1 is loosely termed a 'representation' against the Forum's decision, and the Ombudsman must pass a reasoned order under Regulation 11(b) (facilitating settlement by agreement, conciliation, mediation, or passing an award), Regulation 12.8 expressly permits either party, aggrieved by the Ombudsman's decision, to approach 'any Court or Tribunal having jurisdiction' — meaning there is no hierarchical finality of the kind that defines an 'appeal' (per Shiv Shakti Cooperative Housing Society v. Swaraj Developers, Tirupati Balaji Developers v. State of Bihar, and Snehadeep Structures v. Maharashtra SSIDC: an appeal requires removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior forum with corrective, binding authority). The Ombudsman is accordingly not an Appellate Authority. On the 'Tribunal' question: applying the features enumerated in Union of India v. R. Gandhi, President, Madras Bar Association, and the 'trappings of a Court' test (Committee of Management v. Regional Deputy Director of Education, Agra), the Ombudsman lacks power to compel witness attendance and examine on oath, does not sit in public, and its award (an alternative-dispute-resolution outcome akin to a private conciliation/mediation, not an Arbitration and Conciliation Act award) carries no finality. It is accordingly not a Tribunal, and the Single Judge, in deciding the writ petition, did not exercise Article 227 superintendence over a Tribunal. Rule 5's exclusion is therefore inapplicable, and the Special Appeal is maintainable.

cases.title: Prakash Chandra Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Ombudsman cannot withdraw unappealed CGRF part-relief on the consumer's own representation
cases.holding: No. The Ombudsman exceeded jurisdiction by withdrawing, in representation/appeal no. 228/2017 filed by the consumer, part of the relief granted by CGRF on 26.9.2016, there being no appeal or representation by respondent no. 4. Applying Authorised Officer (Land Reforms) v. M.M. Krishnamurthy Chetty, even an order that may not be strictly legal becomes final and binding between the parties if it is not challenged before a superior forum; a dispute that has attained finality cannot be reopened. The Ombudsman order dated 8.2.2021 is set aside. On remand, CGRF cannot withdraw that part-relief, there being no appeal or writ by the licensee against the 26.9.2016 order.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite s.42(6). It treated respondent no. 2 (Electricity Ombudsman, U.P.) as the 'appellate Court' on the consumer's representation. Keyed to s.42(6) as the Ombudsman provision. The judgment recites that CGRF decided 'against the petitioner' (para 2) yet also that 'relief which was granted in part' cannot be withdrawn (paras 10, 13-14); the content of that part-relief is not identified.

cases.title: Barnala Steel Industries Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: ombudsman
cases.holding: The Court did not decide the challenge to system loading charges levied on load enhancement, or the related office-memorandum conditions, and disposed of both writs by directing the consumer to approach the Electricity Ombudsman for that grievance.

EA2003::43.clause: s.43 (duty to supply); reconnection vs fresh connection
EA2003::43.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Duty to supply is not absolute; consumer-premises synergy; reconnection = same premises
cases.holding: The duty to supply under s.43 is not absolute and is subject to the charges and compliances stipulated by the utility as part of the application for supply; it is owed to the owner or occupier of particular premises, and one becomes a 'consumer' only with respect to those premises for which electricity is sought and provided. An application for the same premises for which supply was earlier provided is a 'reconnection'; different premises make it a fresh connection even if the consumer is the same.

cases.title: Ram Raji v. State of U.P. — tubewell not energised due to private obstruction
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: energisation of supply despite third-party obstruction
cases.holding: Where a tubewell has not been energised because private incumbents are causing obstruction, the Court will not itself mandamus a connection. It will direct the Executive Engineer to finalise the proceedings in accordance with law within a stated time and, if the applicant has fulfilled the prerequisite formalities and private incumbents raise a dispute, to resolve that dispute as directed in Chandu Khamaru v. Nayan Malik.
cases.flag: The order cites the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 without a numbered clause; s.43 is identified from Chandu Khamaru as applied.

cases.title: Radhe Shyam Singh v. State of U.P. & 2 Ors.
cases.topic: Duty to supply to owner or occupier; landlord's consent not a precondition for a tenant's connection
cases.holding: No. Section 43 casts a duty to supply to the owner or occupier of premises; the landlord's refusal of consent (here to pressure the tenant to vacate) is no ground to refuse the tenant a new connection. A mandamus was issued to install the connection in the tenant's name, subject to his completing the Code formalities.

cases.title: Sri Chandu Khamaru v. Smt. Nayan Malik & Ors.
cases.topic: Statutory duty to supply owner/occupier; a pending private dispute is no ground to deny supply
cases.holding: No. Sections 42(1) and 43(1) cast a statutory duty on the licensee to supply an owner or occupier of premises in its area on application, and confer a correlative statutory right to obtain supply. A pending private dispute between the applicant and third parties (here over the passage of land, the subject of a civil suit) cannot be a ground to deny the applicant supply to his house; pending resolution of that dispute the applicant cannot be denied electricity.

cases.title: Neelam Gupta v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: New connection — disputed occupation and refusal of spot inspection
cases.holding: The writ court will not interfere. Settled possession cannot be resolved because the petitioner herself resisted spot inspection, so Abhimanyu Mazumdar (person in settled possession entitled to electricity) cannot be applied. Seema Mansoor is distinguishable: that case concerned a tenant; here the petitioner claims residence as wife of a son from one of her mother-in-law's marriages. Impleadment of other occupants is pointless for the same reason. Dismissal does not bar a written application to the supply company to make spot inspection.
cases.flag: Order does not number the section. It quotes Seema Mansoor on the licensee's obligation to supply under the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Supply Code, 2005; s. 43 is the duty-to-supply provision that quotation paraphrases.

cases.title: Abdul Waheed v. Smt. Fatima Begum And Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: connection to lawful occupier without owner's title or NOC
cases.holding: Ownership of the premises is not a condition for grant of electric connection. Even Regulation 3(i)(b) of the superseded 1984 Regulations required only lawful occupation, and where the owner declined a no-objection certificate the occupier could execute an indemnity and obtain supply. Nothing showed respondent 1 was not in lawful occupation; the Permanent Lok Adalat's finding of possession on ration card, electric connection card, children's educational documents and Nagar Palika water-tax receipt called for no interference.

EA2003::45.clause: 45 (read with s. 14 and Chapter VII) vis-a-vis SICA ss. 18, 19(2), 32(1)
EA2003::45.topic: Licensee's tariff-recovery obligation vs. a binding BIFR-sanctioned demand-charge waiver

cases.title: U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. v. Appellate Authority for Industrial & Financial Reconstruction & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Licensee's tariff-recovery obligation vs. a binding BIFR-sanctioned demand-charge waiver
cases.holding: No. Although a licensee under Section 14 of the Act of 2003 is obliged to demand charges per the tariff fixed by the UPERC (Section 45; Chapter VII), where it participated in and was heard during the sanction of a rehabilitation scheme under Section 18 SICA (and was represented at the appellate stage), consented to the scheme within the meaning of Section 19(2) SICA, and did not challenge the sanctioning/clarificatory orders, it is bound by the scheme and by the BIFR/AAIFR orders directing waiver of demand charges and cannot resile from that waiver years later. The reliance on Indian Maize and Chemical Ltd. was distinguished because there the scheme had not been sanctioned by the BIFR, whereas here the Corporation was heard. The Court declined to interfere.

cases.title: M/s. Shree Gopala Iron (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Levy of demand charge / 75% billable demand for a period of temporary disconnection raises a question of tariff interpretation, not of jurisdiction; the 'wholly without jurisdiction' exception to the alternative-remedy rule is not attracted and no show-cause notice is required
cases.holding: It raises a question of tariff interpretation, not of jurisdiction. The petitioners' plea that after the UPERC abolished minimum consumption charges for HV-2 consumers the licensee cannot demand charges for a disconnection period, and the licensee's defence that the 2006-07 tariff permits billable demand of the actual maximum demand or 75% of the contracted load whichever is higher, cannot be lightly brushed aside; but the point does not relate to jurisdiction - it is the interpretation of the provisions of the tariff, which can more appropriately be gone into by the Forum. No show-cause notice was required before raising the bills. The 'wholly without jurisdiction' exception to the alternative-remedy rule (Whirlpool, Harbanslal Sahnia, Gujarat Ambuja, Pradeep Kumar Singh) was therefore not attracted, and the writ court declined to decide the merits.

EA2003::46.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (read with Clauses 4.6 & 4.21, Supply Code 2005)
EA2003::46.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Recoverable expenditure — actual expenses proved vs the licensee's own statutory obligation
cases.holding: Under Section 46 a licensee may recover only “expenses reasonably incurred in providing any electric line or electrical plant”, and the burden to prove actual expenditure lies on the licensee (as the Supreme Court's remand directed). Extension of distribution mains and commissioning of new sub-stations is the licensee's own statutory obligation under the first proviso to Section 43(1) and cannot be loaded onto the consumer. On the evidence the 4-pole structure and service line were actually constructed, so Rs. 5,49,181 and Rs. 4,65,000 were rightly retained; the processing fee of Rs. 5,000 is non-refundable per the Cost Data Book.
cases.flag: The Supreme Court's remand order dated 29.11.2022 (in this very case) fixed the frame: refund is to be denied only “to the extent” the respondents prove “the actual expenses incurred.”

EA2003::47.clause: s.47(1) ('subject to the provisions of this section')
EA2003::47.topic: 'Subject to the provisions of this section' in s.47(1) means s.47 read as a whole, not subservient to sub-section (5) alone

cases.title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
cases.topic: 'Subject to the provisions of this section' in s.47(1) means s.47 read as a whole, not subservient to sub-section (5) alone
cases.holding: The words 'subject to the provisions of this section' in Section 47(1) indicate that the fixation of reasonable security is governed by Section 47 read as a whole; sub-sections (1) and (2) are not made subject to sub-section (5) alone, rejecting the petitioners' submission (relying on the Black's Law Dictionary meaning of 'subject to' as explained in Saurashtra Chemicals) that sub-section (5) overrides sub-sections (1)-(4).

cases.title: Tehri Girders Limited and another v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited and others (with R.A. Castings, Sikka Papers and connected petitions)
cases.topic: Nature of security: advance payment / depositor-depositee, not a recoverable debt
cases.holding: Security under s.47 is in the nature of an advance payment of charges (a running current account) - the relationship being depositor-depositee, not debtor-creditor (Ferro Alloys) - and is only an amount demanded as a condition of supply, not owed as an enforceable debt; hence it is not 'dues' and cannot be recovered as arrears of land revenue (Mirzapur Electric Supply, on s.47-A of the 1948 Act). By contrast, a load-factor rebate once given in the bill and later withdrawn does become a 'due', and a bank-guarantee demand for that amount cannot be faulted.

cases.title: M/s Shri Ganga Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. Managing Director, Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: security deposit — penalty on delayed bank-guarantee renewal
cases.holding: Prima facie, s.47 EA 2003 does not provide a penalty for delay in renewing a bank guarantee given as security; the licensee's statutory remedy for missing or insufficient security is disconnection. Stay granted on the penalty demanded under Note 10, Chapter-III of the 08.07.2019 Cost Data Book (Rs.500 per lakh per day of BG) till disposal. Petitioners must continue timely bill payment and maintain security/BG as per law, failing which the licensee may disconnect.

cases.title: M/S Awadh Steels & Alloys (P) Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: security deposit
cases.holding: Section 47 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for reasonable security to be determined by the Regulation.

cases.title: M/s R.A. Castings (Pvt.) Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reasonable security determined by regulation
cases.holding: Section 47 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for reasonable security to be determined by the regulation.

cases.title: M/S Prem Steels (Pvt.) Limited v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Others
cases.topic: Interest on security deposit at bank rate from 10.6.2003
cases.holding: Yes. The consumer is to be given interest at the bank rate from 10.6.2003, when Section 47(4) enacted the obligation to pay interest on security. Respondents nos. 2 and 3 were directed to pay interest at the RBI bank rates notified from time to time from that date. Want of a Commission notification, and continued use of the 2002-Code rate, did not displace s.47(4). The writ was allowed.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing, adjournment, an 18.4.2012 dismissal as infructuous (recalled 4.1.2013), a 7.4.2014 roster/vires referral, and other interlocutory orders from 24.11.2011 to 18.10.2022; the operative judgment is 2.12.2022 (Siddhartha Varma and Ajit Singh JJ.). That order is unnumbered; paragraph numbers are of its recitals and directions. Catalog key is EA2003::47 (no EA2003::47(4) key). Catalog false-positives (BIHAR-2007, CPC::47, UP-2005::4.4/4.44/4.49 and allied occupancy/arrears tags) are not used.

cases.title: M/s G.M.K. Steels Pvt. Ltd. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: pre-payment meter and interest on security
cases.holding: Relief under section 47(4) and 47(5) of the Electricity Act, 2003—installation of a pre-payment meter, restraint from levying security under the repealed law, and refund or adjustment of Rs 60,10,900 security with 12% interest—was refused along with the rest of the writ.

cases.title: M/s L. Kant Paper Mills Ltd. v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: security-deposit
cases.holding: The Court refused to quash the additional security demand of Rs. 16,30,647, to compel installation of a pre-payment meter under Section 47(5), or to refund, credit or adjust Rs. 43,52,247 already deposited as security with 12% interest under Section 47(4).

cases.title: R.A. Castings Pvt. Limited v. PVVNL and Others
cases.topic: Additional security under s.47 is not arrears of electricity dues; load-factor rebate cannot be withdrawn on that footing
cases.holding: No. The tariff orders deny the rebate only to a consumer with arrears. The respondents' own case was that the rebate had been disallowed because additional security was treated as arrears on a letter of the Director (Licensing), UPERC. Following Tehri Girders, Mirzapur Electric Supply and K.L. Concast, additional security does not fall within the definition of dues and cannot be termed arrears of electricity dues. It is a condition of supply, not money owed as a debt; the consequence of not giving it is discontinuance of supply, not recasting the amount as bill arrears. The petitioner therefore cannot be disallowed load-factor rebate. The letters dated 6.10.2008, 11.11.2008 and 21.11.2008 and the bill dated 31.10.2008 are quashed. A fresh bill is to be issued strictly in the light of that holding.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing orders of 23.9.2011, 17.10.2011, 2.11.2011, 17.11.2011, 20.11.2018 and 29.11.2018 with the reserved 18.12.2018 judgment (delivered by B. Amit Sthalekar, J.), which is unnumbered. Clauses 6.1 and 6.1(g) of the Supply Code, 2005 were recited (billing/arrears and bill particulars) but not independently construed. Ratio is the s.47 characterisation of additional security, applied to the tariff arrears-bar on load-factor rebate.

cases.title: M/s Suresh Furnace Pvt. Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: additional security
cases.holding: A 2011 Division Bench framed additional-security litigation as requiring s.47 of the Electricity Act, 2003 to be read with cl. 4.20 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, called for affidavits, and continued interim protection subject to security other than cash or bank guarantee. The consumer’s prepaid-scheme argument was not decided. In 2023, none appearing for the petitioner, the writ was dismissed in default and the interim order vacated.

cases.title: Vardhman Casting Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Limited
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: additional security
cases.holding: The writ challenging the additional security demand under s.47 of the Electricity Act, 2003 was dismissed in default for non-appearance on an oldest-pending list; the 2011 interim continuing protection on security other than cash or bank guarantee was vacated, with liberty to seek recall within one month.

EA2003::50.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.50, Electricity Supply Code; s.181(2)(x), regulation-making power) — ultra vires invalidation of Kerala Electricity Supply Code, 2014, Regulation 153(15)
EA2003::50.clause: s.50/s.181(2)(x) rule-making power — a Supply Code Regulation cannot create a substantive exemption from s.126 liability not found in the parent Act; such a Regulation is ultra vires and invalid
EA2003::50.topic: Regulation 153(15) of the Kerala Electricity Supply Code, 2014 (exempting 'unauthorised additional load in the same premises and under same tariff' from being reckoned as 'unauthorised use of electricity') is ultra vires Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and invalid, since a State Commission's delegated Supply Code rule-making power under s.50/s.181(2)(x) cannot create substantive exemptions from liability that the parent Act's own self-contained s.126/s.127 scheme does not provide

cases.title: Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors. v. Thomas Joseph Alias Thomas M.J. & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.topic: Regulation 153(15) of the Kerala Electricity Supply Code, 2014 (exempting 'unauthorised additional load in the same premises and under same tariff' from being reckoned as 'unauthorised use of electricity') is ultra vires Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and invalid, since a State Commission's delegated Supply Code rule-making power under s.50/s.181(2)(x) cannot create substantive exemptions from liability that the parent Act's own self-contained s.126/s.127 scheme does not provide
cases.holding: No, Regulation 153(15) is ultra vires and declared invalid. Applying the settled doctrine that delegated legislation cannot travel beyond, or be inconsistent with, its parent enabling Act (Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram Sardar Singh Raghuvanshi; General Officer Commanding-in-Chief v. Dr. Subhash Chandra Yadav; State of Karnataka v. H. Ganesh Kamath; Kunj Behari Lal Butail v. State of H.P.; St. Johns Teachers Training Institute v. Regional Director, NCTE; State of T.N. v. P. Krishnamurthy; Global Energy Ltd. v. CERC; Pratap Chandra Mehta v. State Bar Council of M.P.; Dr. Mahachandra Prasad Singh v. Chairman, Bihar Legislative Council; McEldowney v. Forde), the Court held that s.50 empowers a Supply Code to address recovery of charges, billing intervals, disconnection/restoration, and tampering-prevention — following its own earlier ruling in U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. v. Anis Ahmad that the Supply Code 'need not provide provisions relating to, [and does] not relate to, assessment of charges for unauthorised use of electricity under Section 126.' Since s.126/127 constitute a complete, self-contained code (Seetaram Rice Mill), a Supply Code Regulation carving out an exemption from that code's liability — however well-intentioned to protect domestic-type consumers from disproportionate billing — travels beyond the delegated rule-making power and directly frustrates the object of s.126 (restricting unauthorised consumption to protect the supply system), rendering it inconsistent with the parent Act and therefore void.

cases.title: Sub Divisional Officer Vidyut Nagariye v. Hameed Khan
cases.topic: permanent-lok-adalat-billing-jurisdiction
cases.holding: The Court entertained the licensee’s writ to examine whether, in view of Section 50 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and Clause 7(10) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the Permanent Lok Adalat had jurisdiction to entertain a billing dispute; held that the matter required consideration; issued notice to the consumer; and directed the petition to be connected and listed with Writ-C No. 39818 of 2018. No finding was recorded on the jurisdictional question.

cases.title: M/s. Suvidha Engineers India Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: The Supply Code is not confined to s.50's subjects; it is regulation-making under s.181 and s.86(1) 'supply'
cases.holding: No. The Supply Code specified under Section 50 is a compilation of regulations traceable to Section 181(2)(p)-(x) and the general power in Section 181(1); the headings, marginal notes and Statement of Objects confirm this. 'Supply' in Section 86(1) is read liberally to include ancillary measures for protecting/preserving revenue, and the power to legislate on a substantive topic subsumes ancillary matters. The Code is therefore not confined to Section 50's enumerated subjects, and Clause 4.49 is within the Commission's regulation-making power.

cases.title: Abdul Waheed v. Smt. Fatima Begum And Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: 1984 Regulations superseded by 2003 Act and 2005 Supply Code
cases.holding: Electricity Supply (Consumers) Regulations, 1984 have no application after enforcement of the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, framed in exercise of powers under sections 50 and 181 read with sections 43 to 48, 50 and 55 to 59 of the Act.

EA2003::55.topic: Releasing an electricity connection without installing a meter is illegal; the proviso to Section 55(1) lets a consumer install a purchased meter

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Company Ltd. & Another v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Releasing an electricity connection without installing a meter is illegal; the proviso to Section 55(1) lets a consumer install a purchased meter
cases.holding: No. The Statute clearly contemplates that an electricity connection shall be released by installing a meter, and the petitioners' counsel could not dispute that releasing a connection without installing a meter was illegal, unsupported by any provision of law and ex facie contrary thereto. The plea that a meter was unavailable was unsubstantiated - no material showed how or why the meter was unavailable - and in any event the proviso to Section 55(1) permitted a consumer to install a meter himself by purchase, a facility the licensee could have availed. The meterless release, followed by installation only on 21.12.2009, was wholly illegal and unauthorized.

EA2003::56.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power

cases.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: (2023) SCC OnLine SC 603; Civil Appeal Nos. 2109-2110 of 2004 (batch)
cases.topic: Recovery by suit is independent of the disconnection power
cases.holding: The power to initiate recovery proceedings by filing a suit against a defaulting consumer is independent of the power to disconnect supply as a means of recovery under Section 56.

cases.title: Sandeep Kesarwani v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: For assessed dues, the sum 'first becomes due' under s.56(2) only on final assessment, not on the date of provisional assessment or the underlying checking/inspection
cases.holding: No — under s.126, a sum cannot be held 'due' against a consumer until the final assessment is made (here, 21.6.2013); the recovery citation issued 19.11.2013 was therefore well within two years of the sum first becoming due, and s.56(2) was not attracted.

cases.title: Shyam Ferrous Ltd. Gopal Nagar v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: The s.56(2)/Clause 6.15 two-year recovery bar applies only prospectively, to liabilities arising after the Electricity Act, 2003 came into force; liabilities from the pre-2003 regime (here, 2002 peak-hour-restriction violations) are governed by the earlier law (s.24, 1910 Act) which imposes no such limitation on the power to demand/recover, per s.6 of the General Clauses Act preserving accrued liabilities on repeal
cases.holding: No. Section 56(2) applies only after the Electricity Act, 2003 came into force; liabilities incurred under the pre-2003 regime continue to be governed by s.24 of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (which imposes no limitation on the licensee's power to demand/recover, only providing a separate, non-exclusive suit remedy) by virtue of s.6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which preserves rights/liabilities accrued under a repealed enactment — following Kusumam Hotels (P) Ltd. v. Kerala SEB. Electricity Supply Code 2002's Clause 6.31.2 (an analogue to Clause 6.15) similarly bars only recovery via the 1958 Dues Recovery Act route after two years from when a sum 'first became due' — and a sum 'first becomes due,' for this purpose, only when a proper bill is raised and remains unpaid, not from the date of the underlying default (following MCD v. H.D. Shourie and NDMC v. Karam Chandra Thapar). Here, the correct penalty (per the Supreme Court's 25.7.2006 formula in U.P. Power Corp. v. Lohia Brass) was billed for the first time on 4.2.2009, with follow-up notices in 2009, and recovery proceedings under the 1958 Act commenced well within any two-year window measured from that billing — the intervening 13 years since the 2002 violations reflects an earlier (unauthorised, later-corrected) waiver by a Deputy General Manager lacking power to grant it, not licensee inaction after proper billing. Service of the demand notices by registered post to the recorded address was deemed sufficient under Explanation 1 to s.3 of the 1958 Act, notwithstanding the petitioner's claimed non-receipt (particularly given the petitioner's own subsequent conduct — seeking temporary reconnection, earlier partial payment under protest — evidencing awareness of the liability). Writ petition dismissed, with six months allowed for deposit and recovery held in abeyance meanwhile.

cases.title: RKG Industries LLP v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited & 4 Others
cases.topic: Electricity dues are statutory in character, not purely contractual, and a clearance condition for a fresh connection is not unreasonable
cases.holding: Electricity dues under the Act and the terms and conditions of supply are statutory in character, cannot be waived in view of Section 56, and do not partake of the character of purely contractual dues. A condition that the arrears in respect of the premises be cleared before a fresh connection is granted is neither arbitrary nor unreasonable and will not be interfered with in judicial review; and such dues are recoverable as arrears of land revenue under the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 read with Clause 6.15.

cases.title: M/S Om Food Manufacturing Center v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: supplementary demand after paid bills — no disconnection, no upward revision, civil recovery only
cases.holding: A subsequent demand on discovery of a billing mistake can be made under Section 56 as declared in Rahamatullah Khan, but there cannot be recovery to the distress of the consumer. Section 56(1) provides 15 days' written notice including disconnection; sub-section (2) is limitation; Rahamatullah Khan says coercive action cannot be taken, so the licensee must obtain a civil remedy for the principal (and may claim interest in that action). There cannot be upward revision of the demand after it is made. Notices that allege discovery of a mistake without stating a bona fide error, without opportunity to test correctness, and without particulars of charge and rebate, are deficient. The supply company is directed to present the discovery of mistake and a proper calculation with applicable rebate for payment within the prescribed time; on non-payment it must sue. Prem Cottex distinguished Rahamatullah Khan on facts and did not overrule it. Writ allowed and disposed of.
cases.flag: The bound source PDF also contains the 23 April 2026 interlocutory order (demand stayed; listed 6 May 2026). Clause 6.5 was invoked as a maintainability bar on 23 April and was not applied or decided on 6 May.

EA2003::56(2).topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Limitation on recovery — recurring companion provision in Supply Code litigation
cases.holding: "Sum due" means an amount adjudicated between the parties; un-adjudicated, escalating demands raised years after the service ended are barred.
cases.flag: Respondent pleaded this as "Clause 56(2) of the U.P. Supply Code"; the provision quoted and applied is s.56(2) of the Act. Recorded, not merged.

cases.title: Assistant Engineer (D1), Ajmer Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Rahamatullah Khan alias Rahamjulla
cases.topic: Meaning of 'first due'; disconnection barred after two years but recovery not
cases.holding: 'First due' means when the bill is first issued (the liability arises on consumption but the sum becomes due only on billing). Section 56(2) bars only the remedy of disconnection after two years from the sum first becoming due (unless continuously shown as arrears); it does not bar a supplementary/additional demand or other modes of recovery. In a case of bona fide mistake, limitation for the additional demand runs from discovery (s.17(1)(c), Limitation Act, 1963), but the licensee still cannot disconnect supply — only pursue other recovery.

cases.title: Joginder Singh v. D.V.V.N. Ltd. thru' its Managing Director & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Section 56(2)'s two-year bar on recovery applies to default in payment of charges, not to theft cases
cases.holding: Prima facie, no. Section 56(2) is applicable to default in payment where a person neglects to pay any charge for electricity, or any sum other than a charge for electricity, due to a licensee or the generating company in respect of supply, transmission, distribution or wheeling of electricity; it is not applicable to theft cases. The petitioner's contention that recovery of the tampering/theft assessment beyond two years was barred therefore could not be sustained at the prima facie stage.
cases.flag: Order-sheet with no printed page numbers or numbered paragraphs; pins are order dates. The substantive observations are in the 29.9.2010 order (Sunil Ambwani and Kashi Nath Pandey, JJ.), while coram/date reflect the 2.5.2023 disposal (Manoj Kumar Gupta and Prashant Kumar, JJ.).

cases.title: Smt. Mamta Devi Srivastava v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: The s.56(2) two-year bar does not apply to a continuing consumer's regular current bills
cases.holding: No. The s.56(2) bar does not apply where it is not a case of a belated demand after disconnection but of non-payment of regular bills by a continuing consumer being supplied electricity; the consumer, having paid nothing since re-energisation while consuming, cannot invoke the 12/24-month bar. Whether bills were sent is a disputed fact not for writ jurisdiction, and the remedy lies under Clause 6.5; the Court declined Article 226 relief to a gross defaulter.

cases.title: Managing Director, D.V.V. Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others v. Sri Kartar Singh & Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: No recovery of old arrears where the licensee produces no bills or ledgers showing them continuously as recoverable
cases.holding: No. Section 56(2) provides that no sum due from a consumer shall be recoverable after two years from the date it first became due unless it has been shown continuously as recoverable as arrears of charges for electricity supplied. The Forum found that the licensees had produced records only for 25.02.2009–19.03.2009 and 20.12.2009–20.03.2010, with no bills or ledgers for the period before 2009 and no disconnection despite alleged non-payment since 1990. In the writ they still gave no justification for that default. They cannot be given the benefit of their own defaults. The Forum's order limiting recovery to 26.02.2007–31.03.2010 excluding surcharge, and setting aside the demand of Rs. 1,76,431.60, cannot be faulted on the evidence.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. The Electricity Consumer Grievances Redressal Forum & Anr.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Two-year bar on recovery of overload arrears
cases.holding: Section 56(2) provides that no sum due from a consumer under that section shall be recoverable after two years from the date when such sum became first due unless it has been shown continuously as recoverable as arrears of charges for electricity supplied. A 51-month overload demand is not open.

EA2003::57.clause: s.57(2) (compensation when the licensee misses specified standards of performance)
EA2003::57.topic: Section 57, with Clause 8.2, is the statutory consequence of missing the 24-hour FIR / 30-day Special Court timeline

cases.title: Satish Kumar Bharti alias Chhotu v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Section 57, with Clause 8.2, is the statutory consequence of missing the 24-hour FIR / 30-day Special Court timeline
cases.holding: Section 57(2) requires the licensee, without prejudice to penalty or prosecution, to pay such compensation as the Commission determines if it fails to meet the standards specified under s.57(1). Read with Clause 8.2 of the Code (24-hour police complaint; 30-day Special Court filing), it supplies the consequence for breach of the s.135(1-A) 24-hour lodging rule, and is why Indresh Patel's 'no consequences' premise does not hold.
cases.flag: Deployed only as the consequence that makes the 24-hour rule mandatory; the Court did not award s.57 compensation.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Standards of performance of the licensee are irrelevant to waiver of consumer minimum charges
cases.holding: No. The Ombudsman sidestepped the licensee's 3.8/3.9 and Tariff Order argument by referring to Section 57, which the Court held was irrelevant for the purpose. Section 57 concerns Commission-specified standards of performance of the licensee and compensation to the person affected if those standards are not met. It does not support waiving the consumer's tariff liability.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Standards of performance of the licensee are irrelevant to waiver of consumer minimum charges
cases.holding: No. The Ombudsman sidestepped the licensee's 3.8/3.9 and Tariff Order argument by referring to Section 57, which the Court held was irrelevant for the purpose. Section 57 concerns Commission-specified standards of performance of the licensee and compensation to the person affected if those standards are not met. It does not support waiving the consumer's tariff liability.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Standards of performance of the licensee are irrelevant to waiver of consumer minimum charges
