Section 57 concerns Commission-specified standards of performance of the licensee and compensation to the person affected if those standards are not met. It does not support waiving the consumer's tariff liability.

EA2003::64.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination

cases.title: BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.topic: Truing up cannot change the methodology of the original tariff determination
cases.holding: No. A tariff order under s.64 is quasi-judicial and binding until amended/revoked under s.64(6); truing up is only the adjustment of actuals against projections and cannot be used to re-think de novo the basic principles or retrospectively change the methodology of the initial determination. The DERC's changes on Issues 1, 2, 3 and 5 (LPSC/collection efficiency, depreciation, FR/SR salary, fringe benefit tax) were impermissible and are set aside; interest on Consumer Security Deposit (Issue 4) is a legitimate expense the appellants may recover.

cases.title: Chandra Bhan Singh v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Commission determines tariff; LMV-5 of 22.11.2004 was not a licensee-made rate
cases.holding: No. Under Section 64, on a licensee's application and after considering public objections and suggestions, the Appropriate Commission issues a tariff order. Section 62(3) permits differentiation by load factor, power factor, voltage, consumption, time of supply, geographical position, nature and purpose of supply. The 22.11.2004 Rate Schedule LMV-5, notified for 2004-05 and effective from 1.12.2004 for four distribution companies, was fixed by the U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission. Newspaper publication (Annexure 8) was on the record and unchallenged. There is no inconsistency with Sections 62 and 64. The contention that urban rates were being charged is incorrect: the area being exempted from schedule rostering, LMV-5 clause 4(b) applies.
cases.flag: EA2003::62 is not a catalog key; it is folded here because the Court quoted ss.62 and 64 together. Petitioner sought readjustment under s.62(4); the Court quoted 62(4) and 62(6) but did not apply either. Catalog hit OFFTOPIC::s62-6-interest-generation-tariff is not used.

EA2003::67.topic: Drawing a line over land whose owner objects: alternative route, else the s.67(2) permission procedure

cases.title: Sri Chandu Khamaru v. Smt. Nayan Malik & Ors.
cases.topic: Drawing a line over land whose owner objects: alternative route, else the s.67(2) permission procedure
cases.holding: The licensee must first ascertain whether there is any other way to draw the line to the applicant's house; if there is none, it must follow the procedure under Section 67(2) — the rules specifying the cases where consent is required and the authority which may grant permission where an owner/occupier objects to the works. The exercise is to be completed within six months, and until supply is effected by some other route the applicant's existing supply is not to be disconnected.

cases.title: Consumer forum has no jurisdiction over EA assessment
cases.topic: consumer-forum jurisdiction over assessment
cases.holding: Applying UPPCL v. Anis Ahmad, the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum has no power to redress a dispute that is not a “service” or “complaint” under CPA 1986 ss. 2(1)(o) and 2(1)(c). A complaint before the District Consumer Forum over an assessment under the Electricity Act, 2003, and the Executive Engineer’s appeal from that forum, were both not maintainable. Both orders were set aside. Parties may seek their remedy under the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Writ allowed.

cases.title: Art.226 declined for tubewell bill; statutory correction remedies available
cases.topic: Art.226 vs statutory bill-correction remedies
cases.holding: Where the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 afford remedies to approach the authorities for correcting an electricity bill, the High Court will not interfere directly under Article 226 at that stage.

ESA1948::sixth-schedule.topic: Reasonable return; power-purchase rate by reverse application of the Sixth Schedule

cases.title: Noida Power Company Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Reasonable return; power-purchase rate by reverse application of the Sixth Schedule
cases.holding: NPCL being entitled to a reasonable return, the power-purchase rate may be determined by reverse application of the principles of the Sixth Schedule, which is one of the most appropriate, accurate and secure methods. The Commission's year-wise determination rested on settled norms and did not call for interference.

IBC::238.topic: Section 238 IBC overrides the Electricity Act, 2003 (including ss.173/174)

cases.title: South East U.P. Power Transmission Company Ltd. v. Prescribed Authority & Ors. (with Tata Steel Ltd. v. State of U.P.)
cases.topic: Section 238 IBC overrides the Electricity Act, 2003 (including ss.173/174)
cases.holding: No. Although s.174 gives the Electricity Act overriding effect (subject to the s.173 carve-outs), that clause is itself subject to s.238 IBC, a later and unambiguous non-obstante provision that prevails over all other laws in case of inconsistency. In insolvency, the IBC prevails notwithstanding ss.173 and 174 of the Electricity Act; the contention that electricity dues, being statutory, cannot be extinguished is unacceptable.
cases.flag: Applies the Supreme Court's ratio in Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. (s.238 IBC overrides the Electricity Act).

cases.title: Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: IBC overrides the Electricity Act — even 'arrears on premises' cannot be demanded for the pre-effective-date period
cases.holding: Because the IBC has overriding effect, statutory authorities cannot enforce extinguished claims or resort to coercive recovery; and dues or arrears 'on premises' that would ordinarily be demandable under the Electricity Act cannot be demanded for the pre-effective-date period, the IBC prevailing. For any post-effective-date dues the parties have their remedy under the Electricity Act.

cases.title: S.K. Construction Co. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: IBC override of the Supply Code; auction purchaser not liable for the corporate debtor's pre-CIRP electricity dues
cases.holding: Yes. Section 238, being a non-obstante provision in a subsequent parliamentary enactment, gives the Code overriding effect over the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Supply Code, 2005 wherever inconsistent (following NCLAT in PVVNL v. Raman Ispat). Clause 4.3(f), which makes outstanding dues a first charge and casts joint liability on seller and purchaser, is inconsistent with the Section 53 scheme and cannot be enforced against the auction purchaser; the licensee's plea to recover pre-CIRP dues from the purchaser before energising the connection was rejected.

cases.title: HSA Traders v. Office of the Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division, Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited & Anr.
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: IBC override of the Supply Code; auction purchaser not liable for the corporate debtor's pre-CIRP electricity dues
cases.holding: Yes. Section 238, being a non-obstante provision in a subsequent parliamentary enactment, gives the Code overriding effect over the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Supply Code, 2005 wherever inconsistent (following NCLAT in PVVNL v. Raman Ispat). Clause 4.3(f), making outstanding dues a first charge and casting joint liability on seller and purchaser, is inconsistent with Section 53 and cannot be enforced against the auction purchaser; the licensee's demand of pre-CIRP dues as a pre-condition to the connection was rejected.

IBC::31.topic: Approved resolution plan extinguishes pre-CIRP claims not part of it (clean slate)

cases.title: South East U.P. Power Transmission Company Ltd. v. Prescribed Authority & Ors. (with Tata Steel Ltd. v. State of U.P.)
cases.topic: Approved resolution plan extinguishes pre-CIRP claims not part of it (clean slate)
cases.holding: No. On approval under s.31, the resolution plan binds all stakeholders including statutory authorities and extinguishes all claims not filed during CIRP or not forming part of the plan; such claims cannot be resurrected under the guise of statutory recovery. The authorities admittedly filed no claim during CIRP and the dues were not in the plan, so the impugned pre-CIRP demands cannot be enforced. Continuity of the corporate name does not make the reborn entity liable for pre-CIRP unclaimed dues, and CIRP publication is sufficient notice to all stakeholders.
cases.flag: Paras 102.1-102.3 are the Supreme Court's holding (Ghanashyam Mishra) reproduced; the deciding Court's own reasoning is at paras 101-116.

cases.title: Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Extinguishment of all pre-effective-date claims; liability crystallises at the plan's 'effective date'
cases.holding: All claims for the periods before the plan's effective date — pre-CIRP dues, CIRP-period operational costs, and the monitoring/transition phase up to the effective date — that were not filed during the CIRP or not provided for in the approved plan stand extinguished under s.31 and are unenforceable; the corporate debtor emerges on a clean slate notwithstanding continuity or change of name. Liability crystallises only from the 'effective date' (here 22-12-2022, the actual transition of control on deposit of the resolution amount), determined by the plan's implementation structure — not merely the date of approval — especially where implementation was delayed by litigation; and the exclusion of time taken in litigation benefits the petitioner, not the respondent authorities.

cases.title: Trimurti Concast Pvt. Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: Clean slate on approval of a resolution plan: pre-CIRP electricity dues extinguished; new connection cannot be denied to the corporate debtor under new management
cases.holding: No. Once a resolution plan is approved under Section 31, all claims not forming part of the plan stand frozen and extinguished and no person may initiate or continue proceedings in respect of them (Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons). The corporate debtor, being an independent entity under new management, is not liable for pre-CIRP dues; the licensee cannot invoke Clause 4.3(f) to refuse a new connection on account of such dues and must energise the connection to support the corporate debtor as a going concern, subject otherwise to the Electricity Act, 2003 and Supply Code, 2005.

IBC::32A.topic: Statutory bar on action against the property of the corporate debtor for pre-CIRP liabilities after a change of control

cases.title: Trimurti Concast Pvt. Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: Statutory bar on action against the property of the corporate debtor for pre-CIRP liabilities after a change of control
cases.holding: Yes. By Section 32A(2), no action can be taken against the property of the corporate debtor in relation to an offence/liability committed prior to commencement of CIRP where the property is covered by an approved resolution plan resulting in a change of control to a person who was not a promoter/related party of the erstwhile management. The licensee (a State instrumentality) therefore cannot proceed against the corporate debtor's property or premises for pre-CIRP dues.

IBC::53.topic: Liquidation waterfall: licensee a secured operational creditor recovering pre-CIRP dues only under Section 53; extinguishment of the right to recover from the purchaser

cases.title: S.K. Construction Co. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: Liquidation waterfall: licensee a secured operational creditor recovering pre-CIRP dues only under Section 53; extinguishment of the right to recover from the purchaser
cases.holding: The licensee is at most a secured operational creditor and is entitled to receive its pre-CIRP dues only through the Section 53 distribution of liquidation proceeds; it cannot recover them from the successful auction purchaser. On completion of the liquidation the right to recover those dues stands extinguished, and where the Electricity Act casts a duty to supply, the licensee is bound to energise a fresh connection without insisting on the pre-CIRP dues.

cases.title: HSA Traders v. Office of the Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division, Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited & Anr.
cases.court: National Company Law Tribunal, Allahabad Bench (Prayagraj)
cases.topic: Liquidation waterfall: licensee a secured operational creditor recovering pre-CIRP dues only under Section 53; extinguishment of the right to recover from the purchaser
cases.holding: The licensee is at most a secured operational creditor entitled to receive its pre-CIRP dues only through the Section 53 distribution of liquidation proceeds; it cannot realise them from the successful auction purchaser (Maithan Alloys). On completion of the liquidation the right to recover the pre-CIRP dues stands extinguished, and where the Electricity Act casts a duty to supply the licensee must energise the connection without insisting on those dues.

IEA1910::26(6).code: Indian Electricity Act, 1910 (s.26(6), Electrical Inspector reference for meter-correctness disputes) read with Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission Distribution (Conditions of Supply) Code, 1998 (Clauses 56, 64, 105, 110, 115)
IEA1910::26(6).clause: s.26(6), 1910 Act — inapplicable where the licensee's case is fraud/tampering (not mere meter defectiveness); governing framework for tampering-based penal charges is the licensee's own statutory Supply Code, not s.26
IEA1910::26(6).topic: Section 26(6) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 applies only to genuine disputes over a meter's inherent correctness/defectiveness, referable to an Electrical Inspector, and has no application where the licensee alleges fraud/deliberate tampering with the meter or metering equipment; such tampering-based penal assessments are governed instead by the licensee's own statutory Supply Code provisions (here, Clauses 56, 64, 105 of the Orissa Code, 1998), and a consumer who never applied to the Electrical Inspector under s.26(6) cannot resist a tampering-based penal bill by merely asserting the meter was 'defective'

cases.title: Western Electricity Supply Co. of Orissa Ltd. & Ors. v. M/s Baba Baijanath Roller and Flour Mill Pvt. Ltd.
cases.topic: Section 26(6) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1910 applies only to genuine disputes over a meter's inherent correctness/defectiveness, referable to an Electrical Inspector, and has no application where the licensee alleges fraud/deliberate tampering with the meter or metering equipment; such tampering-based penal assessments are governed instead by the licensee's own statutory Supply Code provisions (here, Clauses 56, 64, 105 of the Orissa Code, 1998), and a consumer who never applied to the Electrical Inspector under s.26(6) cannot resist a tampering-based penal bill by merely asserting the meter was 'defective'
cases.holding: Yes, the High Court erred. Following Madhya Pradesh Electricity Board v. Smt. Basantibai and State of W.B. v. Rupa Ice Factory (P) Ltd., a dispute over fraud/tampering with the meter, metering equipment, or seals falls entirely outside s.26(6)'s scope (confined to genuine correctness/defectiveness disputes referable to an Electrical Inspector); the consumer here never applied to the Electrical Inspector under s.26(6), undermining any claim to that provision's protection. The High Court further erred in factually finding the inspection occurred without the consumer's representative present, when the record showed the Manager was present and signed the inspection report; unsubstantiated allegations of duress/coercion, never raised before any appropriate authority, could not displace that finding. Clauses 56, 64, and 105 of the Orissa Code, 1998 (sealing/tampering prohibition, disconnection for tampering after 7-day show-cause notice, and penal energy/demand charges at twice the applicable rate for unauthorised use) — not s.26(6) of the 1910 Act — governed the penal-bill dispute, and the High Court's failure to consider these Code provisions vitiated its judgment. The penal bill, inspection report, and consequent disconnection were accordingly valid, and the High Court's quashing order (including its direction to refund amounts and to not charge delayed-payment surcharge) was set aside.

cases.title: U.P. Rajya Vidyut Parishad v. Panjab Corbohydrate
cases.topic: Meter-correctness dispute (no theft) must go to the Electrical Inspector; licensee cannot self-assess
cases.holding: It must refer the dispute to the Electrical Inspector under s.26(6), whose opinion on whether the meter has ceased to be correct is final; the licensee cannot raise a supplementary/assessment bill on the ground of under-recording. If the Inspector finds the meter faulty, only the Inspector estimates the energy consumed (for a period not exceeding six months) and fixes the amount. Here no check meter was installed and no reference was made, and the licensee could show no provision authorising the assessment, so the assessment was illegal.

cases.title: I.G. Shoes Pvt. Ltd. v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. and Others
cases.topic: Electrical Inspector's jurisdiction confined to meter-correctness disputes, not bill disputes or theft/fraud
cases.holding: No. Section 26(6) applies only where a difference arises as to whether the meter is correct; the Inspector first examines the meter and, if it has ceased to be correct, estimates consumption for up to six months (the meter register otherwise being conclusive, absent fraud). It does not reach disputes over the correctness of bills, nor theft/fraud/tampering assessments (which fall outside s.26). Here no meter-correctness dispute was raised while the meter was installed; it was removed and replaced without objection, destroying the material evidence, and the consumer only later disputed old bills. The CEI's order revising the bills was without jurisdiction and a nullity, and no mandamus could issue to enforce a patently illegal order.

JH-2005::9.2.code: Jharkhand SERC (Electricity Supply Code) Regulations, 2005 (framed under s.50, EA 2003)
JH-2005::9.2.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement

cases.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cases.topic: Reduction of contract demand — the 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement
cases.holding: The initial agreement. Enhancement 'fresh agreements' for the same connection are merely supplementary amendments of the initial agreement (contract demand can be varied even by written communication, Reg. 2(l); reduction itself is by supplementary agreement, Reg. 9.2.6). So the three-year 'initial period' runs from the initial agreement (2004), not the last enhancement (2007); the 2007 reduction application was beyond it and is deemed allowed under Reg. 9.2. The Regulations are liberally construed for the consumer.

LSAA1987::22-C(8).topic: Permanent Lok Adalat has no adjudicatory jurisdiction over a dispute relating to an offence

cases.title: Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat, Moradabad & Anr.
cases.topic: Permanent Lok Adalat has no adjudicatory jurisdiction over a dispute relating to an offence
cases.holding: No. The first proviso to s.22-C(1) preserves only conciliatory jurisdiction (ousted only for non-compoundable offences), so the PLA could conciliate the theft dispute. But once conciliation fails, adjudicatory jurisdiction under s.22-C(8) does not arise if the dispute 'relates to an offence', and — in contrast to the first proviso — compoundability is irrelevant under s.22-C(8). The award adjudicating the dispute was therefore without jurisdiction and a nullity, and is quashed.
cases.flag: Section 175 of the Electricity Act (Act 'in addition to' other laws) was pleaded but does not save the PLA's adjudicatory jurisdiction, which the Legal Services Act itself ousts.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Riyasat Ali and others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Conciliation under s.22-C is a mandatory step before a Permanent Lok Adalat may adjudicate on merits
cases.holding: The Court did not finally decide. It recorded that Canara Bank holds conciliation under Section 22-C to be mandatory and that Section 22-C(8) operates only once an agreement under Section 22-C(7) has failed. On a perusal of this award, no conciliation proceeding under Section 22-C(7) had been undertaken before the Permanent Lok Adalat proceeded to adjudicate on merits. That finding, with the unused Clause 6.5 remedy, was treated as a reason the matter requires consideration. Notice issued.
cases.flag: Interlocutory listing order. Award not quashed or stayed. Canara Bank is cited as 2022 LiveLaw (SC) 499; the fingerprint has no Indian Kanoon doc-id.

NIACT::138-security-cheque-electricity-d.code: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (s.138, dishonour of cheque; Explanation, 'debt or other liability'; s.141, offences by companies) applied to a Power Supply Agreement's security cheque
NIACT::138-security-cheque-electricity-d.clause: s.138 Explanation ('debt or other liability') and its application to a cheque issued as 'security' at the commencement of a commercial power-supply relationship, later dishonoured after electricity dues accrued and went unpaid
NIACT::138-security-cheque-electricity-d.topic: A cheque issued as 'security' under a Power Supply Agreement, close in time to commencement of electricity supply, matures into an instrument for a legally enforceable debt once monthly power-supply dues accrue and are unpaid, and its dishonour is prosecutable under s.138 NI Act notwithstanding the security label; whether the cheque was truly non-presentable security is a triable defence, not a ground for quashing

cases.title: Sunil Todi & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
cases.topic: A cheque issued as 'security' under a Power Supply Agreement, close in time to commencement of electricity supply, matures into an instrument for a legally enforceable debt once monthly power-supply dues accrue and are unpaid, and its dishonour is prosecutable under s.138 NI Act notwithstanding the security label; whether the cheque was truly non-presentable security is a triable defence, not a ground for quashing
cases.holding: Yes, s.138 is attracted. The Explanation's phrase 'debt or other liability' is broader than 'debt' alone and is not confined to a liability existing at the exact moment of drawing the cheque; a post-dated or security cheque issued in the context of a commercial transaction that is thereafter carried into effect (here, three months of actual power supply consumed by the company) matures for presentation once payment for that supply falls due and is not met, irrespective of the cheque's original security label — merely labelling a cheque 'security' does not obviate its character as an instrument designed to meet a legally enforceable debt once that debt accrues. Indus Airways is distinguished because there the underlying purchase order was cancelled before any debt arose, whereas here the PSA was acted upon and power was actually supplied and billed. Following Sampelly Satyanarayana Rao and Sripati Singh, and per HMT Watches and Womb Laboratories, whether the cheque was given as non-presentable security and whether an enforceable liability existed are factual defences for trial, not grounds for quashing under s.482 Cr.P.C. On s.141 NI Act company-director liability (Sunil Bharati Mittal, SMS Pharmaceuticals, Mainuddin Abdul Sattar Shaikh), the complaint's averments sufficed prima facie, and the proviso's due-diligence defence is available only at trial, not at the summoning stage. The Magistrate's summoning order, having considered the complaint, affidavit, evidence list and submissions, was not vitiated by non-application of mind; s.145 NI Act dispenses with mandatory oral examination of witnesses on oath at the s.202 Cr.P.C. inquiry stage for NI Act complaints.

OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.code: General (abuse of the writ process; supervisory direction)
OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.clause: direction for departmental inquiry into collusive non-recovery
OFFTOPIC::abuse-of-process-departmental-.topic: Nine-year evasion of a lawful assessment, including grant of a fresh connection without full payment, warranted a departmental inquiry

cases.title: M/S Hind Industries Limited v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Nine-year evasion of a lawful assessment, including grant of a fresh connection without full payment, warranted a departmental inquiry
cases.holding: Where the record showed apparent collusion between the consumer and the licensee's officers — a modification application concealed as 'pending' when it had in fact been decided over a year earlier, and a fresh connection released to a nine-year defaulter on a bank guarantee rather than full payment — the Court, while dismissing the writ petition as an abuse of process, directed the Principal Secretary (Energy) to hold a detailed inquiry into the officers' and the petitioner's conduct and take consequential action against those responsible.

OFFTOPIC::anticipatory-bail-electricity-.code: Cr.P.C. s.438 (anticipatory bail) — special-circumstances framework for direct High Court application; Clause 4.44, U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (transfer of connection) as background facts only
OFFTOPIC::anticipatory-bail-electricity-.clause: s.438 Cr.P.C. anticipatory bail, applying Vinod Kumar/Ankit Bharti special-circumstances test and Sushila Aggarwal
OFFTOPIC::anticipatory-bail-electricity-.topic: Anticipatory bail granted to an electricity department official prosecuted for fraud/forgery in connection with a disputed tubewell-connection transfer and disconnection, applying the settled special-circumstances test for direct High Court applications under s.438

cases.title: Sunil Kumar v. State of U.P. And Another
cases.topic: Anticipatory bail granted to an electricity department official prosecuted for fraud/forgery in connection with a disputed tubewell-connection transfer and disconnection, applying the settled special-circumstances test for direct High Court applications under s.438
cases.holding: Anticipatory bail allowed. The applicant, an Assistant/Executive Engineer who had ordered disconnection of a tubewell connection at the request of the transferee-consumer (Smt. Shashi Kanta, whose transfer application under Clause 4.44 of the Supply Code was supported by a registered sale deed, mutation records, and regular bill payments), was found to have no personal antecedents, held a public-servant post without sanction to prosecute under s.197 Cr.P.C., and the case fell within the recognised special circumstances (Vinod Kumar, Ankit Bharti) justifying direct High Court recourse; following Sushila Aggarwal v. State (NCT of Delhi), anticipatory bail was granted till conclusion of trial subject to standard conditions.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its criminal-procedure/anticipatory-bail subject matter; the Clause 4.44 transfer-of-connection background is incidental to the bail analysis and not independently adjudicated.

OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.79, 111, 121, 178) — APTEL's appellate jurisdiction vis-a-vis CERC's delegated regulation-making power
OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.clause: s.111 (appeal to APTEL) vis-a-vis s.178 (CERC's power to make Regulations) and s.121 (APTEL's general powers)
OFFTOPIC::aptel-jurisdiction-over-cerc-r.topic: APTEL has no jurisdiction under s.111 to decide the vires of CERC Regulations made under s.178 (a delegated-legislation function reviewable only via Article 226); s.121 does not confer judicial-review power on APTEL; CERC was empowered under the residuary s.178(1)/(2)(ze) to cap electricity-trading margins by Regulation

cases.title: PTC India Ltd. v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission, thr. Secy. (and connected appeals)
cases.topic: APTEL has no jurisdiction under s.111 to decide the vires of CERC Regulations made under s.178 (a delegated-legislation function reviewable only via Article 226); s.121 does not confer judicial-review power on APTEL; CERC was empowered under the residuary s.178(1)/(2)(ze) to cap electricity-trading margins by Regulation
cases.holding: (i) Section 178 (CERC's regulation-making power) is wider than the enumerated Order/decision-making functions under s.79(1). (ii) A s.178 Regulation, as delegated legislation, intervenes in and can override existing contracts between regulated entities. (iii) Because a s.178 Regulation is delegated legislation, its validity can be tested only by judicial review before the courts (Article 226), not by appeal to APTEL under s.111. (iv) Section 121 does not confer a power of judicial review on APTEL — the words 'orders', 'instructions', or 'directions' therein do not extend to invalidating subordinate legislation. (v) Where a dispute concerns the interpretation (not the validity) of a s.178 Regulation, an appeal lies to APTEL under s.111, but no appeal lies on the Regulation's validity. (vi) Applying the 'generality versus enumeration' principle, CERC was empowered, under the residuary s.178(1) read with s.178(2)(ze), to cap trading margins in inter-State electricity trading by Regulation. The reference was accordingly answered: APTEL has no jurisdiction to decide the validity of CERC Regulations framed under s.178; such validity may only be challenged by judicial review under Article 226. All appeals dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~3670 lines) and its subject (APTEL/CERC regulatory-jurisdiction architecture for inter-State electricity trading), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's retail billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::arbitration-s11-appointment.topic: Section 11 court examines only the existence of an arbitration agreement; merits and other objections (including a Code-forum bar) are left to the arbitrator

cases.title: M/S Ambuja Cements Limited v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited
cases.topic: Section 11 court examines only the existence of an arbitration agreement; merits and other objections (including a Code-forum bar) are left to the arbitrator
cases.holding: The Court is confined, under s.11(6A) as explained in Mayavati Trading (following Duro Felguera paras 48 and 59; reiterated in GOQII Technologies), to a narrow examination of the existence of an arbitration agreement. On a prima facie finding that a clause exists and that the parties had not appointed a consented arbitrator, and with counsel's consent, the Court appointed Mr. Justice Sudhir Agarwal (former Judge) as sole arbitrator subject to s.11(8) consent. No final conclusion was drawn on the merits; all objections the Act permits remain open before the arbitrator.

OFFTOPIC::cauvery-interstate-water-dispu.code: Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956; Constitution of India, Article 262
OFFTOPIC::cauvery-interstate-water-dispu.clause: Not applicable — interstate river-water apportionment, no Electricity Act/Supply Code provision at issue
OFFTOPIC::cauvery-interstate-water-dispu.topic: Cauvery river water allocation among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, modifying the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's final award

cases.title: The State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu & Ors. (with connected appeals of State of Kerala and State of Tamil Nadu)
cases.topic: Cauvery river water allocation among Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, modifying the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's final award
cases.holding: The Supreme Court modified the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's award, revising the inter-State water-sharing formula (including recognition of Bangalore's drinking-water requirements and groundwater considerations), while broadly upholding the Tribunal's equitable-apportionment framework. No electricity-law question was presented or decided.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its complete absence of electricity/Supply Code nexus and enormous scale (a landmark interstate water-dispute judgment); not exhaustively digested against this corpus's doctrinal framework.

OFFTOPIC::contempt-civil.code: Contempt of Courts Act / civil contempt (not the Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::contempt-civil.clause: civil contempt of a writ-disposal order
OFFTOPIC::contempt-civil.topic: An order relegating the petitioner to a Code procedure is not a direction whose non-compliance is contempt

cases.title: Smt. Jama Begum v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: An order relegating the petitioner to a Code procedure is not a direction whose non-compliance is contempt
cases.holding: From a perusal of the writ order — which only observed that the petitioner must raise her bill dispute under the prescribed Clause 6.5 procedure and disposed of the petition — no case for contempt is made out. Application dismissed as misconceived.
cases.flag: Contempt-procedure holding; retained because the alleged contempt was of a Supply-Code relegation order.

cases.title: Devendra Nath Dubey v. Executive Engineer, Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: Contempt of a Clause 6.5 relegation order becomes infructuous once the representation has been decided
cases.holding: Where the writ court's direction was only to consider and decide a Clause 6.5 representation, and that representation has been decided, the contempt application is infructuous; the notice stands discharged.
cases.flag: Contempt-procedure holding; retained because the alleged contempt was of a Supply-Code relegation order.

OFFTOPIC::criminal-bail-s376.code: Indian Penal Code / Code of Criminal Procedure
OFFTOPIC::criminal-bail-s376.topic: Criminal bail application — no electricity-law content

cases.title: Rishipal v. State of U.P. [OFF-TOPIC: criminal bail, s.376 IPC]
cases.topic: Criminal bail application — no electricity-law content
cases.holding: Bail application under s.376 IPC rejected on the facts; no Supply Code or Electricity Act issue arises. File mis-indexed into the electricity corpus.

OFFTOPIC::criminal-interim.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition

cases.title: Dr. Vinod Kumar Bassi v. The State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Interlocutory stay in a s.482 complaint-quashing petition
cases.holding: On the applicant's contention that the complaint was proceeded with without the Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. enquiry (applicant residing in Lucknow, complaint filed in Hardoi), notice was ordered and further proceedings stayed till the next date. No merits were decided.
cases.flag: Off-topic for the Supply Code: a two-line interlocutory criminal order under Section 482 Cr.P.C.; no Electricity Supply Code provision is involved. Retained only for queue completeness.

OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.14(b), 42) & Special Economic Zone Act, 2005 (s.49) — CSS/open-access wholesale regime, not the retail Supply Code
OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.clause: s.14(b) deemed-licensee proviso vis-a-vis 'consumer' status and CSS liability
OFFTOPIC::cross-subsidy-surcharge-sez-de.topic: A single-unit SEZ developer deemed a distribution licensee under s.14(b) remains liable, as a 'consumer', to pay Cross Subsidy Surcharge to the area distribution licensee when procuring its entire power for captive use from another generator

cases.title: M/S Sesa Sterlite Ltd. v. Orissa Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: A single-unit SEZ developer deemed a distribution licensee under s.14(b) remains liable, as a 'consumer', to pay Cross Subsidy Surcharge to the area distribution licensee when procuring its entire power for captive use from another generator
cases.holding: The deeming fiction in the proviso to Section 14(b) (SEZ developer = deemed distribution licensee) presupposes actual distribution of power to others; it cannot be stretched to exempt a developer who establishes an SEZ solely for its own single unit and consumes the entire power itself, from CSS liability as a 'consumer' under Section 2(15). CSS compensates the area distribution licensee for the loss of cross-subsidy revenue when a consumer situated in its area procures power from elsewhere via open access, regardless of whether the licensee's own line is physically used, and applies whether or not the deemed-licensee status is held. The appellant's transmission line was found (on the facts) not to be a 'dedicated transmission line' exempting it from this liability. The appeal was dismissed.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale and its subject (CSS/open-access/SEZ interplay), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::delay-and-laches-writ-jurisdic.clause: delay and laches bar equitable relief even for similarly-situated claimants
OFFTOPIC::delay-and-laches-writ-jurisdic.topic: A consumer who did not timely challenge withdrawal of a benefit cannot invoke a later favourable judgment obtained by other litigants more than two decades afterward

cases.title: M/S Three Star Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 5 Ors.
cases.topic: A consumer who did not timely challenge withdrawal of a benefit cannot invoke a later favourable judgment obtained by other litigants more than two decades afterward
cases.holding: Those who were vigilant and raised their dispute in time are entitled to the benefit of a subsequent favourable judgment (here, Pawan Alloys, 1997, on promissory estoppel for a development rebate); a consumer who accepted withdrawal of the rebate without protest, and made no claim until a year after the judgment (1998) and pursued it in this writ only decades later, is guilty of extraordinary delay and laches disentitling equitable relief under Article 226, irrespective of being similarly situated to successful litigants.

OFFTOPIC::director-personal-liability-fo.code: Recovery of a company's electricity dues from its Director — personal liability
OFFTOPIC::director-personal-liability-fo.topic: Director not personally liable for the company's electricity dues absent a personal guarantee

cases.title: Rajee Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Director not personally liable for the company's electricity dues absent a personal guarantee
cases.holding: As a well-settled position, a Director cannot be held personally liable for the company's electricity dues unless he has given an undertaking or personal guarantee for recovery from his personal assets. On the facts, however, the plea did not avail the petitioner because the impugned recovery citation had been issued in the name of the company (M/s Rajee Steels Pvt. Ltd. through its Director), not against petitioner no. 2 in his personal capacity. This determination did not affect the result, which turned on limitation.

OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.code: Delhi Electric Reforms Act, 2000 (ss.14-16, 57) and Delhi Electricity Reforms (Transfer Scheme) Rules, 2001 (Rules 3, 6, 8) — successor-DISCOM liability for erstwhile Board employees' pension/terminal benefits
OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.clause: Rule 6(8)/(9) (personnel-related liability transfer) and Rule 8(3) (litigation-liability cap) of the Transfer Scheme Rules, 2001
OFFTOPIC::discom-unbundling-employee-pen.topic: Successor DISCOM liability for pension/terminal-benefit claims of Delhi Vidyut Board employees who had already retired/been dismissed before unbundling — an employer-succession dispute among privatised distribution companies, unrelated to consumer billing/Supply Code

cases.title: North Delhi Power Ltd. v. Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi & Ors. (with BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Govt. of N.C.T. of Delhi & Anr.)
cases.topic: Successor DISCOM liability for pension/terminal-benefit claims of Delhi Vidyut Board employees who had already retired/been dismissed before unbundling — an employer-succession dispute among privatised distribution companies, unrelated to consumer billing/Supply Code
cases.holding: Rule 6 of the Transfer Scheme Rules, 2001 is a complete, self-contained code governing 'personnel and personnel-related matters' (Rule 3(2)), broad enough to cover retired, dismissed, and deceased employees, not merely those formally on the transfer list; under Rule 6(8), the relevant successor DISCOM stands substituted for the Board for all statutory/employment-related schemes including pension and superannuation funds for 'existing pensioners'. The litigation-liability cap in Rule 8(3) (Rs. 1 crore per annum per DISCOM) applies equally to personnel-related claims, not only third-party/consumer litigation. The successor DISCOMs (NDPL, BSES Rajdhani) were accordingly held liable for the pension/terminal-benefit claims of pre-unbundling retirees/dismissed employees of the erstwhile DVB, subject to the Rule 8(3) cap.
cases.paras: paras 15-56 (~209-para judgment; core reasoning at paras 15-33, 44-51)
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~2000 lines) and its subject (post-privatisation employer-successor pension/personnel liability dispute among DISCOMs), which has no nexus to the U.P. Electricity Supply Code's consumer billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::disproportionate-assets-quashi.code: Cr.P.C. s.482 (inherent power to quash) applied to a Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 s.13(1)(d)/13(2) disproportionate-assets charge sheet against a former electricity department Junior Engineer
OFFTOPIC::disproportionate-assets-quashi.clause: s.482 Cr.P.C. — quashing standard (R.P. Kapur, Bhajan Lal, P.P. Sharma, Zandu Pharmaceutical) applied to disputed factual defences in a disproportionate-assets prosecution
OFFTOPIC::disproportionate-assets-quashi.topic: A s.482 Cr.P.C. application to quash a disproportionate-assets charge sheet is dismissed where the defence (agricultural land income, family gifts explaining the excess assets) raises disputed questions of fact not resolvable at the quashing stage

cases.title: Vijay Kumar Sachan v. State of U.P. And Another
cases.topic: A s.482 Cr.P.C. application to quash a disproportionate-assets charge sheet is dismissed where the defence (agricultural land income, family gifts explaining the excess assets) raises disputed questions of fact not resolvable at the quashing stage
cases.holding: Application dismissed. Applying R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal, State of Bihar v. P.P. Sharma, and Zandu Pharmaceutical Works Ltd. v. Mohd. Sharaful Haq, the Court held that at the s.482 stage only a prima facie case need be examined, and the applicant's explanations (agricultural income from family land, gifts from a retired father) for the alleged disproportionate assets (Rs. 31,66,841) were disputed questions of fact requiring evidence, not resolvable on a quashing application; the Court left it open to the applicant to raise his health condition (kidney ailment requiring dialysis) before the trial court in any future bail application.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its criminal-procedure/PC Act disproportionate-assets subject matter and absence of Supply Code nexus; the applicant's former employment in the electricity department is incidental background only.

OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (ss.9, 10, 14, 15, 19, 42(2)) and Distribution of Electricity (Additional Requirement of Capital Adequacy...) Rules, 2005
OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.clause: ss.9/10 (captive plant vs generating company); Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply); s.19 (revocation); s.142 (penalty/natural justice)
OFFTOPIC::distribution-licensing-minimum.topic: Distribution licence grant/cancellation; minimum-area Explanation is a guideline, not a rigid bar, on these unusual facts; penalty requires a hearing

cases.title: M/S Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. v. Chhattisgarh State Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cases.neutral_citation: Civil Appeal Nos. 3607-3610 of 2008, with C.A. Nos. 4104-4107 of 2008
cases.topic: Distribution licence grant/cancellation; minimum-area Explanation is a guideline, not a rigid bar, on these unusual facts; penalty requires a hearing
cases.holding: The Supreme Court restored a distribution licence earlier granted to JSPL (a captive-power-plant owner, governed by s.9 not s.10 of the Act) to supply a private industrial estate it had itself developed under a State Government MoU/permission predating the 2003 Act's full commencement and the 2005 Rules. The Appellate Tribunal had wrongly treated the Explanation to Rule 3 (minimum area of supply = a municipal area or revenue district) as an inflexible bar to a second/parallel licence in a smaller area; the Court held the historical background — investment made, the State's own power shortage, CSEB's admitted inability to supply the area, and long-term supply contracts already in place before the Rules existed — justified treating the case as an exception, and estoppel/vested-rights principles militated against retrospectively invalidating the licence. Separately, the Commission's Rs. 1 lakh penalty under s.142 for supplying without a licence was rightly set aside by the Tribunal for want of a hearing, since the licensing proceeding itself never framed the question of JSPL's liability to penalty.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~57 pages) and its subject (distribution licensing, not Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection); not exhaustively digested. General electricity-law background only.

cases.title: Mukesh Kumar v. State of U.P.

OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.code: Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (s.2(1)(c)) vis-a-vis Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 (s.81) and IPC s.21
OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.clause: s.2(1)(c)(iii), 1988 Act (public servant) vis-a-vis s.81, 1948 Act (deemed public servant under IPC s.21)
OFFTOPIC::electricity-board-employee-pub.topic: An Electricity Board employee is a 'public servant' under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 independently of the 1948 Act's IPC-specific deeming provision, since the Board is a statutory corporation within s.2(1)(c)(iii) of the 1988 Act

cases.title: Naresh Kumar Madan v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.topic: An Electricity Board employee is a 'public servant' under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 independently of the 1948 Act's IPC-specific deeming provision, since the Board is a statutory corporation within s.2(1)(c)(iii) of the 1988 Act
cases.holding: A term defined in one statute cannot be construed solely by reference to its definition in a different statute; s.81 of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 deems Board employees 'public servants' only for purposes of s.21 IPC, but that does not exhaust the question of their status under the differently-and-more-broadly-worded 'public servant' definition in s.2(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, which independently captures any person in the service or pay of a corporation established by or under a Central, Provincial or State Act. The appellant, a Board employee, therefore answered the description of 'public servant' under the 1988 Act, and his prosecution for taking illegal gratification in connection with grant of an electrical connection was maintainable. The single-judge decision in Bimal Kumar Gupta v. Special Police Establishment Lokayukt holding otherwise was overruled as not laying down the correct law.
cases.flag: Recorded for corpus completeness; concerns the criminal-law 'public servant' status of Electricity Board employees for anti-corruption prosecution, not the Supply Code's consumer-facing billing/assessment/disconnection framework.

OFFTOPIC::embezzlement-quashing-electric.clause: s.528 BNSS / s.482 Cr.P.C. — pre-trial quashing of ss.409/420 IPC embezzlement prosecution of an electricity-department Office Assistant
OFFTOPIC::embezzlement-quashing-electric.topic: 528 BNSS quashing of a departmental-enquiry embezzlement prosecution is refused where a prima facie case is disclosed; disputed defences are for trial

cases.title: Natthi Prasad v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: 528 BNSS quashing of a departmental-enquiry embezzlement prosecution is refused where a prima facie case is disclosed; disputed defences are for trial
cases.holding: No. The Court held that many grounds taken related to disputed questions of fact; appreciation of evidence is a function of the trial court and cannot be assumed under section 482 Cr.P.C. so as to end the trial. Inherent power at the pre-trial stage is used sparingly, only where there is a legal bar to the proceeding or the FIR and charge-sheet, taken at face value, do not disclose an offence. Disputed facts and the accused's defence cannot be considered at that stage. Applying R.P. Kapur, Manik B., Bhajan Lal, P.P. Sharma and Zandu Pharmaceutical, no ground for quashing was made out. The FIR and witness statements supported the prosecution case of embezzlement of Rs. 1,45,00,775 after departmental enquiry; the Investigating Officer had since submitted a charge-sheet; a prima facie offence was made out. The application of Natthi Prasad was dismissed.
cases.flag: Not a Supply Code construction. The Code appears only in the quoted 22.04.2022 Division Bench listing order in Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 4363 of 2022 (irregularity in permanent disconnection attributed to the Executive Engineer). Source PDF also contains listing/adjournment orders from 11.04.2025 to 26.08.2025 (including an amendment allowed on 20.08.2025); the operative dismissal is 02.09.2025. Paragraph 5 contains a garbled sentence mixing the applicant's abuse-of-process prayer with the 482-sparingly principle; the operative result is dismissal.

cases.topic: Family pension dispute between two wives of a deceased municipal employee — no Supply Code content; cites electricity-board pension cases only as general persuasive analogues

OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.code: U.P. Government Servant (Discipline & Appeal) Rules, 1999 (Rule 4) — suspension pending disciplinary inquiry; incidental reference to U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 4.6(e), supervision charges)
OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.clause: Rule 4 (suspension requires application of mind to gravity of allegations) — Clause 4.6(e) (supervision charges payable to licensee before work begins) cited only as a factual defense
OFFTOPIC::government-servant-suspension-.topic: Suspension of a Development Authority engineer for alleged financial irregularity in an electric-line-shifting project quashed for want of application of mind; Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code (supervision charges due before work commencement) was invoked only to show the petitioner's processing of such charges was procedurally correct, not to establish any independent Supply Code holding

cases.title: Shabih Haider v. State of U.P. thru. Prin. Secy., Housing & Urban Planning & Ors.
cases.topic: Suspension of a Development Authority engineer for alleged financial irregularity in an electric-line-shifting project quashed for want of application of mind; Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code (supervision charges due before work commencement) was invoked only to show the petitioner's processing of such charges was procedurally correct, not to establish any independent Supply Code holding
cases.holding: The suspension order was quashed as passed without application of mind to Rule 4's requirement that suspension be resorted to only where allegations, if established, would warrant a major penalty; the record showed the petitioner had no substantive role in project conception, tender approval, or contract award, and had merely forwarded files in the ordinary course. On the specific supervision-charges allegation, the respondents conceded that Clause 4.6(e) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 requires such charges to be deposited with the licensee before commencement of work — meaning the charge that the petitioner had improperly processed centage payment 'prior to commencement of work' was, on the correct reading of Clause 4.6(e), based on a mistaken premise.
cases.flag: Recorded for completeness of the source corpus; the operative holding is a service-law suspension ruling, with Clause 4.6(e) of the Supply Code invoked only incidentally as a factual defense regarding timing of a supervision-charge payment — not itself a substantive Supply Code determination relevant to this project's consumer-facing focus.

OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.code: General maxim (lex non cogit ad impossibilia) applied to billing where the consumer's own meter cannot yield a reading
OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.clause: exceptional reliance on an outside/check meter for billing
OFFTOPIC::impossibility-billing-on-outsi.topic: Where the consumer's own meter is physically incapable of providing a reading, an independent check meter outside the premises may exceptionally found billing, if reliably maintained

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.topic: Where the consumer's own meter is physically incapable of providing a reading, an independent check meter outside the premises may exceptionally found billing, if reliably maintained
cases.holding: No statutory provision permits billing/assessment based on a meter other than the one installed at the consumer's premises; ordinarily the answer must go against the licensee for want of such a provision. However, the law does not require compliance with the impossible: where the consumer's own meter is destroyed (e.g. by fire) or stolen and cannot yield a reading, an independent/check meter installed by the licensee outside the premises may exceptionally be relied upon for billing, provided it is shown to be reliably and authentically maintained with the consumer's knowledge — applying lex non cogit ad impossibilia, impotentia excusat legem and nemo tenetur ad impossibilia, following the Division Bench in Inter College Kusmaul, Gorakhpur v. State of U.P.

OFFTOPIC::interim-relief-after-withdrawa.code: Constitutional/writ procedure (Article 226) — power to grant interim relief after a petition is dismissed as withdrawn
OFFTOPIC::interim-relief-after-withdrawa.topic: A writ court has no jurisdiction to grant interim protection for the interregnum once a petition is dismissed as withdrawn or the party is relegated to another forum, since Article 226 interim relief is only ancillary to a final relief obtainable on merits in a proceeding still pending before that court

cases.title: Om Prakash s/o Gauri Shankar v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: A writ court has no jurisdiction to grant interim protection for the interregnum once a petition is dismissed as withdrawn or the party is relegated to another forum, since Article 226 interim relief is only ancillary to a final relief obtainable on merits in a proceeding still pending before that court
cases.holding: Following the Constitution Bench in State of Orissa v. Madan Gopal Rungta (and its consistent subsequent approval), the Court held it lacks jurisdiction to grant interim relief (such as a stay of recovery) for the period during which a petitioner intends to approach the Clause-based Supply Code authority, once the writ petition itself has been dismissed as withdrawn; interim relief under Article 226 can only be granted as ancillary to final relief in a matter still pending before the court on merits.
cases.flag: General writ-jurisdiction/interim-relief principle applied in an electricity-recovery context; not itself a Supply Code holding, but the Supply Code recovery notice was the underlying dispute in which it arose.

OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.code: Indian Penal Code, 1860 / Cr.P.C., 1973 (unrelated to the Electricity Act/Supply Code)
OFFTOPIC::ipc-405-406-entrustment.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry

cases.title: Kishore Biyani v. State of U.P. & Anr.
cases.topic: Criminal breach of trust — commercial sale is not 'entrustment'; mandatory Section 202(1) enquiry
cases.holding: A mere commercial sale transaction (unpaid supply of goods) does not amount to 'entrustment' of property under Section 405 IPC; absent entrustment and dishonest misappropriation, no offence under Section 406 is made out. Where the accused resides outside the trial court's jurisdiction, Section 202(1) Cr.P.C. mandates an enquiry before summoning, and its omission vitiates the summoning order.
cases.flag: Entirely off-topic to the Supply Code jurisprudence; recorded only to keep the source-corpus review complete. No provision-holdings or authorities from this case are added to the Supply Code index.

OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.clause: no jurisdiction by consent, acquiescence, or waiver
OFFTOPIC::jurisdiction-not-by-consent.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order

cases.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
cases.topic: Jurisdiction of a tribunal of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot be conferred by consent, acquiescence, or an unreasoned prior order
cases.holding: A tribunal or forum of limited/statutory jurisdiction cannot derive jurisdiction beyond the statute; no acquiescence, consent, or waiver can confer it, and a defect of jurisdiction cannot be cured even by consent, rendering any resulting order a nullity.

OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.clause: Article 227; interim injunction to restore supply
OFFTOPIC::landlord-tenant-civil.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction

cases.title: Dipali Dey (Baxi) v. Mira Das
cases.topic: Restoration of a tenant's electric supply by civil injunction
cases.holding: Where a tenant in possession has had supply disconnected by the landlord, the civil court may by injunction direct restoration pending the tenancy suit; the High Court should not interfere with such concurrent orders under Article 227. The tenancy dispute abides the trial.

OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.code: Power Purchase Agreements (contractual Change-in-Law and Late Payment Surcharge clauses) — bulk generation procurement, unrelated to the retail Supply Code
OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.clause: Change-in-Law clause vis-a-vis RBI PLR-to-Base-Rate/MCLR transition
OFFTOPIC::lps-change-in-law-ppa.topic: RBI's replacement of PLR with Base Rate/MCLR did not entitle the distribution company to recompute LPS at the new (lower) rate, given concurrent factual findings and the company's own prior acceptance of invoices

cases.title: Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. v. Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.
cases.topic: RBI's replacement of PLR with Base Rate/MCLR did not entitle the distribution company to recompute LPS at the new (lower) rate, given concurrent factual findings and the company's own prior acceptance of invoices
cases.holding: The Supreme Court declined to disturb the concurrent findings of MERC and APTEL rejecting the distribution company's claim that the RBI's introduction of the Base Rate (2010) and MCLR (2016) systems, replacing the PLR methodology, constituted a 'Change in Law' under the Power Purchase Agreements entitling it to pay Late Payment Surcharge at the lower Base Rate/MCLR-linked rate instead of the PLR-based SBAR rate defined in the agreements; the distribution company had accepted and reconciled the invoiced LPS without dispute for years, and could not introduce fresh material in a second appeal under Section 125 not tendered before the regulatory authorities below.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its scale (~5170 lines) and its subject (bulk power-procurement PPA/LPS contract dispute), which is distinct from the U.P. Electricity Supply Code billing/assessment/disconnection framework central to this project; not exhaustively digested.

OFFTOPIC::mala-fide-impleadment.clause: plea of mala fide requires eo nomine impleadment
OFFTOPIC::mala-fide-impleadment.topic: A plea of mala fide cannot be entertained unless the official against whom it is alleged is impleaded eo nomine

cases.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: A plea of mala fide cannot be entertained unless the official against whom it is alleged is impleaded eo nomine
cases.holding: It is settled law that a plea of mala fide/bias against a named official cannot be entertained unless that official is impleaded eo nomine and given an opportunity to meet the allegation; the petitioner's mala fide plea failed for want of such impleadment.

OFFTOPIC::mining-royalty-enhancement-sta.code: Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (s.15) and Punjab Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964 (Rules 10, 21) — enhancement of royalty/dead rent during subsistence of a mining lease
OFFTOPIC::mining-royalty-enhancement-sta.clause: s.15(3) MMDR Act and Rule 21(1)(i)(a)/(iii), 1964 Rules — statutory power to revise royalty/dead rent surviving despite silence in the executed lease deed
OFFTOPIC::mining-royalty-enhancement-sta.topic: A statutory contract's silence on rate-revision does not foreclose the government's independent statutory power to enhance royalty/dead rent; such power is an implied condition of every lease traceable to the enabling statute, and judicial review of the quantum of enhancement is confined to Wednesbury unreasonableness

cases.title: The State of Haryana & Ors. v. M/s Faridabad Gurgaon Minerals & Anr. (with M/s Ganpati Enterprises Slate Mines)
cases.topic: A statutory contract's silence on rate-revision does not foreclose the government's independent statutory power to enhance royalty/dead rent; such power is an implied condition of every lease traceable to the enabling statute, and judicial review of the quantum of enhancement is confined to Wednesbury unreasonableness
cases.holding: The appeals were allowed. Though the mining lease deed itself (unlike the preceding Auction Notice and Letter of Acceptance) did not expressly incorporate Rules 10 and 21 of the 1964 Rules, those Rules formed an implied condition of the lease because the lease is a statutory grant, not a purely private contract, and mere contractual silence cannot denude the State of a power expressly conferred by s.15(3) MMDR Act and the Rules. Distinguishing Indian Aluminium Co. v. Kerala SEB (which applies only where a contract expressly and validly fetters a statutory power), the Court held that a lease deed merely fixing a rate without expressly barring future enhancement does not fetter the State's statutory revision power; following J.K. Synthetics, statutory rate-revision provisions override contrary lease terms. The 50% royalty enhancement after a 5.5-year gap (exceeding the 3-year minimum interval) was not arbitrary — judicial review of the quantum is confined to Wednesbury unreasonableness, not a merits reassessment. On the Rules of Business (Article 166(3)) challenge, the Court held that approval by the Chief Minister personally (distinguishing MRF Ltd. v. Manohar Parrikar, where an individual minister acted without Chief Ministerial knowledge) satisfied the constitutional requirement of collective responsibility, and deemed Finance Department consent could be inferred absent evidence of the Finance Minister's disagreement.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given complete absence of electricity/Supply Code nexus; this is a pure mining-royalty/MMDR Act ruling collected incidentally, not exhaustively digested against Supply Code doctrine.

OFFTOPIC::panchayat-raj-act-pradhan-remo.code: U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 (s.95(1)(g) and proviso) read with U.P. Panchayat Raj (Removal of Pradhans, Up-Pradhans and Members) Enquiry Rules, 1997
OFFTOPIC::panchayat-raj-act-pradhan-remo.clause: Proviso to s.95(1)(g) — preliminary/fact-finding enquiry must be conducted by a person qualifying as 'Enquiry Officer' under Rule 2(c) of the 1997 Rules, or by the District Magistrate himself, before financial/administrative powers may be ceased
OFFTOPIC::panchayat-raj-act-pradhan-remo.topic: A report submitted by an officer not validly appointed as 'Enquiry Officer' under Rule 2(c) of the 1997 Rules (and not a District-Level Officer) cannot constitute a valid preliminary enquiry report for ceasing a Gram Pradhan's financial and administrative powers under the proviso to s.95(1)(g)

cases.title: Usha Devi (Smt.) v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: A report submitted by an officer not validly appointed as 'Enquiry Officer' under Rule 2(c) of the 1997 Rules (and not a District-Level Officer) cannot constitute a valid preliminary enquiry report for ceasing a Gram Pradhan's financial and administrative powers under the proviso to s.95(1)(g)
cases.holding: The District Magistrate's order was quashed. Applying the Full Bench ruling in Vivekanand Yadav v. State of U.P., a valid preliminary enquiry report for purposes of ceasing a Pradhan's powers under the proviso to s.95(1)(g) must be submitted either by the District Magistrate himself or by a person appointed and qualifying as 'Enquiry Officer' under Rule 2(c) of the 1997 Rules (ordinarily a District-Level Officer). Here, the officer (Assistant Director, Savings) who submitted the report relied upon by the District Magistrate was never validly appointed as Enquiry Officer (the only such appointment, of the District Savings Officer, never resulted in a submitted report) and did not, in any event, qualify as a District-Level Officer under Rule 2(c); his report was accordingly not a valid basis for the impugned order.
cases.flag: Recorded compactly given its complete absence of electricity/Supply Code nexus; not exhaustively digested against this corpus's doctrinal framework.
