cases.title: M/s Bharti Retail Ltd. v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: delay in sanction of 65 KW connection
cases.holding: Complaint of delay in sanctioning a 65 KW connection under the Supply Code, 2005, was disposed of without examining entitlement: the petitioner may file a fresh representation with a certified copy; respondent no. 3 must within one week of receipt specify remaining formalities; the petitioner has ten days from that letter to complete them; and respondent no. 3 must then decide the claim in accordance with law, preferably within ten days of receiving the completed papers.

cases.title: Prem Shanker Pandey v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: provisional-assessment-objections
cases.holding: On the licensee's statement that no final assessment had been passed and the recovery citation was being withdrawn, the writ challenging a theft-related demand was disposed of without a merits decision: the consumer may file objections to the provisional assessment; the assessing officer shall consider them after hearing and pass a reasoned order in accordance with the Electricity Act, 2003 and the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; and no coercive measures shall be taken until that decision or a specified outer date, whichever is earlier.

cases.title: Raj Kumar Didwania v. State of U.P. And Others
cases.topic: demand notice after provisional assessment
cases.holding: Once the licensee withdrew a recovery demand issued only after provisional assessment, the writ seeking quash of that demand became infructuous. Against the remaining provisional assessment the consumer may file a written objection before the Executive Engineer within the date fixed; the Executive Engineer shall finalise the assessment within two weeks of the objection.

cases.title: Chandra Kanti Rai v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: recovery citation without final assessment
cases.holding: A recovery citation for electricity dues is set aside where the licensee has itself recalled the recovery for reconsideration; the licensee remains free to take fresh recovery steps after making assessment in accordance with law.

cases.title: Kamlawati Devi v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: demand-notice-writ-relegation
cases.holding: The Court declined to entertain a writ seeking quashing of a demand notice, holding it was not a fit case for writ proceedings. The petitioner having already filed a complaint before the District Consumer Forum, it was open to her to pursue that complaint or to file an objection in accordance with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The writ was disposed of on that observation.
cases.flag: Order cites the Supply Code 2005 generally; no clause numbered.

cases.title: Ram Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: bill-complaint-remedy
cases.holding: An objection to an electricity bill, including a bill issued on a check that supply is used for commercial purposes, is to be pursued by making an appropriate complaint under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ court will not decide such a representation on merits.

cases.title: Tek Chand v. State of U.P. — recovery certificate and restoration of supply
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: recovery of dues and restoration of connection
cases.holding: A writ challenging a recovery certificate for electricity dues will not be entertained where the consumer has already approached the District Consumer Forum and the dues have been recovered. The claim may be pursued before the Forum under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and restoration of connection may be sought by application to the competent authority. Writ dismissed.
cases.flag: Order cites the Supply Code generally with no clause number. It treats the District Consumer Forum as under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Murli Manohar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ-alternate-remedy-bill-dispute
cases.holding: Where the licensee asserts that a decree-compliant revised bill has already been served and is unpaid, and the consumer disputes payment through execution, the writ court will not recast the bill or order reconnection. A dispute to a fresh electricity bill is to be pursued under the Electricity Act, 2003 and the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Bechan Lal v. State of U.P. — demand-notice writ declined for alternative remedy
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: writ maintainability — statutory alternative remedy
cases.holding: Where a consumer challenges an electricity demand notice in writ and statutory alternative remedies under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 or the Electricity Act, 2003 are available, the High Court will decline to entertain the petition and dismiss it without examining the demand on merits.
cases.flag: order cites Supply Code 2005 and Electricity Act 2003 without a clause or section number

cases.title: Vijay Pal Singh v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitaran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: alternate-remedy-theft-bill
cases.holding: A writ petition disputing a theft-related electricity bill will not be entertained when statutory remedies under the Electricity Act, 2003 or the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 have not been availed. The petition is dismissed with liberty to pursue those remedies.
cases.flag: No section or Supply Code clause is numbered. The order invokes unspecified remedies under the 'Uttar Pradesh Electricity Act, 2003' (misnomer for the Electricity Act, 2003) and the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 in a case described as electricity theft.

UP-2005::152.topic: compounding fee — refund after compounding of theft

cases.title: Compounding fee under Clause 152 not refundable as double deposit
cases.topic: compounding fee — refund after compounding of theft
cases.holding: Where compounding fee under Clause 152 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 has been deposited and the alleged theft stands compounded, and the assessed amount has also been paid, the compounding fee is not a double deposit and is not refundable. The Executive Engineer's refusal to return that sum warrants no interference.
cases.flag: Order cites Clause 152 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 as the compounding power; s.152 EA 2003 is the statutory compounding provision. Recorded as cited, not corrected.

cases.title: Val Kishan v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: instalment-facility
cases.holding: Where a consumer facing a Tehsildar recovery citation for unpaid Power Corporation dues seeks only that the amount be accepted in instalments, Clause 16.1.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 affords that facility before the Competent Officer. The writ was disposed of with liberty to approach that officer; the recovery citation was not quashed.

cases.title: Pokhpal v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: new connection — co-owner consent; writ vs pending partition suit
cases.holding: A writ under Article 226 to restrain the licensee from granting a new connection to a co-occupant without the petitioner's consent under the Supply Code will not be entertained where a partition suit between the parties is already pending; that relief is left to the civil proceedings.

cases.title: Brij Kishore v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: alternative-remedy
cases.holding: A writ challenging a bill of demand will be dismissed where Clause 16.5 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 furnishes a statutory alternative remedy, with liberty to the petitioner to pursue that remedy.
cases.flag: Order cites cl. 16.5; Supply Code 2005 has no such clause (likely 6.5 or 6.8).

cases.title: Kaushal Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: disputed bill — representation to Executive Engineer
cases.holding: Where a domestic consumer disputes a recovery citation, alleging that no bill was issued and load was enhanced without notice, paragraph 16.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 furnishes a remedy of representation before the Executive Engineer. The Court disposed of the writ with a direction that if such a representation was filed before respondent no. 4 within a week, it be considered and decided within one month, and stayed coercive action on the citation for that period.

cases.title: Bihari Lal (Deceased) v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: alternative-remedy
cases.holding: The Court recorded that the petitioner had an alternative remedy under clause 17.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Without going into merits, and on an innocuous prayer, it disposed of the writ by directing the Executive Engineer (Prescribed Authority) to decide the pending representation by a reasoned speaking order preferably within six weeks, independently and as permissible in law, and directed that no action be taken against the petitioner until that order was passed and communicated.
cases.flag: Clause 17.10 is cited as the Supply Code alternative remedy; the order does not quote or construe the clause, and the ticket catalog has no matching 17.10 hit.

UP-2005::18(v).topic: expeditious disposal of pending Supply Code appeal

cases.title: Amit Kumar Samaiya v. President (Prabandhak Nideshak) Discom Committee KESCO
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: expeditious disposal of pending Supply Code appeal
cases.holding: Where a consumer's appeal under section 18(v) of the Electricity Supply Code is pending before the Discom Committee and was filed only recently, the High Court will not issue mandamus to decide that appeal out of turn; it may still direct that the appeal be heard and decided as early as possible.
cases.flag: clause cited as section 18(v); numbering does not match the UPESC 2005 clause scheme

UP-2005::2(oo).topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree

cases.title: Dr. Ashok Kumar Sharma & Another v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: 'Occupier' requires authorised occupation — tenant under an unstayed eviction decree
cases.holding: A tenant is ordinarily an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply for a connection on an indemnity bond and cannot be denied supply merely for want of the landlord's NOC. But 'occupier' means a person authorised to occupy; a tenant faced with an unstayed eviction decree is not so authorised, and the court declined, in its discretion under Article 226, to direct a connection at that stage — with liberty to apply if the decree is set aside, recalled or stayed.

cases.title: Anil Shastri v. State of U.P. Thru. Principal Secy. Power & Others
cases.topic: Occupier of the premises where energy is used is liable for the theft assessment
cases.holding: Yes. Occupier in Clause 2.2(oo) means the owner or authorised person in occupation of the premises where energy is used or proposed to be used. The petitioner, Secretary of the registered society and occupier of the premises of the electrical connection from which electricity was drawn by a cable put directly on the distribution line, is liable to pay the amount to the Power Corporation.
cases.flag: The Court cites 'clause 2.2. (oo)'; keyed to catalog UP-2005::2(oo) (SCJ-021). Not keyed to UP-2005::2.2, which is the general definitions heading.

UP-2005::2.2.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.62(6)) with U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 2.2 definitions of tariff order/schedule, energy/demand/fixed charge)
UP-2005::2.2.clause: s.62(6) (interest only for overcharging above tariff) vis-a-vis a rebate under the tariff order
UP-2005::2.2.topic: Delayed crediting of a tariff-order rebate does not attract Section 62(6) interest, since a rebate is a bill-level concession, not itself part of the chargeable tariff

cases.title: M/S. Kamla Cold Storage And Ice Factory v. M.V.V.N.L. & Anr.
cases.topic: Delayed crediting of a tariff-order rebate does not attract Section 62(6) interest, since a rebate is a bill-level concession, not itself part of the chargeable tariff
cases.holding: No. Under Clause 2.2 of the Code, 'tariff order' and 'tariff schedule' fix the rates (fixed charge, energy charge, demand charge) a licensee may charge; a rebate is a distinct concession applied to reduce the bill generated from those tariff-calculated charges, not itself an element of the chargeable tariff. Since the fixed and energy charges billed to the consumer were correctly calculated as per the tariff order, and the rebate (also provided for in the tariff order) was in fact eventually credited, this is not a case of the licensee recovering a price or charge 'exceeding the tariff determined' within Section 62(6); a rebate cannot be equated to excessive tariff so as to bring delayed crediting within the ambit of Section 62(6). No interest was payable on the delayed rebate.

UP-2005::2.2(ff).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 2.2(ff), 'independent feeder' definition) vis-a-vis UPERC Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum & Ombudsman Regulations, 2007 (Regulation 11)
UP-2005::2.2(ff).clause: 2.2(ff) ('independent feeder' — single consumer/similar-process group) vis-a-vis a licensee's 'mixed feeder' (serving multiple unrelated consumers)
UP-2005::2.2(ff).topic: A licensee's mixed feeder is not an 'independent feeder' under Clause 2.2(ff), so Clause 3.4(d)'s tapping-permission provision cannot justify an Electricity Ombudsman directing supply of a Clause 3.4(a)-covered load via a mixed feeder; such an award, being inconsistent with the Supply Code, exceeds the Ombudsman's Regulation 11 jurisdiction and is quashed

cases.title: Sigma Castings Ltd. & Another v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others (with Kundan Castings (P) Ltd.; PVVNL v. Vidyut Lokpal; M/s Shyam Ferrous Ltd.)
cases.topic: A licensee's mixed feeder is not an 'independent feeder' under Clause 2.2(ff), so Clause 3.4(d)'s tapping-permission provision cannot justify an Electricity Ombudsman directing supply of a Clause 3.4(a)-covered load via a mixed feeder; such an award, being inconsistent with the Supply Code, exceeds the Ombudsman's Regulation 11 jurisdiction and is quashed
cases.holding: No. Clause 2.2(ff) defines 'independent feeder' as one supplying a single consumer or group of consumers with a similar process; a mixed feeder serving thousands of differently-processed industries (here, ~5110-11250 industries) does not qualify, so Clause 3.4(d) (which permits tapping of an existing independent feeder where separate-feeder construction is infeasible) has no application to a mixed feeder. The Electricity Ombudsman's award directing supply via the mixed feeder — vague as to duration and contrary to Clause 3.4(a) — exceeded its Regulation 11 jurisdiction (which confines awards to what is consistent with the Act and Supply Code, per Punjab SEB v. Vishwa Calibere Builders) and was quashed. Prior instances of the licensee mistakenly supplying other Clause 3.4(a) consumers via the mixed feeder (M/s Nitin Spat) do not found a valid discrimination claim, since Article 14 guarantees no negative equality (Chandigarh Administration v. Jagjit Singh; State of Orissa v. Mamata Mohanty) — a prior illegality cannot be perpetuated on that ground.

cases.title: M/s Kesarwani Sheetalaya & Ors. v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: A feeder supplying a group of similar-process consumers on contiguous premises is an 'independent feeder' under the 2005 definition, which governs, not the narrower 2002 definition
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 2.2(ff) of the 2005 Code defines an independent feeder (for 11 KV supply) as one emanating from a 33 KV or higher sub-station for supplying a single consumer or a group of consumers having a similar process on the same or contiguous premises; a feeder shared by such a group therefore remains an independent feeder. As the impugned order was passed on 20/12/2008, after the 2005 Code came into force, the 2005 definition governs, and the narrower 2002 definition (2.2(aa) — single consumer) relied on by the respondents does not apply. The Corporation, having throughout treated the cold-storage feeder as independent — in its 1979 letters and by levying the 15% independent-feeder charge in the bills — could not take a contrary stand.

UP-2005::2.2(oo).topic: Registered meter-holder remains liable for the charges notwithstanding a tenant in occupation; the 'Occupier' definition does not shift liability

cases.title: Dinesh Kumar Gupta v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Registered meter-holder remains liable for the charges notwithstanding a tenant in occupation; the 'Occupier' definition does not shift liability
cases.holding: The meter-holder remains liable. The petitioner relied on Clause 2.2(oo), which defines 'Occupier' as the owner or authorized person in occupation of the premises where electricity is used, to contend that his tenant (respondent no.5, running a coaching centre) alone was liable. The Court rejected this: since the electricity meter stood in the name of the petitioner, the petitioner is liable to meet the charges. The induction of a tenant, and the recording in the checking report that the tenant was in occupation, did not by itself transfer the statutory liability away from the registered meter-holder.
cases.flag: Order-sheet: 11 pages, multiple dated orders from 23.12.2011 to the disposal of 1.12.2025, no printed page numbers (the final order carries a single '2' page marker); pins are order dates. The interim stay of recovery is of 23.12.2011 (Vineet Saran and Ashok Pal Singh, JJ.); the operative disposal is the 1.12.2025 order (Ajit Kumar and Vivek Saran, JJ.).

UP-2005::2.2(ss).topic: Recovery/sealing for a defaulter's dues is confined to the 'premises' for which the connection was sanctioned; scope disputes go to the Collector on facts

cases.title: M/S Birla Aircon v. District Magistrate, Meerut & Ors.
cases.topic: Recovery/sealing for a defaulter's dues is confined to the 'premises' for which the connection was sanctioned; scope disputes go to the Collector on facts
cases.holding: No, not without that determination. 'Premises' under Clause 2.2(ss) of the Code means the area/portion of the building/shed/field for which the connection was applied for or sanctioned to a single consumer; recovery as arrears of land revenue against the defaulter can proceed only against premises so defined. Since the record lacked sufficient material on the ownership/occupation of the two firms and the precise extent of the premises sanctioned to the defaulter (M/s Beeco Electricals India) as of the date of sanction (26.5.2004), the Court could not resolve the scope issue on the writ record and remitted the objection to the Collector (with liberty to conduct spot inspection) for a reasoned decision within three weeks, after hearing the licensee.

UP-2005::2.2(tt).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with UPERC Tariff Orders)
UP-2005::2.2(tt).topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division v. The Electricity Ombudsman & 2 Others
cases.topic: Protective-load charge requires the consumer's option and sanction
cases.holding: No. A 'Protective Load' (Clause 2.2(tt): a load not subject to normal rostering) charge under the Tariff Orders is attracted only where the consumer has opted for the facility and it has been sanctioned by the licensee. The Aviation College never exercised such option; the demand — raised suo motu for eight years' arrears on an audit objection — was illegal (following Allahabad Inter Prises v. State of U.P.).

UP-2005::3.3(e).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 3.3(e), professional use of residential space) read with the rate schedules (LMV-1 domestic, LMV-2 non-domestic/commercial) approved by the U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission
UP-2005::3.3(e).clause: 3.3(e) (professionals including lawyers using up to 50 sq. m. of residential space for practice/consultancy do not attract non-domestic tariff) — extended in principle to advocates' chambers within court premises
UP-2005::3.3(e).topic: Electricity consumption in lawyers' chambers within a court compound must be billed under the domestic rate schedule (LMV-1), not the commercial/non-domestic rate schedule (LMV-2), since the legal profession is not a commercial activity and the residuary 'not covered under any rate schedule' clause (assigning unclassified consumption to LMV-2) cannot override this classification

cases.title: Tehsil Bar Association, Sadar Tehsil Parisar, Gandhi Nagar, Ghaziabad v. U.P. Power Corporation Limited And 3 Others
cases.topic: Electricity consumption in lawyers' chambers within a court compound must be billed under the domestic rate schedule (LMV-1), not the commercial/non-domestic rate schedule (LMV-2), since the legal profession is not a commercial activity and the residuary 'not covered under any rate schedule' clause (assigning unclassified consumption to LMV-2) cannot override this classification
cases.holding: LMV-1 (domestic) applies, not LMV-2. Applying the noscitur a sociis principle (Dr. D.M. Surti v. State of Gujarat) that associated words take their colour from one another, LMV-2's illustrative list (shops, hotels, restaurants, cinemas, commercial/trading establishments, etc.) reflects purely commercial/trading activities, which the legal profession — carried on through personal skill, intelligence, and individual characteristics, and traditionally prohibited from advertising or profit-sharing arrangements by Bar Council rules — is not (Dr. D.M. Surti; V. Sasidharan v. Peter and Karunakar; M.P. Electricity Board v. Shiv Narayan; Sudha v. President, Advocates Association Chennai; Ramanathan v. State of Kerala; Sakharam v. Nagpur Corporation; Arup Sarkar v. CESC). Clause 3.3(e) of the Supply Code already recognises professionals' (including lawyers') use of residential space for practice as not attracting non-domestic tariff, and pre-existing licensee circulars (28.11.1983 and 8.10.1985) classified lawyers' offices as LMV-1; while the current tariff schedule's rate-classification list does not expressly enumerate 'lawyers' chambers,' the residuary Clause 13 (assigning unclassified LMV consumers to LMV-2) cannot be applied where the activity in question is affirmatively non-commercial. The fact that the chambers are located within a court compound rather than a residential building does not change this analysis, since the court compound is itself part of judicial premises historically billed at LMV-1. Discrimination between advocates' chambers in different court compounds within the same State, where a single Electricity Regulatory Commission-approved rate schedule applies uniformly, is impermissible regardless of which distribution company serves a given district.

UP-2005::3.4.clause: 3.4(d)(ii) (consent of the 'original consumer' for tapping an independent feeder)
UP-2005::3.4.topic: Only the consumer who funded construction of the independent feeder itself is the 'original consumer' whose consent is needed for further tapping; a mere connecting-line-cost-bearing tapping consumer is not

cases.title: M/S Shri Parasnath Alloys (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Only the consumer who funded construction of the independent feeder itself is the 'original consumer' whose consent is needed for further tapping; a mere connecting-line-cost-bearing tapping consumer is not
cases.holding: No. The 'original consumer' whose consent is required under Clause 3.4(d)(ii) is the consumer at whose instance and cost the independent feeder itself was constructed — here, the consumer that paid the entire feeder-construction cost (over Rs. 1.25 crore) and was sanctioned load first. Subsequent consumers permitted to tap the feeder, who bore only the cost of their own connecting line (not the feeder's construction), do not thereby acquire 'original consumer' status or a consent right over further tapping; nor is there evidence that the petitioner itself obtained the true original consumer's consent, which would be necessary to stand in its shoes (as in Kesarwani Sheetalaya, factually distinguishable since there the objecting party had obtained consent from, and shared cost with, the true original consumer). Since the true original consumer raised no objection to the further sanction, and was not even a party to the writ, the petitioner (itself only a downstream tapping consumer) had no justiciable ground to object to a further consumer's tapping of the same feeder.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar Agarwal s/o M.P. Agarwal v. State of U.P. thru. Secretary & Ors.
cases.topic: Clause 3.4(a)'s list of industries requiring mandatory independent-feeder supply is specific/restrictive, not illustrative; consumers outside that list (or below the 1000 KVA threshold) have only an option, not an obligation, to take an independent feeder, and cannot be compelled to bear its cost where a shared feeder is technically feasible
cases.holding: No — Clause 3.4(a)'s enumerated industries (Arc/Induction furnaces, Rolling Mills, Re-rolling Mills, Mini steel plants) are specific and restrictive, not illustrative; a textile unit does not fall within it. Clause 3.4(b) gives such other consumers with load above 500 KVA merely an *option* to seek an independent feeder — it is not compulsory, and the licensee cannot insist on or compel independent-feeder supply where a dependent/shared feeder has been found technically feasible (as the respondents' own committee had found here). A generalized theft-prevention rationale does not override the Code's clear text, since the Code itself provides other anti-theft mechanisms. The condition imposed (independent-feeder connection, at ~Rs. 19 lakh cost to the consumer) was quashed, and the licensee directed to provide the sanctioned 3000 KVA connection from the existing 33 KV Fatehpur feeder within two weeks.

cases.title: Sigma Castings Ltd. & Another v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others (with Kundan Castings (P) Ltd.; PVVNL v. Vidyut Lokpal; M/s Shyam Ferrous Ltd.)
cases.topic: Clause 3.4(a)'s mandatory independent-feeder requirement for the specified heavy industries applies to load-enhancement applications as well as new connections, regardless of whether the enhancement changes the system/voltage of supply under Clause 4.43(b)/(c)
cases.holding: Clause 3.4(a) applies to both. It is wide enough, and uses the word 'only', to cover both new connections and additional-load applications without qualification — Clause 4.43 (which only prescribes time-frames/procedure) cannot be read to narrow this substantive requirement; a harmonious construction requires reading Clause 4.43 alongside, not divorced from, Clause 3.4. Accordingly, after the Supply Code's 18.2.2005 commencement, any release of 1000 KVA-plus load to Clause 3.4(a) industries — whether by new connection or load enhancement, and whether or not it changes the system/voltage — must be through an independent feeder.

cases.title: Stay of PLA independent-feeder direction; rural-line connection if requested
cases.topic: independent feeder
cases.holding: Operation of the Permanent Lok Adalat's direction requiring the discom to give the consumer an independent-feeder connection is stayed. If the consumer is ready to take supply through the rural electricity line, he may request it and the department shall be free to grant that connection. Notice issued; writ listed.

cases.title: Raj Narayan Singh v. State of U.P. and Others
cases.topic: Clause 3.4 (independent feeders / consent to tapping) does not protect a small consumer who has no independent feeder
cases.holding: No. Clause 3.4 governs supply through independent feeders (Arc/Induction furnaces, Rolling/Re-rolling Mills, mini steel plants of 1000 KVA and above, or other loads above 500 KVA on request) and the conditions for tapping such feeders, including the original consumer's consent. A 2 HP / 2 KW tube-well consumer who merely paid for ordinary lines and a transformer has no independent feeder and no right under Clause 3.4 to object to tapping. Tapping may nonetheless be permitted only if technically feasible and after the licensee records satisfaction that the petitioner's own supply will not be affected.

cases.title: Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd., Bhikaripur & Anr. v. Vidyut Lokpal (Electricity Ombudsman) & Anr.
cases.neutral_citation: 2008 SCC OnLine All 376 : AIR 2008 All 127 : (2008) 5 All LJ 683
cases.topic: Tapping of an existing feeder permitted where an independent feeder cannot be constructed
cases.holding: Yes, under the Clause 3.4(d) exception. Where construction of a separate feeder is not possible (non-availability of corridor/right of way/bay - here a railway track and agricultural land intervened), tapping of the independent feeder may be permitted to another connection having a similar process, which includes such furnace/rolling-mill consumers. The Ombudsman's direction for temporary tapping of the 33 KV Fatehpur feeder (with an independent meter for energy audit) was not contrary to Clause 3.4(a) but within the 3.4(d) exception, and was upheld; the licensee's objection confined to 3.4(a) ignored the exception.

cases.title: Independent feeder — third consumer not to be reconnected pending writ
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: independent feeder — connecting another consumer
cases.holding: If respondent no. 3's supply on the petitioner's independent feeder had already been disconnected, it shall not be reconnected pending further orders. The Court recorded the plea under clause 3.4 that no other consumer may be connected to an independent feeder without the original consumer's consent, but did not decide that plea. The writ remains pending.

cases.title: M/s Suyash Craft And Papers Ltd. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: tapping through original consumer; consent
cases.holding: Paragraph 3.4 of the Supply Code permits a connection through an original consumer to another consumer if, among other requirements, the prospective consumer takes the original consumer's consent. The writ alleging tapping without such consent was later dismissed for want of prosecution, without a merits decision on the tapping dispute.

cases.title: Kirti Sheet Grah Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corp. Ltd.
cases.topic: independent-feeder load thresholds
cases.holding: Independent feeder under clauses 3.4(a) and (b) can be given only at 1000 kVA and 500 kVA (with applicable charges and technical feasibility). The petitioner's 150 kVA feeder was not independent, was Corporation property, and the Corporation was entitled to supply others through it.

cases.title: Indian Industries Association v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: tapping of dedicated industrial feeder
cases.holding: A writ seeking to quash an office memorandum directing tapping of a third consumer onto the petitioner's 11 kV dedicated industrial feeder, and to restrain such tapping under Clause 3.4(d) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and related Government Orders, was dismissed. After perusing the record in the petitioner's absence, the Court held that no case for interference was made out and that the cause of action appeared no longer to survive or the petition had become infructuous; the earlier stay of the memorandum was vacated. Clause 3.4(d) was not construed.

cases.title: M/s Kesarwani Sheetalaya & Ors. v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: Clause 3.4(d) governs tapping of an independent feeder in both the 3.4(a) and 3.4(b) categories, not only steel/furnace plants, and requires the original consumer's consent
cases.holding: On a conjoint reading of Clause 3.4, sub-clause (d) governs supply through an independent feeder for both category (a) (Arc/Induction furnaces, rolling, re-rolling and mini steel plants of 1000 KVA and above) and category (b) (other cases, including townships/complexes and domestic, non-domestic or institutional loads above 500 KVA); its applicability cannot be restricted to steel/furnace plants. The conditions in sub-clause (d) — including the consent of the original consumer, cost-sharing and technical feasibility — must therefore be fulfilled before a fresh consumer is tapped in. Here the petitioners had never consented and had objected, so the direction to connect respondent no.4 was in breach of Clause 3.4(d); the order was also unsustainable because it was passed mechanically on the Energy Minister's endorsement, without application of mind and contrary to Clause 3.4.
cases.flag: Source judgment is not paragraph-numbered; pins reference the page breaks of the source order. Clause 3.4 is reproduced at pp.6-7.

UP-2005::3.8.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.24(7), U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999; Regulation 139, UPERC (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2004)
UP-2005::3.8.clause: 3.8(a) (tariff takes effect seven days after publication; no retrospective application)
UP-2005::3.8.topic: A revised tariff cannot be applied retrospectively to a date preceding its publication

cases.title: M/S Shokumbhari Pulp & Paper Mills Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others (with connected petitions)
cases.topic: A revised tariff cannot be applied retrospectively to a date preceding its publication
cases.holding: No. Clause 3.8(a) of the Supply Code, read with Section 24(7) of the Reforms Act, 1999 and Regulation 139(2) of the 2004 Conduct of Business Regulations, provides that a published tariff takes effect only seven days after the last date of its publication in at least two widely-circulating daily newspapers, and remains in force until amended and published afresh; none of these provisions empowers retrospective application. Following Binani Zinc Ltd. v. Kerala SEB (the Regulatory Commission has not been empowered to frame tariff with retrospective effect, and all laws are presumptively prospective absent express provision or necessary intendment to the contrary), the licensee's notification purporting to apply the revised tariff from 1.10.2012 — though published only on 23.10.2012 and notified on 25.10.2012 — was without legal authority. The tariff was held effective only from 1.11.2012, and amounts realised on the earlier (retrospective) basis were directed to be adjusted in the consumers' future bills.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Minimum monthly/fixed charges cannot be waived; consumer who does not seek permanent disconnection remains liable
cases.holding: No. Adopting the Coordinate Bench in Writ-C No. 1003603 of 2008 (paras 12–16), the Court held that the Ombudsman's logic — that a consumer need not pay charges if no electricity is consumed for reasons beyond his control, mirroring the licensee's freedom from compensation for interruption beyond its control — is beyond the Electricity Act, 2003 and the Supply Code, 2005. Paragraphs 3.8 and 3.9, with the Tariff Orders, provide that minimum monthly/fixed charges are announced by the Commission; the licensee may decide other charges mentioned in paragraph 3.8, and may realise charges not in the Tariff Orders only with the Commission's prior approval. The published tariff schedule is to be paid. If the consumer (the saw-mill operator in the sister writ) was prevented from running the mill, the remedy was to approach the Executive Engineer for permanent disconnection. He did not. Minimum monthly charges therefore had to be paid. Because those charges are part of the notified Tariff Order, the licensee could not waive them on a consumer request, and the Ombudsman could not ask the licensee to ignore the Tariff Order. The Ombudsman order dated 23.05.2008 is set aside, and this petition is allowed in terms of the 21.03.2023 orders.

cases.title: Chandra Bhan Singh v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Classification and differential charges with Commission approval are not discriminatory and not inconsistent with ss.62 and 64
cases.holding: No. Clause 3.7 permits the licensee to classify or reclassify consumers and to fix different tariffs for different categories with the Commission's approval. Clause 3.8(a) provides that tariff and other charges are announced by the licensee with that approval, in accordance with Section 24 of the U.P. Electricity Reforms Act, 1999 to the extent consistent with the 2003 Act, and take effect only seven days after publication in at least two daily newspapers having wide circulation in the area of supply. LMV-5 rates are charges for consumers classified under Clause 3.7. The classification and different charges cannot be said to be discriminatory or unreasonable. Consumers are reasonably classified and the tariff is fixed by the Appropriate Commission under Sections 62 and 64; the prayer to quash Regulations 3.7 and 3.8 is devoid of merit.

Dates of the impugned schedule appear as 20.12.2004, 22.11.2004, 1.12.2004 and 1.1.2005 as the judgment states them.

cases.topic: independent feeder
cases.holding: On 1 December 2009 the Court issued an interim mandamus directing the respondents to provide an independent power line as per clause 3D(8) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 within one month or show cause. On 13 August 2019 the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution after counsel stated the client was not responding, and the interim order was vacated.

cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: On the second respondent's statement that grant of an electricity connection is governed by the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and that, subject to the petitioner completing all formalities, the pending application would be disposed of within two weeks, the Court disposed of the writ. The petitioner was directed to approach the second respondent within one week with a copy of the order; the second respondent was to apprise remaining formalities and decide the application for a fresh connection within two weeks thereafter. cases.title: Dinesh Kumar Agarwal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: A writ directing grant of a new electricity connection is not maintainable where the petitioner has not applied in the prescribed format under the Electricity Act, 2003 read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and has come straight to the High Court. If he thereafter applies after fulfilling every prerequisite formality, the Executive Engineer is expected to consider and redress the grievance within the time frame provided in the Code and in accordance with law.

cases.title: No mandamus for a new connection without a prescribed Supply Code application
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-prescribed-application
cases.holding: The Electricity Act, 2003 (styled in the order as the U.P. Electricity Act, 2003) read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 is a self-contained code with a full mechanism for claiming a new connection after fulfilling the prescribed formalities. Where the petitioner has not applied in the prescribed format, the Court will not mandamus the licensee to give a connection. The writ is dismissed, with liberty to apply; any such application is to be dealt with on the parameters laid down for grant of connection.

UP-2005::4(i).topic: contempt of connection direction; dues on brother's connection on same land

cases.title: M/s S.K. Rice Mill v. Aditya Pandey
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: contempt of connection direction; dues on brother's connection on same land
cases.holding: A writ-court direction to give an electricity connection within four weeks, following counsel's statement that a connection would be given, is only a direction to provide connection in accordance with law. An Executive Engineer's later speaking order refusing the connection under paragraphs 4(i) and 4(ii) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 — because dues stood against the applicant's brother's connection on the land on which the mill is established — is not willful disobedience of that writ. Alleged illegalities in the refusal go to merits and cannot be considered in contempt; the applicant has the remedy of challenging the order before the appropriate authority. Application disposed of; notice discharged.
cases.flag: Order recites 'paragraph nos. 4 (i) and 4 (ii)' of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 without identifying the parent clause; not silently mapped to 4.3/4.4.

UP-2005::4.1.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Arrears-bar is premises-specific; connection to a tenant/occupier of a distinct premises
cases.holding: No. The arrears-bar in the third proviso to Clause 4.1 applies only to dues on the same 'premises' (Clause 2(ss)); the shop is a distinct premises and the tenant is an 'occupier' (Clause 2(oo)) entitled to apply. Clause 4.3(h) forbids refusal on the ground of dues on other portions; the licensee must instead pursue the defaulters under Clause 4.3(f)(v).

cases.title: Chandra Prakash Gupta v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Auction-purchaser and arrears — the Code as the missing statutory provision
cases.holding: No. Ahmedabad Electricity Co. v. Gujarat Inns turned on the absence of a statutory provision; Clause 4.1 of the 2005 Code (promulgated after that 2004 decision) now supplies one, requiring a No-Dues Certificate before a fresh connection on premises where ownership has changed and arrears exist. A SARFAESI auction-purchaser is bound by it and may obtain a connection only on furnishing a No-Dues Certificate.

cases.title: Smt. Meenu Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: refusal of new connection for others' arrears
cases.holding: An interlocutory Division Bench held, prima facie, that Clause 4.1 permits refusal of a fresh connection only where there is default in respect of the premises applied for, and is not attracted merely because other tenants occupying different portions of the same building have arrears. On final hearing another Division Bench did not decide that question, holding that whether the arrears related to the same premises and whether the licensee was legally justified in refusing the connection were issues of fact for the Managing Director of Kanpur Electricity Supply Company to examine on a representation; the writ was disposed of with directions for a reasoned speaking order.

cases.title: Sneha Devi v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection; completed application; one-month period
cases.holding: Clause 4.1 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 requires the licensee, on an application by the owner or occupier of premises in its area of supply, to give supply within one month after receipt of a completed application. An application with many columns unfilled is not a completed application, and a writ of mandamus for a new connection filed before expiry of that period is premature and liable to be dismissed.

cases.title: Executive Engineer, U.P. Power Corporation Nigam Ltd. v. K.K. Singh
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interlocutory stay of Permanent Lok Adalat award
cases.holding: Where a licensee seeks to quash a Permanent Lok Adalat award as illegal, contrary to the record and contrary to Clause 4.1 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the writ requires consideration: notice issues to the consumer and the award remains stayed till the next date of listing.

cases.title: Smt. Soni Dwivedi v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. thru. its Chairman & Ors.
cases.topic: Clearing the premises' arrears is a condition precedent to a new connection to a purchaser of the premises
cases.holding: Yes. Though Clause 4.1 obliges the licensee to supply on application, its provisos provide that where ownership of premises has changed and arrears subsist, a new connection is released to the new owner only on a No-Dues Certificate under Clause 4.3(f), and shall not be released to a new applicant on the same premises while arrears remain. The 2005 Code governs the field and makes clearing the previous dues a condition precedent to a new connection; the purchaser's liability to the department is not absolved by a sale-deed clause casting the dues on the seller (which she may enforce against the seller). The refusal was upheld and the writ dismissed.

cases.title: Kalawati Rana v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. Thru its M.D./Chairman and Another
cases.topic: New connection to a purchaser conditioned on a No-Dues Certificate for the premises' arrears
cases.holding: Yes. The third proviso to Clause 4.1 provides that where arrears exist on premises whose ownership has changed, a new connection is released to the new owner only on submission of a No-Dues Certificate under Clause 4.3(f). Consistently with PVVNL v. DVS Steels and Haryana SEB v. Hanuman Rice Mills (as applied by the coordinate bench in Pawan Jha), the distributor may stipulate clearing the premises' arrears as a condition of a fresh connection, and an inter-party sale-deed clause fixing the dues on the seller does not bind the licensee. The refusal was upheld, with liberty to deposit the erstwhile owner's dues and obtain a No-Dues Certificate.

cases.title: Gaurav Gupta v. Managing Director, Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: fresh connection — previous premises dues
cases.holding: As per paragraph 4.1 of the Electricity Supply Code, unless previous dues on the premises are cleared, no fresh electricity connection can be given. Purchasers of a house with dues exceeding ten lakh rupees were directed to pay those dues as indicated by the distribution licensee and recover them from their seller; mandamus for a connection without clearing the arrears was refused.

cases.title: M/S Aditri Agro Infratech Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: restoration-subject-to-prior-dues
cases.holding: Without deciding whether Tata Power's clear-slate principle or para 4.1(3) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (cited as requiring clearance of premises dues before a new connection or restoration) governed the claim, the Court directed respondent no.3 to communicate within three weeks its decision on whether restoration could be granted and, if not, the reasons; any representation already made was to be considered. The writ was disposed of.
cases.flag: as_cited

cases.title: Lakshmi Oil And Vanaspati Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Others
cases.topic: Auction purchaser without prior contract is not a defaulter; Clause 4.1 duty to supply remains
cases.holding: No. Following Isha Marbles, the new purchaser cannot be said to be a consumer or occupier under the Electricity Act, there having been no contract with the licensee before purchase. The factual position was the same: the petitioner was not previously connected, cannot be said to be a defaulter, and it cannot be said that there are dues against him. The Power Corporation cannot be exempted from the Clause 4.1 obligation to supply. The writ is allowed; the order dated 19.4.2006 is quashed; connection is to be given within one month of production of a certified copy. If dues exist against the previous owner, the Corporation may recover them from that owner in accordance with law.
cases.flag: Isha Marbles was decided under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910; this Court applies it to Clauses 4.1 and 4.3(f) of the 2005 Code. The quoted last proviso to Clause 4.1 also recites the associate/relative/control bar (Companies Act, 1956 ss. 2 and 6); those limbs were not applied.

cases.title: Trinmurti Buildwell Pvt Ltd v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd And Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Auction purchaser without prior contract is not a defaulter; Clause 4.1 duty to supply remains
cases.holding: No. Following Isha Marbles, the new purchaser cannot be said to be a consumer or occupier under the Electricity Act, there having been no contract with the licensee before purchase. The Court treated the facts as the same as an SFC section 29(1) auction purchaser: the petitioner was not previously connected, cannot be said to be a defaulter, and it cannot be said that there are dues against him. The Power Corporation cannot be exempted from the Clause 4.1 obligation to supply. The writ is allowed; the order dated 10.4.2008 is quashed; connection is to be given within one month of production of a certified copy. If dues exist against the previous owner, the Corporation may recover them from that owner in accordance with law.
cases.flag: Isha Marbles was decided under the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, on an SFC s.29 sale; this Court applies it to Clauses 4.1 and 4.3(f) of the 2005 Code on a Union Bank recovery auction. The quoted last proviso to Clause 4.1 also recites the associate/relative/control bar (Companies Act, 1956 ss. 2 and 6); those limbs were not applied.

cases.title: Kamlesh Sisodiya v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: permanent disconnection after theft-assessment dues
cases.holding: A writ seeking consideration of an application for permanent disconnection, where an unchallenged theft assessment remains outstanding, is disposed of by directing that if the consumer deposits electricity dues including that assessment, the licensee shall consider and decide the application; if the consumer objects to or appeals the assessment, permanent disconnection awaits the result, and regular bills must be paid in the meantime.
cases.flag: cited as 4.1.4(g)

cases.title: Ghanshyam v. State of U.P. Thru. Prin. Secy. Energy Deptt. & 3 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Lucknow Bench)
cases.topic: paid final bill after consumer-initiated termination bars further demand
cases.holding: No. The 10.11.2016 receipt for Rs 1,696 stamped 'P.D. Final Amount' was not denied; a departmental letter of 9.5.2024 said records of the connection were unavailable, so the Court saw no reason to doubt the receipt. The same Rs 1,696 is recited in the 28.5.2025 demand, identifying the same connection. Clause 4.14(g) requires, after 30 days' notice, a reading, disconnection, removal of meter and cable, and a final bill including arrears; payment yields a receipt stamped FINAL BILL, treated as a no-dues certificate. Once permanent disconnection is approved and that bill paid, there is no occasion to issue further bills or to assess the consumer again for an unusual amount. Missing records cannot be used to subject him to illegal billing. The demand of Rs 1,66,916 is quashed.
cases.flag: Licensee also cited Clause 4.38 (permanent disconnection); the Court reproduced and applied only Clause 4.14(g).

cases.title: Ghanshyam v. State of U.P. Thru. Prin. Secy. Energy Deptt. & 3 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Lucknow Bench)
cases.topic: prescribed format or last receipt not a ground to refuse processing a disconnection application
cases.holding: No. There is no justification for insisting on a prescribed-format application annexing the last receipt when those materials are with the department itself. Any disconnection application is to be processed forthwith: supply disconnected and a final bill on the last reading. Mere non-use of the prescribed format, or failure to annex the bill or receipt, is not a ground to reject or not process the application. The department is under a duty to frame consumer-friendly rules. The application itself indicates cessation of the consumer-supplier relationship; under paragraph 4.14, supply is to be disconnected and a reading taken within 30 days so that a final bill can be submitted, which the consumer must clear or dispute under the Code.
cases.flag: Observations made while quashing a post-PD demand, not on a pending disconnection application. The prescribed format referred to is Annexure 4.7, quoted in Clause 4.14(g).

cases.title: DLF Universal Limited v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: termination of agreement / permanent disconnection
cases.holding: A consumer seeking permanent disconnection must terminate the agreement by notice in the specified format (Annexure 4.7) under clause 4.14(g) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (pari materia with the 2002 Code). An application not in that format does not entitle the consumer to mandamus; the writ was dismissed with liberty to proceed in accordance with law.

UP-2005::4.15.topic: single-point connection; two connections in same premises

cases.title: Executive Engineer, Electricity Distribution Division v. Aneeta Garg
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: single-point connection; two connections in same premises
cases.holding: On the licensee's writ asserting that Clause 4.15(C) permits only a single-point connection inside the premises and that both the husband's and wife's connections were therefore rightly disconnected after theft on the husband's supply, the Court issued notice and stayed the Permanent Lok Adalat award dated 29.5.2014, except that respondent Aneeta Garg's connection no. 6110/058072 was directed to be restored forthwith. Later listing orders continued the stay. The Clause 4.15(C) contention and the alleged perversity of the Adalat's finding that the two connections stood at different places were not decided.
cases.flag: Counsel cited Clause 4.15 (C); the Court neither verified the sub-clause letter nor construed it.

cases.title: M/S Atul Industrial Corporation And Another v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited And Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: HT/EHT consumer must provide independent entry to meter/metering cubicle; licensee fixes accessible point of supply
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.15(b) (cited as Clause 4.1.5(b)) requires all EHT and HT consumers/applicants to provide independent entry to the meter or metering cubicle, and Clause 4.15(a) requires the licensee to determine the point of supply so that meters and other equipment are always accessible without obstruction for inspection. There is no jurisdictional error in the 21.07.2007 order. If the meter is already independently accessible, the consumer may bring that fact to the Executive Engineer, who shall take appropriate action in accordance with law; in any case the impugned order is not illegal. The writ is dismissed.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing orders from 18.11.2010 to 29.1.2019; the operative disposal is 22.5.2023 (unnumbered). The Court wrote 'Clause 4.1.5 (b)' for the independent-entry duty whose text is Clause 4.15(b); Clause 4.15(a) was cited correctly. Keyed to UP-2005::4.15, not UP-2005::4.1 or BIHAR-2007::4.15.

cases.title: S. R. Traders v. Kanpur Electricity Supply Company
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: more than one connection in one premises
cases.holding: Para 4.15 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 indicates that it is the discretion of the concerned authority to permit more than one connection in one premises. The Court saw no ground to quash the 11.05.2010 inspection report and directed the Executive Engineer, Electricity Urban Distribution Division, Jajmau, KESCO, to decide any representation of the petitioners in accordance with law within four weeks.
cases.flag: Court attributed the multiple-connection discretion to 'para 4.15' of the 2005 Code; clause number taken as stated.

cases.title: Instalments of electricity dues — relegated to Executive Engineer under clause 4.16
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: instalment of dues — competent authority
cases.holding: A consumer’s request to pay electricity dues in instalments and to adjust a sum already deposited is a factual matter for the competent authority under clause 4.16 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not for the writ court. The petitioner was directed to apply to the concerned Executive Engineer within ten days; the Engineer is to decide on merits preferably within one month of receipt.
cases.flag: Court attributed instalment competence to cl. 4.16 without extracting the clause text.

cases.title: Mahboob v. State of U.P. — instalment plea relegated to EE under cl. 4.16
cases.topic: instalment of dues / competent authority
cases.holding: A consumer's request to pay electricity dues in instalments and to have an amount already deposited adjusted is a factual matter the High Court will not resolve; clause 4.16 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 empowers the competent authority to do so, and the consumer is to approach the concerned Executive Engineer for a decision on merits, preferably within one month.

cases.title: M/s Baba Cold Storage and Ice Factory v. DVVNL
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: OCB installation liability
cases.holding: The writ petition invoking para 4.16(c) of the Electricity Supply Code, which the consumer had pleaded as placing the liability to install an 11 kV oil circuit breaker on the distribution licensee, was dismissed as having become infructuous by efflux of time, without any adjudication of that clause.

cases.title: Neelam Sharma v. U.P. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-title-dispute-indemnity
cases.holding: Where a new connection is refused because of a pending civil title dispute, clause 4.2 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 — applied with s.43 of the Electricity Act, 2003 as construed in Smt. Sushama Chowdhary — requires the licensee, on the applicant filing an indemnity bond, to take necessary steps in accordance with law for grant of supply. The writ court will not adjudicate the pending civil dispute.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: transformer capacity enhancement
cases.holding: Clause 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 obliges the distribution licensee to extend transformer capacity if load increases to 80% of installed capacity. Where a 100 KVA transformer carried only about 54 KVA, it did not require enhancement, strengthening or replacement, and the Permanent Lok Adalat's direction to install an additional 25 KVA transformer for a 7.5 KVA tubewell was, prima facie, illegal. Operation of the award dated 12.12.2015 was stayed until further orders, the writ being listed for admission/final disposal with Writ C No. 23246 of 2016.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: transformer capacity extension at 80% load
cases.holding: Clause 4.2 obliges the licensee to extend, strengthen or replace a transformer only when load on it increases to 80% of installed capacity. Load of about 54 kVA on a 100 kVA transformer is within capacity, so a Permanent Lok Adalat cannot, prima facie, direct installation of an additional transformer for one consumer.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat
cases.topic: transformer-capacity-extension-at-80-percent-load
cases.holding: Clause 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code 2005 obliges the distribution licensee to extend the capacity of a transformer if the load increases to 80% of the installed capacity. Where the admitted load on an existing 100 KVA transformer is about 54 KVA, the load is within capacity and the transformer need not be increased, strengthened, or replaced by one of higher capacity. A Permanent Lok Adalat direction to install an additional 25 KVA transformer for a 7.5 KVA tubewell is, prima facie, illegal. Operation of the award is stayed until further orders.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: transformer capacity enhancement at 80% loading
cases.holding: Clause 4.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 obliges the licensee to extend transformer capacity if load increases to 80% of installed capacity. Where a 100 KVA transformer carries about 54 KVA (77.5 HP), the load is within existing capacity and the transformer need not be increased, strengthened, or replaced. Prima facie a Permanent Lok Adalat award directing installation of an additional 25 KVA transformer for a 7.5 KVA tubewell is illegal, and its operation is stayed pending disposal.

cases.title: Ishwari Prasad v. U.P. Power Corporation Lucknow
cases.topic: fresh application after Code compliance
cases.holding: The writ was not pressed. The Court granted liberty to approach the concerned authority afresh after complying with all requirements of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, in particular Clauses 4.2 and 4.3, and directed that an application so presented shall be considered and decided within ten days.

UP-2005::4.20.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.47(5), EA 2003)
UP-2005::4.20.topic: Prepayment-meter exemption from security deposit is conditional on availability of the meter; Clause 4.20(l) not ultra vires s.47(5)

cases.title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
cases.topic: Prepayment-meter exemption from security deposit is conditional on availability of the meter; Clause 4.20(l) not ultra vires s.47(5)
cases.holding: No, the clause is intra vires, and no, mere willingness does not suffice. Section 47(5) exempts a consumer from security only where the consumer is 'prepared' to take supply through a prepayment meter, and this preparedness is itself contingent on the actual availability of such a meter; Section 55 separately mandates only a 'correct meter', not a prepayment meter. Since prepayment meters for HT consumption are neither manufactured nor available in the Indian market, the licensee is under no obligation to install one merely on request, and the exemption in Section 47(5) does not arise. Clause 4.20(l) of the Supply Code, which links the exemption to the licensee 'providing a choice to consumer to opt' for a prepaid meter, does no more than track Section 47(5) and is not an independent or additional fetter; it is not ultra vires. Consequently, a demand for additional security on account of increased HT consumption, made while prepayment meters remain unavailable, is valid.

cases.title: Challenge to 2002 Code cl. 4.55 security distinction dismissed as infructuous after Supply Code 2005
cases.topic: security deposit — no load-capacity distinction
cases.holding: The U.P. Electricity Distribution Code, 2002 having been repealed and replaced by the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 made under the Electricity Act, 2003, clause 4.20 of the 2005 Code does not distinguish consumers of different load capacities and security is now common for all categories of heavy consumers. Counsel submitted that the challenge to clause 4.55 of the 2002 Code (bank-guarantee option confined to contracted load exceeding 10 MW) had therefore become infructuous; the writ petition was dismissed as such. Section 47 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for reasonable security to be determined by the Regulation.

cases.title: M/S Prem Steels (Pvt.) Limited v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Others
cases.topic: Interest on security at the RBI bank rate
cases.holding: Clause 4.20(i), inserted on 14.6.2008, requires the licensee to credit interest on security deposited by cash, cheque or bank draft at the bank rate as on 1 April of the applicable financial year — meaning the rate notified by the Reserve Bank of India — in the April, May or June billing cycle; no interest if the deposit is not so made. The Court applied that RBI bank rate, together with s.47(4), from 10.6.2003, rejecting the plea that absence of a contemporaneous Code clause when the deposit was made confined the consumer to the 2002-Code rate.
cases.flag: The quoted clause is printed '4.20 (i).)' in the source. The Court reproduced 4.20(i) and its Explanation because the petitioner relied on them; the start date of interest is s.47(4) (10.6.2003), not the 14.6.2008 amendment itself.

UP-2005::4.21(a).topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised

cases.title: Suman Engineering and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P.P.C.L. & 4 Others
cases.topic: System-loading charges — refundability where the connection is cancelled and never energised
cases.holding: Yes, refundable. A system-loading charge is a compulsory exaction on one who enjoys the benefit of the distribution system; the liability accrues only once the applicant starts consuming electricity using the licensee's system. A prospective consumer who never takes supply cannot be fastened with it. Refund of Rs. 32,00,000 with interest @ 8.5% p.a. from the date of deposit ordered.

cases.title: Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. v. State of U.P. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Parallel-operating charges under pre-existing ("old") agreements
cases.holding: No. The clause preserves the charge only till termination and is read subject to the maxim that no party may take advantage of its own wrong. Charges end with actual disconnection (28.9.2007); the demand for January 2008-30.11.2018, with interest, is quashed.

UP-2005::4.29.topic: transformer overload; additional connection; alternative remedy

cases.title: Brijesh Kumar Singh v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: transformer overload; additional connection; alternative remedy
cases.holding: Complaints that a consumer's transformer is overloaded, that no further connection can be given from it without his consent, and that another connection would reduce effective supply or threaten the transformer, are to be raised under para 4.29 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 to the concerned Executive Engineer, who may consider the complaint expeditiously. The writ was dismissed on the ground of alternative remedy.

cases.title: Smt. Dujiya v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: sharing of existing consumer's service line with other consumers
cases.holding: Supply of electricity to other consumers from the connection given to an existing consumer is permissible under Clause 4.29 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The licensee's conduct in giving such connections from the petitioner's cable was not defective. The licensee must, however, ensure that while doing so, supply of electricity to the original consumer is not affected.
cases.flag: Court cited Clause 4.29 without specifying sub-clause (a) or (b).

cases.title: Kirti Sheet Grah Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corp. Ltd.
cases.topic: service-line sharing with other consumers
cases.holding: Clause 4.29(a) permits the licensee to use the petitioner's service line and apparatus to give supply to neighbouring cold storages so long as the petitioner's supply is not affected; the Court refused to quash the Managing Director's 23.03.2011 tapping order and found no discriminatory or arbitrary alignment.

cases.title: M/S Skmr Healthcare v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: permanent disconnection and service-line handover
cases.holding: A representation seeking permanent disconnection after adjustment of electricity duty and security deposit with interest, and handover of the service line under Clause 4.29(b), is to be decided by a reasoned order of the Executive Engineer in accordance with law after hearing the consumer; the High Court will not itself grant the mandamus on merits.

cases.title: Sabdar Ali v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: licensee use of consumer-paid service line for other consumers
cases.holding: Under clause 4.29 the licensee may use a service line and other apparatus paid for by a consumer to give supply to other consumers provided that consumer's own supply is not affected. The supply company was directed to examine the petitioner's representation for adjustment of the line-installation expenses he had borne and to pass an order keeping that clause in view; the writ was disposed of without an injunction against the proposed connection.
cases.flag: Court cited Clause 4.29 generally; quoted text is 4.29(b).

cases.title: M/S Skmr Healthcare v. Purvanchal Vidhut Vitrana Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reasoned decision on return of service line, security and post-PD fixed charges
cases.holding: The Executive Engineer’s 02.07.2025 order on the Clause 4.29 claim was mechanical and gave no reasons for rejecting return of the service line paid for by the consumer, while the grievance against fixed charges after permanent disconnection remained pending. The writ was disposed of without deciding those claims: on a comprehensive representation filed within two weeks, respondent No.2 shall decide the claims for return of the service line and cessation of fixed-charge liability on merits after brief hearing, by a reasoned order within two months, including a tabular chart of security deposits (and any interest thereon) and amounts claimed by the licensee.
cases.flag: court referred to Clause 4.29 generally, not 4.29(b)

cases.title: Ram Magan Chauhan @ Ram Magan v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: sharing of consumer-funded transformer
cases.holding: A connection to a subsequent consumer from a transformer installed at the petitioner's expense is permissible under para 4.29 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Counsel for the petitioner could not show the legal position was otherwise. The Court declined to interfere and disposed of the writ, without prejudice to other remedies prescribed in law.
cases.flag: Court cited para 4.29 generally; catalog hit is 4.29(b).

cases.title: Prabhat Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: connection from consumer's private line or pole
cases.holding: The Court did not decide whether clause 4.29 of the Supply Code permits the licensee to give electricity connections to other persons from the petitioner's private line or pole. On the petitioner stating that his own connection had been disconnected, the writ was disposed of with liberty to approach the concerned authorities or seek remedies prescribed in law.
cases.flag: order cites Rule 4.29 without a subclause

cases.title: M/s Kesarwani Sheetalaya & Ors. v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: Para 4.29 (service line) cannot be invoked to bypass the independent-feeder tapping conditions of Clause 3.4
cases.holding: No. 'Service line' (Clause 2.2(vv)) and 'independent feeder' are distinct concepts, and paras 4.29 and 3.4 must be given a harmonious construction so that both survive. If para 4.29 were read to allow the licensee to use a consumer's service line/independent feeder to supply others in disregard of Clause 3.4, the conditions of Clause 3.4 would be rendered redundant. Para 4.29 therefore in no manner dilutes the conditions required for supply through an independent feeder under Clause 3.4.
cases.flag: The judgment refers to 'para 4.29' without a sub-clause; keyed to 4.29(b), the corpus's existing key for the service-line-usable-for-other-consumers proposition.

UP-2005::4.3.topic: Clause 4.3(ii)-(iii) supports withholding a fresh connection pending dues, but does not by itself authorise coercive recovery of the previous owner's dues from a purchaser who never held the connection

cases.title: M/S Rayana Paper Board Industries Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Clause 4.3(ii)-(iii) supports withholding a fresh connection pending dues, but does not by itself authorise coercive recovery of the previous owner's dues from a purchaser who never held the connection
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.3(ii) obliges the vendor to clear outstanding dues before sale (or disclose them in the sale deed), and Clause 4.3(iii) allows the purchaser to seek a no-dues certificate, with the licensee bound to disclose pending dues or issue the certificate within 30 working days; the Code does not, however, contain any penal/recovery provision empowering the licensee to coercively recover the vendor's dues from the vendee. In the absence of a provision enabling such recovery, the licensee's right is confined to withdrawing/declining the electricity connection to the premises (i.e. refusing a fresh connection until dues are cleared, consistent with Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Paramount Polymers Pvt. Ltd.) — it cannot issue a coercive recovery citation against the purchaser for dues never incurred by the purchaser. The impugned recovery citation was quashed, with liberty to recover from the original owner (who, moreover, already had a pending dispute before the Electricity Ombudsman over the same dues).
cases.flag: An early (2010) ruling in the arrears/transferee cluster (cf. SCJ-005/012/031/036/037/054), drawing a distinction between (a) withholding a NEW connection pending dues (permissible leverage) and (b) coercive RECOVERY of the previous owner's dues from a non-consumer transferee (requires an express enabling provision). This narrower point about the mode of enforcement may retain force even after K.C. Ninan (SCJ-037) recognised that a Supply Code condition CAN create a statutory charge enabling recovery from a transferee where the Code so expressly provides.

cases.title: New connection withheld for predecessor's old dues
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection — old dues
cases.holding: The Court will not decide disputed questions of fact as to the validity of old dues. Clause 4.3 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 provides the procedure for a new connection and includes payment of old dues. The licensee shall furnish details of the arrears; the applicant may pay them under protest, after which the new connection shall be considered in accordance with law.

cases.title: Mohd. Iqbal Ansari v. Roshan Jacob (Incharge M.D./G.M., K.E.S.C. Ltd.)
cases.topic: contempt enforcement of writ direction to decide on clause 4.3 compliance
cases.holding: Where a writ court has directed the licensee to take an appropriate decision in accordance with law if the consumer complies with clause 4.3 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the licensee is bound by that direction. On a contempt application alleging non-decision after service of the writ order, the Court disposed of the application at this stage, warning that failure to comply within two months of receipt of this order, without reasonable cause, would invite proceedings under the Contempt of Courts Act, with liberty to the applicant to approach the Court again.

cases.title: Mohd. Iqbal Ansari v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection — consider application in accordance with law
cases.holding: If the petitioner complies with Clause 4.3 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the licensee shall take a decision on the new-connection application in accordance with law expeditiously, electricity being an essential service.

cases.title: Landlady's writ against tenant's connection and arrears consigned to records
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: owner-occupier-liability-and-occupant-connection
cases.holding: The Court found no reason to interfere with the impugned order granting the tenant an electricity connection and leaving previous dues of Rs. 19,002 on the landlady, keeping in view Clauses 4.3 and 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Recovery of those dues as between landlady and tenant was treated as a private dispute to be raised by interim application in the pending civil suit, to be disposed of expeditiously if filed. The writ was consigned to records.

cases.title: Smt. Pawan Jha @ Priya Jha v. State of U.P. And Others
cases.topic: An ADA EWS-flat allottee is not distinguishable from a private purchaser for purposes of the arrears-liability doctrine: pre-existing dues of the erstwhile occupier may lawfully condition the grant of a fresh connection to the new allottee, subject to equitable moulding
cases.holding: Yes, applying the DVS Steels Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. (SCJ-099) and Hanuman Rice Mills doctrine that arrears follow the premises/connection and not merely the person of the departed consumer, an ADA-allotment context is not meaningfully distinguishable from a private purchase for this purpose; the licensee may insist on clearance of dues as a precondition to a fresh connection. However, exercising equitable jurisdiction, the Court moulded relief: the petitioner was permitted to deposit the outstanding amount in three equal monthly installments, with the licensee directed to release the electricity connection within 72 hours of the first installment being deposited, and the petitioner was given liberty to pursue recovery of any amounts paid from the erstwhile owner/occupier through appropriate independent proceedings.

cases.title: Rakesh Kumar Srivastava v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: change of name
cases.holding: Where a recovery citation for electricity arrears stands in the name of a deceased consumer, a successor seeking transfer of the connection must deposit the demanded amount and move an application for change of name under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the High Court will not itself order the transfer in writ.

cases.title: Virendra Kumar Mittal v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: A new connection cannot be withheld for a theft-assessment amount whose liability is undetermined
cases.holding: No. The right to supply on deposit of the estimate is independent of the theft-assessment liability, which is still to be fixed by the Special Judge (E.C. Act). The licensee cannot treat the undetermined theft assessment as an 'outstanding due' under Clause 4.3 to refuse the connection; instead the amount is secured by the consumer furnishing security (other than cash or bank guarantee), whereupon the new connection is to be provided. Whether it is an 'outstanding due' under Clause 4.3 abides the Special Judge's decision.

cases.title: Usman Husain v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad (Lucknow Bench)
cases.topic: new connection withheld for alleged premises dues
cases.holding: Where the licensee withholds a new connection under paragraph 4.3 on alleged premises dues and the applicant asserts that the buildings are different, the writ court will not adjudicate identity of the premises; the applicant may apprise the Executive Engineer, who shall re-verify the facts and take such decision as may be required in law.
cases.flag: Order cites 'Paragraph no. 4.3' without a sub-clause.

cases.title: Smt. Pushpa Jain v. Executive Engineer, Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam
cases.topic: new-connection-premises-arrears
cases.holding: Until outstanding electricity dues of an earlier connection to the same premises are cleared, a new connection cannot be released.
