The Electricity Supply Code, as amended, places liability for those earlier dues on the person taking the new connection. The writ petition was disposed of on that basis.

cases.title: Santosh Kumar Yadav v. State of U.P. through M.D., U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection application before writ
cases.holding: A writ seeking a direction to install a new electricity connection, without first making an application in accordance with clauses 4.3 to 4.9 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005—which require particulars including payment of any dues of the connection in the premises and the consent of the owner/landlord—is misconceived and liable to be dismissed. If the consumer thereafter applies in accordance with the Code, the application is to be considered expeditiously.

UP-2005::4.3(f).topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises

cases.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Liability of an auction-purchaser for arrears attaching to the premises
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f)(i) & (viii) place the duty to ascertain and clear outstanding dues on both seller and purchaser and permit the application to be processed only on clearance. The auction-purchaser, buying 'as-is-where-is', is fixed with 'buyer beware' and cannot escape the statutory charge by relying on the encumbrance-free recital or the vendor's non-consumption.

cases.title: Jitendra Kumar Gupta & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: Subsequent purchaser liable for premises dues, including a theft assessment
cases.holding: Yes. 'Outstanding dues' under Clause 4.3(f) means all dues pending on the premises, including a post-theft assessment, and attach to the premises; the purchaser must obtain a No-Dues Certificate. The theft being a personal criminal liability of the previous occupant does not exclude the assessed civil amount. But recovery from the purchaser is subject to adjustment against any amount recovered from the original defaulter (no double recovery); here, a practical direction to deposit 50% to obtain the connection.

cases.title: Sri Piyush Kumar v. State of U.P. Thru' Secretary Lucknow And Others
cases.topic: A director who signed an electricity supply agreement as agent of the company (not personally) is not liable for the company's electricity dues absent a personal guarantee or specific statutory provision; Clause 4.3(f) of the 2005 Supply Code, which for the first time addresses director liability, did not apply to dues/demand notices predating the Code's notification, and in any event requires exhaustion of company assets before recovery from directors
cases.holding: No. A company, being an artificial person, acts only through agents; a director signing an agreement 'on behalf of the Company' under s.46 of the Companies Act, 1956 incurs no personal liability unless the Articles/Board resolution otherwise permit, or the director acts beyond his powers, misrepresents, or gives a personal guarantee/undertaking — none of which was shown here. Following this Court's own precedents (Adesh Kumar Jain v. UPSEB; M/s Meekin Transmission Ltd.), the 'consumer' under the pre-2003 Electric Supply (Consumers) Regulations, 1984 and under s.2(15) of the Electricity Act, 2003 is the company, not its directors personally. The U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 — whose Clause 4.3(f)(iv) first makes outstanding dues a first charge on company assets and whose Clause 4.3(f)(v) permits recovery from directors — was notified after the dues were ascertained and the recovery citation issued, and so had no application; even prospectively, recovery from directors is permissible only after the company's assets prove insufficient to satisfy the dues, and the counter affidavit contained no averment that the licensee had first proceeded against the company's assets. The recovery citation against the petitioner-director was accordingly quashed, without prejudice to recovery proceedings against the company itself.

cases.title: Anoop Goyal v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: auction-purchaser-fresh-connection-predecessor-arrears
cases.holding: A purchaser of premises by auction who seeks a fresh electricity connection is bound under clause 4.3(f) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, to search out and clear predecessor electricity dues on the same plot. Non-disclosure of that liability in the sale deed does not entitle the purchaser to a connection without payment. The Permanent Lok Adalat's dismissal of the complaint was without error, and the writ petition was dismissed.

cases.title: Raman Ispat (Pvt.) Ltd. & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Clearing predecessor's arrears may be stipulated as a condition of a fresh connection / load enhancement to the same premises
cases.holding: Yes. Following PVVNL v. DUS Steels, though past dues are not a charge on the premises and cannot be recovered from a transferee as such, the distributor may, when the purchaser seeks a fresh connection or enhanced load to the same premises, stipulate clearing of the arrears as a condition of supply; such a stipulation is not unreasonable or arbitrary. The amended Clause 4.3(f)(i) reinforces this by making the seller and purchaser jointly and severally liable for the outstanding dues and making those dues a first charge on the company's assets, entered in the agreement with the new applicant.

cases.title: Raman Ispat (Pvt.) Ltd. & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Lifting the corporate veil to fix arrears liability where the same person controls the defaulting and the applicant entities
cases.holding: Yes. The department was justified in lifting the veil and finding R.P. Singh to be the person behind M/s Sai Steels (the defaulter), M/s Singh Alloys and the petitioner M/s Raman Ispat, so that the dues of Sai Steels could be recovered from him and made a condition precedent to enhancement of Raman Ispat's load. The petitioners failed to prove the absence of relationship between the entities, withheld material facts to obtain an interim order, and did not come with clean hands; all three petitions were dismissed with costs.

cases.title: Mukesh Kumar and 3 Others v. State of U.P. and 4 Others
cases.topic: Director liability sequenced after recovery from company assets; vires challenge left open
cases.holding: On the agreed arrangement, recovery is to proceed first against the company's assets; only if the dues remain unrecovered even after their sale may the Corporation proceed against the directors, and that step abides the outcome of the pending writ petitions (Writ-C Nos. 39095 of 2015 and 8370 of 2016). The petitioners' contentions, including the challenge to the vires of Clause 4.3(f)(v) and the s.2(15) definition of 'consumer', were expressly kept open; the Court did not decide them.

cases.title: RKG Industries LLP v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited & 4 Others
cases.topic: Auction purchaser's co-extensive duty to clear a predecessor's electricity dues on an "as is where is" distress sale; duty not confined to private sales
cases.holding: Yes, the dues can be recovered. Clause 4.3(f)(i) casts a co-extensive duty on both seller and purchaser to find out and pay the outstanding electricity dues up to the date of sale and obtain a no-dues certificate, and Clause 4.3(f)(iii) obliges a purchaser who has no such certificate to apply to the licensee before purchase; this duty is not confined to private sales. Where the property is sold "as is where is" with the Recovery Officer disclaiming knowledge of encumbrances, the purchaser is put to enquiry and, having made none, cannot escape the erstwhile owner's dues. The licensee is entitled to recover them from the purchaser as arrears of land revenue.

cases.title: Lakshmi Oil And Vanaspati Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Others
cases.topic: SFC auction sale certificate free from encumbrances is a Clause 4.3(f) no-dues certificate
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f) requires a purchaser of existing property to verify that the old owner has paid all dues and obtained a no-dues certificate, and the last proviso to Clause 4.1 withholds a new connection until that certificate is produced. The petitioner bought the factory in an auction sale for recovery of U.P. Financial Corporation dues; the sale certificate transferred the factory and premises free from all encumbrances. That certificate is itself a no-dues certificate so far as the petitioner is concerned, and the authorities ought to have treated it as no objection towards electricity dues on the petitioner.
cases.flag: The Court quotes Clause 4.3(f) as a single paragraph (purchaser's duty to verify dues and obtain no-dues). Later numbered sub-clauses 4.3(f)(i)–(viii) are not cited. Source PDF concatenates listing and impleadment orders (22.10.2009–6.10.2010) with the operative 30.11.2010 judgment of Prakash Chandra Verma and Virendra Singh JJ., which is unnumbered.

cases.title: Trinmurti Buildwell Pvt Ltd v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd And Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Bank-recovery auction sale certificate free from encumbrances is a Clause 4.3(f) no-dues certificate
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.3(f) requires a purchaser of existing property to verify that the old owner has paid all dues and obtained a no-dues certificate, and the last proviso to Clause 4.1 withholds a new connection until that certificate is produced. The petitioner bought the factory in an auction sale for recovery of Union Bank of India dues; the sale certificate transferred the factory and premises free from all encumbrances. That certificate is itself a no-dues certificate so far as the petitioner is concerned, and the authorities ought to have treated it as no objection towards electricity dues on the petitioner.
cases.flag: The Court quotes Clause 4.3(f) as a single paragraph (purchaser's duty to verify dues and obtain no-dues). Later numbered sub-clauses 4.3(f)(i)–(viii) are not cited. Source PDF concatenates an 11.3.2010 pass-over (R.K. Agrawal and Jayashree Tiwari JJ.) with the operative 24.9.2010 judgment of Prakash Chandra Verma and Ram Autar Singh JJ., which is unnumbered. Same construction as SCJ-655 (SFC auction).

UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 4.3(f)(v), 6.15) read with Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (ss.14, 31, 238) and Indian Contract Act, 1872 (s.128)
UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).clause: 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 (Director's liability for company's electricity dues) vis-a-vis IBC moratorium/resolution-plan discharge
UP-2005::4.3(f)(v).topic: Approval of a CIRP resolution plan and liquidation of the defaulter consumer-company does not extinguish a Director's independent personal-guarantor liability for the company's electricity dues; recovery against the Director under Clause 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 survives

cases.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Approval of a CIRP resolution plan and liquidation of the defaulter consumer-company does not extinguish a Director's independent personal-guarantor liability for the company's electricity dues; recovery against the Director under Clause 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 survives
cases.holding: No. The s.14 IBC moratorium, on its plain text, applies only to the Corporate Debtor and its own assets/proceedings — it has no application to a personal guarantor (State Bank of India v. V. Ramakrishnan). Approval of a resolution plan under s.31 IBC does not ipso facto discharge a personal guarantor's independent, co-extensive liability under s.128 of the Contract Act (Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India); the release of the principal debtor by an involuntary process such as insolvency/liquidation does not absolve the guarantor. Since one of the Company's Directors had furnished a notarized undertaking/affidavit with the application for supply, undertaking to be liable for the Company's dues, and Clauses 4.3(f)(v)/6.15 of the Supply Code empower recovery against Directors as arrears of land revenue under the 1958 Dues Recovery Act, the demand notice against the Directors jointly was not vitiated merely by the Corporate Debtor's insolvency/liquidation. The vires challenge to Clause 4.3(f)(v) was not entertained for want of foundation in the pleadings. Writ petition dismissed.

cases.title: Brijesh Kumar Agrawal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: director-recovery-where-consumer-is-company
cases.holding: On a challenge that clause 4.3(f)(v), which provides that where the defaulting consumer is a company recovery from its directors shall be ensured, is ultra vires section 2(15) of the Electricity Act, 2003 because a director is not the consumer, the Court held that the issue requires consideration, issued notice to the Advocate General, and directed that the recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner-director in the meantime, without restraining recovery of the amount due against the company-consumer.

cases.title: Mukesh Goel v. State of U.P. (stay of recovery pending clause 4.3(f)(v) challenge)
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interim stay of recovery citation pending challenge to clause 4.3(f)(v)
cases.holding: Pending admission of a writ connected with a challenge to clause 4.3(f)(v) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, a recovery citation against the petitioner shall not be enforced; the respondents remain free to recover the same dues from respondent no. 7.

cases.title: Yatendra Singh Panwar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interim stay of recovery pending challenge to clause 4.3(f)(v)
cases.holding: Pending admission of a connected writ challenging clause 4.3(f)(v) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, notice is to issue to the Advocate General and respondent no. 6; a recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner, though the respondents remain free to recover the dues from respondent no. 6.

cases.title: Virendra Verma v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: challenge to cl. 4.3(f)(v); interim stay of recovery citation
cases.holding: Noting that clause 4.3(f)(v) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 was under challenge in connected Writ-C No. 8370 of 2016, the Court connected this writ, issued notice to the Advocate General and respondent no. 7, and directed that the recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner, while leaving it open to the respondents to recover the dues from respondent no. 7.

cases.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interim stay of recovery pending challenge to clause 4.3(f)(v)
cases.holding: Because clause 4.3(f)(v) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 was under challenge in the connected writ, the Court issued notice to the Advocate General and respondent no. 7, directed that the recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner, and left it open to the respondents to recover the dues from respondent no. 7, while connecting and listing the petition.

cases.title: Izharul Hauque v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: Director liability for a company-consumer's dues — vires challenge (interim)
cases.holding: Interlocutory. The challenge to the vires of clause 4.3(f)(v) requires consideration; notice was issued to the Advocate General, and by way of interim protection the recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner-Director, without restraining recovery of the dues against the company (the seventh respondent) in accordance with law.
cases.flag: Interlocutory order; the vires question is not decided. A later order dated 24 February 2023 is a listing order, indicating the matter remained pending.

cases.title: Renu Aggarwal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: interlocutory stay of recovery pending challenge to clause 4.3(f)(v)
cases.holding: Because clause 4.3(f)(v) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 is under challenge in connected Writ-C No. 8370 of 2016, the Court listed this writ with that petition, issued notice to the Advocate General and respondent no. 7, and directed that the recovery citation shall not be enforced against the petitioner in the meantime, while leaving it open to the respondents to recover the dues from respondent no. 7.

cases.title: RKG Industries LLP v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited & 4 Others
cases.topic: Financial-institution-auction sub-clause does not make a claim against the institution the sole recovery route; SARFAESI priority of the secured creditor
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.3(f)(v) merely enables the licensee to lodge a claim with the financial institution that auctioned a company's property; it does not bar recovery of the outstanding dues from the auction purchaser. In any event Section 26-E of the SARFAESI Act gives the secured creditor priority, and the purchaser did not show that the sale consideration exceeded the bank's debt so as to leave a surplus from which the electricity dues could have been met; the licensee could therefore proceed against the purchaser.

cases.title: Vinod Kumar Jaiswal And Another v. State of U.P. And 6 Others
cases.topic: interim stay of recovery against directors pending vires challenge
cases.holding: The Court did not decide the vires. Because the same issue is pending in Writ-C No. 11426 of 2016 (Brijesh Kumar Agarwal), the petitioners (ex-Directors) were given the same interim on 16 March 2021: the recovery citation dated 21.9.2020 shall not be enforced against them; proceedings against the company (respondent no. 7) are not stayed. Later benches continued that interim and listed the writ with connected matters. The last order (16 December 2025) listed the matter for 6 January 2026 after the Advocate General did not appear.
cases.flag: Interlocutory only. No construction of Clause 4.3(f)(v). Vires vis-à-vis s.2(15) left to the connected lead writ.

UP-2005::4.3(f)(vi).clause: 4.3(f)(vi) (landlord's co-extensive liability to clear tenant's electricity dues before tenant vacates) read with 4.4(a)(vi) (owner's consent for new connection)
UP-2005::4.3(f)(vi).topic: A landlord's liability for a tenant's electricity dues becomes co-extensive under Clause 4.3(f)(vi) once the connection was given with the landlord's consent (which may be evidenced by a tenancy-agreement clause, even absent a direct undertaking to the licensee), requiring the landlord to clear arrears before the tenant vacates

cases.title: Smt. Beena Dubey v. M.D. Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.topic: A landlord's liability for a tenant's electricity dues becomes co-extensive under Clause 4.3(f)(vi) once the connection was given with the landlord's consent (which may be evidenced by a tenancy-agreement clause, even absent a direct undertaking to the licensee), requiring the landlord to clear arrears before the tenant vacates
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.4(a)(vi) requires the owner's consent for a new connection; here such consent, while not directly endorsed to the Electricity Department, is evidenced by Clause 5 of the tenancy agreement between the landlord and tenant contemplating the tenant obtaining the connection in his own name and bearing its charges — the landlord accordingly did not object to (and effectively agreed to) the connection. Separately and independently, Clause 4.3(f)(vi) makes the landlord's liability co-extensive with the tenant's for clearing all electricity arrears/dues before the tenant vacates the premises — a liability arising from the Supply Code itself, not from any direct undertaking to the Department. Since the tenant had already vacated without clearing dues, recovery from the landlord was lawful and the recovery proceedings were not quashed, though the landlord retains recourse against the tenant (civil suit, s.138 Negotiable Instruments Act prosecution over a dishonoured cheque, or the licensee's own separate action against the tenant) and may seek installment or other relief available under the Code.

cases.title: Kiran Singh v. State of U.P. and others
cases.topic: landlord liability for tenant dues
cases.holding: Clause 4.3(f)(vi) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 fastens on the landlord a duty to ensure payment of all electricity dues of the tenant before the tenant vacates. Where the landlord consented to a connection in the tenant’s name at premises owned by her, no writ of mandamus will issue to compel a fresh connection at the same premises unless that duty is first discharged; otherwise recovery would be prejudiced and the landlord would circumvent the Code.

UP-2005::4.3(g).topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises

cases.title: Anubhav Jaiswal v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Pro-rata apportionment of arrears on a sub-divided premises
cases.holding: Only his pro-rata share. Though outstanding dues are the first charge on the premises (Clause 4.3(f)(iv)), on a legal sub-division they are apportioned pro-rata (Clause 4.3(g)) and a connection to the sub-divided portion is given on payment of that portion's share alone (Clause 4.3(h)); the licensee cannot demand the whole. The matter is remanded for fresh pro-rata determination after notice to the original owner.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. v. M/s DVS Steels & Alloys Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Electricity dues are not a charge on the premises and cannot be recovered from a transferee absent contract/stipulation, but a distributor may lawfully condition a fresh connection to a sub-divided plot on pro-rata clearance of the predecessor's arrears
cases.holding: (a) No — electricity dues do not constitute a charge on the premises; a transferee with no privity of contract cannot be sued or subjected to revenue recovery for a predecessor's dues, absent a contract to the contrary. (b) Yes — this legal position affords no practical protection to a purchaser seeking a fresh connection: the distributor may validly stipulate, as a condition for supply, that a predecessor's arrears (or, for a legally sub-divided property, the pro-rata share under Clause 4.3(g)/(h)) be cleared first; such a condition is not unreasonable or arbitrary and legitimately protects the distributor against consumers evading dues by selling and relocating. (c) No — the purchaser here voluntarily paid the pro-rata dues as a condition for connection before any Commission order or injunction; a subsequent Commission direction restraining the distributor from *demanding* such payments from future applicants (issued because the predecessor furnished a bank guarantee for its disputed liability) did not itself direct refund of amounts already paid, and the purchaser — having paid pursuant to its own undertaking to obtain connection — is estopped from reclaiming it except on the agreed terms (i.e., refundable only if the predecessor's liability is ultimately negated or the predecessor actually clears the dues).

cases.title: Shri Balajee Laboratories v. Executive Engineer
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-sub-divided-premises-outstanding-dues
cases.holding: Quoting clause 4.3(h) (new connection to sub-divided premises only after the applicant pays the share of outstanding dues attributed to those premises), the Court held the U.P. Power Corporation was not without power to recover such amount from the transferee-petitioner; there was no inconsistency with Hanuman Rice Mills; the Corporation's claim suffered from no infirmity; the writ was dismissed without costs.
cases.flag: Court applied 4.3(h) (sub-divided premises) to a transferee/previous-owner dues challenge; 4.3(f) is the usual analogue and was not cited.

UP-2005::4.35.topic: examination of bills and restoration after temporary disconnection

cases.title: Satyapal Singh v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: examination of bills and restoration after temporary disconnection
cases.holding: On a consumer's challenge to a bill and prayer for restoration after deposit following a temporary-disconnection notice, the Court, having perused Clauses 4.35 and 4.36 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, disposed of the writ by directing the concerned officer to examine the grievance as to bills and restoration of supply (if not permanently disconnected) and pass an appropriate order within six weeks.

UP-2005::4.36.topic: Deemed-disconnection plea does not defeat a theft assessment in a writ where unauthorised drawing continued; left for the appeal

cases.title: Ashok Kumar Ajmera v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Deemed-disconnection plea does not defeat a theft assessment in a writ where unauthorised drawing continued; left for the appeal
cases.holding: Not in this writ. The petitioner contended that, having paid nothing after 29.12.2006, his connection stood deemed temporarily and then permanently disconnected under Clauses 4.36, 4.37 and 4.38 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, so no theft liability could be fastened on him. The Court did not accept this as a basis to interfere: he was found to be unauthorisedly drawing electricity even after disconnection, a theft case was registered and a final assessment order passed. The deemed-disconnection contention was expressly left open to be raised as a ground in the Section 127 appeal.

UP-2005::4.37.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default

cases.title: Harihar Cold Storage v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
cases.topic: Minimum-guarantee charges on temporary disconnection — only for consumer's default
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.37 permits minimum-charge billing on a temporary disconnection only where the disconnection is on account of the consumer's default; here the disconnection was due to a burnt transformer the licensee failed to repair for about five months (breaching Clause 7.07's 24-hour restoration / 15-day replacement norms), so no minimum-guarantee charges lie. Where no fixed minimum sum is committed, minimum-guarantee charges require the licensee to ensure the minimum guaranteed supply.

cases.title: Parvati Devi v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.topic: Clauses 4.37 and 4.38 empower the licensee to permanently disconnect after six months of unremedied temporary disconnection; a consumer who disputes the bill cannot compel that step in writ
cases.holding: The licensee is empowered by Clauses 4.37 and 4.38 to permanently disconnect a line that was temporarily disconnected, where the cause has not been removed (Clause 4.37(a): minimum-charge billing after TD, Annexure 4.9 notice, permanent disconnection after six months, then dormant connection and a final account; Clause 4.38(b): PD if the cause is not removed within six months). Whether the consumer can compel the licensee to exercise that power is not a question for consideration in a writ petition in which the bill itself is disputed. The petition, which sought a recast bill from inception without fixed charges after TD and without surcharge, and quashing of the 20.02.2026 bill, was dismissed.

cases.title: Smt. Rani Agrawal v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: minimum-charges-temporary-disconnection
cases.holding: Whether minimum charges under clause 4.37 are payable for a period of Apex Court-ordered disconnection, when the connection was not permanently disconnected and no energy was supplied, raises disputed questions of fact that cannot be decided in writ. The petitioners may move the Appropriate Authority/Consumer Forum within two weeks; that authority shall decide the representation by a reasoned speaking order within four months and, if filed in time, without examining limitation.
cases.flag: Respondent cited cl. 4.37 as the source of minimum charges on temporary (non-permanent) disconnection; the Court did not examine or apply the clause.

cases.title: Surbeer Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: minimum charges after disconnection
cases.holding: Read with Regulation 17 of the Electricity Supply Consumer Regulations, 1984, clauses 4.37 and 4.38 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 were treated as limiting the period for which minimum charges may be recovered after disconnection to seven or eight months, and recovery on the 11.11.2009 citation was stayed on that interlocutory footing. The writ was later dismissed in default without a merits determination.
cases.flag: Court cites 4.37 and 4.38 together with 1984 Regulation 17 for a seven-or-eight-month cap without isolating which clause supplies that period.

cases.title: Ex. Eng. E.D.D. Dakshinanchal V.V. Nigam Ltd. v. Jagdish Verma
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: permanent disconnection on consumer request
cases.holding: Permanent disconnection under Clause 4.38 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 may be made on the request of the consumer. An application in the name of a person who had died in 1985, acted on the same day without verifying genuineness or calling for a report of outstanding dues, is not in accordance with that procedure. The Permanent Lok Adalat's award directing restoration of the connection therefore called for no interference, and the licensee's writ was dismissed.
cases.flag: Counsel referred to the provision as Section 38 of the Code; the Court cited Clause 4.38.

cases.title: Mohd. Asif v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: permanent disconnection grounds
cases.holding: A connection once granted may be disconnected only in accordance with clause 4.38. That clause does not contemplate disconnection for a property-ownership dispute, and none of its grounds were attracted on the licensee's case that the consumer's father had produced documents denying the consumer's title.

cases.title: Sagufta Ishrar v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: permanent disconnection
cases.holding: On a consumer's prayer to finalize permanent disconnection under clause 4.38 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the High Court directed the licensee to inspect the meter at the consumer's residence in her presence, intimate pending dues, and, upon payment within three weeks of knowledge of those dues, permanently disconnect the electricity line.

cases.title: Petitioner v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. and Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: permanent disconnection after temporary disconnection
cases.holding: On a prayer for mandamus directing permanent disconnection from the date of temporary disconnection under Clause 4.38(i)(b), the Court did not decide whether the licensee is bound to permanently disconnect after six months of temporary disconnection. It disposed of the writ by permitting the petitioner to make a representation to the Executive Engineer, EDD-1, PuVVNL, Allahabad, who shall consider and decide it by a reasoned speaking order after notice and hearing, preferably within one month.

cases.title: Bipin Kumar Tripathi v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited & Another
cases.topic: Special sympathetic reduction of arrears with no-dues certificate; not a construction of Clauses 4.36/4.38 or s.56
cases.holding: The Court did not decide the disconnection-duty or s.56 grounds. On the petitioner offering to pay some amount under a one-time settlement and the licensee stating that 50% could be waived, it directed deposit of Rs. 50,000 of outstanding bills of Rs. 1,19,850 on or before 30.05.2026. After deposit the concerned officer is to pass an order within two weeks, settle the excess after accepting Rs. 50,000 as a genuine amount, and issue a no-dues certificate. The Court took a sympathetic view because the father had died in 2018 and the premises were not in occupation; if anyone used electricity without authorisation, the petitioner should not in this case be saddled with the entire dues.
cases.flag: Petitioner cited Clauses 4.36 and 4.38 (order dated 6.6.2024) and s.56 of the Electricity Act, 2003. Clause 4.36 is not a catalog key (catalog has 4.37 and 4.38). The operative order of 14.05.2026 cites no clause number.

cases.title: Satish Kumar @ Yatish Sharma v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Consecutive default requires TDC then PDC within six months; post-TDC billing is limited to that period; 2016-disconnection claim not proved
cases.holding: No. Licensee's counsel admitted that under the 2005 Code the licensee ought to carry out temporary disconnection on consecutive default in payment, followed by permanent disconnection within six months. On the records, TDC was in September 2022 and billing was only for the subsequent six months because of deemed PDC. The petitioner conceded he had no evidence of a 2016 disconnection. Outstanding dues of Rs. 1,52,261 plus surcharge Rs. 99,723.82 were reduced under OTS to Rs. 1,52,261. By consent the petitioner is to pay that sum in six equal monthly installments, the first due on 30 September 2024 and the rest by the end of each succeeding month; default lapses the order and the department may proceed in accordance with law.
cases.flag: The Court did not number the clause. Listing orders of 1.8.2024 and 14.8.2024 recorded the licensee's admission of the TDC-then-PDC-within-six-months duty; the 3.9.2024 order applies that admission to the September 2022 TDC and six-month billing. Keyed to Clauses 4.37/4.38 as the pattern that matches; Clause 4.36 (TDC for non-payment) is not a catalog key.

UP-2005::4.39.clause: 4.39 r/w second proviso to Section 135(1A), Electricity Act, 2003
UP-2005::4.39.topic: After a permanent disconnection recorded on theft allegations, reconnection or fresh connection is available under Clause 4.39 r/w the second proviso to Section 135(1A); the authority is directed to consider the request, subject to clearance of dues

cases.title: Satya Prakash Singhal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: After a permanent disconnection recorded on theft allegations, reconnection or fresh connection is available under Clause 4.39 r/w the second proviso to Section 135(1A); the authority is directed to consider the request, subject to clearance of dues
cases.holding: Such provisions are available and the matter is remitted for consideration. The connection's status was recorded as 'PDC final'. The Court did not order automatic restoration on the strength of the discharge; on perusing Clause 4.39 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 read with the second proviso to sub-section (1A) of Section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003, it found that provisions for reconnection or fresh connection in the event of permanent disconnection are available under those provisions. It therefore disposed of the writ with a direction to respondent no.3 to consider the petitioner's request in the light of those provisions - either by reconnecting and restoring the connection or by granting a fresh connection in accordance with law - within six weeks of production of a certified copy of the order, provided the petitioner has cleared off all dues pending against him.
cases.flag: Order-sheet of 11 pages, dated orders from 3.4.2012 to the operative disposal of 5.3.2014, no printed page numbers; pins are order dates. The 5.3.2014 recall order refers to the want-of-prosecution dismissal as 'dated 6.11.2012', whereas that dismissal order is itself dated 6.11.2013 in the record - an apparent slip.

cases.title: Mohd. Asif v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reconnection after permanent disconnection
cases.holding: The consumer was directed to apply to the Executive Engineer for reconnection under clause 4.39 or any other relevant provision. The Executive Engineer shall consider that application in accordance with law, preferably within six weeks of filing, after hearing the concerned parties including the consumer's father.

cases.title: Dharmendra Kumar Kesarwani v. Purwanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: reconnection application after disconnection
cases.holding: A grievance seeking reconnection of a disconnected supply, including where a provisional bill has been paid and an FIR lodged, is to be redressed under Clause 4.39 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, by the competent authority considering the reconnection application; the High Court will not itself grant reconnection on the writ.
cases.flag: Order cites Clause 4.39 generally, without specifying sub-clause (b).

cases.title: Smt. Neelam Jaiswal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: instalments after disconnection for unpaid bills
cases.holding: The writ was disposed without directing restoration or instalments. The petitioner was left free to seek instalments of the unpaid bills under clause 4.39 of the Supply Code, as stated by the licensee.
cases.flag: order cites clause 4.39 generally, not 4.39(b)

cases.title: Harish Agrawal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reconnection after temporary disconnection
cases.holding: Regulation 4.39(b), which provides that supply shall be reconnected after the cause of disconnection has been removed, is an enabling clause for the benefit of the person whose supply was temporarily disconnected. It does not bar the licensee from restoring supply by another mechanism if the licensee is protected in relation to payment of the bills.

cases.title: Manoj Kumar v. State of U.P. — permanent disconnection bars reconnection
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: reconnection after permanent disconnection
cases.holding: A permanently disconnected connection cannot be reconnected under the Supply Code; the consumer must apply for a new connection. The 10.08.2023 direction that DVVNL reconnect supply on deposit of Rs 1,80,000 is modified: if the petitioner deposits that amount within one month and applies for a new connection, the Executive Engineer, EDD-II, DVVNL, Aligarh shall take necessary steps. Modification application disposed; writ listed before the appropriate Bench and not treated as tied up; interim order continues.
cases.flag: order cites clause 4.39 without a sub-clause; the PD/new-connection rule is 4.39(b)

UP-2005::4.4.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent

cases.title: Anand Kumar v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant's connection on an indemnity bond absent owner's consent
cases.holding: Following Seema Mansoor, an occupier (including a tenant) has a statutory right to supply under Sections 42-43 read with Clause 4.4; where the owner's consent is unavailable, the tenant may file an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) to obtain the connection.

cases.title: Devendra Sharma v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Clause 4.4 governs new connections, not disconnection over a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 applies to new-connection applications, not to disconnecting an existing connection. A landlord-tenant dispute is not a ground to cut a valid connection on which bills are paid; a connection may be disconnected only on grounds authorised by the Act/Code (theft, unauthorised use, non-payment). The disconnection here was illegal, arbitrary and malafide, and offended Article 21.

cases.title: Divya Sahani v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: Pendency of a property dispute is not a ground to refuse/disconnect a connection
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 does not prohibit a connection because of a pending property dispute; Clause 4.4(a)(i) only requires that a court-order copy be furnished where ownership is in litigation. A connection is not proof of title (Note-3, Annexure 4.1). Disconnection solely for the pendency of a suit is dehors the law and violates Article 21; mandamus issued to grant the connection.

cases.title: Gaurav Sharma v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Connection to a genuine occupier on an indemnity bond, without the owner's NOC
cases.holding: No. Section 43(1) confers on an occupier a statutory right to supply; Clause 4.4 read with Annexure 4.2 lets a genuine occupier unable to obtain the owner's NOC furnish an indemnity bond and obtain a connection. The object of the bond is only to exclude a trespasser/house-grabber; a family dispute or want of the owner's consent is no ground to refuse. Refusal quashed and remitted for reconsideration.

cases.title: Husna Bano v. State of U.P. & 9 Others
cases.topic: Tenant/occupier's connection on an indemnity bond amid a landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: No. Annexure 4.2 (Clause 4.4) enables an occupier who cannot obtain the owner's NOC to obtain a connection on an indemnity bond; possession can be shown by a Ration Card and Aadhaar (cash rent often leaving no receipt). The bond is not a document of title, and a connection does not bar an eviction suit; the landlord's refusal of NOC is no ground to deny supply. Refusal set aside and remitted for reconsideration.

cases.title: Mohd. Ashfaq Khan @ Ashfaq Khan v. State of U.P. thru. Addl. Chief Secy., Energy Deptt., Lucknow & 3 Others
cases.topic: An occupant/tenant whose connection was disconnected at the instance of a transferee-owner may seek a fresh connection under Clause 4.4 by furnishing an indemnity bond and proof of possession, subject to licensee inspection and without prejudice to the parties' civil rights
cases.holding: The petitioner was directed to apply for an electricity connection with an indemnity bond and proof of possession under Clause 4.4; the licensee may inspect to verify possession (hearing the transferee-owner in the process), and if there is no legal impediment and possession is proved, the connection shall be granted — without prejudice to either party's rights to pursue separate proceedings regarding possession/title.

cases.title: Ashwani Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: landlord-objection-before-tenant-connection
cases.holding: The distribution licensee shall not grant an electricity connection to persons claiming tenancy of the petitioner's premises without first considering the landlord's objection already filed before the Executive Engineer.
cases.flag: Order cites the Electricity Supply Code generally for landlord no-objection on tenanted premises; no clause number is given.

cases.title: Priya Tiwari v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: tenant connection — landlord NOC
cases.holding: Without a landlord no-objection certificate, a tenant’s writ for an electricity connection is not granted. Under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 a tenant may apply in his own name only after the landlord’s NOC. A valid application accompanied by that certificate shall be considered and decided by the distribution corporation in accordance with law.

cases.title: Priya Prem v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. & 4 Others
cases.topic: A new-connection grievance (including a s.43(3) penalty claim) is routed through the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum rather than decided directly in writ jurisdiction
cases.holding: The petitioner was directed to file a representation before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum (presided over by the Sub Divisional Officer, Electricity Urban Distribution, Sub Division-IX Raptinagar, Gorakhpur) within two weeks; the Forum was directed to decide the representation within four weeks of receipt, by a reasoned order after affording the petitioner a hearing.

cases.title: Seema Mansoor v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & 3 Others
cases.topic: A tenant/occupier cannot be refused a new electricity connection solely for want of the landlord's consent, since the Supply Code provides an alternative indemnity-bond route (Annexure 4.2) precisely for such situations; refusing connection on landlord-consent grounds alone nullifies Rent Control Act protections and is against public policy
cases.holding: No. Section 43 of the Electricity Act, 2003 obliges the licensee to supply electricity to any owner OR occupier (a term the Supply Code, Clause 2.2(oo), defines to include an authorised person in occupation, i.e. a tenant) making a proper application. While Clause 4.4(a)(i) of the Code lists owner's consent (Annexure 4.3) among required documents, the Code simultaneously provides Annexure 4.2 — an indemnity bond specifically designed for the situation where 'the intending consumer is not the owner' and 'is not able to obtain the consent' of the owner — as an alternative route, indemnifying the licensee against loss/claims from the owner, recoverable under the Revenue Recovery Act if needed. Reading the Code holistically, a tenant cannot be denied connection merely for lack of landlord consent; to hold otherwise would let an unscrupulous landlord (here, one in an ongoing rent dispute who had already gotten the existing connection disconnected to pressure the tenant to vacate) defeat Rent Control Act protections by simply withholding consent — an interpretation contrary to both the statutory scheme and public policy. Two prior Division Bench rulings to the contrary (Ravi Shankar Giri; the Iftikhar Ahsan/Tanveer Azam line) were held not to lay down correct law, having overlooked ss.42/43 of the Act and Clause 4.4(a)(i)/Annexure 4.2 of the Code. Mandamus issued directing the licensee to consider and grant connection to the petitioner-tenant, subject to a proper application, indemnity bond, and fulfilment of other requirements.

cases.title: Hem Chand Saini v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection on occupancy and indemnity despite disputed title
cases.holding: Where applicants are prima facie in occupancy of the premises and are prepared to furnish an indemnity bond, applications for a new electricity connection are to be entertained and considered under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and a permanent or temporary connection may be granted notwithstanding that the underlying lease is disputed and under litigation; want of proof of ownership is not a ground to refuse to process the application. The Sub-Divisional Officer was directed to take steps for providing the connections subject to the writ and the indemnity required by the rules.

cases.title: Smt. Chandra Kala Singh v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupier connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 provides for a provisional connection to an intending consumer who is not the owner, on execution of an indemnity bond as per Annexure 4.2, with proof of occupancy (valid power of attorney, latest rent-paid receipt, or registered lease deed) where landlord consent cannot be obtained. Denial of a new connection solely because a civil case is pending between tenant and landlord is not warranted. The SDO was directed to inspect and, if the petitioner is the occupier, sanction the connection provisionally on the indemnity bond within two weeks.

cases.title: Sunil Kumar Srivastava v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Where a tenant seeks independent supply after the landlady applies for permanent disconnection, the licensee is to consider the occupant's application under Clause 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, including an indemnity bond, and pass an appropriate order; the Court does not itself grant the connection.

cases.title: Gajanand Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: tenant/occupier entitlement to fresh connection
cases.holding: A tenant seeking a fresh electricity connection after disconnection is entitled only if he fulfils the criteria in Clause 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. Occupancy rights remain for the pending landlord-tenant suit. The application must be in the prescribed form; the Executive Engineer is to decide after putting the landlord to notice.

cases.title: Ram Surat v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: indemnity bond; disputed title; tube-well restoration
cases.holding: Pending a civil title suit and a revenue partition, the High Court will not direct restoration of a permanently disconnected tube-well supply. If the consumer obtains interim permission from the court seised of the dispute, the Electricity Department shall consider a temporary or indemnity-bond connection under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 so the tube well can run until the dispute is decided.
cases.flag: Order cites only ‘relevant clauses’ of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 for the indemnity-bond path; it does not number 4.4.

cases.title: Rajesh Kumar Gupta v. U.P.P.C.L.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection — indemnity bond / landlord-tenant
cases.holding: A writ challenging denial of an electricity connection in a landlord–tenant dispute is disposed of by directing the concerned officer to consider the petitioner's request in accordance with law and Clause 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, after putting the landlord and tenant to notice, preferably within six weeks; the Court does not itself grant the connection or decide the indemnity-bond issue.

cases.title: Ajay Kumar Gupta v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: new connection — occupancy dispute
cases.holding: Where a new-connection application is made for premises whose occupancy is disputed between the applicant and his brother, the writ court will not determine occupancy or direct supply. The Executive Engineer must hear the disputing parties and pass appropriate orders in accordance with the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, within three months of production of a certified copy of the order.

cases.title: Sneha Devi v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupant connection; notice to landlord
cases.holding: The Executive Engineer's power under Clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 must be exercised after putting the landlord to notice. A tenant's pending application for connection in tenanted premises is to be decided under that clause, preferably within two months of production of a certified copy of the order.

cases.title: Smt. Mahendri Devi v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: tenant connection without landlord permission
cases.holding: Where a tenant seeks a new connection and the SDO has reported that supply cannot be granted for want of the landlord’s permission, the Executive Engineer must hear the landlord and pass appropriate orders keeping in view clause 4.4 read with annexure 4.1 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, within six weeks of production of a certified copy; the writ court will not itself grant or refuse the connection.

cases.title: Gopal Babu v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: mutation
cases.holding: The Court directed the competent authority to treat the petitioner's application to mutate a connection standing in his father's name as an application under paragraph 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and to decide it by a reasoned and speaking order after hearing, within four weeks. The Court did not grant mutation or a connection on merits.
cases.flag: ambiguous_clause

cases.title: Rakesh Srivastava v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: processing of new domestic connection application
cases.holding: Clauses 4.4 and 4.8 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 contain sufficient provisions to cover a request for a domestic connection. The writ petitioner is left to pursue the application, and the competent authority shall take action in accordance with law.

cases.title: Allahabad U.P. Gramin Bank v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: new connection — compliance then consideration
cases.holding: Where a consumer seeks a decision on an application for a new electric connection, the Court may dispose of the writ by permitting compliance with clauses 4.4 and 4.8 of the 2005 Supply Code, after which the licensee shall consider the application in accordance with law expeditiously.

cases.title: Deep Mohan Agarwal v. District Magistrate, G.B. Nagar
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: independent connection for non-owner occupant on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Where supply has been cut off amid a dispute between co-occupants and the intending consumer is not the owner, the writ court will not decide disconnection or entitlement on merits. The occupant may apply in the prescribed form for an independent connection under clause 4.4 of the 2005 Code (indemnity bond by a non-owner intending consumer); the distribution licensee shall examine the application in accordance with law, decide preferably within 15 days after hearing the parties including the co-occupant, and provide the connection expeditiously if entitlement is found. The impugned order shall abide by that decision.

cases.title: Sachchidanand v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: A writ of mandamus directing a new electric connection will not issue where the applicant has not moved a prescribed-form application (Annexure 4.1) complete in all respects, with the registration-cum-processing fee and requisite documents, under Clause 4.4; a plain request for connection is not compliance, and dismissal of the writ does not bar a subsequent Clause 4.4 application, after which Clause 4.7 governs the processing timeframe.

cases.title: Keshav Dev Tyagi v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: The 2005 Code is a complete Code. A new connection is to be obtained under Clause 4.4, with the time schedule in Clause 4.7. Where the petitioners have not moved the required application, the High Court will not grant mandamus in writ jurisdiction; they remain free to pursue the Code remedy.

cases.title: Vijaya Bhusan v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: new-connection-application
cases.holding: The U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, read with the Electricity Act, 2003, is a self-contained code. An applicant for a fresh electricity connection must fulfill the requirements of clause 4.4. Where the form, on a prima facie view, does not satisfy those prerequisites, the writ court will not compel acceptance of the application; the licensee is only to look into the claim and decide it in accordance with law if a complete clause 4.4 application is submitted.

cases.title: Abhisek Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection — indemnity bond and time-bound consideration
cases.holding: A writ seeking a new electricity connection will not itself grant supply where Supply Code formalities, including the indemnity bond under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, remain incomplete. If the applicant completes those formalities within two weeks, the licensee shall consider and decide the application within two weeks thereafter; any rejection must be by speaking order communicated within one further week.
cases.flag: Order requires an indemnity bond under the Supply Code, 2005 but does not number the clause.

cases.title: Harpreet Singh Bedi v. U.P.P.C.L. — co-sharer NOC for fresh connection remitted to EE
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: fresh-connection-co-sharer-no-objection
cases.holding: Without construing whether clause 4.4 requires a no-objection from co-sharers for a fresh connection, the Court granted liberty to represent the claim to the Executive Engineer, Division Gajraula, District Amroha, who is to decide it in accordance with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 preferably within two months of receipt of a certified copy.

cases.title: Kranti Kumar Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: fresh-connection-application
cases.holding: A consumer seeking a fresh electricity connection may apply afresh to the concerned authority with the documents contemplated by clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. If such an application is made, the authority shall consider and decide it within two weeks of presentation. The writ was disposed on those terms without directing that a connection be granted.
cases.flag: Cited as Section 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Vikram Agrawal v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new connection — indemnity bond where title is disputed
cases.holding: An applicant refused a new connection for want of proved title, and because a civil dispute is pending, may apply afresh with a duly executed indemnity bond in the form of Annexure 4.2 to Clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the licensee shall then scrutinise the application and pass appropriate orders, and the earlier refusal stands ineffective. No connection is directed on the merits.

cases.title: Vijay Kumar Tiwari v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: A tenant’s writ for commercial and domestic connection was disposed of with liberty to apply on the prescribed Supply Code format. If the landlord refuses the no-objection certificate required by Clause 4.4, the occupant shall be permitted to furnish an indemnity bond in conformity with Annexure 4.2 after depositing the requisite fee, and the licensee is to pass appropriate orders on a timely application.

cases.title: Vandana Srivastava v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: Clean hands required; concealment of an adverse civil finding on tenancy bars writ relief
cases.holding: No. Although the distribution licensee was not a party to the suit and no connection relief was sought there, the trial court's finding on the petitioner's status as tenant is relevant to the writ grievance, at least for interim relief. Suppression of that material fact means the petitioner did not approach the Court with clean hands, and the writ court will not interfere; the petition is dismissed.

cases.title: Hari Om v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitaran Nigam Limited
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: mandamus to decide application/objection
cases.holding: A writ of mandamus commanding the licensee to decide the consumer's 17.03.2018 application/objection as per clause 4.4 (I & IV) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 was refused: on perusal of the petition the Court found no ground entitling the petitioner to that relief, dismissed the writ, and vacated any interim order.
cases.flag: Prayer cites 'Section 4.4 (I & IV)' in roman capitals; recorded as pleaded, not recast as 4.4(i)/(iv).

cases.title: Shahina Parveen v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: tenant/occupier new connection
cases.holding: Mandamus to compel a tenant's new connection under clauses 4.4 and 4.5 was not granted on merits. The Court directed the petitioner to apply afresh to the Executive Engineer with supporting papers, and directed that authority to consider and decide the application in accordance with law by a speaking order within two weeks of receipt.

cases.title: Akash Joshi v. State of U.P. — tenant connection relegated to clause 4.4
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-forum
cases.holding: A person seeking electricity connection, including a tenant, must ventilate the claim before the appropriate forum under clause 4.4 of the Uttar Pradesh Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the High Court will not issue mandamus for connection in the first instance. If an application under clause 4.4 is filed, the concerned authority shall take action expeditiously.

cases.title: Smt. Sunita Kalra v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: tenant connection despite pending rent-release proceedings
cases.holding: An admitted tenant is entitled to an electricity connection under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 notwithstanding a pending landlord application under Section 21 of the U.P. Act XIII of 1972 for release of the tenanted shop. The licensee must consider and grant the connection on an application made in the prescribed manner, an indemnity bond as contemplated by Clause 4.4 read with Annexure 4.2, and fulfilment of the other requirements of the Code.

cases.title: Pramod Kumar Sharma v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond despite landlord-tenant dispute
cases.holding: Where the licensee withholds a new connection because of a landlord-tenant dispute over the premises, the Executive Engineer is directed to consider and grant the connection subject to the applicant applying under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, furnishing the indemnity bond contemplated by Clause 4.4 and Annexure 4.2, and fulfilling the other requirements of the Code.

cases.title: Yogesh Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: non-owner occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Without deciding entitlement, the Executive Engineer was directed to dispose of the intending consumer's pending representation for a new connection within two weeks, keeping in view Clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and Annexure 4.2, which prescribe the procedure for a provisional connection to a non-owner occupant on execution of an indemnity bond and production of proof of occupancy (valid power of attorney, latest rent-paid receipt, or registered lease deed) where landlord consent cannot be obtained. Police assistance may be sought from the local SHO if required.

cases.title: Dr. Mamta Tripathi v. State of U.P. & 6 Ors.
cases.topic: Occupier's connection on an indemnity bond where the owner's consent is unavailable
cases.holding: Yes. Clause 4.4, which aids the s.43 statutory duty to supply, provides that where an occupier cannot produce the owner's consent — especially in an owner-occupier dispute — a connection may be granted on furnishing an Indemnity Bond (Annexure 4.2). Absence of the landlord's consent is therefore no bar; the authority must process the tenant's application on that basis, subject to her fulfilling the other legal requirements.

cases.title: Teena Sehgal v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Occupier's connection on an indemnity bond, conditioned on clearing the portion's dues
cases.holding: Yes, on conditions. The petitioner residing on the ground floor (undisputed) is entitled to a connection, but not without paying the dues attributable to that portion. The Court fixed the ground-floor liability at Rs. 1,20,000 (50% in two weeks, balance in four instalments), required an Indemnity Bond (Annexure 4.2) for her ground-floor residence and payment of regular bills, and directed the authority to provide the new connection on the 50% payment and completion of formalities.

cases.title: Deepak Jain v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Tenant's connection: owner's consent letter OR indemnity bond
cases.holding: No. A lessee/tenant/occupier cannot be refused a connection merely for want of the landlord's consent; under Clause 4.4 read with Annexures 4.2 and 4.3, the application is considered either on a consent letter of the owner or, in its absence, on an Indemnity Bond furnished by the tenant. The competent authority must decide the tenant's application within four weeks after hearing the stakeholders.

cases.title: Iftakhar Ahsan v. State of U.P. and others
cases.topic: Owner's consent is a mandatory pre-condition for a new connection to an occupier/tenant
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4(a)(vi) of the 2005 Code makes the owner's consent mandatory for a new supply connection to an occupier. A pre-2005 precedent (Rajesh Kumar Gupta) decided under the then-existing provisions does not aid the petitioner, and the Code provision was neither challenged nor its consent requirement satisfied; the landlord was also not impleaded. Accordingly no mandamus could issue, and the petition was consigned to records with liberty to approach the appropriate authority or seek remedy in the pending suit.

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Permanent Lok Adalat and Another
cases.topic: Occupier's new connection requires proof of occupancy plus indemnity bond; Lok Adalat cannot order otherwise
cases.holding: The Permanent Lok Adalat has jurisdiction over such a public-utility grievance (in addition to, not in derogation of, the Act's fora), but it cannot direct action contrary to law. Section 43 obliges the licensee to supply an owner or occupier; under Clause 4.4 a non-owner occupier may apply on an indemnity bond (Annexure 4.2) instead of the owner's consent (Annexure 4.3), but must produce proof of occupancy (valid power of attorney / latest rent receipt / registered lease deed). As the applicant was not the owner (property in his father's name, civil suit pending) and furnished no proof of occupancy, the award directing a connection on a mere indemnity bond was contrary to Clause 4.4 and was quashed, with liberty to apply afresh in compliance with the Code.

cases.title: Smt. Sushama Chowdhary v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. thru. Chairman & 4 Ors.
cases.topic: Occupier's connection on an indemnity bond where the owner's consent is unavailable in an owner-occupier dispute
cases.holding: No. Clause 4.4 is in aid of the Section 43 duty to supply, and Annexure 4.2 provides expressly for the case of an occupier who cannot produce the owner's consent — the paradigm being an owner-occupier dispute. Having furnished an indemnity bond describing herself as occupier unable to obtain consent because of pending litigation, the petitioner could not be refused a connection by an order that merely referred to Clause 4.4 without reasons; such an order shows total non-application of mind and unawareness of the Section 43 obligation. The rejection was quashed, the licensee directed not to insist on the owner's consent, and the connection ordered to be granted on a fresh indemnity bond within ten days.

cases.title: Mohd. Rizvan v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant/occupier's application for a connection refused for want of the owner's NOC; disposal by direction to decide in light of Gaurav Sharma
cases.holding: The Court, without expressing any opinion on the merits, disposed of the petition by directing the licensee to take a final call on the petitioner's pending representation strictly in accordance with law and taking into account the Division Bench in Gaurav Sharma — which holds that a genuine occupier who is not the owner is entitled to a connection under the Code by furnishing an Annexure 4.2 indemnity bond in aid of Clause 4.4, and that a connection cannot be declined merely because the landlord refuses an NOC in a landlord-tenant dispute — within three months.

cases.title: Sanjay Kumar v. State of U.P. & Another
cases.topic: Transfer of a connection is by prescribed-form application to the Executive Engineer under Clause 4.4; the writ court will not itself transfer on a representation to the supply company
cases.holding: He must apply in the prescribed form to the Executive Engineer. The Court recorded that the proper authority is the Executive Engineer and that the procedure stands provided in Clause 4.4. A fresh application is to be properly made to the Executive Engineer in terms of that procedure. If it is duly made, it is to be considered for necessary action to transfer. The petitioner needs to fulfill all the requirements. Writ disposed of.
cases.flag: The Court cited Clause 4.4 as the licensee put it. Mutation/transfer of an existing connection is more typically Clause 4.44 (SCJ-174, SCJ-196: Executive Engineer; arrears to be cleared). Recorded, not merged. The order does not mention arrears, indemnity, or owner's consent.

cases.title: Shabanam Begam v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Tenant connection without landlord consent — Clause 4.4 indemnity and 4.4(vii) prepaid raised; not applied; landlord's son added; listed
cases.holding: No construction of Clause 4.4. The licensee submitted that supply can be given on indemnity where the tenant cannot obtain landlord consent, that arrears then attach to the premises, and that prepaid connection under 4.4(vii) is for jhuggi/hutment/patri shopkeepers, whereas the petitioner wants a regular connection. The Court added Akash Gaurav (son of the deceased landlord) as respondent no.4, granted leave to amend, and listed 22 May 2026 as fresh. No direction to give the connection.
cases.flag: Interlocutory only. Clause 4.4 indemnity (SCJ-006, SCJ-027 occupier-on-indemnity cluster) and 4.4(vii) prepaid were invoked by the licensee, not applied. The tension — indemnity without consent vs arrears attaching to the landlord's premises — is on the table, not decided.

cases.title: Ashish Pal v. State of U.P. and others
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Clause 4.4 of Chapter 4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 permits a new connection to a person who lacks standard ownership proofs, or who seeks supply as a tenant without the landlord's consent, on the indemnity form in Annexure-4.2. Where a status-quo order is operating and the occupant offers that indemnity, the licensee shall, on receipt of the form, consider and grant the connection in accordance with law. The petitioner was given two weeks to furnish the form; the authority four further weeks to grant supply.

cases.title: Lalit Kumar Tripathi v. State of U.P. and 5 Others
cases.topic: Occupier in possession (not a tenant) — connection on Clause 4.4 indemnity; subject to pending s.145 petition; no NOC from rival claimant
cases.holding: Respondent no. 5 is directed to consider the petitioner's application for an electricity connection if there is no legal impediment, provided he submits the indemnity form required under Clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, within two weeks. The connection is subject to the final outcome of the pending petition. The Court recorded that possession of the ground floor was not disputed and that the petitioner was not shown to be a tenant so as to require a no-objection from the first-floor occupant claiming to be sole owner. Disconnection had been only upon the SDM's order in the s.145 CrPC matter.
cases.flag: The writ prayer is restoration of a disconnected first-floor connection; the operative direction is to consider a fresh application on a Clause 4.4 indemnity. The body discusses ground-floor possession. Section 145 is CrPC 1973 (possession proceedings), not EA2003 s.145; catalog EA2003::145 / 4.44 / 4.49 hits are false positives and were not used.

cases.title: Afzal Ahmad v. State of U.P. Thru. Secy. Energy, Lucknow and Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: On the licensee's statement that an indemnity bond under Clause 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 would remove any objection to a new supply, a pending property dispute is not a ground to refuse a domestic connection. The rejection dated 3 February 2026 is set aside and the Executive Engineer, Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Limited, is directed to grant a fresh connection within one week of a complete application with Clause 4.4 compliance.

cases.title: Jayant Singh v. Pradeep Kumar Verma
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: occupancy certificate required in addition to indemnity bond; contempt of conditional connection writ
cases.holding: No. The 24.08.2023 writ in Writ-C No. 7126 of 2023 directed the competent officer to provide the connection within two weeks if the applicant completed the formalities. An indemnity bond under Clause 4.4 does not by itself complete those formalities. On the affidavit of compliance the Court found that the occupancy certificate had not been provided. The contempt application is disposed of with liberty to furnish the occupancy certificate in accordance with Clause 4.4 read with Annexure 4.2 of the Code, 2005. If the required formalities are completed, the opposite party is expected to ensure compliance with the writ.
cases.flag: Contempt disposal. The Court used 'occupancy certificate' without listing the Clause 4.4 occupancy proofs (power of attorney / rent receipt / registered lease). Annexure 4.2 is the indemnity-bond proforma; the Court read it with Clause 4.4 as requiring occupancy proof as well as the bond. The writ was already conditional on completing formalities. No finding of wilful disobedience.

cases.title: Gudiya @ Sapna v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: owner NOC for connection
cases.holding: Paragraph 4.4 of the Electricity Supply Code 2005 provides that an electricity connection cannot be given without a no-objection certificate from the owner of the premises. The review applicants produced none and showed no error apparent on the face of the 21.09.2024 dismissal of their writ seeking restoration or a new connection without that NOC. Review rejected.

cases.title: Smt. Uma Chauhan v. State of U.P. And 2 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Tenant/occupier entitled to a connection on occupancy proof and indemnity; additional meter in tenanted premises is not fraud
cases.holding: The occupier is entitled to the connection. Clause 4.4 requires proof of occupancy (including a latest rent-paid receipt or valid lease) and, where the intending consumer is not the owner and cannot obtain consent, an Annexure 4.2 indemnity bond. Following Seema Mansoor, a tenant has a legal right to obtain electricity connection and the licensee cannot refuse solely for want of the owner's consent. No tenant can enjoy the premises without electricity. The additional meter was installed by the electricity department under the Act and the Code. In view of that Division Bench law, it cannot be said that the revisionist obtained the connection by playing fraud.
cases.flag: The Court quoted Clause 4.4 and Annexure 4.2 in full and referred to the Indian Electricity Act and the U.P. Electricity Supply Code (Thirteenth Amendment), 2018 without numbering an Act section. The Hindi extract labelled as rent-agreement clause 4 is OCR of a possession-at-sale clause; the Court's English recital is the additional-meter billing term. Source PDF also contains listing orders from 27.07.2023 to 14.07.2025; the operative judgment is 28.07.2025.

cases.title: Smt. Uma Chauhan v. State of U.P. And 2 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Supply Code is self-sufficient; s.420 complaint for a tenant's additional meter is abuse of process where no Code proceeding for removal is taken and civil/criminal pleas contradict
cases.holding: No. The Code is a self-sufficient code. No proceeding was initiated by the landlady under it for disconnection or removal of the additional meter on the ground of fraud. Once the rent agreement itself provides that the tenant shall pay the electricity bill as per the additional meter, it does not stand to reason that the lessee played fraud in getting that meter installed. The civil plea of unpaid additional-meter bills and the criminal plea of fraudulent installation are contradictory. Dishonest intention from the inception, required for Section 420 IPC (N. Raghvender), is not made out: the revisionist entered possession under the rent deed and was entitled to a connection. The complaint was engineered to gain mileage in the pending ejectment suit, was initiated by Yogesh Kumar Goel who is not the owner (the Section 200 statement being that of Smt. Priya Goel, who is not a party), and is malicious and an abuse of process. Revision allowed; the 14.11.2022 discharge-rejection and the entire complaint are quashed.

cases.title: Guddi Kesarwani v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupancy proof for new connection
cases.holding: Rejection of a new domestic connection solely for want of ownership proof is unsustainable. An occupier, even a trespasser, is entitled to electricity as a fundamental right under Article 21; domicile certificate, gas passbook and ration card showing residence suffice. The 26 July 2024 rejection is quashed and the licensee is directed to grant the connection within eight weeks upon statutory payment.

cases.title: Dharampal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: mutation of connection after consumer's death
cases.holding: A claim to mutate an existing electricity connection in the occupier's name after the recorded consumer's death raises factual issues for the competent authority under clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not for a writ court. The petitioner may make an exhaustive representation to the third respondent, who shall consider the issues and pass orders within four weeks.

cases.title: M/s Rudransh Hotel and Resorts v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: occupier-indemnity-new-connection
cases.holding: Where the licensee is willing to release a fresh connection to a lessee on completion of an indemnity bond, charges and other formalities, the Court will not mandamus release or waive the owner's NOC, but will allow a short time for those steps and direct the licensee to take an appropriate decision thereafter.

cases.title: Smt. Vinita Verma v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: Where the petitioner-wife resides in premises whose electricity connection stands in the owner-husband's name amid matrimonial discord, the licensee is to consider her online application for a new connection under Electricity Supply Code, 2005 clause 4.4 on submission of an indemnity bond, on the same footing as a tenant in possession where the landlord does not cooperate, and to decide as per law within three weeks of completing those formalities, without prejudice to the owner's property rights.

cases.title: Mohd. Afaq v. U.P. Power Corporation Limited
cases.topic: occupier connection on indemnity bond
cases.holding: A tenant cannot be deprived of an electricity connection only because a landlord-tenant dispute is pending, unless there is some other impediment, subject to an indemnity bond under clause 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. If the occupier applies with an indemnity bond, the licensee shall consider the application in accordance with law within three weeks of submission, inform any legal impediment in writing, and verify that the applicant is in possession; the order does not decide title or possession.

cases.title: Tasneem Kazmi v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: occupant connection on indemnity bond
