cases.title: Bhim Singh v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: forum-ombudsman-route-for-billing-grievances
cases.holding: A writ raising a disputed question of fact as to whether tariff is payable at rural or urban rates is not to be decided by the High Court in the absence of evidence. The consumer's remedy is before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and/or the Ombudsman under Clause 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The writ was disposed of at admission with a direction to apply to that forum, which shall hear and decide the application by a reasoned order after fullest opportunity of hearing, within one month of communication of the order.

cases.title: Pushpa Rani v. Noida Power Company Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF and Ombudsman route for billing grievances
cases.holding: A consumer challenging an electricity bill in writ has a remedy by approaching the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and the Ombudsman under clause 7.10 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ was disposed of with a direction that any application so filed be decided expeditiously.

cases.title: M/S Ekdil Mini Floor Mill v. The Executive Engineer
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF and Ombudsman as alternative remedy for billing grievances
cases.holding: Where a consumer remains dissatisfied with a modified electricity demand after a representation decided pursuant to earlier court and contempt directions, the alternative remedies of the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and thereafter the Ombudsman under para 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code are to be pursued; the writ is disposed with a direction that a CGRF complaint, if preferred, be decided expeditiously.

cases.title: Pawan Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF as alternative remedy for billing grievances
cases.holding: Where clause 6.5 is not attracted, the consumer's remedy is to approach the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under clause 7.10 of the Supply Code. The writ petition challenging the recovery certificate was dismissed on the ground of alternative remedy.

cases.title: Ajeet Kumar v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: CGRF route for tariff and billing grievance
cases.holding: A grievance as to the rate of tariff and alleged excess billing is to be placed before the Consumer Grievances Redressal Forum constituted under Clause 7.10 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The High Court will not mandamus the District Consumer Protection Forum to decide such a complaint; the consumer is to approach the functioning CGRF (here Mirzapur, looking after Sonebhadra) with a certified copy of the order, for time-bound disposal.

cases.title: Kalwa Khan v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.topic: cgrf-alternative-remedy-billing
cases.holding: A consumer challenging an electricity-bill demand as arbitrary has an adequate alternative remedy before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum constituted under Clause 7.10 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, even after the District Consumer Redressal Forum has rejected the grievance; the writ is dismissed on that ground.

cases.title: Chandra Pal Singh v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: cgrf-route-for-billing-dispute
cases.holding: On a dispute of electricity bill, the Court followed Ram Autar and disposed of the writ by directing the petitioners to appear before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum created under Clause 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, making clear that if they approach the Forum their application will not be thrown out only on account of delay.

cases.title: Mahaveer Prasad v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF as forum for billing disputes
cases.holding: Where the controversy is a dispute of electricity bill, the writ petitioner is to appear before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum created under clause 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; if the petitioners approach the Forum, the application will not be thrown out only on account of delay.

cases.title: Jawahar Lal Vishwakarma v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: CGRF route for billing grievances
cases.holding: Where a consumer seeks quashing of an electricity bill in writ and the licensee points to the statutory grievance remedy, the High Court will not decide the bill and will direct the consumer to the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under clause 7.10 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; if an appropriate application is filed, the Forum shall decide the complaint expeditiously, preferably within three months of production of a certified copy of the order.

cases.title: Smt. Saroj Devi v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: statutory-grievance-remedy
cases.holding: A writ petition challenging an Executive Engineer's dismissal of a consumer's representation cannot be entertained when paragraph 7.10(II) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 provides a statutory remedy for redressal of the grievance; the petitioner may avail that remedy.
cases.flag: Court cites para 7.10 (II) in roman numerals; catalog has 7.10, 7.10(i) and 7.10(iv), not 7.10(ii).

cases.title: Foran Singh v. Executive Engineer, Dakshinanchal Electricity Distribution Division & Anr.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: forum bar on subsequent writ after 7.10 liberty
cases.holding: Where an earlier writ has already been disposed of with liberty to pursue the remedy under Clause 7.10 read with Clauses 7.7.1 to 7.7.5 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 against the licensee's decision on a representation, a subsequent writ seeking mandamus to decide a further representation cannot be entertained; the consumer must avail that statutory forum.

cases.title: Raj Bahadur v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: alternative remedy for bill dispute
cases.holding: A writ challenging an electricity bill and the recovery certificate issued on it will not be entertained where the consumer has a statutory alternative remedy before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum and thereafter the Ombudsman under para 7.10(i) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 read with the UPERC (Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum & Ombudsman) Regulations, 2003, and para 7.10(iv) of those Regulations. The petition was dismissed on that ground.
cases.flag: Court cites para 7.10(i) of Code, 2005 for CGRF (not 6.7) and para 7.10(iv) of Regulations, 2003 for Ombudsman; clause numbering as stated, not corrected.

UP-2005::7.10(iii).topic: CGRF after Executive Engineer decides a clause 6.5 complaint

cases.title: Smt. Sharda Sharma v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: CGRF after Executive Engineer decides a clause 6.5 complaint
cases.holding: Once the Executive Engineer has decided a clause 6.5 complaint, the consumer's next remedy is a complaint to the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under clause 7.10(iii) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, not a writ. The petition is dismissed on that alternative remedy. The consumer may file the complaint within six weeks; if so filed, the Forum shall entertain it without examining limitation and decide it on merits after hearing the parties.
cases.flag: CGRF cited as clause 7.10(iii); not recast

UP-2005::7.10(iv).topic: Ombudsman as statutory remedy against CGRF order

cases.title: Santosh Stationary (P) Ltd. v. PuVVNL — CGRF order, Ombudsman under 7.10(iv)
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Ombudsman as statutory remedy against CGRF order
cases.holding: If a consumer is aggrieved by a decision of the Electricity Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum, including a finding that the complaint is not covered within Clause 7.10 of the Uttar Pradesh Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the statutory alternative remedy is to approach the Ombudsman under Clause 7.10(iv). A writ against the Forum order was dismissed with liberty to approach the Ombudsman within four weeks; the Ombudsman was directed to decide the grievance on merits preferably within eight weeks of receipt.

cases.title: Haneefa Begam v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: ombudsman-statutory-remedy
cases.holding: A writ petition against a Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum order cannot be entertained where clause 7.10(iv) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 provides a statutory remedy before the Ombudsman; the petitioner may avail that remedy.

cases.title: Sanjay Kumar Upadhayaya v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: authority to assess electricity theft
cases.holding: The writ challenging the 31.7.2010 theft assessment, including the plea that respondent no.4 was not authorised under clause 7.3(I) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 to assess theft, was dismissed as withdrawn. Interlocutory orders had stayed further action on the assessment, later modified so that proceedings on the provisional assessment notice remained stayed if the petitioner filed a bank guarantee of half the billed amount within three weeks and continued to pay future charges.
cases.flag: clause cited as 7.3 (I); not restated as 7.3.1 or 7.3(i)

cases.title: Yogendra v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: theft-assessment-authority
cases.holding: On the petitioner's statement and withdrawal application, the writ challenging the 2 March 2012 theft assessment as unauthorised under clause 7.3(I) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 was dismissed as withdrawn. The interim order was vacated and no liberty was granted to file a fresh writ on the same cause of action.

cases.title: Mohd. Rashid v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: compounding of s.135 offence
cases.holding: If the alleged s.135 offence is compoundable, the accused may seek compounding under the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; the writ court does not itself compound or stay the FIR on that score.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Company Ltd. & Another v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Damages under paragraph 7.7.2 for the licensee's delay and laches, concurrently found and Ombudsman-confirmed
cases.holding: Yes. Both the authorities below found the delay and laches on the part of the petitioners fully proved and fortified; damages in accordance with the rules prescribed in paragraph 7.7.2 were therefore to be imposed, were imposed by the DCGRF (Rs.9095 at Rs.85 per day for 114 days) and were confirmed by the Electricity Ombudsman. The licensee could not point out any error apparent on the face of the record warranting interference under Article 226.
cases.flag: Judgment marked 'AFR' (Approved For Reporting) with numbered paragraphs 01-14; pins are paragraph numbers. Pages 1-6 carry order-sheets (3.12.2010 to 15.11.2011, including a Division-Bench reference to a Single Judge) preceding the reasoned single-judge judgment of 22.11.2011; the DCGRF order of 29.7.2009 is reproduced partly in Hindi.

cases.title: Kanpur Electricity Supply Co. Ltd. and another v. Uttar Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission, Lucknow and others
cases.topic: Charitable institution providing free/subsidised service is billed under LMV-4(A); wrong-billing penalty upheld; concurrent findings of fact not interfered
cases.holding: It is governed by LMV-4(A). Both tariff schedules mention charitable institutions, but LMV-4(A) covers those providing service free of cost or at charges not exceeding those of similar Government institutions, and the rest fall under LMV-4(B). The consumer having pleaded and proved (and the licensee having conceded) that it provided free/subsidised service, the concurrent findings of fact of the CGRF and Ombudsman were unimpeachable and were not interfered with; the para 7.7.2 penalty for wrong billing was also sustained. The writ, filed by a State-owned licensee against its own correct billing determination, was dismissed as frivolous and vexatious with costs.

cases.title: Munnu Lal v. State of Uttar Pradesh
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: appeal against rejection of new connection
cases.holding: Whether ownership documents were filed with a new-connection application is a question of fact for the competent authority under Clause 7.7.6; a writ under Article 226 will not be entertained. The petition is dismissed for alternative remedy. If the petitioner prefers a representation under Clause 7.7.6 within two weeks, the authority shall decide it expeditiously, preferably within two weeks of filing.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Licensee's force-majeure freedom from SOP compensation does not waive the consumer's minimum charges
cases.holding: No. Paragraph 7.7 concerns standards of customer service (supply, new connections, disconnections, re-connections, metering, billing, transfer of ownership and conversion). A licensee must ensure uninterrupted supply, but is not liable to pay compensation if it fails to do so for reasons beyond its control because of an act of God. That does not support the converse: that a consumer need not pay electricity charges when he consumes none for reasons beyond his control. Applying that analogy in Appeal No. 96 of 2008 was beyond the Act and the Code.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Licensee's force-majeure freedom from SOP compensation does not waive the consumer's minimum charges
cases.holding: No. Paragraph 7.7 concerns standards of customer service (supply, new connections, disconnections, re-connections, metering, billing, transfer of ownership and conversion). A licensee must ensure uninterrupted supply, but is not liable to pay compensation if it fails to do so for reasons beyond its control because of an act of God. That does not support the converse: that a consumer need not pay electricity charges when he consumes none for reasons beyond his control. Applying that analogy in Appeal No. 96 of 2008 was beyond the Act and the Code.

cases.title: U.P. Power Corp. Ltd. Through Executive Engineer v. Ombudsmen and 2 Others
cases.topic: Licensee's force-majeure freedom from SOP compensation does not waive the consumer's minimum charges
cases.holding: No. Paragraph 7.7 concerns standards of customer service (supply, new connections, disconnections, re-connections, metering, billing, transfer of ownership and conversion). A licensee must ensure uninterrupted supply, but is not liable to pay compensation if it fails to do so for reasons beyond its control because of an act of God. That does not support the converse: that a consumer need not pay electricity charges when he consumes none for reasons beyond his control. Applying that analogy in Appeal No. 96 of 2008 was beyond the Act and the Code.

UP-2005::7.7.4.topic: load enhancement as billing; CGRF exclusive under 7.10

cases.title: Shamshul Qamar v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: load enhancement as billing; CGRF exclusive under 7.10
cases.holding: Reduction or enhancement of load falls under billing in Clause 7.7.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. A grievance about a licensee's load-enhancement communication, payment and increased consumption can be adjudicated only by the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum under Clause 7.10. The Court declined to decide the writ on merits and directed the petitioner to apply to the Forum within one week of receiving a certified copy, to be heard and disposed of within one month thereafter.

cases.title: Dhanee Ram v. State of U.P. and others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: billing dispute — CGRF forum
cases.holding: A dispute over being billed for 10 HP when the sanctioned and inspected load is 3 HP is a billing matter under clause 7.7.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and is squarely covered by clause 7.10(ii). The High Court will not exercise extraordinary writ jurisdiction; the consumer must proceed before the Consumer Grievance Redressal Forum. Pending that complaint, he is to pay at the 3 HP rate from 2006 and, on payment of an interim 3 HP bill issued within 15 days, the connection is not to be disconnected until the Forum disposes of the complaint, which he must file within 30 days.

cases.title: Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Kranti Gupta
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: theft-inspection-procedure-mandatory-leave-to-appeal-refused
cases.holding: Where the prosecution case is that CT/PT terminals were tampered so as to slow the meter, leave to appeal against acquittal will not be granted if the trial court found that the mandatory provisions of Chapter VIII of the Electricity Supply Code were not complied with, DW-1's evidence that the meter-room key lay with the licensee's officials was not denied, and the alleged meters were not sent to a laboratory for testing. Failure to follow that procedure is not a ground to reverse the acquittal. Leave to appeal is dismissed.
cases.flag: The Court referred to Chapter VIII of the Electricity Supply Code and to 'paragraph-20 and 33 of the UP Electricity Code 2005' (not standard clause numbers). Counsel described the offence as Section 135B of the Electricity Act, 2003.

cases.title: Dharmi v. U.P.P.C.L. — recovery citation; writ dismissed for want of prosecution
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: recovery citation; want of prosecution
cases.holding: On 2 July 2013 the Court connected this writ with Writ-C No. 53470 of 2012 in view of Clause 8(1)(b)(iii) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, as quoted in the petition, and directed that no coercive steps be taken on the citation dated 19 June 2013 till the next listing, following reasons given in an earlier order about lack of opportunity of hearing on the objection. On 11 April 2023, none having appeared for the petitioner even in revised call, the writ was dismissed for want of prosecution without deciding that challenge.

UP-2005::8(1)(b)(iv).topic: final assessment for theft after police final report

cases.title: Mohd. Shahjad v. U.P. Power Corpn. Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: final assessment for theft after police final report
cases.holding: Prima facie, final assessment for theft of electricity cannot proceed where theft was not established (police final report; criminal proceedings withdrawn), in view of paragraph 8(1)(b)(iv) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005; recovery on the 4 March 2010 assessment is stayed until further orders.
cases.flag: Order cites paragraph no.8(1)(b)(iv) without quoting the clause; numbering taken as written.

UP-2005::8.0(5).topic: committee to inquire into inspection procedure

cases.title: Devendra Kumar Bansal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: committee to inquire into inspection procedure
cases.holding: A writ seeking constitution of a committee under Clause 8.0(5) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 to inquire into inspection procedure will not be entertained once a provisional assessment notice has been served; the consumer may raise all objections, including as to the checking procedure, in reply to that notice or pursue the remedies under the Code.

cases.title: Nirmala Devi v. President (Prabandhak Nideshak) Discom Committee, KESCO, Kanpur
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: expedition of pending Clause 8.0(5) Committee application
cases.holding: If the petitioner's application dated 9/13.5.2013, made in accordance with the prescribed procedure, is maintainable under Clause 8.0(5) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the Committee may dispose of it in accordance with law as expeditiously as possible.

cases.title: Rajendra Kumar Agarwal v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: theft penalty — writ jurisdiction and statutory appeal
cases.holding: A writ challenging a theft-assessment demand and penalty will not be entertained where disputed questions of fact are involved. The consumer was given fifteen days to file an appeal; the appellate authority was directed to dispose of it in accordance with law within three months; deposit of Rs. 2,00,000/- was required, with the remaining amount subject to the result of the appeal.

cases.title: Manoj Kumar Agarwal v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: assessment-writ-appeal
cases.holding: Disputed questions of fact attending a theft-assessment penalty bar writ interference with the demand notice and with the prayer for a committee enquiry under Clause 8.0 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. The consumer is to file an appeal before the appellate authority within 15 days, depositing Rs.2,00,000, the remaining amount remaining subject to the appeal; the appellate authority shall dispose of the matter in accordance with law within three months of filing.
cases.flag: order cites Clause 8.0 generally, not 8.0(5)

UP-2005::8.1.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.126, EA 2003 & 1958 Dues Recovery Act)
UP-2005::8.1.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery

cases.title: Gauri Shankar Gupta v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cases.topic: Proper assessment (with hearing) is a precondition to recovery
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(a)&(b) read with Section 126 require notice, service of the provisional assessment, and an opportunity of hearing before a final assessment; only on such an assessment, and non-payment of the demand thereunder, can recourse be had to the 1958 Act. The department failed to show the demand notice was served or that any assessment order was passed; the recovery order and citation are quashed, with liberty to reassess after hearing.

cases.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cases.topic: Theft cannot be inferred from an unexplained divergence between the billing meter and untested outside check-meters
cases.holding: No. Under para 8.1(b)(iv) of the Code, a case of theft must be established, not presumed. Since the three outside meters (maintained under the licensee's own seal/custody) recorded consumption comparable to the billing meter for nearly the whole assessment period, were never independently tested, and no report of tampering with them was ever lodged, there was no material basis to infer theft at the consumer's premises merely from a late-period divergence (occurring only around the time the billing meter was destroyed by fire); an unsupported suggestion at the hearing that all four meters had been remotely tampered could not be explained by the licensee's own technical officer and did not constitute evidence. The assessment and confirming appellate order (itself unreasoned/non-speaking, contrary to para 8.1) were quashed.

cases.title: Theft-dues recovery without prior provisional assessment
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional assessment before recovery
cases.holding: Where a licensee recovered alleged theft dues without first making a provisional assessment, serving it, and inviting and deciding objections before final assessment, the recovery citation is unsustainable. The licensee may still issue a provisional assessment, serve it, invite objections, and then make a final assessment, against which the consumer may appeal.
cases.flag: Order cites a theft case under Supply Code 2005 and the Electricity Act with no clause number; 8.1 keyed from the provisional-assessment, objections, final-assessment and appeal sequence directed.

cases.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.topic: A 'final notice' demanding payment of a provisionally assessed amount, issued without any hearing on the consumer's timely-filed objections and without an actual reasoned final assessment order, is dehors the Section 126/Clause 8.1 procedure and must be quashed
cases.holding: No. Section 126(1)'s provisional assessment requires the assessing officer's recorded conclusion of unauthorised use, which itself cannot be reached without a fair opportunity of hearing given the potential overlap with s.135 investigation. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) of the Supply Code specifically requires a personal hearing after the consumer files objections to the provisional assessment/show-cause notice, before any final order is passed. Here, after the petitioner filed timely objections (pursuant to an earlier court order permitting him to do so and deposit 50% of the provisional amount for restoration), the licensee neither gave notice of hearing nor considered the objections, yet issued 'final notice' letters (4.3.2017, repeated 17.3.2017) simply reiterating the original provisional-assessment figure as though finally established, without ever serving any actual reasoned final assessment order. This is dehors the statutory procedure (following Ashok Kumar, Kamil, and Hazi Mohd. Yaseen) — a consumer cannot be compelled to pay a provisional-assessment amount as if final, absent a proper final assessment after hearing. The two impugned notices were quashed, with liberty to the licensee to conduct the final assessment properly, in accordance with the Act and the Code.

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: For assessment of theft of electricity under s.135, Clauses 8.1/8.2 of the Supply Code (not Clause 6.8) govern; Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires 15 working days' show-cause notice and Clause 8.1(b)(iv) mandates assessment at 1.5 times (not 3 times) the applicable tariff if theft is established after hearing
cases.holding: Following Mohit Paper Mills (applying the specific-prevails-over-general canon), Clauses 8.1/8.2 govern theft-based assessment, not Clause 6.8. On the facts, the assessing officer's provisional-assessment notice (25.5.2007) gave only one week (not the mandated 15 working days), lacked specificity as to which s.135(1) clause was invoked, and calculated the provisional assessment at thrice (not 1.5 times) the applicable tariff — all procedural lapses reflecting negligence or lack of legal clarity by the (technically-trained, non-legal) assessing officer, for which the licensee bears responsibility to provide adequate training. However, since the petitioner's only reply (31.5.2007) addressed occupancy, not the theft allegation or quantum, and the assessing officer's own subsequent (albeit procedurally chaotic) self-correction reduced the assessment to the correct 1.5x multiplier (Rs. 21,17,016, down from Rs. 42,78,355), and given the clearly-established theft on the inspection record (a 160 KVA transformer improperly connected via temporary L.T. line to run an ice factory with no sanctioned connection), the Court declined to interfere with the corrected final assessment despite the demonstrated procedural laxity — noting the Court, exercising equity under Article 226, would not assist a demonstrably blameworthy party on technicalities causing loss to public revenue.

cases.title: Arup Kumar Mitra v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Effect of a set-aside theft assessment; duty to pass a fresh reasoned order on remand
cases.holding: The set-aside assessment (18.9.2013) became non est and ceased to exist in law. The assessing authority was bound to pass a fresh, reasoned, speaking order after considering the consumer's objection dated 3.10.2013. The order of 5.5.2014, which merely reaffirmed the quashed assessment without dealing with the 19-page objection, is non-speaking, founded on a non est order and cannot sustain; it is set aside.
cases.flag: The show-cause and assessment refer to assessment 'in accordance with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005' for a s.135 theft; the Court did not cite a specific clause number. Keyed to the Code's theft-assessment clause for indexing.

cases.title: Mohd. Usman v. Dakkshinachal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft-disconnection
cases.holding: Clause 8.1(viii) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 empowers the licensee to disconnect supply forthwith on the spot where the consumer is found committing theft of electricity. After an inspection allegedly disclosing theft and an FIR under section 135 of the Electricity Act, 2003, disconnection on 28 August 2018 was prima facie justified even though a crowd had prevented immediate disconnection. The writ to quash that disconnection and the provisional assessment and to restore supply was dismissed; the consumer was left to raise all grievances before the assessing authority, which was to pass a speaking order.

cases.title: Tehsildar v. State of U.P. and others
cases.neutral_citation: 2009 SCC OnLine All 1931 : (2009) 83 AIC 493 : (2010) 1 All LJ (NOC 84) 22
cases.topic: A final assessment under Clause 8.1(b) is a condition precedent to theft recovery, even absent objections
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b) requires a final assessment to be made before recovery, even if no objection to the provisional assessment has been filed; the authorised officer must record findings that the provisional assessment was served and make the final assessment (at 1.5 times the applicable normal tariff, whichever is higher, per Clause 8.1(b)(iv)). Insisting on recovery without any final assessment violates the Code's procedure. The recovery under the notice was directed to remain in abeyance until a final assessment is made against the petitioner.

cases.title: Subhashis Chatterjee v. U.P. Power Corporation Limited, Lucknow through Chairman and others
cases.neutral_citation: 2011 SCC OnLine All 611 : (2011) 89 ALR 888 : (2011) 6 All LJ 527
cases.topic: No power to disconnect for 'unauthorised use'; Code disconnection power is confined to theft
cases.holding: No. Code 8.1(iv),(vii),(viii) permits disconnection only in cases of 'theft' under s.135, not in cases of 'unauthorised use of electricity' assessed under s.126. Once the licensee treated the case as UUE (issuing a s.126 provisional assessment), the disconnection provisions were not attracted, and neither the Act nor the Code confers power to disconnect a domestic connection for UUE. The remedy for the detected gadget was search and seizure under Clauses 4.33-4.34 (in the person's presence with a signed list), not disconnection. Restoration was ordered, with liberty to file objections to the provisional assessment.

cases.title: M/S Kamakhya Steels Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Final assessment that dismisses objections as 'not accepted' without engaging them, and converts 'possibility of theft' into a theft finding without analysis, is non-speaking and unsustainable
cases.holding: No. The Court found, to its 'utter surprise', that the final assessment of 23.10.2007 (Rs. 29,52,212) referred to the paragraphs of the objection only to reject them, without applying its mind or even reproducing the points so that some consideration could be inferred. The concluding analysis (paras 34–37 of that order) did no more than restate that seals were tampered and energy-flow analysis showed line losses, and therefore unauthorised use by way of theft had taken place. That is not analysis converting possibility of theft into a clear case of theft. The assessment was quashed and remitted for a fresh order under the Code, after reconsidering the objections, with specific findings, within two months of production of a certified copy. Amounts already deposited are to remain with the respondents to abide that order.
cases.flag: The Court remitted for fresh 'provisional and final assessment under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005' on a theft allegation but did not cite a clause number. Keyed to Clause 8.1 (theft-assessment procedure) for indexing; the petitioner had invoked Chapter VIII and Clause 6.8(vi). Internal dates in the judgment are inconsistent (final assessment also referred to as 23.08.2007; appellate order variously 11.10.2007 / 08.04.2010 / 09.04.2012) — recorded as the judgment states them; the operative paragraph quashes the assessment of 23.10.2007, the appellate order in Appeal No. 17 of 2007-08, and recovery dated 09.04.2012.

cases.title: Shah Faisal v. State of Uttar Pradesh & 4 Others
cases.topic: Clause 8.1 challenge to inspection and assessment (no videography / no independent witnesses) — raised, not decided, because the 528 application was not pressed
cases.holding: Not decided. That was prayer (II) of the 528 application. After the State submitted that a prima facie s.135 offence was made out and that the facts were for trial, counsel did not press the application and sought only liberty to apply for bail. The Court disposed of the application on that prayer. This case is not authority on Clause 8.1's videography or witness requirements.
cases.flag: Indexed under Clause 8.1 only because that was the Code ground pleaded. Thin criminal-procedure disposal; no construction of the Code.

cases.title: Shahvez Abdullah v. State of U.P. & 6 Others
cases.topic: A 'final' assessment cannot support recovery where there is no receipt showing service of the provisional assessment notice; it is to be treated as provisional and objections heard
cases.holding: No. The petitioner's case was that no provisional assessment notice was ever issued so as to enable an objection under the Supply Code, 2005. Instructions showed a final assessment dated 24.03.2026 said to rest on a provisional notice dated 27.03.2025, with a recital that the petitioner did not reply. The Court found no receipt appended to the instructions from which service of the provisional notice could be inferred. It therefore directed that the 24.03.2026 order be treated as a provisional assessment; the petitioner may file objections within four weeks; if he does, he shall be heard and a fresh final assessment passed within one further month, and no coercive action shall be taken on the recovery notice, which is put in abeyance to abide that decision.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite a clause number. Petitioner invoked objections 'under Electricity Supply Code, 2005' to a provisional assessment. Keyed to Clause 8.1 (provisional bill, objections, hearing, then final assessment) as the theft-assessment procedure that this pattern matches; it could equally be Clause 6.8 if the demand was for unauthorised use rather than theft — the order does not say. Internal date inconsistency on the recovery citation (07.10.2025 vs 24.03.2026) recorded as the judgment states it; the operative paragraph puts the citation dated 24.03.2026 in abeyance.

cases.title: M/s Kamakhya Steels Pvt. Ltd. & Another v. PVVNL & Another
cases.topic: A final assessment that does not consider the consumer's objections is quashed and remitted for a fresh order under the Code
cases.holding: No. As in the connected Writ-C No. 20210 of 2012, the objections were not accorded due consideration. The petition is allowed. The order of the final assessing authority (Executive Engineer) dated 23.10.2007 and consequential orders are quashed. The matter is remitted to the assessing authority to pass a fresh order after considering the objections and to record how a case of possibility of theft can be taken as actual theft so as to charge the check-meter unit difference. An appropriate order is to be passed under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 within two months of production of a certified copy. Amounts already deposited remain with the respondents to abide that order.
cases.flag: The Court did not cite a clause number. Remand is for a fresh order 'under the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005'. Keyed to Clause 8.1 (theft-assessment procedure) as in SCJ-273; the demand was styled as theft/possibility of theft. The petition also challenged the appellate order; the operative paragraph quashes the 23.10.2007 assessment and 'consequential orders'.

cases.title: M/s S. Milan Agro Industries & 2 Others v. State of Uttar Pradesh & 4 Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: A post-decisional hearing after a completed final assessment puts the order under a cloud; the assessment is quashed and a fresh Code process directed
cases.holding: No. After a provisional assessment (3 December 2023), the consumer's reply and appearance (9 December 2023), and a speaking final assessment (28 December 2023), there is no requirement under the law for the authorities to grant another hearing. A further hearing on 6 January 2025, granted on the petitioner's request, put the entire order under a cloud. All proceedings including that final assessment are quashed and set aside on condition that the petitioner deposit 50% of the assessed amount with the Executive Engineer within two weeks. On such deposit the petitioner may file a fresh objection, shall be heard, and the authorities shall pass an appropriate order in accordance with law. The entire proceedings, including the fresh final assessment, are to be concluded within eight weeks. No appeal having been filed and no recovery attempted for over nine months after the December 2023 order, that situation should not be repeated.
cases.flag: Source PDF also contains listing orders of 24.7.2025 and 7.8.2025; the operative disposal is 11.8.2025. The Court did not cite a clause number. The 24.11.2023 order in Writ-C No. 31951 of 2023 referred to a final assessment 'as stipulated in the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.' Keyed to Clause 8.1 (provisional bill, objections, hearing, then final assessment) as the theft-assessment procedure that this pattern matches; it could equally be Clause 6.8 if the demand was for unauthorised use rather than theft — the order does not say.

cases.title: Sangram Singh Yadav v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: objection to theft notice after provisional assessment
cases.holding: Where a consumer objects to a theft-related notice after provisional assessment, the writ is disposed of by directing the licensee to decide that objection under Clause 8.1 of the Electricity Supply Code within three weeks of a certified copy being filed; disconnection is stayed for four weeks or until the objection is decided, whichever is earlier, without examining the merits of the assessment.

cases.title: Smt. Amna Khatoon v. PVVNL & Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: Alleged Clause 8.1 defects in a provisional assessment are for objections, not writ
cases.holding: No. Counsel challenged the 7.3.2008 provisional assessment on the ground that the procedure to invoke Section 126(4) was not as per Clause 8.1 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, and that the assessment was for 407 days instead of 180 days as contemplated under those provisions. The Court held that those objections, among others, can be raised by filing objections as called for by the respondents, and did not decide whether Clause 8.1 was followed.
cases.flag: Counsel's contention is recorded as 'Clauses and 8.1' (OCR). Treated as Clause 8.1.

cases.title: Sanjay Dadu v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: provisional-assessment-notice
cases.holding: A provisional assessment notice under section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003 and clause 8.1 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 is not defective where it rests on an inspection recording extraction of energy by a direct connection from another consumer's tube-well and it discloses the duration of assessment and the manner of computation. Where an objection to that notice remains pending, the writ court will not quash the notice or order refund, but will direct the licensee to decide the objection by following the procedure prescribed in the Supply Code, 2005.

UP-2005::8.1(VII).topic: 8.1(VII) limited to meter-tampering theft, not unauthorized line

cases.title: Anil Suhala v. Purvanchal Vidhut Vitrana Nigam Ltd., Varanasi
cases.topic: 8.1(VII) limited to meter-tampering theft, not unauthorized line
cases.holding: Clause 8.1(VII) applies only where theft of electricity is on account of tampering of meter etc. It has no applicability where a separate unauthorized line is laid to obtain supply so that consumption is not metered.

cases.title: Shamsul Qamar v. PVVNL and Others
cases.topic: Laboratory report of a meter removed for testing must be supplied before a provisional theft assessment can stand
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(vii) requires that, on prima facie evidence of theft by tampering, the meter be removed, sealed and tested in accordance with clause 5.6. The 19.11.2007 inspection itself recorded that the old meter was sent for laboratory testing and that the report would bind the parties. The petitioner's uncontroverted case was that the meter was not so tested, no testing date was given, and no laboratory result was supplied. The 28.11.2007 bill did not disclose or even mention a laboratory report. The bill is illegal, arbitrary and in violation of clause 8.1(vii), and is quashed. The department may supply the laboratory report and then issue a fresh provisional assessment, to which the petitioner may object.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing orders of 11.11.2011, 14.11.2018, 27.11.2018 and 5.12.2018 with this 14.12.2018 disposal. Cited as clause 8.1(vii); catalog key UP-2005::8.1(VII). The 14.12.2018 order is unnumbered; paras 3-7 are the petitioner's submission, the quoted clause, the uncontroverted pleadings, the quashing and the liberty.

cases.title: M/S Mayur Sheetgrah Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. And Others
cases.topic: MRI report must be supplied before a theft assessment is finalised, not along with the final order
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(a)(vii) imposes a statutory requirement that the MRI report be supplied where there is evidence of tampering. The supplementary counter affidavit and the 24.02.2009 order itself showed that the MRI downloaded on 27.11.2008 was supplied only with that order, which also directed the Executive Engineer to supply it. The Court held it could not see how the assessment was finalised by the same order, and that the order therefore violated natural justice. The 24.02.2009 assessment of Rs. 26,86,316 is set aside. The petitioner may file objections to the MRI within two weeks; respondent no. 3 is to consider those objections together with the replies already on record and pass a fresh assessment.
cases.flag: Cited as para 8.1 (a) (vii); catalog key UP-2005::8.1(VII). The quoted text also refers to clause 5.6 testing on LT meter removal; this case turns on MRI supply, not a 5.6 laboratory test. Source PDF concatenates 2011–2014 listing and adjournment orders with the 9.4.2014 disposal (Ashok Bhushan and Ranjana Pandya, JJ.). That disposal is unnumbered; paras are sequential blocks of the 9.4.2014 order from 'Heard Shri Pramod Kumar Jain'.

UP-2005::8.1(b).topic: Final assessment requires an opportunity of hearing before it is passed

cases.title: Arvind Kumar v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cases.topic: Final assessment requires an opportunity of hearing before it is passed
cases.holding: No. A final assessment under s.126(5) read with Clause 8.1(b) mandates an opportunity of hearing before it is passed. An order that only records that objections were considered and communicated, with no hearing, does not comply with the mandatory provisions, so no valid final assessment order has been passed. The Executive Engineer must pass a final assessment after affording a hearing within 15 days; the recovery/demand/bill are kept in abeyance meanwhile.

cases.title: Mahipal Alias Mahipal Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: objections before final theft assessment
cases.holding: A consumer in a theft case has a right to raise objections before the Executive Engineer under para 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, before final assessment is made. If objections are filed, the Executive Engineer shall consider them expeditiously and if possible within one month. Where no recovery certificate has yet issued, none is stayed in advance; but if a recovery certificate and citation are issued in the meantime, they remain suspended until the final assessment order.

cases.title: Sonu v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft-recovery-citation
cases.holding: A writ against a Tehsildar recovery citation issued pursuant to alleged electricity theft is disposed of without examining whether provisional or final assessment under para 8.1(b) of the 2005 Supply Code preceded recovery; the consumer may represent to the Executive Engineer, who shall consider the claim and pass an appropriate order in accordance with law within one month.

cases.title: Vijaybir Singh v. State of U.P. and Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft assessment — hearing before final order
cases.holding: A final theft assessment and a recovery citation founded on it cannot stand where the licensee has not followed Clause 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 — preparation of a provisional assessment, opportunity of hearing, and then a final order. The citation dated 28.7.2009 based on the Rs.4,60,000 assessment, made without notice or hearing, was set aside, with liberty to make a fresh final assessment only after giving the consumer an opportunity of hearing in accordance with the Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Prem Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft assessment — final assessment before recovery
cases.holding: Clause 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 requires, after service of a provisional theft assessment, a final assessment in which the competent authority records that the consumer was served and given an opportunity of personal hearing. Because no final assessment was made and the provisional bill was sent for recovery merely for want of a reply, the statutory procedure was not followed. The recovery citation is quashed and the matter is remanded for final assessment in accordance with the Code.

cases.title: Dhirendra Pratap Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft assessment procedure
cases.holding: Where a provisional assessment is served, the consumer is heard on reply, a final assessment confirms that demand, and a recovery certificate is issued, the procedure under para 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 is prima facie followed.

cases.title: Rajendra Prasad v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.topic: no recovery of theft assessment without final assessment
cases.holding: Clause 8.1(b) requires a final assessment of theft before recovery can be initiated. That final assessment is necessary even if the consumer files no objections, and must record that the provisional assessment was served. Recovering a provisional theft assessment without a final assessment violates the Supply Code. Recovery of Rs.40,856 under notice dated 4.9.2009 stayed until final assessment.

cases.title: Rajesh Kumar v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: final assessment before recovery of theft assessment
cases.holding: Clause 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 requires a final assessment of theft, recording that the provisional assessment was served, before recovery can be initiated, even if the consumer has not filed objections. Recovering the amount without that final assessment violates the Code. Recovery of Rs 40,856 under the notice dated 4 September 2009 shall remain in abeyance until final assessment is made.

cases.title: Rajendra Kumar Gupta v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft assessment — provisional bill and objections before final bill
cases.holding: Where the licensee treats the consumer as a theft case and issues a final assessment bill without complying with Clause 8.1(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and without notice, the bill cannot be sustained. On the licensee's concession that a fresh provisional bill would be issued, objections invited and a final assessment then passed, the High Court quashed the bill dated 16.8.2010 and directed the licensee to proceed afresh in accordance with the Code.

UP-2005::8.1(b)(iii).topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment

cases.title: Chunni Lal Gupta v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-day provisional-bill notice before final assessment
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires service of a provisional assessment bill with 15 days to reply and a hearing before final assessment. A 'revised bill' issued on the day of the raid, without that procedure, cannot be a final assessment; it is at best provisional, the consumer may file objections to be decided per the Code, and may appeal under Section 127 thereafter.

cases.title: Dr. Munni Lal v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Theft assessment — mandatory 15-working-day show-cause notice and hearing
cases.holding: No. Clause 8.1(b)(iii) requires a show-cause notice giving 15 working days to object and fixing a hearing date before a final assessment; a seven-day notice with no hearing date does not comply. No final order of assessment was passed, so the recovery demand was premature.

cases.title: Mohammad Idrish v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.topic: Unproved service of a provisional assessment presumes non-receipt and denial of hearing
cases.holding: The Court presumes the provisional assessment was never received, so the consumer was deprived of the opportunity of hearing under s.126(3) read with Clause 8.1(b)(iii). The consumer is to be given an opportunity to file objections, which the Executive Engineer must decide by a speaking order after a reasonable opportunity of hearing; recovery stays meanwhile and abides that decision.

cases.title: Ram Das v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: hearing on recovery in s.135 theft
cases.holding: On a challenge to a recovery certificate issued in section 135 theft proceedings without the clause 8.1(b)(iii) hearing, the writ was disposed at admission directing the petitioner to deposit 50% of the recovered amount within one month; subject to that deposit he may file an objection or representation, which the authority shall decide after fullest opportunity of hearing by a reasoned order within a further month; the writ papers may be treated as part of the representation; on deposit, no coercive action until one week after communication of that departmental order.

cases.title: Kartar Singh v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: hearing on recovery in a Section 135 theft proceeding
cases.holding: Without deciding whether recovery without a Clause 8.1(b)(iii) hearing was illegal, the Court directed the consumer in a Section 135 theft recovery to deposit 50% within one month, then file an objection which the authority must hear and decide by reasoned order within a further month, with coercive steps stayed until a week after that order if the deposit is made.

UP-2005::8.1(vi).topic: Restoration of supply during pending theft/UUE provisional assessment; inspection report

cases.title: Vinod Kumar Sahu v. State of Uttar Pradesh And 3 Others
cases.topic: Restoration of supply during pending theft/UUE provisional assessment; inspection report
cases.holding: Mandamus will not restore a domestic connection while a provisional assessment for alleged theft/unauthorised use is pending. The petitioner shall reply to the provisional assessment notice within two weeks; the competent authority shall pass a final assessment order strictly in accordance with law within two months after hearing the petitioner. Restoration of supply shall depend upon that final assessment and the petitioner's compliance. The para 8.1(vi) inspection-report prayer is spent once the report is furnished with the licensee's written instructions.
cases.flag: The licensee called the case both 'theft of electricity' and 'using electricity unauthorisedly'. The Court did not cite EA 2003 ss. 126/135 or distinguish UUE from theft. Para 8.1(vi) appears only in the prayer for the inspection report; the Court does not interpret that sub-clause.

UP-2005::8.2.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h)) — effect of a subsequent criminal acquittal on a theft-based civil assessment
UP-2005::8.2.clause: 8.2(X)(g)/(h) (final theft assessment 'subject to adjudication by the court'; mandatory withdrawal of charges/assessment and meter restoration if the court finds theft not established)
UP-2005::8.2.topic: Where a criminal acquittal on the s.135 charge post-dates the appellate order upholding a theft-based assessment, the matter must be remanded to the appellate authority to independently examine Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) in light of that acquittal

cases.title: Shri Kunwar Sarvesh Kumar Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cases.topic: Where a criminal acquittal on the s.135 charge post-dates the appellate order upholding a theft-based assessment, the matter must be remanded to the appellate authority to independently examine Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) in light of that acquittal
cases.holding: Since the appellate order (1.4.2010) predated the trial court's acquittal judgment (23.1.2011, disclosed only in the petitioner's rejoinder), the Commissioner had no occasion to consider Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h). The appellate order is modified/partly set aside to the extent that the petitioner's appeal shall be treated as pending before the Commissioner, who must independently and objectively examine the acquittal judgment in light of Clause 8.2(X)(g)/(h) and pass a fresh appropriate order, unaffected by the High Court's observations on issues (a)-(c) above (which concerned assessment on the civil/administrative record, not the separate criminal mens rea question).

cases.title: Nandu Engineering Works & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.date: 22 February 2012 interim order (order-sheet 19.1.2012 to 8.1.2018; writ pending)
cases.topic: Interim restoration of a disconnected supply on part-payment and deposit of current bills, pending decision on whether the re-assessment was calculated in accordance with clause 8.2 and whether the exorbitant assessment renders the appeal onerous
cases.holding: Interim protection was granted and the merits left open. The Court held that the petitioner's submissions - that the calculation was not in accordance with clause 8.2 of the Supply Code and that the exorbitant assessment made the appeal onerous (50% pre-deposit) - 'needs consideration', and directed a counter affidavit. The connection having been disconnected after the writ was filed, it provided that subject to payment of Rs.10 lakh to respondent no.3 and deposit of current bills as and when due, the supply be restored, later correcting the order to add that no coercive action be taken against the petitioner in pursuance of the order dated 20.12.2011. This is an interim arrangement; the clause 8.2 calculation challenge and the alternative-remedy plea were not decided and the writ remained pending on the record.
cases.flag: Interim order-sheet of 16 pages, dated orders from 19.1.2012 to 8.1.2018 across several Division Benches, no printed page numbers and no final judgment; pins are order dates. The operative interim relief is the order of 22.2.2012 (Ashok Bhushan and Sunita Agarwal, JJ.), corrected on 6.4.2012. The extract has 'clause 8.2 of the the U.P. Electricity Supply Code 2005' (the doubled 'the' is in the source).

cases.title: Bhure Khan @ Mohd. Jahangeer v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: theft-final-assessment-before-recovery
cases.holding: Recovery of a theft assessment cannot be made on a citation where the demanded amount is reduced from the assessment treated as final without explanation of the discrepancy, and where no final assessment order appears to have been passed as required under Clause 8.2(b) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 even though no objection was received. The citation dated 01.05.2018 is quashed; the petitioner shall file objections before respondent no.4 within two weeks, who shall pass an appropriate order within six weeks.
cases.flag: Court cites Clause 8.2(b); catalog 8.2 sub-clauses are roman (8.2(vii), 8.2(x)). Not silently rekeyed.

cases.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitaran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Commissioner, Moradabad Region & Anr.
cases.topic: Appellate authority on a limited remand cannot reverse the remanding court's final findings
cases.holding: Prima facie, no. The remand was for the limited purpose of examining the acquittal (SST No. 69/2008) under Clause 8.2(X)(G) and (H); the Commissioner travelled beyond it and recorded findings contrary to the High Court's final findings on the owner's liability and the validity of the assessment. The operation of the Commissioner's order is stayed pending the writ petition.
cases.flag: Interim order only (stay). The substantive findings on owner-liability and assessment-validity are reproduced from the earlier final judgment dated 18.11.2011 in Writ-C No. 20679/2010, not originated here.

cases.title: Tariq v. Pashimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: restoration after theft assessment where no Special Court complaint within 30 days
cases.holding: Clause 8.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 provides that if a complaint of theft is not filed before the Special Court within 30 days of disconnection, the consumer may approach the authorised officer for restoration of supply on deposit of one time of the existing tariff. A demand of six times the tariff in that situation is not legally permissible. The Executive Engineer shall consider a restoration representation in accordance with Clause 8.2 and, if the one-time tariff has already been deposited and no such complaint was lodged within 30 days, restore the connection without insisting on the balance.

cases.title: Smt. Urmila Devi v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 3 Others
cases.topic: Effect of a criminal final report/exoneration on a theft assessment — interim stay
cases.holding: The Court held the matter requires consideration and, as interim relief, stayed recovery under the citation dated 30.1.2014 pending affidavits. No final view was expressed on whether the accepted final report entitles the consumer to relief under Clause 8.2(x)(h).
cases.flag: Interim order only; the Clause 8.2(x)(h) question is reserved for final hearing.

cases.title: Vijay Pal Singh & Another v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. and Others
cases.topic: Code's three-times theft-assessment rate is ultra vires the Act's 1.5-times cap under s.126(6)
cases.holding: No. Section 126(6) caps the assessment at 1.5 times the applicable tariff; by virtue of Section 174 the Act overrides, and the Code, being subordinate legislation framed under the Act, cannot travel beyond it. The three-times rate in Clause 8.2(iv) r/w Annexure 6.3(c) was ultra vires and contrary to Section 126(6). The theft assessment (5.7.2005) was quashed with a direction that the petitioner pay only 1.5 times the tariff applicable on the date of checking (4.5.2005).

cases.title: Vijay Pal Singh v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. and Others
cases.topic: Code's three-times theft-assessment rate is ultra vires the Act's 1.5-times cap under s.126(6)
cases.holding: No. Following the identical reasoning in the twin petition (Writ-C 60987 of 2005), the three-times rate in Clause 8.2(iv) r/w Annexure 6.3(c) was ultra vires Section 126(6), which caps the assessment at 1.5 times; the Act overrides by Section 174 and the Code cannot travel beyond it. The assessment (4.7.2005) was quashed with a direction that the petitioner pay only 1.5 times the tariff applicable on the date of checking (4.5.2005).

cases.title: M/s. Citi Hotel v. Commissioner, Lucknow Division, Lucknow & Ors.
cases.neutral_citation: 2009 SCC OnLine All 346 : AIR 2009 All 137 : (2009) 4 All LJ 741
cases.topic: Acquittal of theft after trial requires withdrawal of the theft assessment and restoration through the original meter
cases.holding: Under Clause 8.2(x)(g)-(h), the final theft assessment is subject to adjudication by the court, and where the court holds theft not established, the charges and assessment must be withdrawn in writing and the connection restored through the original meter. The appellate authority acted perversely and irrationally in dismissing the appeal without considering the acquittal (which had attained finality) or recording reasons for disagreeing with it, and in ignoring Clause 8.2. As the charge was only theft (not dishonest consumption), no wrongful loss was shown, there were no pre-raid dues, and the SDO's report placed the load within the permissible +/-10%, no civil liability survived either. The appellate order and the theft assessment were quashed and the deposits ordered refunded.

cases.title: Satish Kumar Bharti alias Chhotu v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cases.topic: Clause 8.2's 24-hour police-complaint / 30-day Special Court filing, read with s.57, supplies the 'consequences' that make the s.135(1-A) 24-hour FIR rule mandatory; breach voids the criminal case
cases.holding: Mandatory. Clause 8.2 of the Code requires the police complaint within 24 hours and the case before the Special Court within 30 days; failure attracts the licensee's obligations under Section 57 of the Act (compensation for missing specified standards of performance). Those are the consequences Indresh Patel said were missing. That Division Bench decision, having been given without looking at s.57 and Clause 8.2, is per incuriam and not binding. Following Varun Kumar Yadav (a thing required to be done in a particular manner is void if done otherwise — Dr. Arun Kumar), and it being admitted that the FIR was lodged four days after the inspection, well beyond 24 hours, the entire sessions case is quashed. The licensee is directed to proceed against the officer who failed to lodge the FIR in time.
cases.flag: The statutory 24-hour clock in s.135(1-A) second proviso runs from disconnection, not from inspection; the applicant and the Court treated the four-day gap from inspection (26.10.2020 → 30.10.2020) as the breach. No separate finding on the date of disconnection. The operative direction at para 12 refers to the mandate as 'Section 135(1)(a)' — the 24-hour rule is the second proviso to s.135(1-A); (1)(a) is the tapping/direct-connection offence. Recorded as a slip, not merged. Tension with Indresh Patel (DB, directory) is stated, not papered over; this is a Single Judge holding a DB per incuriam.

cases.title: Vishwas Malik v. State of U.P. and Another
cases.topic: clause 8.2 time-bar of s.135 complaint — left to trial court
cases.holding: The Court did not quash the complaint and did not decide whether clause 8.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 bars a sections 135/136/138 complaint filed more than 30 days after disconnection. Where the applicant's 29.09.2011 application raising that time-bar remained pending, and the AGA had no objection, the 482 application was disposed of by directing the trial court to decide that application in accordance with law within 30 days of production of a certified copy of the order, and then to proceed further.
cases.flag: Thin disposal. The 30-day-from-disconnection period is the applicant's reading of an amending notification to clause 8.2, recorded in the 02.01.2012 listing order and restated on 15.07.2024; the Court did not verify or construe the clause. The 2011 prayer was to quash Case No. 784 of 2006; the 2024 hearing recast it as a direction to decide the pending application. The source PDF also contains listing/stay-extension orders of 02.01.2012, 12.10.2023, 21.11.2023, 04.01.2024, 13.03.2024, 16.04.2024 and 03.07.2024; the judgment under record is the 15.07.2024 order (neutral citation 2024:AHC:113658).

cases.title: Ramesh Chandra Kasera v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: clause 8.2 not ultra vires Cr.P.C.
cases.holding: The challenge that clause 8.2 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 is ultra vires because it 'hammers' the overriding effect of the Cr.P.C. was rejected as per se absurd. The writ was dismissed and the Special Court directed to conclude the section 135 case within four months.

cases.title: M/S Laxmi Oil Expeller v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: fresh assessment under first amendment
cases.holding: Where the period of assessment relates to the first amendment of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, the licensee must make a fresh assessment in accordance with the Code as so amended; the existing assessment and consequential orders cannot stand.

cases.title: Akhalak Ahmad v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitaran Nigam Ltd. Thru' G.M. & Others
cases.topic: Assessing officer must pass a fresh order in the spirit of Clause 8.2(X)(h) after considering objections and the police final report
cases.holding: Yes, as a direction, not a merits withdrawal. The petitioner is at liberty to file the police final report said to have been filed in the FIR alleging unauthorised theft. The Assessment Authority is directed to pass an order in view of the spirit of Clause 8.2(X)(h) after considering the petitioner's objections. The Court did not itself withdraw the assessment or restore the connection.
cases.flag: Cited as 'Rule 8.2 (X) (h)'; treated as Clause 8.2(X)(h). The 2005 Code was not in force on 16.12.2003; applied in spirit to the remanded decision.

cases.title: M/S Sri Dauji Cold Storage Pvt Ltd And Another v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd And Others
cases.topic: Code's three-times theft-assessment rate (quoted as unamended 8.2(iv)) is ultra vires s.126(6)
cases.holding: No, as applied via Vijay Pal Singh, which the Court followed. That Division Bench held that unamended Clause 8.2(iv) (three times) was contrary to Section 126(6) (1.5 times) and ultra vires by Section 174; the Commission's 3rd amendment of 14.9.2006 later aligned the Code at 1.5 times. This Bench quashed the 29.3.2008 three-times demand on that law. It did not independently construe Clause 8.2 on these facts.
cases.flag: The quoted Vijay Pal Singh extract mixes 8.1(iv), 8.1(b)(iv) and 8.2(iv); keyed to catalog UP-2005::8.2 as in SCJ-227. Checking here was 1.11.2004 (2002 Code still in force); Pankaj Kumar (relied on by the petitioner) had read s.126(6) against the 2002 Code. The Court rested on Vijay Pal Singh and s.126(6), not on a 2002-Code clause.

cases.title: M/S Mayur Sheetgrah Pvt. Ltd. v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. And Others
cases.topic: An assessment cannot be finalised in the same order that records clause 8.2(i) as still uncomplied
cases.holding: No. The 24.02.2009 order itself stated that paragraph 8.2(i) had not been complied with and that the Executive Engineer might now take further proceedings, yet it finalised the assessment at Rs. 26,86,316. That contradiction, with the simultaneous direction to supply the MRI report, vitiated the order.
cases.flag: The Court did not quote clause 8.2(i). Catalog key is UP-2005::8.2.

UP-2005::8.2(vii).topic: assessment of electricity dues at one-time tariff

cases.title: Mohd. Mansoor v. State of U.P.
cases.topic: assessment of electricity dues at one-time tariff
cases.holding: On the licensee's admission that assessing outstanding electricity dues at twice the normal tariff was a calculation mistake—the petitioner having invoked clause 8.2(vii) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 as permitting assessment only at one time the tariff—the High Court quashed the recovery citation for Rs.1,25,141 and directed the petitioner to deposit the recast dues of Rs.45,194 within two months, failing which the licensee could recover that amount in accordance with law.

cases.title: Mohd. Kasim v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: post-acquittal restoration after theft prosecution
cases.holding: The Court did not itself apply clause 8.2(x) or order withdrawal of theft charges or restoration of supply. By consent it disposed of the writ with a direction that if the acquitted consumer files a fresh application before the Executive Engineer with a certified copy of the order, the application shall be considered and decided in accordance with law by a reasoned speaking order, preferably within six weeks.

cases.title: Radha Rani v. State of U.P. and others
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: closure of theft proceedings after accepted police final report
cases.holding: On admitted facts that the police final report in the theft investigation had been accepted by the criminal court and the Executive Engineer had no objection, the Court held that realization of electricity dues on the theft assessment was not justified, stayed recovery under the 19 March 2018 final assessment until further orders, listed the writ for admission, and left it open to the petitioner to apply under Section 8.2(X)(g) of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005 for closure of all proceedings in view of that acceptance.
cases.flag: Court cited 'Section 8.2(X)(g)' of the 2005 Code (catalog parent 8.2(x)); numbering of nested (g) taken as written.

cases.title: M/S Radha Krishna v. M.D., D.V.V.N. and Another
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: refund of restoration deposit after s.135 theft charge not made out, against security while revision pending
cases.holding: The petitioner, having had the theft charge held not made out, sought refund of the Rs.10 lakh restoration deposit under Clause 8.2(x)(f) and (h). Because a criminal revision against the acquittal is pending, the proceedings have not attained finality, but there is no impediment to refund if the petitioner furnishes security other than cash or bank guarantee to the satisfaction of the concerned Executive Engineer. The amount shall be refunded within two months after that security is furnished. The writ is disposed of finally on that direction and on the consent of counsel.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing orders of 14.12.2010, 22.12.2010 and 20.1.2011; the operative disposal is 13.4.2011 (unnumbered). Petitioner invoked Clause 8.2(x)(f) and (h); the Court directed refund against security rather than construing those sub-clauses as an unconditional cash refund.

cases.title: M/s Liladhar Tularam Ice Factory v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: restoration after acquittal
cases.holding: The writ claiming restoration of supply after acquittal, invoking clause 8.2(x)(g)(h) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005, was dismissed for want of prosecution when counsel stated he had no instructions; the 21 February 2012 interim mandamus to restore supply or show cause stood discharged, without any merits determination of the clause 8.2(x) claim.

cases.title: Shyam Kumar Awasthi v. U.P.P.C.L.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: objection-to-provisional-assessment
cases.holding: Clause 8.5 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, with Section 126 of the Electricity Act, 2003, is the path for a reply to a provisional theft bill; the Executive Engineer must consider the objection and pass an assessment order.

cases.title: Govind v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.topic: checking-report billing dispute — objection before licensee
cases.holding: A writ questioning the correctness of a checking report is a pure billing dispute. The consumer is to file an objection before the concerned officer within ten days; that officer shall then decide the objection keeping the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 and the rules framed thereunder, within three weeks. The High Court does not examine the checking report on merits.

UP-2005::9.1.clause: 9.1 (MCG waiver; read with para 11 of the Commercial and Revenue Manual)
UP-2005::9.1.topic: MCG for a disconnection period cannot be waived if electricity dues are pending

cases.title: Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. Through Its Executive v. Electricity Ombudsman, U.P., Lucknow and Others
cases.topic: MCG for a disconnection period cannot be waived if electricity dues are pending
cases.holding: No. The Forum had waived energy charges but directed payment of MCG. The Ombudsman waived MCG. The licensee pleaded that paragraph 11 of the Commercial and Revenue Manual does not permit waiver of MCG except in circumstances under Clause 9.1 of the Code, and that MCG cannot be waived if dues are pending. Paragraphs 12 and 13 of the writ petition pleaded that, under paragraph 11 of the Manual, MCG for the disconnection period is not charged provided there are no pending dues. The consumer's counter-affidavit did not dispute that dues were pending. The Ombudsman had itself found pending bill dues. Once dues were pending, there was no occasion to waive MCG; the waiver was against paragraph 11 of the Manual. The writ is allowed and the 25.01.2008 Ombudsman order is quashed.
cases.flag: Source PDF concatenates listing/adjournment orders of 8.4.2022 and 20.4.2022 (Shree Prakash Singh, J.) and 19.7.2022, 30.8.2022, 10.10.2022 and 22.11.2022 (Manish Kumar, J.); the operative judgment is 12.12.2022 (paras 1–11, Manish Kumar, J.). Caption spells the licensee 'Vidut'; the mill is styled 'Floor Mill'. Respondent no. 2 is unnamed. Catalog hits EA2003::42, EA2003::42(6) and individual-grievance-via-s42-not-commission mark the CGRF/Ombudsman path, not a construction of s.42. UP-2005::9.1 is not a catalog key; keyed as the Code clause the petitioner invoked. No precedent is cited.

UP-2005::9.3.code: Electricity Act, 2003 (s.126(3)) read with U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (Clauses 8.1(b)(iii), 9.3)
UP-2005::9.3.clause: 9.3 (mode of service of orders/notices) read with 8.1(b)(iii) (right to object to provisional assessment)
UP-2005::9.3.topic: Failure to serve a provisional assessment in the Clause 9.3-prescribed manner deprives the consumer of the s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii) right to object; a subsequent demand notice/recovery certificate premised on treating the unserved provisional assessment as final cannot stand without first affording a genuine objection opportunity

cases.title: Shiv Shankar Giri v. Purvanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Others
cases.topic: Failure to serve a provisional assessment in the Clause 9.3-prescribed manner deprives the consumer of the s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii) right to object; a subsequent demand notice/recovery certificate premised on treating the unserved provisional assessment as final cannot stand without first affording a genuine objection opportunity
cases.holding: No — the licensee's own instructions were silent on whether the provisional assessment was sent by registered or ordinary post, and the consumer denied receiving both the provisional assessment and the subsequent demand notice (sent by ordinary post). This deprived the consumer of the statutory right to object under s.126(3)/Clause 8.1(b)(iii). The Court directed that the petitioner be given six weeks (from receipt of a certified copy of the order and the now-supplied provisional assessment/checking report) to file objections before the Executive Engineer, who must decide them by a reasoned, speaking order after a hearing, preferably within six weeks; recovery proceedings under the impugned citation were stayed until the earlier of a fixed date or disposal of the objections, with recovery to thereafter abide by that decision.

cases.title: Ramji Lal v. Dakshinanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: service of provisional assessment
cases.holding: Service of the checking report and provisional assessment under certificate of posting is not proper under regulation 9.3, which prescribes registered post, courier post, or newspaper publication. Respondent no. 2 was directed to serve the provisional assessment by registered post; after receipt the petitioner has two weeks to object; objections are to be decided in accordance with law; recovery under the citation dated 22.09.2009 stays until final assessment. Writ allowed.

cases.title: Mohan Bajpai v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: mode of service of provisional assessment
cases.holding: Service of documents sent by ordinary post cannot be presumed sufficient, as it does not conform to Clause 9.3 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005. A copy of the provisional assessment having been served with the counter affidavit, the writ was disposed of by directing the petitioner to file objections within fifteen days, to be decided in accordance with law within a month, with no recovery until those objections are decided.

UP-2005::Annexure 4.2.topic: meter in own name — pending title suit

cases.title: Atul Narain v. S.D.O. Vidyut Vitran
cases.topic: meter in own name — pending title suit
cases.holding: Where the petitioner has already filed a civil suit claiming a share in the property, a writ seeking installation of a meter for supply in his own name is disposed of without a merits direction; he may apply in the pending suit or approach the Executive Engineer under Annexure 4.2 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005.

cases.title: Praveen Bano v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: new-connection-prerequisite-formalities
cases.holding: Mandamus to restore electricity to a tenant's premises will not issue unless the applicant first completes the prerequisite formalities in Annexures 4.2 and 4.4 of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005; once those formalities are completed, the competent authority is to consider the request, preferably within two weeks.
cases.flag: Court referred to 'Annexures 4.2 and 4.4'. Catalog has Annexure 4.2 and clause 4.4, not Annexure 4.4.

cases.title: Mohd. Nadeem Siddiqui v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, Lucknow Bench
cases.topic: new connection — disputed title — indemnity bond
cases.holding: Even if the premises are disputed property, the licensee cannot decline to grant an electricity connection. At best it may take an indemnity bond under Annexure 4.2 of the Electricity Supply Code, 2005, even if the applicant is not the owner. Opposite party no.4 was directed to intimate the documents still required within one week of production of a certified copy; the petitioner to supply them within three days; and, on compliance, to grant the connection no later than one week thereafter in accordance with law.

cases.title: Harish Agrawal v. State of U.P.
cases.court: High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
cases.topic: occupier indemnity bond
cases.holding: Where the licensee has accepted an indemnity bond from the occupier of a portion of the premises and restored supply, there is no illegality and no impediment to granting connection to a person in occupation on an Annexure 4.2 indemnity bond.
