Hanum.proposition: Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge over the property, so a transferee of premises cannot in general law be made liable for the dues of the previous owner/occupier; but where statutory rules or statutory conditions of supply authorise the supplier to demand the previous owner/occupier's arrears from a purchaser seeking re-connection or a fresh connection, the supplier can recover the arrears from the purchaser.

cited_in.title: Vijay Lakshmi v. Bihar State Electricity Board & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Relied on to hold that, absent an applicable statutory condition, the petitioner-transferee could not be saddled with the former tenant's arrears.

SCJ-031.name: Haryana State Electricity Board v. Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri
SCJ-031.proposition: Electricity arrears are not a charge on the property, but where statutory rules or statutory terms and conditions of supply authorise it, the supplier may demand the previous owner's arrears from a purchaser claiming a fresh/re-connection.

cited_in.title: Kalawati Rana v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. Thru its M.D./Chairman and Another
cited_in.how_treated: Applied; the U.P. Code (unlike the position in Haryana) contains express rules enabling recovery, so the refusal was justified.

1336616.name: Haryana State Electricity Board v. Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
1336616.proposition: Electricity arrears do not constitute a charge over the property (following Isha Marbles); a transferee cannot be made liable for a predecessor's electricity dues absent a specific enabling clause (such as Clause 21A considered in Paramount Polymers) in the terms and conditions of supply authorising such recovery from a purchaser.

cited_in.title: Palika Towns LLP v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Surveyed as part of the settled electricity-dues transferee-liability position; held of no assistance to the petitioner here since the lease deed did contain an express first-charge stipulation (unlike the absence of such a clause in the electricity context there).

cited_in.title: Smt. Pawan Jha @ Priya Jha v. State of U.P. And Others
cited_in.how_treated: Applied alongside DVS Steels as controlling authority.

cited_in.title: Special Officer, Commerce, North Eastern Electricity Company of Orissa (NESCO) & Anr. v. M/s Raghunath Paper Mills Private Limited & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Followed as the summarising statement of law.

Haryana State Electricity Board Vs. Hanu.name: Haryana State Electricity Board Vs. Hanuman Rice Mills and others

cited_in.title: Shri Balajee Laboratories v. Executive Engineer

Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. Paschimanchal Vidyu.name: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd.
Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. Paschimanchal Vidyu.proposition: Same procedural-fairness principle for s.126/Clause 8.1 assessment.

cited_in.title: Shishir Jain v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Another
cited_in.how_treated: Followed as supporting authority.

Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P..name: Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P.
Heinz India Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P..proposition: Judicial review of administrative action is confined to legality, procedural propriety, and Wednesbury unreasonableness — illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety, or abuse of power.

cited_in.title: M/S Om Ice Factory Thru' Its Partner Satyapal Singh v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Held inapplicable — none of the five grounds of judicial review was shown to be violated.

Himalayan Coop. Group Housing Society v..name: Himalayan Coop. Group Housing Society v. Balwan Singh
Himalayan Coop. Group Housing Society v..proposition: A counsel's admission binds only if unequivocal and authorised; the client is not bound by an unauthorised concession, nor by statements on matters of law or legal conclusions; the court should ascertain authority before accepting a concession that surrenders substantial rights.

cited_in.title: Smt. Ranjana Gupta v. Executive Engineer (Distribution), Asst. General Manager & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Followed. The petitioner relied on para 32; the Court also applied para 21, holding that the Appellate Committee should have been cautious in accepting a concession against the client's interest, recorded only in the operative portion.

Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. RERC.name: Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. RERC
Hindustan Zinc Ltd. v. RERC.proposition: Subordinate legislation, including regulations framed under statutory authority, carries a presumption of constitutionality; the burden lies on the challenger to establish invalidity.

cited_in.title: Ramayana Ispat Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. v. State of Rajasthan & Ors. (with connected appeals)
cited_in.how_treated: Applied to place the burden on the appellants to demonstrate the Regulations of 2016 were invalid, a burden they failed to discharge.

HMT Ltd. v. Mudappa.name: HMT Ltd. v. Mudappa
HMT Ltd. v. Mudappa.proposition: Malice in law doctrine applied to administrative/service action.

cited_in.title: Smt. Vimla Tiwari v. State of U.P. And Others
cited_in.how_treated: Cited in the malice-in-law discussion.

HMT Watches Ltd. v. M.A. Habida.name: HMT Watches Ltd. v. M.A. Habida
HMT Watches Ltd. v. M.A. Habida.proposition: Whether a cheque was given as security or towards an outstanding liability is a factual question determinable only at trial, not in s.482 Cr.P.C. proceedings.

cited_in.title: Sunil Todi & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Followed.

Hoosein Kasam Dada (India) Ltd. v. State.name: Hoosein Kasam Dada (India) Ltd. v. State of M.P.
Hoosein Kasam Dada (India) Ltd. v. State.proposition: Unless the new Act expressly or by necessary implication is retrospective, the right of appeal crystallises on institution and a new deposit condition cannot be imposed.

cited_in.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cited_in.how_treated: Referred (within Ramesh Singh).

Hotel Adityaz Ltd. v. M.P. Kshetra Vidyu.name: Hotel Adityaz Ltd. v. M.P. Kshetra Vidyut Vitran Co. Ltd.
Hotel Adityaz Ltd. v. M.P. Kshetra Vidyu.proposition: Theft cases fall only under Section 135, and Section 126 has no application to them.

cited_in.title: West Bengal State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd. (WBSEDCL) v. M/s Orion Metal Pvt. Ltd.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished — the view that Section 126 has no application to theft cases was not accepted.

Hyderabad Vanaspathi Ltd. v. A.P. State.name: Hyderabad Vanaspathi Ltd. v. A.P. State Electricity Board
Hyderabad Vanaspathi Ltd. v. A.P. State.proposition: Electricity dues under the terms and conditions of supply partake of the character of statutory dues; the agreements with individual consumers only bring the statutory terms to their notice and do not render the terms purely contractual.

cited_in.title: RKG Industries LLP v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited & 4 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Referred (through Telangana SPDCL) to affirm the statutory, non-contractual character of the dues.

Hyderabad Vanaspati Ltd. v. A.P. State E.name: Hyderabad Vanaspati Ltd. v. A.P. State Electricity Board
Hyderabad Vanaspati Ltd. v. A.P. State E.proposition: Terms and conditions of supply notified by an Electricity Board under Section 49 of the Electricity (Supply) Act are statutory, not contractual; a condition for recovery of dues from a transferee is not ex facie unauthorised or unreasonable.

cited_in.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Referred (within Paramount Polymers) for the statutory character of the conditions of supply.

21266288.name: I.C. Golak Nath and others v. State of Punjab
21266288.proposition: Introduced the doctrine of prospective overruling into Indian constitutional jurisprudence, distinguishing the Blackstonian (purely retrospective) theory from Cardozo's prospective-overruling approach.

cited_in.title: Sri Chandra Mohan Goyal v. U.P. Power Corporation Ltd. & Others
cited_in.how_treated: Cited as the foundational source of the prospective-overruling doctrine.

In Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under.name: In Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under Section 138 of the N.I. Act 1881
In Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under.citation: Suo Motu Writ Petition (Crl) No. 2 of 2020, decided 16.4.2021
In Re: Expeditious Trial of Cases under.proposition: s.145 NI Act dispenses with mandatory oral examination of witnesses on oath for the s.202 Cr.P.C. inquiry in s.138 complaints; complainant's evidence may be by affidavit.

cited_in.title: Sunil Todi & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Applied to hold the Magistrate's summoning process procedurally valid.

In re: Natural Resources Allocation, Spe.name: In re: Natural Resources Allocation, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012
In re: Natural Resources Allocation, Spe.proposition: Clarifies that the binding 'law declared' under Article 141 is the ratio decidendi culled from the judgment as a whole, not every observation.

cited_in.title: State of Gujarat & Ors. v. Utility Users' Welfare Association & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Cited by counsel on how to read the Tamil Nadu Generation ratio.

1286590.name: Indian Aluminium Co. v. Kerala State Electricity Board
1286590.proposition: A stipulation entered into by a public authority in exercise of a statutory power, even if it fetters future exercise of the same or another statutory power, is valid and binding on the principle of harmonious construction — but this applies only to express stipulations in exercise of statutory power, not silence in a private-contract-style term.

cited_in.title: The State of Haryana & Ors. v. M/s Faridabad Gurgaon Minerals & Anr. (with M/s Ganpati Enterprises Slate Mines)
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished — no express fettering stipulation existed in the lease deed here.

Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala.name: Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala
Indian Aluminium Co. v. State of Kerala.proposition: The legislature cannot by mere declaration overrule a judicial decision, but may render it ineffective by validly altering the law fundamentally and retrospectively.

cited_in.title: M/s. Suvidha Engineers India Ltd. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished: the tests for a validating act do not arise, Clause 4.49 being a protective provision unconnected with overriding any decision.

63772460.name: Indian Overseas Bank v. RCM Infrastructure Ltd.
63772460.proposition: Once CIRP is initiated and a moratorium is ordered, SARFAESI Act proceedings against the Corporate Debtor cannot continue; IBC, being a later Parliamentary code, overrides inconsistent provisions of other laws under s.238.

cited_in.title: Narendra Singh Panwar v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Relied on by the petitioner for the general overriding-effect proposition, but distinguished on facts — that case concerned action against the Corporate Debtor's own assets, not a personal guarantor.

752151.name: Indira Sohanlal v. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Delhi
752151.proposition: Observed that the right of appeal in a pending action may be a substantive vesting right, but left the question open.

cited_in.title: Aruna Bhargava v. PuVVNL & Another
cited_in.how_treated: Referred; the open question was later settled in Garikapati.

Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. Stat.name: Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. Stat.citation: Criminal Misc. Writ Petition No. 265 of 2023, decided 6.2.2013 (as cited)
Indresh Patel @ Indreshwar Singh v. Stat.proposition: The 24-hour requirement in the second proviso to s.135(1-A) is directory; no consequences are specified for its breach.

cited_in.title: Satish Kumar Bharti alias Chhotu v. State of U.P. & 2 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Held per incuriam and not a binding precedent, because it did not notice s.57 of the Act or Clause 8.2 of the Code, which do specify consequences. (The citation as given is internally inconsistent: a 2023 writ number with a 2013 decision date — recorded as the judgment states it.)

Indus Airways Private Ltd. v. Magnum Avi.name: Indus Airways Private Ltd. v. Magnum Aviation Private Ltd.
Indus Airways Private Ltd. v. Magnum Avi.proposition: A cheque issued as advance payment for a purchase order later cancelled (with no goods ever supplied) does not secure a legally enforceable debt or liability; s.138 requires a subsisting debt/liability on the date of drawing.

cited_in.title: Sunil Todi & Ors. v. State of Gujarat & Anr.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished — here, unlike Indus Airways, the underlying commercial transaction (power supply) was actually performed and a debt accrued.

Innovative Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank.name: Innovative Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank
Innovative Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank.proposition: The IBC, by its non-obstante clause (Section 238), has overriding effect over any other law for the time being in force in case of inconsistency.

cited_in.title: S.K. Construction Co. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Referred in support of the IBC's overriding effect over the Electricity Supply Code.

Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Ban.name: Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank
Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Ban.proposition: The IBC is a complete, self-contained code with overriding effect over inconsistent State/other laws.

cited_in.title: Reliance Projects and Property Management Services Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Others
cited_in.how_treated: Referred on the primacy and self-contained nature of the IBC.

181931435.name: Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank & Anr.
181931435.proposition: Section 238 of the IBC, containing the widest possible non-obstante clause, ensures that no right of the corporate debtor under any other law can come in the way of the Code.

cited_in.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Relied on for the general primacy of IBC s.238 over conflicting sectoral statutes.

840038.name: Inter College Kusmaul, Gorakhpur & Anr. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
840038.proposition: Expounds the maxims lex non cogit ad impossibilia, impotentia excusat legem and nemo tenetur ad impossibilia (the law does not compel the impossible).

cited_in.title: M/S Mohit Paper Mills Ltd. & Anr. v. PVVNL & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Followed to permit exceptional reliance on an outside/check meter for billing where the consumer's own meter cannot yield a reading.

738683.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board
738683.proposition: Absent a charge over the property or a statutory rule authorising a demand for the previous occupant's dues, an auction-purchaser seeking a fresh connection cannot be required to clear the pre-sale arrears; such a purchaser is not a 'consumer' liable for the predecessor's contractual dues.

cited_in.title: Haryana State Electricity Board v. M/s Hanuman Rice Mills, Dhanauri & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Explained and confined — its ratio applies where there is no enabling statutory rule/condition; it does not bar recovery where such a condition exists.

Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity.name: Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity Board
Isha Marbles v. Bihar State Electricity.proposition: A fresh purchaser / auction-purchaser could not be saddled with the previous owner's electricity arrears in the absence of a statutory charge; the duty to supply could not be conditioned on clearing another's dues.

cited_in.title: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished / substantially qualified — the Court recognised that a statutory charge can be created under the Supply Code (ss.50/181, and s.49 of the 1948 Act), so arrears are recoverable from a transferee where such a Condition of Supply exists.

cited_in.title: Raman Ispat (Pvt.) Ltd. & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Cited by the petitioner for the proposition that past dues cannot be enforced against a subsequent purchaser; distinguished/limited in light of DUS Steels where a fresh connection/enhancement to the same premises is sought.

cited_in.title: Smt. Soni Dwivedi v. Madhyanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. thru. its Chairman & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished: it arose under the Electricity Act, 1910 r/w the Bihar and Orissa Public Demands Recovery Act, 1914 (auction-purchaser context), whereas the 2005 Code governs the present field and makes clearing prior dues a condition precedent to a new connection.

cited_in.title: Vijay Lakshmi v. Bihar State Electricity Board & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Referred (through Rekha Gupta) as affirming the Patna High Court's view that unconnected purchasers are not liable for a predecessor's dues.

cited_in.title: RKG Industries LLP v. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited & 4 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished: it applied where the auction had no clause dealing with electricity dues, whereas here the property was sold "as is where is" with the terms putting the purchaser to notice, so its reasoning did not aid the review applicant.

cited_in.title: Lakshmi Oil And Vanaspati Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Others
cited_in.how_treated: Followed as covering the same facts: an auction purchaser without a prior connection is not a consumer or occupier and cannot be said to have dues against him.

cited_in.title: Trinmurti Buildwell Pvt Ltd v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd And Another
cited_in.how_treated: Followed as covering the same facts: an auction purchaser without a prior connection is not a consumer or occupier and cannot be said to have dues against him. The Court analogised the Union Bank recovery auction to a sale under section 29(1) of the State Financial Corporations Act.

J.M. Baxi & Co., Gujarat v. Commissioner.name: J.M. Baxi & Co., Gujarat v. Commissioner of Customs, New Kandla & Anr.
J.M. Baxi & Co., Gujarat v. Commissioner.proposition: Where recourse to an alternative remedy was onerous, involving deposit of a huge amount, and the demand itself was barred by limitation, interference by the High Court on merits was necessary despite the alternative remedy being available.

cited_in.title: M/s. Shree Gopala Iron (India) Ltd. & Anr. v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished - here there was no precondition to deposit the entire amount and the demand was not barred by limitation.

J.M.D. Alloys Ltd. v. Bihar State Electr.name: J.M.D. Alloys Ltd. v. Bihar State Electricity Board
J.M.D. Alloys Ltd. v. Bihar State Electr.proposition: Where the period of unauthorised use cannot be established, the maximum (fallback) period may be taken for computing the assessment.

cited_in.title: Ram Bahadur v. State of U.P. & Others
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished: there the period could not be established; here it was ascertainable from the date of connection.

cited_in.title: M/s. Citi Hotel v. Commissioner, Lucknow Division, Lucknow & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished: here there was a full trial with oral and documentary evidence ending in acquittal, unlike the mere acceptance of a final report in J.M.D. Alloys, so it did not aid the licensee.

1803208.name: J.N. Banavalikar v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi
1803208.proposition: In the absence of impleadment of the person who allegedly passed a mala fide order, a contention of malice in fact should not be countenanced.

cited_in.title: M/S Beeco Electrical India & Anr. v. Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Relied on to the same effect.

Jharkhand State Electricity Board v. Lax.name: Jharkhand State Electricity Board v. Laxmi Business and Cement Company Pvt. Ltd.

cited_in.title: Jharkhand State Electricity Board & Others v. M/s Ramkrishna Forging Limited
cited_in.how_treated: Distinguished on facts as relating to minimum-guarantee charge.

93465500.name: Jindal Poly Films Limited v. U.P. Electricity Regulatory Commission, Lucknow
93465500.proposition: Regulation 8.1(i) of the 2007 Regulations, giving the Distribution Licensee a remedy of representation to the Electricity Ombudsman, is intra vires the Act, 2003, on a 'read as a whole' construction.

cited_in.title: Kisan Cold Storage & Ice Factory v. Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. (Full Bench reference)
cited_in.how_treated: Overruled — did not engage Section 42(5)-(7) specifically; does not lay down the correct law.

JMD Alloys Ltd..name: JMD Alloys Ltd.
JMD Alloys Ltd..proposition: Sending a meter for testing to the accredited laboratory of its manufacturer/supplier (Secure Meters Ltd.) is likely to create a strong bias on the part of the supplier/manufacturer.

cited_in.title: Rituraj v. State of U.P. & Others
cited_in.how_treated: Noticed within the quoted Modern Rice Mill extract in support of the manufacturer-bias point.

73508068.name: K. Kishan v. Vijay Nirman Company Private Limited
73508068.proposition: Upholds the primacy of IBC s.238 over the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

cited_in.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Referred as another instance of IBC primacy.

K. Sambasivaraju v. M.V.S.R. Chandrayya.name: K. Sambasivaraju v. M.V.S.R. Chandrayya Chetty
K. Sambasivaraju v. M.V.S.R. Chandrayya.proposition: The word 'instrument' (as defined in s.2(14) of the Stamp Act, 1899) must receive an extensive meaning including an affidavit.

cited_in.title: M/s L.M.L. Ltd. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Relied on to hold that the affidavit of undertaking qualified as an 'instrument' acceptable under the unamended Clause 4.49.

28868630.name: K. Shashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank
28868630.proposition: Once the conditions of s.33 IBC are met, the Adjudicating Authority must initiate liquidation as a matter of course, with no discretion to evaluate the CoC's commercial decision.

cited_in.title: Paschimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Raman Ispat Private Limited & Ors.
cited_in.how_treated: Cited for the mandatory, non-discretionary nature of liquidation initiation under s.33.

160269658.name: K.C. Ninan v. Kerala State Electricity Board
160269658.proposition: Electricity utilities can, by subordinate legislation or statutory conditions of supply, create a charge enabling recovery of electricity arrears from a subsequent transferee; recoupment of arrears protects the public good of electricity supply.

cited_in.title: Amir Ahmad v. State of U.P. & 4 Others
cited_in.how_treated: Followed and applied to hold the auction-purchaser liable to clear arrears before a new connection is released.

cited_in.title: M/S Dharti Agro Industries Pvt. Ltd. v. The Managing Director, Pashchimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & 2 Others

K.K. Bhalla v. State of U.P..name: K.K. Bhalla v. State of U.P.

cited_in.title: M.D., Pakshimanchal Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. v. Electricity Ombudsman & Anr.
